translation.text:
“I could not put it back on without hooks,” said Lucien, blushing.

“Bérénice will go and fetch some; they will not be superfluous here,” said the tradesman with a horribly mocking air.

“Papa Camusot,” said Coralie, casting him a look filled with atrocious contempt, “have the courage of your cowardice! Come, say everything you are thinking. You think monsieur’s boots look like mine? I forbid you to take off your boots,” she said to Lucien. “Yes, Monsieur Camusot, yes, those boots are exactly the same as the ones that stood with their arms crossed before my hearth the other day, while monsieur, hidden in my dressing room, was waiting for them; he had spent the night here. That is what you think, eh? Think it; I want you to. It is the plain truth. I am deceiving you. And then? It pleases me!”

She sat down without anger and with the most unconstrained air in the world, looking at Camusot and Lucien, who did not dare look at each other.

“I shall believe only what you wish me to believe,” said Camusot. “Do not jest; I am in the wrong.”

“Either I am a shameless wanton who, in a single moment, has become infatuated with monsieur, or I am a poor, wretched creature who has felt for the first time the true love after which all women run. In either case, you must leave me or take me as I am,” she said, making a sovereign gesture by which she crushed the merchant.

“Can it be true?” said Camusot, who saw from Lucien’s bearing that Coralie was not joking and who was begging to be deceived.

“I love mademoiselle,” said Lucien.

On hearing those words spoken in an emotional voice, Coralie flung herself upon her poet’s neck, clasped him in her arms, and turned her head toward the silk merchant, showing him the admirable tableau of love that she formed with Lucien.

“Poor Musot, take back everything you have given me; I want nothing from you. I love this boy madly, not for his wit, but for his beauty. I prefer poverty with him to millions with you.”

Camusot sank into an armchair, put his head in his hands, and remained silent.

“Would you like us to go away?” she asked him with incredible ferocity.

A chill ran down Lucien’s back when he saw himself burdened with a woman, an actress, and a household.

“Stay here, keep everything, Coralie,” said the tradesman in a faint, sorrowful voice that came from his soul. “I do not want to take anything back. There are, however, sixty thousand francs’ worth of furnishings here, but I could not reconcile myself to the thought of my Coralie in poverty. And yet, before long, you will be in poverty. However great monsieur’s talents may be, they cannot provide you with a living. That is what awaits all of us old men! Leave me, Coralie, the right to come and see you sometimes: I can be useful to you. Besides, I confess it, it would be impossible for me to live without you.”

The gentleness of this poor man, dispossessed of all his happiness at the moment when he believed himself happiest, deeply touched Lucien, but not Coralie.

“Come, my poor Musot, come as often as you like,” she said. “I shall love you better when I am no longer deceiving you.”

Camusot appeared content not to be driven from his earthly paradise, where he would doubtless suffer, but where he hoped later to regain all his rights, trusting to the hazards of Parisian life and to the temptations that were going to surround Lucien. The crafty old merchant thought that sooner or later this handsome young man would permit himself some infidelities, and in order to spy on him, to ruin him in Coralie’s estimation, he wished to remain their friend. This cowardice of true passion frightened Lucien. Camusot offered to give them dinner at Véry’s in the Palais-Royal, and the offer was accepted.

“What happiness!” cried Coralie when Camusot had gone. “No more garret in the Latin Quarter; you will live here, we shall never part, and, to keep up appearances, you will take a small apartment in the rue Charlot—and let the ship sail where it may!”

She began to dance her Spanish step with a vigor that expressed an indomitable passion.

“I can earn five hundred francs a month by working hard,” said Lucien.

“I have just as much at the theater, not counting the performance fees. Camusot will always provide my clothes; he loves me! With fifteen hundred francs a month, we shall live like Croesuses.”

“And the horses, and the coachman, and the servant?” said Bérénice.

“I shall run into debt,” cried Coralie.

She began dancing a jig with Lucien.

“Then I must accept Finot’s proposals,” cried Lucien.

“Come,” said Coralie, “I shall dress and take you to your newspaper; I shall wait for you in the carriage on the boulevard.”

Lucien sat down on a sofa, watched the actress dress, and gave himself up to the gravest reflections. He would have preferred to leave Coralie free rather than be thrust into the obligations of such a marriage; but he saw her so beautiful, so well formed, so alluring, that he was seized by the picturesque aspects of this Bohemian life and threw down the gauntlet in Fortune’s face. Bérénice was ordered to oversee Lucien’s move and installation. Then Coralie—triumphant, beautiful, happy—carried off her beloved lover, her poet, and crossed all Paris to go to the rue Saint-Fiacre. Lucien ran lightly up the stairs and presented himself as a master in the newspaper’s offices. Coloquinte, still with his stamped paper on his head, and old Giroudeau again told him, with a fair degree of hypocrisy, that no one had come.

“But the editors must meet somewhere to agree on the contents of the newspaper,” he said.

“Probably, but the editorial staff is no concern of mine,” said the captain of the Imperial Guard, who went back to checking his wrappers while making his eternal “Brrum! Brrum!”

At that moment, by a chance that one must call fortunate or unfortunate, Finot came to tell Giroudeau of his sham abdication and to commend his interests to his care.

“No diplomacy with monsieur; he is on the newspaper,” Finot said to his uncle, taking Lucien’s hand and shaking it.

“Ah! Monsieur is on the newspaper,” cried Giroudeau, surprised by his nephew’s gesture. “Well, monsieur, you did not have much trouble getting onto it.”

“Your Grace was almost a prophet,” he said in a charming voice, “and I shall endeavor to make you one altogether. I count myself fortunate to have come here this evening, since I am able to pay you my respects.”

Lucien drew His Lordship into a conversation that lasted ten minutes. All the women looked upon Lucien as a phenomenon. His unexpected impertinence had left Madame du Châtelet without voice or answer. Seeing Lucien the object of every woman’s admiration; following, from group to group, the whispered account each gave the others of the exchanged remarks in which Lucien had as good as crushed her while appearing to disdain her, she felt a pang at her heart from wounded pride.

“If he did not come tomorrow, after that remark, what a scandal!” she thought. “Where does this pride of his come from? Could Mademoiselle des Touches be in love with him?…”

“He is so handsome!—They say she rushed to his home in Paris the day after the actress’s death!… Perhaps he came to save his brother-in-law and happened to find himself behind our carriage at Mansle through an accident of travel. That morning, Lucien looked Sixte and me over in a most singular fashion.” A myriad thoughts arose, and, unfortunately for Louise, she yielded to them as she watched Lucien conversing with the bishop as though he were the king of the drawing room: he bowed to no one and waited for people to come to him, sweeping his gaze about with varied expressions and with an ease worthy of de Marsay, his model. He did not leave the prelate to go and greet Monsieur de Sénonches, who appeared a short distance away.

At the end of ten minutes, Louise could bear it no longer. She rose, walked over to the bishop, and said to him, “What are they saying to you, then, Your Grace, to make you smile so often?”

Lucien stepped back a few paces, discreetly leaving Madame de Châtelet with the prelate.

“Ah! Madame la Comtesse, this young man is very witty!… He was explaining to me how he owed all his strength to you…”

“I, madame, am not ungrateful!…” said Lucien, casting her a reproachful glance that delighted the countess.

“Let us come to an understanding,” she said, drawing Lucien back toward her with a gesture of her fan. “Come with His Lordship, this way!… His Grace shall be our judge.”

And she indicated the boudoir, drawing the bishop into it.

“She is putting His Lordship to a strange use,” said a woman from the Chandour camp, loudly enough to be heard.

“Our judge!…” said Lucien, looking in turn at the prelate and the prefect’s wife. “Then there is to be a guilty party?”

Louise de Nègrepelisse sat down on the sofa in her former boudoir. After seating Lucien beside her and His Lordship on her other side, she began to speak.

Lucien did his former friend the honor, the surprise, and the kindness of not listening. He assumed the attitude and gestures of Pasta in _Tancredi_ when she is about to say, _O patria!_… With his countenance he performed the famous _del Rizzo_ cavatina. Finally, Coralie’s pupil managed to bring a few tears to his eyes.

“Ah! Louise, how I loved you!” he whispered in her ear, heedless of the prelate and of the conversation, the moment he saw that the countess had noticed his tears.

“Dry your eyes, or you would ruin me here once again,” she said, turning toward him in an aside that shocked the bishop.

“And once is enough,” Lucien promptly replied. “That remark from Madame d’Espard’s cousin would dry all the tears of a Magdalen. My God!… For a moment I had recovered my memories, my illusions, my twenty years, and you…”

His Lordship abruptly returned to the drawing room, realizing that his dignity might be compromised between these two former lovers. Everyone made a show of leaving the prefect’s wife and Lucien alone in the boudoir. But a quarter of an hour later, Sixte, displeased by the talk, the laughter, and the pacing about at the threshold of the boudoir, entered it with a more than anxious air and found Lucien and Louise in a state of great animation.

“Madame,” Sixte whispered in his wife’s ear, “you, who know Angoulême better than I do, should you not be giving some thought to the prefect’s wife and to the government?”

“My dear,” said Louise, looking her responsible publisher up and down with a haughty air that made him tremble, “I am discussing with Monsieur de Rubempré matters of importance to you. We are concerned with saving an inventor who is on the point of becoming the victim of the basest maneuvers, and you will help us do so… As for what these ladies may think of me, you shall see how I am going to conduct myself so as to freeze the venom on their tongues.”

She left the boudoir leaning on Lucien’s arm and led him to sign the contract, openly parading their association with the audacity of a great lady.

“Shall we sign together?…” she said, handing Lucien the pen.

Lucien allowed her to show him the place where she had just signed, so that their signatures would be side by side.

“Monsieur de Sénonches, would you have recognized Monsieur de Rubempré?” said the countess, forcing the insolent huntsman to bow to Lucien.

She led Lucien back into the drawing room and placed him between herself and Zéphirine on the formidable sofa in the center. Then, like a queen upon her throne, she began, at first in a low voice, an obviously epigrammatic conversation in which several of her former friends and several women who were paying court to her joined. Soon Lucien, now the hero of a circle, was prompted by the countess to speak of Parisian life, upon which he improvised a satire with incredible verve, interspersed with anecdotes about famous people, true conversational delicacies for which provincials are exceedingly greedy. His wit was admired as the man himself had been admired. Madame la Comtesse Sixte triumphed so patiently in Lucien, handled him so skillfully like a woman enchanted with her choice, supplied him with rejoinders with such aptness, and solicited approval for him with such compromising glances, that several women began to see in the coincidence of Louise’s and Lucien’s return a deep love that had fallen victim to some mutual misunderstanding. Resentment had perhaps brought about the ill-fated Châtelet marriage, against which a reaction was now setting in.

Under a promise of profound secrecy, Ève and her mother listened to Lucien’s confidences. Both wept as they listened to the ambitious young man; and when he wished to know the cause of their sorrow, they told him that everything they possessed had been absorbed by table and household linen, by Ève’s trousseau, and by a multitude of purchases that David had not thought of and that they were glad to have made, for the printer acknowledged that Ève brought a dowry of ten thousand francs. Lucien then told them of his idea of taking out a loan, and Madame Chardon undertook to go and ask Monsieur Postel for a thousand francs for one year.

“But, Lucien,” said Ève with a pang at her heart, “then you will not be at my wedding? Oh! Come back; I shall wait a few days! Surely she will let you come back here in a fortnight, once you have accompanied her! Surely she will grant us eight days—to us who raised you for her! Our marriage will turn out badly if you are not there... But will a thousand francs be enough for you?” she said, suddenly interrupting herself. “Although your coat suits you divinely, you have only one! You have only two fine shirts, and the other six are of coarse linen. You have only three batiste cravats; the other three are of ordinary jaconet; and besides, your handkerchiefs are not handsome. Will you find a sister in Paris to wash and whiten your linen the very day you need it? You need much more of it. You have only one pair of nankeen trousers made this year; last year’s are tight on you, so you will have to have clothes made in Paris, and Paris prices are not Angoulême prices. You have only two white waistcoats fit to wear; I have already mended the others. Listen, I advise you to take two thousand francs with you.”

At that moment David, who was coming in, appeared to have heard those last two words, for he looked at the brother and sister and remained silent.

“Do not hide anything from me,” he said.

“Well!” cried Ève, “he is leaving with her.”

“Postel,” said Madame Chardon, entering without seeing David, “agrees to lend the thousand francs, but for six months only, and he wants a bill of exchange from you accepted by your brother-in-law, for he says that you offer no security.”

The mother turned, saw her son-in-law, and the four of them remained in profound silence. The Chardon family felt how greatly they had taken advantage of David. They were all ashamed. A tear welled in the printer’s eyes.

“Then you will not be at my wedding?” he said. “Then you will not stay with us? And I, who have spent everything I had! Ah, Lucien, as I was bringing Ève her poor little bridal jewels, I did not know,” he said, wiping his eyes and drawing jewel cases from his pocket, “that I would have cause to regret having bought them.”

He placed several morocco-covered boxes on the table before his mother-in-law.

“Why do you think so much of me?” said Ève with an angelic smile that softened her words.

“Dear mother,” said the printer, “go and tell Monsieur Postel that I consent to give my signature, for I can see from your face, Lucien, that you are quite determined to leave.”

Lucien bowed his head listlessly and sadly, adding a moment later, “Do not judge me harshly, my beloved angels.” He took hold of Ève and David, kissed them, drew them close to him, and clasped them as he said, “Wait for the results, and you will know how much I love you. David, what use would our loftiness of thought be if it did not allow us to disregard the petty ceremonies in which laws entangle feelings? Despite the distance, will my soul not be here? Will thought not unite us? Have I not a destiny to fulfill? Will the booksellers come here in search of my Archer of Charles IX and the Daisies? A little sooner or a little later, must I not in any event do what I am doing today? Could I ever encounter more favorable circumstances? Is it not my entire fortune to make my Paris debut in the Marquise d’Espard’s salon?”

“He is right,” said Ève. “Did you not tell me yourself that he had to go to Paris promptly?”

David took Ève by the hand, led her into the narrow room where she had slept for seven years, and whispered in her ear, “He needs two thousand francs, you said, my love? Postel is lending only a thousand.”

Ève looked at her betrothed with a terrible gaze that expressed all her suffering.

“Listen, my adored Ève, we are going to begin life badly. Yes, my expenses have absorbed everything I possessed. I have only two thousand francs left, and half of that is indispensable to keep the printing house going. To give your brother a thousand francs is to give away our bread, to jeopardize our peace of mind. If I were alone, I know what I would do; but there are two of us. You decide.”

Distraught, Ève threw herself into her lover’s arms, kissed him tenderly, and whispered in his ear, all in tears, “Act as though you were alone; I shall work to earn that sum back!”

Despite the most ardent kiss ever exchanged by two betrothed lovers, David left Ève dejected and returned to Lucien.

“Do not grieve,” he told him. “You shall have your two thousand francs.”

“Go and see Postel,” said Madame Chardon, “for you must both sign the paper.”

When the two friends came back upstairs, they surprised Ève and her mother on their knees, praying to God. Although they knew how many hopes his return was to fulfill, at that moment they felt all that they were losing in this farewell; for they found the happiness to come too dearly purchased by an absence that was about to shatter their lives and plunge them into a thousand fears concerning Lucien’s fate.

“If you ever forgot this scene,” David whispered in Lucien’s ear, “you would be the lowest of men.”

The printer doubtless judged these grave words necessary: Madame de Bargeton’s influence alarmed him no less than the disastrous fickleness of character that might just as readily cast Lucien onto a bad path as onto a good one. Ève soon finished packing Lucien’s bundle. This literary Hernán Cortés was taking little with him. He kept on his best frock coat, his best waistcoat, and one of his two fine shirts. All his linen, his famous coat, his belongings, and his manuscripts formed so slight a bundle that, in order to conceal it from Madame de Bargeton’s eyes, David proposed sending it by stagecoach to his correspondent, a paper merchant, to whom he would write instructing him to hold it at Lucien’s disposal.

Everyone returned to the gaming tables. The gleams of dawn soon made the candles grow pale.

“Your friends from the rue des Quatre-Vents were as gloomy as men condemned to death,” Coralie said to her lover.

“They were the judges,” replied the poet.

“Judges are more amusing than that,” said Coralie.

For a month Lucien found his time taken up by suppers, dinners, luncheons, evening parties, and was swept along by an irresistible current into a whirlpool of pleasures and easy work. He ceased to calculate. The power of calculation amid the complications of life is the seal of great wills, which poets, weak people, or those who are purely spiritual never counterfeit. Like most journalists, Lucien lived from day to day, spending his money as he earned it, giving no thought to the periodic expenses of Parisian life, so crushing for these bohemians. His dress and bearing rivaled those of the most celebrated dandies. Coralie, like all fanatics, loved to adorn her idol; she ruined herself to give her dear poet that elegant furniture of the fashionable which he had so greatly desired during his first walk in the Tuileries. Lucien then possessed marvelous canes, a charming lorgnette, diamond studs, rings for his morning cravats, signet rings, and, finally, enough wondrous waistcoats to allow him to match the colors of his attire. He soon passed for a dandy. On the day when he attended the German diplomat’s invitation, his metamorphosis aroused a kind of restrained envy among the young men present, who held pride of place in the realm of fashion, such as de Marsay, Vandenesse, Ajuda-Pinto, Maxime de Treilles, Rastignac, the Duc de Maufrigneuse, Beaudenord, Manerville, etc. Men of the world are jealous of one another after the manner of women. The Comtesse de Montcornet and the Marquise d’Espard, for whom the dinner was being given, seated Lucien between them and lavished coquetries upon him.

“Why, then, did you leave society?” the marquise asked him. “It was so ready to welcome you warmly, to celebrate you. I have a quarrel to take up with you! You owed me a visit, and I am still waiting for it. I caught sight of you at the Opera the other day; you did not deign to come and see me or even greet me.”

“Your cousin, madame, dismissed me in such unequivocal terms...”

“You do not know women,” Madame d’Espard replied, interrupting Lucien. “You wounded the most angelic heart and the noblest soul I know. You have no idea of all that Louise wished to do for you, or how much subtlety she put into her plan. Oh! she would have succeeded,” she said in response to a silent denial from Lucien. “Was not her husband, who has now died, as he was bound to die, of indigestion, going to restore her freedom sooner or later? Do you think she wanted to be Madame Chardon? The title of Comtesse de Rubempré was well worth conquering. You see, love is a great vanity which must accord, especially in marriage, with all the other vanities. Were I to love you madly—that is to say, enough to marry you—it would be very hard for me to be called Madame Chardon. Admit it. Now you have seen the difficulties of life in Paris; you know how many detours must be made to reach one’s goal. Well, admit that, for an unknown man without a fortune, Louise was aspiring to an almost impossible favor, and therefore she could afford to neglect nothing. You have a great deal of wit, but when we love, we have even more of it than the wittiest man. My cousin intended to make use of that ridiculous Châtelet... I owe you some pleasures; your articles against him made me laugh heartily!” she said, interrupting herself.

Lucien no longer knew what to think. Initiated into the betrayals and perfidies of journalism, he knew nothing of those of society; and so, despite his perspicacity, he was destined to receive some harsh lessons.

“What, madame,” said the poet, whose curiosity had been keenly aroused, “are you not the Heron’s patroness?”

“But in society one is forced to show courtesy to one’s cruelest enemies, to appear to enjoy oneself with bores, and often one seemingly sacrifices one’s friends in order to serve them better. Are you still so very inexperienced? What! you, who wish to write, are ignorant of the ordinary deceptions of society. If my cousin appeared to sacrifice you to the Heron, was it not necessary in order to turn his influence to your advantage? For our man is very well regarded by the present Ministry; and so we demonstrated to him that, up to a certain point, your attacks were serving him, so that one day we might reconcile the two of you. Châtelet has been compensated for your persecutions. As des Lupeaulx said to the ministers: While the newspapers are making Châtelet ridiculous, they leave the Ministry in peace.”

“Monsieur Blondet has led me to hope that I shall have the pleasure of seeing you at my home,” said the Comtesse de Montcornet while the marquise left Lucien to his reflections. “You will find a few artists and writers there, and a woman who has the keenest desire to meet you, Mademoiselle des Touches, one of those talents rare among our sex, and whose home you will doubtless visit. Mademoiselle des Touches—Camille Maupin, if you prefer—has one of the most remarkable salons in Paris; she is prodigiously rich. She has been told that you are as handsome as you are witty, and she is dying to see you.”

Lucien could do nothing but overwhelm her with thanks, and cast an envious glance at Blondet. There was as much difference between a woman of the kind and quality of the Comtesse de Montcornet and Coralie as between Coralie and a streetwalker. This countess, young, beautiful, and witty, possessed, as her distinctive beauty, the extreme fairness of Northern women; her mother had been born Princess Scherbellof, and so, before dinner, the minister had lavished his most respectful attentions upon her. The marquise had by then finished disdainfully sucking a chicken wing.

“My poor Louise,” she said to Lucien, “had so much affection for you! I was privy to the splendid future she dreamed of for you: she would have endured many things, but what contempt you showed her by sending her letters back! We forgive cruelties—one must still believe in us in order to hurt us—but indifference!... Indifference is like the ice of the poles; it stifles everything. Come, admit it: through your own fault you have lost treasures. Why break it off? Even had you been spurned, do you not have your fortune to make, your name to win back? Louise was thinking of all that.”

“Well!” one of them was saying, “that poor Naïs, you know? I do not believe it myself; she has a whole blameless life behind her; she is far too proud to be anything other than Monsieur Chardon’s protectress. But if it is true, I pity her with all my heart.”

“She is all the more to be pitied because she is making herself dreadfully ridiculous; for she could be Monsieur Lulu’s mother, as Jacques called him. That little would-be poet is twenty-two at most, and Naïs, between ourselves, is a good forty.”

“For my part,” Châtelet was saying, “I find that the very position in which Monsieur de Rubempré was proves Naïs’s innocence. One does not go down on one’s knees to ask again for what one has already had.”

“That depends!” said Francis with a roguish air that earned him a disapproving glance from Zéphirine.

“But do tell us exactly what happened?” people asked Stanislas as they formed a secret committee in a corner of the drawing room.

Stanislas had ended by concocting a little tale full of obscenities, accompanying it with gestures and poses that made the affair look exceedingly incriminating.

“It is unbelievable,” they kept repeating.

“At noon,” said one of them.

“Naïs would have been the last person I should have suspected.”

“What is she going to do?”

Then came endless comments and suppositions!... Du Châtelet defended Madame de Bargeton; but he defended her so clumsily that he fanned the flames of gossip instead of extinguishing them. Lili, devastated by the fall of the most beautiful angel on the Olympus of Angoulême, went in tears to spread the news at the Bishop’s Palace. When the whole town was most certainly in an uproar, the delighted du Châtelet went to Madame de Bargeton’s, where, alas, there was only a single whist table; he diplomatically asked Naïs to go and talk with him in her boudoir. They both sat down on the little sofa.

“You doubtless know,” du Châtelet said to her in a low voice, “what all Angoulême is talking about?...”

“No,” she said.

“Well,” he resumed, “I am too much your friend to leave you unaware of it. I must enable you to put a stop to slanders doubtless invented by Amélie, who has the effrontery to consider herself your rival. I was coming to see you this morning with that ape Stanislas, who was a few paces ahead of me, when, on reaching there,” he said, pointing to the boudoir door, “he claims to have seen you with Monsieur de Rubempré in a situation that did not permit him to enter; he rushed back to me in utter dismay and dragged me away without giving me time to collect myself; and we were at Beaulieu when he told me the reason for his retreat. Had I known it, I would not have budged from your house, so as to clear up this affair to your advantage; but returning to your house after having left it would no longer have proved anything. Now, whether Stanislas saw wrongly or whether he is right, *he must be wrong*. Dear Naïs, do not let a fool gamble with your life, your honor, your future; silence him at once. You know my position here? Although I need everyone here, I am entirely devoted to you. Dispose of a life that belongs to you. Although you have rejected my suit, my heart will always be yours, and on every occasion I shall prove to you how much I love you. Yes, I shall watch over you like a faithful servant, without hope of reward, solely for the pleasure I find in serving you, even without your knowledge. This morning I told everyone that I had been at the drawing-room door and had seen nothing. If you are asked who informed you of the things being said about you, make use of me. I should be very proud to be your acknowledged defender; but, between ourselves, Monsieur de Bargeton is the only man who can demand satisfaction from Stanislas... Even if that little Rubempré had committed some folly, a woman’s honor cannot be left at the mercy of the first scatterbrain who throws himself at her feet. That is what I said.”

Naïs thanked du Châtelet with an inclination of her head and remained thoughtful. She was weary, to the point of disgust, of provincial life. At du Châtelet’s first words, her thoughts had turned to Paris. Madame de Bargeton’s silence placed her learned admirer in an awkward position.

“Dispose of me,” he said. “I repeat it.”

“Thank you,” she replied.

“What do you intend to do?”

“I shall see.”

A long silence.

“Do you love that little Rubempré so much, then?”

She let a superb smile escape her and folded her arms as she looked at the curtains of her boudoir. Du Châtelet left without having been able to decipher that proud woman’s heart. When Lucien and the four faithful old gentlemen who had come to play their game, unmoved by this dubious gossip, had departed, Madame de Bargeton detained her husband, who was preparing to go to bed and was opening his mouth to wish his wife good night.

“Come over here, my dear, I have something to say to you,” she said with a kind of solemnity.

Monsieur de Bargeton followed his wife into the boudoir.

“Monsieur,” she said to him, “perhaps I was wrong to put into my protective attentions toward Monsieur de Rubempré an ardor as badly misunderstood by the foolish people of this town as by the young man himself. This morning, Lucien threw himself at my feet, there, and declared his love for me. Stanislas entered at the very moment when I was raising the child to his feet. In contempt of the duties that courtesy imposes upon a gentleman toward a woman in every kind of circumstance, he has claimed to have surprised me in a compromising situation with this boy, whom I was then treating as he deserves. If that thoughtless young man knew the slanders to which his folly has given rise, I know him: he would go and insult Stanislas and force him to fight. That action would be tantamount to a public avowal of his love. I do not need to tell you that your wife is pure; but you will understand that there would be something dishonorable for both you and me if Monsieur de Rubempré were the one to defend her. Go to Stanislas’s at once and formally demand satisfaction for the insulting remarks he has made about me; bear in mind that you must not allow the matter to be settled unless he retracts them in the presence of numerous and important witnesses. In that way you will win the esteem of all decent people; you will conduct yourself as a man of intelligence, as a gentleman, and you will earn a claim to my esteem. I am going to send Gentil on horseback to l’Escarbas; my father must be your second. Despite his age, I know he is a man capable of trampling underfoot that little puppet who is blackening the reputation of a Nègrepelisse. You have the choice of weapons; fight with pistols—you are a marvelous shot.”

“My friend, your letter made us all weep. Let those noble hearts toward whom your good angel is guiding you know this: a mother and a poor young woman will pray to God for them morning and evening; and if the most fervent prayers rise to His throne, they will obtain some favors for all of you. Yes, my brother, their names are engraved upon my heart. Ah! I shall see them someday. I shall go, even if I have to make the journey on foot, to thank them for their friendship toward you, for it has poured balm, as it were, upon my raw wounds. Here, my friend, we are working like poor laborers. My husband, that great unknown man whom I love more with each passing day as, from moment to moment, I discover new riches in his heart, is neglecting his printing house, and I can guess why: your poverty, ours, and our mother’s are killing him. Our adored David is like Prometheus devoured by a vulture, a sallow grief with a sharp beak. As for him, the noble man, he scarcely thinks of it; he has hopes of a fortune. He spends all his days conducting experiments on the manufacture of paper; he has asked me to attend to the business in his stead, in which he helps me as much as his preoccupation allows. Alas! I am with child. This event, which would have filled me with joy, saddens me in the situation in which we all find ourselves. My poor mother has grown young again; she has recovered the strength needed for her exhausting work as a nurse. Were it not for our financial worries, we should be happy. Old Father Séchard will not give his son a farthing; David went to see him to borrow a little money from him so as to help you, for your letter had driven him to despair. ‘I know Lucien; he will lose his head and do foolish things,’ he said. I scolded him thoroughly. My brother, fail in any way whatsoever?... I replied to him, Lucien knows that I should die of grief. Without David’s suspecting it, my mother and I have pawned a few things; my mother will redeem them as soon as she comes into some money. In this way we have managed to raise one hundred francs, which I am sending you by the coach service. If I did not answer your first letter, do not be angry with me, my friend. We were in a situation that kept us up at night; I was working like a man. Ah! I did not know I had so much strength. Madame de Bargeton is a woman without soul or heart; even if she no longer loved you, she owed it to herself to protect and help you after tearing you from our arms only to cast you into that dreadful Parisian sea, where one needs a blessing from God to encounter true friendships amid those waves of men and interests. She is not to be regretted. I wanted some devoted woman beside you, a second self of mine; but now that I know you have friends who carry on our feelings, I am at peace. Spread your wings, my beloved, beautiful genius! You will be our glory, as you are already our love.

Thus, two days later, Lucien was able to repay his friends the loan they had so graciously offered him. Perhaps life had never seemed more beautiful to him, but the stirring of his self-esteem did not escape his friends’ penetrating eyes and delicate sensibility.

“You would think you were afraid of owing us anything,” exclaimed Fulgence.

“Oh! the pleasure he displays is very serious in my eyes,” said Michel Chrestien; “it confirms the observations I have made: Lucien is vain.”

“He is a poet,” said d’Arthez.

“Do you hold it against me that I feel something as natural as this?”

“We must give him credit for not having concealed it from us,” said Léon Giraud. “He is still candid; but I am afraid that later he may come to fear us.”

“And why?” asked Lucien.

“We read your heart,” replied Joseph Bridau.

“There is in you,” Michel Chrestien told him, “a diabolical mind with which you will justify in your own eyes the things most contrary to our principles: instead of being a sophist of ideas, you will be a sophist of action.”

“Ah! I am afraid so,” said d’Arthez. “Lucien, within yourself you will conduct admirable debates in which you will be noble, and which will end in blameworthy deeds... You will never be in agreement with yourself.”

“And on what, then, do you base your indictment?” asked Lucien.

“Your vanity, my dear poet, is so great that you even put it into your friendship!” exclaimed Fulgence. “All vanity of that kind betrays a dreadful selfishness, and selfishness is the poison of friendship.”

“Oh! my God,” exclaimed Lucien, “you cannot know how much I love you.”

“If you loved us as we love one another, would you have shown such eagerness and made such a show of returning what it gave us so much pleasure to give you?”

“Here we do not lend anything to one another; we give,” Joseph Bridau told him bluntly.

“Do not think us harsh, my dear child,” Michel Chrestien told him; “we are being farsighted. We are afraid that one day we shall see you preferring the joys of some petty revenge to the joys of our pure friendship. Read Goethe’s Tasso, the greatest work of that splendid genius, and you will see in it that the poet loves brilliant fabrics, feasts, triumphs, splendor: well then, be Tasso without his madness. Will the world and its pleasures call to you? Stay here... Transfer to the realm of ideas everything your vanities demand. If there must be folly, put virtue into your actions and vice into your ideas, instead of thinking well and behaving badly, as d’Arthez was telling you.”

Lucien lowered his head: his friends were right.

“I confess that I am not as strong as you are,” he said, casting an adorable glance at them. “I do not have the back and shoulders to bear up under Paris, to struggle courageously. Nature has given us different temperaments and faculties, and you know better than anyone the reverse side of vices and virtues. I am already weary, I confess it to you.”

“We shall support you,” said d’Arthez. “That is precisely what faithful friendships are for.”

“The help I have just received is precarious, and we are all as poor as one another; need will soon pursue me again. Chrestien, in the pay of the first comer, can do nothing in the book trade. Bianchon stands outside that circle of business. D’Arthez knows only publishers of scientific or specialized works, who have no influence over publishers of new literature. Horace, Fulgence Ridal, and Bridau work in a realm of ideas that places them a hundred leagues away from publishers. I must decide on a course.”

“Then adhere to ours: suffer!” said Bianchon. “Suffer courageously and put your trust in Work!”

“But what is only suffering for you is death to me,” Lucien said sharply.

“Before the cock has crowed three times,” said Léon Giraud with a smile, “this man will have betrayed the cause of Work for that of Idleness and the vices of Paris.”

“Where has work brought you?” said Lucien, laughing.

“When one leaves Paris for Italy, one does not find Rome halfway there,” said Joseph Bridau. “For you, green peas ought to grow already dressed with butter.”

“They grow that way only for the eldest sons of peers of France,” said Michel Chrestien. “But we sow and water them ourselves, and find them better.”

The conversation became jocular and moved to another subject. Those discerning minds, those sensitive hearts sought to make Lucien forget this little quarrel, and from then on he understood how difficult it was to deceive them. He soon fell into an inward despair that he carefully concealed from his friends, believing them to be implacable mentors. His southern temperament, which ran so easily over the keyboard of feelings, led him to make the most contradictory resolutions.

“Ève! Ève!” David replied, “I wish I were Lucien’s brother. You alone can give me that title, which would allow him to accept everything from me, which would give me the right to devote myself to him with the holy love you bring to your sacrifices, but with the discernment of a calculating mind added to it. Ève, dear beloved child, see to it that Lucien has a treasure from which he may draw without shame. Will not a brother’s purse be as his own? If you knew all the thoughts Lucien’s new position has prompted in me! If he wishes to visit Madame de Bargeton, he must no longer be my foreman, he must no longer live in L’Houmeau, you must no longer remain a working girl, and your mother must no longer ply her trade. If you would consent to become my wife, every difficulty would be smoothed away: Lucien could live on the second floor of my house while I had an apartment built for him above the lean-to at the back of the courtyard, unless my father were willing to add another story. In this way we would arrange for him a life free of cares, an independent life. My desire to support Lucien will give me a courage to make my fortune that I would not have if only I myself were concerned; but it rests with you to authorize my devotion. Perhaps one day he will go to Paris, the only stage on which he can make his appearance, and where his talents will be appreciated and rewarded. Life in Paris is expensive, and the three of us will be none too many to maintain him there. Besides, will not you and your mother need support? Dear Ève, marry me for love of Lucien. Later, perhaps, you will love me when you see the efforts I shall make to serve him and to make you happy. We are both equally modest in our tastes; we shall need little; Lucien’s happiness will be our great concern, and his heart will be the treasure into which we shall put fortune, feelings, sensations—everything!

“Propriety separates us,” said Ève, moved to see how this great love made itself humble. “You are rich and I am poor. One must love very much to surmount such a difficulty.”

“Then you do not love me enough yet?” cried David, dismayed.

“But perhaps your father would object...”

“Good, good,” David replied, “if only my father need be consulted, you shall be my wife. Ève, my dear Ève! You have just made life very easy for me to bear at this moment. Alas, my heart was very heavy with feelings that I neither could nor knew how to express. Only tell me that you love me a little, and I shall summon the courage needed to speak to you of all the rest.”

“Truly,” she said, “you make me feel thoroughly ashamed; but since we are confiding our feelings to each other, I shall tell you that never in my life have I thought of anyone but you. I saw in you one of those men to whom a woman may feel proud to belong, and I dared not hope for myself, a poor working girl with no future, for so great a destiny.”

“Enough, enough,” he said, sitting down on the crossbeam of the weir to which they had returned, for they had been pacing back and forth like mad people over the same stretch.

“What is the matter?” she asked him, expressing for the first time that graceful concern women feel for a being who belongs to them.

“Nothing but good,” he said. “At the sight of an entire happy life, the mind is as though dazzled, the soul overwhelmed. Why am I the happier of us?” he said with an expression of melancholy. “But I know why.”

Ève looked at David with a coquettish and questioning air that demanded an explanation.

“Dear Ève, I receive more than I give. Therefore I shall always love you better than you will love me, because I have more reason to love you: you are an angel, and I am a man.”

“I am not learned enough to understand that,” Ève replied with a smile. “I do love you...”

“As much as you love Lucien?” he said, interrupting her.

“Enough to be your wife, to devote myself to you, and to try never to cause you any distress in the life, somewhat difficult at first, that we shall lead.”

“Have you noticed, dear Ève, that I have loved you since the first day I saw you?”

“What woman does not feel when she is loved?” she asked.

“Then let me dispel the scruples caused in you by my supposed fortune. I am poor, my dear Ève. This is not a lover’s declaration, but a thinker’s reflection. I must acquaint you with my faults, and they are enormous in a man obliged to make his fortune. My character, my habits, the occupations that please me make me unfit for anything involving business and speculation, and yet we can become rich only by pursuing some industry. Though I may be capable of discovering a gold mine, I am singularly inept at working it. But you, who, for love of your brother, have stooped to the smallest details, who possess the genius of economy and the patient attentiveness of the true merchant, will reap the harvest I have sown. Our situation—for a long time now I have placed myself within the bosom of your family—so oppresses my heart that I have consumed my days and nights in seeking an opportunity to make our fortune. My knowledge of chemistry and my observation of the needs of commerce have set me on the path of a lucrative discovery. I can tell you nothing about it yet; I foresee too many delays. We may suffer for several years, but I shall ultimately discover the industrial processes whose trail I have been following for the past few days and which will bring us a great fortune. “I too had guessed,” Ève said, interrupting him, “that you were one of those inventors who, like my poor father, need a woman to take care of them.”

“Then you love me! Ah! Tell me so without fear—to me, who have seen in your name a symbol of my love. Eve was the only woman in the world, and what was materially true for Adam is morally true for me. My God! Do you love me?”

“Yes,” she said, lengthening that simple syllable by the way she pronounced it, as though to portray the extent of her feelings.

For the first time, the sublime belief in success that sustains inventors and gives them the courage to press forward into the virgin forests of the land of discoveries was greeted by Ève with an almost sorrowful smile, and David bowed his head with a funereal motion.

“Oh! my dear, I am not making fun of you, I am not laughing, I do not doubt you!” cried the beautiful Ève, kneeling before her husband. “But I see how right you were to maintain the deepest silence about your experiments, about your hopes. Your Ève could not help smiling when she heard you say, ‘I have found it!...’ for the seventeenth time in a month.”

David began to laugh so frankly at himself that Ève took his hand and kissed it reverently. It was a delightful moment, one of those roses of love and tenderness that bloom beside the most arid roads of poverty and sometimes at the bottom of precipices.

Ève redoubled her courage when she saw misfortune redouble its fury. Her husband’s greatness, his inventor’s naïveté, the tears she sometimes surprised in the eyes of that man of heart and poetry—all these developed in her an unheard-of power of resistance. Once again she resorted to the means that had already succeeded so well for her. She wrote to Monsieur Métivier, asking him to announce the sale of the printing house, offering to pay him out of the price obtained for it, and begging him not to ruin David with needless costs. Faced with this sublime letter, Métivier played dead: his chief clerk replied that, in Monsieur Métivier’s absence, he could not take it upon himself to halt the proceedings. “If I allowed my son to put his hand to my lips, to the rim of my cashbox, he would plunge it right down into the depths of my entrails!...” he cried. “Children all eat straight out of the paternal purse.
