She thought for another moment. Suddenly she drew herself up.

Then that is well, she said. No, I ought to have known that. It did not leave so great an impression. Well, well, then we shall speak no more of it.

No, let us not. My impressions are as immaterial to you now as they were before.

Goodbye, she said. Goodbye for now.

Goodbye, he answered. |

They went their separate ways. He stopped and turned around. There she went now. He stretched out his hands and whispered, speaking tender words to himself: I bear you no grudge, no, no, I do not; I still love you, love you ....

Victoria! he called.

She heard it, started, and turned around, but continued walking.

Several days passed. Johannes went about in the greatest agitation and did not work, did not sleep; he spent almost the whole day in the forest. He climbed onto the great mound of pinewood where the Castle’s flagpole stood; there was a flag on the pole. A flag had also been raised on the Castle’s round tower.

A strange excitement seized him. Guests were to come to the Castle; there was to be a celebration.

The afternoon was still and warm; the river ran like a pulse through the hot landscape. A steamship glided in toward land and left a fan of white streaks spreading across the inlet. Now four carriages drove out from the Castle courtyard and took the road down to the landing.

The ship docked; gentlemen and ladies came ashore and took their places in the carriages. Then a succession of shots began to crack from the Castle; two men stood atop the round tower and loaded and fired, loaded and fired hunting guns. When they had discharged twenty-one shots, the carriages rolled in through the Castle gate and the shooting ceased.

Indeed, there was to be a celebration at the Castle; the guests were received with flags and a salute. Several military men sat in the carriages; perhaps Otto, the lieutenant, was among them.

Johannes descended from the mound and set off for home. He was overtaken by a man from the Castle, who stopped him. The man carried a letter in his cap; he had been sent by Miss Victoria and was to have an answer.

Johannes read the letter with a pounding heart. Victoria invited him after all, wrote to him in heartfelt words, and asked him to come. This time she would ask him. Reply by the messenger.

A strange and unexpected joy had befallen him; the blood rose to his head, and he answered the man that he would come—yes, thank you, he would come at once.

There you are!

He handed the messenger a ridiculously large coin and hurried home to dress.

VIII

For the first time in his life, he passed through the Castle gate and went up the stairs to the second floor. The murmur of voices came toward him from within; his heart beat hard; he knocked and entered.

The still-young lady of the Castle came toward him and greeted him kindly, pressing his hand. She was pleased to see him; she remembered him from the time when he had been no taller than this; now he was a great man .... And it was as though the lady of the Castle had meant to say something more; she held his hand for a long time and looked at him searchingly.

The lord of the Castle also came forward and offered him his hand. As his wife had said, a great man, in more than one sense. A famous man. He was very pleased ...

He was introduced to gentlemen and ladies, to the chamberlain, who wore his decorations, to the chamberlain’s wife, to a landowner from the neighboring district, to Otto, the lieutenant. He did not see Victoria.

A considerable time passed. Victoria entered, pale, even uncertain; she was leading a young girl by the hand. They made a circuit of the drawing room, greeted everyone, and spoke a little with each person. They stopped beside Johannes.

9—Hamsun: III
Victoria smiled and said:

Look, here is Camilla; is that not a surprise? You know each other.

She stood for a little while and looked at them both, then left the drawing room.

For the first moment Johannes remained standing rigid and bewildered on the spot. Here was the surprise; Victoria had most kindly provided someone else in her place. Listen here, go now and have each other, you people! Spring is in bloom, the sun is shining; throw open the windows if you wish, for there is fragrance in the garden, and starlings are also playing in the tops of the birches out there. Why do you not speak to each other? But then laugh now!

Besides, money had never been spared at the Castle; the sums were always large there. What, for example, did a dinner like that not cost! But now it was to look empty everywhere, even in the lady of the Castle’s familiar jewel case, and therefore the son-in-law’s money was to restore the splendour.

How much does he have, one wonders?

Oh, fie, he has such an unfathomable amount of money.

Johannes rose again and went down into the garden. The lilacs were in bloom; streams of fragrance from auriculas and narcissi, jasmines and lilies of the valley met him. He sought out a corner down by the wall and sat on a stone; a thicket concealed him from all the world. He was exhausted by emotion, weary as a slave, his reason darkened; he thought of getting up and going home, but remained sitting there, dull and listless. Then he heard murmuring farther along the gravel path; someone was coming, and he recognized Victoria’s voice. He held his breath and waited a little; then the lieutenant’s uniform also flashed through the foliage. The betrothed couple were walking together.

I do not think, he said, that this quite adds up. You listen to what he says, you sit there concerning yourself with his speech and cry out. What did that really mean?

She stopped and stood tall before him.

Do you want to know? she said.

Yes.

She was silent.

It is all the same to me if it meant nothing, he continued. Then you need not say it.

She subsided again.

No, it meant nothing, she replied.

They began walking again. The lieutenant nervously shrugged his epaulettes and said loudly:

He ought to watch himself a little. Otherwise an officer’s hand might box his ears.

They took the path to the summerhouse.

Johannes remained sitting on the stone for a while, dull and tormented as before. Everything was beginning to be a matter of indifference to him. The lieutenant had grown suspicious of him, and his fiancée had given an account of herself on the spot. She said what had to be said, set the officer’s heart at rest, and walked on with him. And the starlings chattered in the branches above their heads. Indeed. May God grant them a long life.... He had spoken on her behalf at dinner and torn out his heart; it had cost him dearly to put right and cover over her insolent interruption, and she had not thanked him for it. She had seized her glass and drunk. Cheers, look at me, how prettily I drink.... For that matter, look at a woman from the side when she drinks. Let her drink from a cup, from a glass, from anything at all, but look at her from the side. She puts on such airs that it is dreadful. She purses her mouth and dips its outermost rim into the drink, and she is in despair if, while she does so, anyone notices her hand. On the whole, do not look at a woman’s hand. She cannot bear it; she capitulates. At once she begins drawing her hand back, placing it in an ever more beautiful position, all to conceal a wrinkle, a crookedness in the fingers, or a less well-shaped nail. In the end she can bear it no longer, but asks, beside herself: what are you looking at?.... She had once kissed him, once, one summer. It was so long ago; God knows whether it had even been true. How was it—had they not been sitting on a bench? They talked together for a long time, and when they left he came so very close to her that he touched her arm. Outside an entrance she kissed him. I love you! she said.... Now they had passed by; perhaps they were still sitting in the summerhouse. The lieutenant would box his ears, he had said. He had heard it perfectly well; he was not asleep, but neither did he rise and step forward. An officer’s hand, he had said. Indeed, it was a matter of indifference to him....

He rose from the stone and followed them to the summerhouse. It was empty. Up by the veranda of the main building, Camilla stood calling to him; would he please come, there was coffee in the garden room. He followed her. The betrothed couple were sitting in the garden room; several others were present as well. He was given his coffee, stepped back, and found himself a place.

Camilla began talking to him. Her face was so bright, and she looked at him with open eyes; he could not resist her, he joined in the conversation, answered her questions, and laughed. Where had he been? In the garden? That was not true at all; she had searched in the garden and had not found him. Far from it, he had not been in the garden.

Was he in the garden, Victoria? she asked.

Victoria replied:

No, I did not see him.

The lieutenant cast her an embittered glance and, to give his fiancée a warning, said unnecessarily loudly across to the landowner:

Was it the case that you wished to take me woodcock shooting at your estate?

Yes indeed, the landowner replied. You are welcome.

The lieutenant looked at Victoria. She said nothing and remained sitting as before, making no effort whatever to dissuade him from this woodcock shoot at the landowner’s estate. His face grew darker and darker; he stroked his moustache with nervous movements.

Camilla addressed another question to Victoria.

Then the lieutenant rose with a sudden movement and said to the landowner:

Very well, then I shall go with you tonight, at once.

With that he left the room.

The landowner and some others followed.

There was a brief pause.

Suddenly the door opened and the lieutenant entered again. He was in a state of extreme agitation.

Have you forgotten something? Victoria asked, rising.

He took a few bounding steps by the door, as though unable to stand still, and went straight over to Johannes, whom, as if in passing, he struck with his hand. Then he ran back to the door and continued hopping about.

Take care, man, you struck me in the eye, Johannes said, laughing hollowly.

You are mistaken, the lieutenant replied. I boxed your ear. Do you understand? Do you understand?

Johannes reached for his handkerchief, wiped his eye, and said:

You do not mean that. You know I can fold you double and put you in my pocket.

At that same moment he rose.

Then the lieutenant hastily opened the door and stepped outside.

I do mean it! he shouted back. I mean it, you nag!

Then he slammed the door with a crash.

Johannes sat down again.

Victoria was still standing approximately in the middle of the floor. She looked at him and was pale as a corpse.

Did he strike you? Camilla asked in the greatest astonishment.

By accident. He caught me in the eye. Would you like to see?

God, it is red; there is blood. No, do not rub it; let me pour water on it. Your handkerchief is so coarse—here, take it back; I shall use my own. Did anyone ever see the like, right in the eye!

Victoria also held out her handkerchief. She said nothing. Then she walked very slowly to the glass door, where she remained standing with her back to the room, looking out. She tore her handkerchief into small strips. A few minutes later she opened the door and left the garden room, silent and mute.

Then he went out into the city. Perhaps she was to be met, to be discovered; perhaps she was sitting in a carriage. He wandered about until evening.

Outside the theatre he saw her; he bowed, smiled and bowed, and she returned his greeting. He was about to step forward to her—it was only a few paces—when he sees that she is not alone; she has Otto with her, the chamberlain’s son. He was in a lieutenant’s uniform.

Johannes thought: perhaps now she will give me a hint, a little sign with her eyes? She hurried into the theatre, red, with bowed head, as though she wished to hide.

Perhaps he could see her in there? He obtained a ticket and went in.

He knew about the chamberlain’s box; yes indeed, these rich people had a box. There she sat in all her splendour and looked about her. Did she look at him? Never!

When the act was over, he waited for her out in the corridor. He bowed again; she looked at him with a little surprise and nodded.

It is in here that you can get water, said Otto, pointing ahead.

They went past.

Johannes looked after them. A strange dimness settled before his eyes. All these people were angry with him and jostled him; he mechanically begged their pardon and remained standing. There she disappeared.

When she came back, he bowed deeply to her and said:

Excuse me, miss.

Otto answered and looked at him through narrowed eyes.

This is Johannes, she said by way of introduction. Do you remember him?

You presumably wish to know how things are at home, she continued, and her face was beautiful and calm. I really do not know, but I am sure all is well. Excellent. I shall give the miller’s family your regards.

Thank you. Will you be leaving soon, miss?

One of these days. Yes, I shall give them your regards.

She nodded and left.

Johannes again looked after her until she had disappeared, then went outside. An endless wandering, a heavy and sorrowful tramping up one street and down another, killed the time. At ten o’clock he stood outside the chamberlain’s house and waited. The theatres would soon be letting out; now she would come. Perhaps he could open the carriage door, take off his hat, open the carriage door and bow himself to the ground.

At last, half an hour later, she came. Could he remain standing there by the gate and once more bring himself to her notice? He hurried up the street and did not look back. He heard the gate at the chamberlain’s house open, the carriage drive in and the gate slam shut again. Then he turned around.

Now he continued pacing back and forth in front of the house for an hour. He was waiting for no one and had no errand. Suddenly the gate opens from within and Victoria steps out into the street again. She has no hat on and has merely thrown a shawl over her shoulders. She smiles, half frightened, half embarrassed, and begins by asking:

Are you walking here thinking?

No, he answers. Am I thinking? No, I am only walking here.

I saw you walking up and down out here, and so I wanted to.... I saw you from my window. I must go back in at once.

Thank you for coming, Victoria. I was so desperate a little while ago, and now it is over. Forgive me for greeting you at the theatre; unfortunately I have also asked for you here at the chamberlain’s house. I wanted to meet you and learn what you meant, what your opinion is.

Yes, she said, you already know that. I said so much the day before yesterday that you could not have misunderstood it.

I am still just as uncertain about everything.

Let us not speak of it any more. I have said enough; I have said far too much, and I am hurting you now. I love you. I did not lie the day before yesterday and I am not lying now; but there is so much that separates us. I am very fond of you, I like speaking with you, with you rather than with anyone else, but.... Yes, I dare not stand here any longer; they can see us from the windows. Johannes, there are so many reasons that you do not know, so you must not ask me any more to say what I mean. I have thought about it night and day; I mean what I have said. But it will be impossible.

What will be impossible?

The whole thing. All of it. Listen, Johannes, spare me from having to be proud for both of us.

Very well. Good, you shall be spared that! But then you deceived me the day before yesterday. What happened was that you met me in the street and then you were in good spirits and then....

She turned and was about to go inside.

Have I done something wrong? he asked. His face was pale and unrecognisable. I mean, by what have I forfeited your....? During these two days and two nights, have I committed some offence?

No. That is not it. I have merely thought it over; have you not? It has been impossible all along, you know. I am fond of you, esteem you....

And respect me.

She looks at him; his smile wounds her, and she continues more vehemently:

My God, do you not understand for yourself that Papa would refuse you that? Why do you force me to say it? You understand it yourself. What could it have come to? Am I not right?

A pause.

Yes, he answers.

Besides, she continues, there are so many reasons.... No, you really must not follow me to the theatre any more; I became frightened of you. You must never do that again.

No, he says.

She takes his hand.

Could you not come home for a visit? I should be very glad of it. How warm your hand is; I am freezing. No, now I must go. Good night.

Good night, he answers.

The street lay cold and grey uphill through the city; it looked like a belt of sand, an endless road to walk. He came upon a boy selling old, ruined roses; he called to him, took a rose, gave the boy a tiny five-kroner gold coin as a gift, and walked on. Shortly afterward he saw a cluster of children playing by a gate. A ten-year-old boy sits quietly watching; he has old blue eyes that follow the game, hollow cheeks and a square chin, and on his head he wore a cap of canvas. It was the lining of a cap. This child wore a wig; a disease of the hair had disfigured this head for good. Perhaps his soul too was utterly withered.

He noticed all this although he had no clear notion of which part of the city he was in or where he was going. It began to rain as well; he did not notice it and did not put up his umbrella, although he had carried it with him all day.

When at last he came to a square where there were benches, he went over and sat down. It rained more and more; unconsciously he put up the umbrella and remained sitting. After a short while an irresistible drowsiness came over him; his brain lay in a fog, he closed his eyes and began to nod and sleep.

After a while he awoke when some passers-by spoke loudly. He rose and drifted onward. His brain had grown clearer; he remembered what had happened, every event, even the boy to whom he had given five kroner for a rose. He imagined the little gentleman’s delight when he discovered this remarkable coin among his small change, that it was not a twenty-five-øre piece, but a five-kroner gold coin. Go with God!

Weeks and months pass again, and spring came. The snow was already gone; far out in space there was a roaring as of waters released from the sun to the moon. The swallows had come, and in the forest outside the town a lively life awoke, of all kinds of leaping animals and birds with foreign tongues. A fresh, sweetish smell drifted up from the earth.

His work has lasted the whole winter. Like a work song, the poplars’ dry branches had creaked against the wall of the house night and day; now spring had come, the storms were past, and the stamping mill had creaked to a halt.

He opens the window and looks out; the street is already quiet although it is not midnight, the stars twinkle in a cloudless sky, and tomorrow promises to be a warm and bright day. He hears the rumble from the town mingling with the eternal roar in the distance. Suddenly a railway whistle shrills; it is the night train’s signal; it sounds like a single cockcrow in the still night. Now the time for work has come; this train whistle has been like a summons to him all winter.

And he closes the window and sits down at the table again. He throws aside the books he has been reading and brings out the papers. He takes up the pen.

Now his great work is almost finished; it lacks only a final chapter, a greeting as though from a ship sailing away, and he already has it in his head:

A gentleman is sitting in an inn by the road; he is passing through and is going far, far out into the world. His hair and beard are gray, and many years have passed over him; but he is still big and strong, and he is hardly as old as he looks. Outside stands his carriage, the horses are resting, the coachman is happy and content; for the stranger has given him wine and food. When the gentleman has entered his name, the innkeeper recognizes him and bows to him and shows him great honor. Who lives at the Castle now? the gentleman asks. The innkeeper answers: The Captain; he is very rich; his wife is good to everyone. To everyone? the gentleman asks himself and smiles strangely, to me as well? And the gentleman sits down to write on a piece of paper, and when it is filled he reads it over; it is a poem, grave and calm, but with many bitter words. But afterward he tears the paper to pieces, and he continues to sit there and tear the paper into still smaller pieces. Then there is a knock at his door, and a woman clad in yellow enters. She lifts her veil; it is the lady of the Castle, Mrs. Victoria. She is like a majesty. The gentleman rises abruptly; his dark soul is as though lit by a flash of lightning at that very moment. You are so good to everyone, he says bitterly; You come to me as well. She does not answer; she merely stands and looks at him, and her face turns a dusky red. What do You want? he asks, just as bitterly as before: have You come to remind me of what is past? For then it is for the last time, gracious lady; now I am leaving forever. And still the young lady of the Castle does not answer, but her mouth trembles. He says: Is it not enough for You that I have acknowledged my folly once? Then hear me, I do so again: my heart was set on You, I was not worthy of You—are You satisfied now? He continues with mounting vehemence: You answered me no, You took another; I was a peasant, a bear, a barbarian who in his youth had blundered into a royal game preserve! But then the gentleman throws himself onto a chair and sobs and begs: Oh, go! Forgive me, go Your way! Now all the flush has left the lady of the Castle’s face. Then she says, pronouncing the words so slowly and distinctly: I love You; misunderstand me no longer, it is You whom I love; farewell! And the young lady of the Castle turned away; she put her hands over her face and went quickly out of the door....

He puts down the pen and leans back. Yes, full stop, the end. There lay the book, all the written pages, nine months’ work. A warm satisfaction ripples through him because his work has been brought to completion. And while he sits there looking toward the window through which day is dawning, it hums and pounds in his head, and his spirit continues to work. He is full of feeling; his brain lies like an unharvested wild garden from whose earth steam rises:

In some mysterious way he has entered a deep, extinct valley where no living thing is to be found. Far away, alone and forgotten, an organ stands playing. He goes nearer to it, he examines it; the organ is bleeding, blood runs from one of its sides while it plays. Farther on he comes to a square. Everything there is deserted; no tree can be seen and no sound can be heard; it is merely an empty square. But in the sand are marks left by people’s shoes, and the last words spoken in the place seem still to remain in the air, so recently was it abandoned. A strange sensation fills him; these words remaining in the air above the square distress him, come nearer to him, press upon him. He strikes them away from himself and they return; they are not words, they are old men, a group of old men dancing; he sees them now. Why are they dancing, and why are they not in the least happy when they dance? A cold, ghastly air emanates from this company of old men; they do not see him, they are blind, and when he calls to them they do not hear him, they are dead. He wanders toward the east, toward the sun; he comes to a mountain. A voice calls: Are you beside a mountain? Yes, he answers, I am standing beside a mountain. Then the voice says: The mountain beside which you stand is my foot; I lie bound in the outermost land; come and free me!

Then he sets out for the outermost land. By a bridge a man stands lying in wait for him; he collects shadows; the man is made of musk. An icy terror grips him at the sight of this man who means to take his shadow. He spits at him and threatens him with clenched fists, but the man stands motionless and waits for him. Turn back! a voice calls behind him. He turns and sees a head rolling along the road and showing him the direction. The head is a human head, and now and then it laughs softly and soundlessly. He follows it. It rolls for days and nights, and he follows it; at the seashore it slips down into the earth and hides. He wades out into the sea and dives. He stands before a mighty gate and encounters a large, barking fish. It has a mane on its neck and barks at him like a dog. Behind the fish stands Victoria. He stretches his hands out toward her; she has no clothes on, she laughs toward him, and a storm blows through her hair. Then he calls out to her, he himself hears his scream—and wakes.

Johannes rises and goes to the window. It has grown almost light, and in the little mirror on the window jamb he sees that his temples are red. He puts out the lamp and, once more, in the gray light of day, reads the last page of his book. Then he lies down.

By the afternoon of that same day Johannes had paid for his room, delivered his manuscript, and left the town. He had gone abroad; no one knew where.

But after speaking of many kinds of love, the monk Vendt tells of yet another kind and says:

For so intoxicating is a peculiar kind of love!

The young master and mistress have just come home, their long honeymoon is over, and they retire for the night.

A shooting star flared above their roof.

In summer the young master and mistress walked together and never left each other’s side. They picked yellow, red, and blue flowers, which they gave to one another; they watched the grass move in the wind and heard the birds singing in the forests, and every word they spoke was like a caress. In winter they drove with bells on the horses, and the sky was blue, and high above, the stars rushed across the eternal plains.

Thus many, many years passed. The young master and mistress had three children, and their hearts loved one another as on the first day beneath the first kiss.

Then the proud master contracted his illness, the illness that chained him to his bed for so long and put his wife’s patience to so severe a test. The day he recovered and rose from his bed, he did not recognize himself; the illness had disfigured him and taken his hair.

He suffered and brooded. Then one morning he said:

Now you surely do not love me anymore?

But his wife, blushing, threw her arms around him and kissed him as passionately as in the springtime of youth, and answered:

I, I love, love you always. I never forget that it was me and no one else whom you chose, and who became so happy.

And she went into her chamber and cut all the yellow hair from her head so as to resemble her husband, whom she loved.

And again many, many years passed; the young master and mistress grew old, and their children were grown. They shared every happiness as before; in summer they still walked in the fields and watched the grass ripple, and in winter they wrapped themselves in their furs and drove beneath the starry sky. And their hearts continued to be warm and glad, as if from wondrous wine.

Then the mistress became paralyzed. The old mistress could not walk on her feet; she had to be pulled in a wheeled chair, and the master himself pulled her. But the mistress suffered so unspeakably in her misfortune, and her face acquired deep furrows of sorrow.

Then one day she said:

Now I should like to die. I am so paralyzed and hideous, and your face is so handsome; you can no longer kiss me, and you cannot love me as before.

But the master embraces her, red with emotion, and answers:

I, I love you more, more than my life, my dear; I love you as on the first day, the first moment when you gave me the rose. Do you remember? You held out the rose to me and looked at me with your beautiful eyes; the rose was fragrant like you, you blushed like it, and I became intoxicated in all my senses. But I love you even more now; you are more beautiful than in your youth, and my heart thanks and blesses you for every day you have been mine.

The master goes into his chamber, pours acid on his face to disfigure it, and says to his wife:

I had the misfortune of getting acid on my face; my cheeks are covered with burns, and surely you do not love me anymore?

Oh, you, my bridegroom, my beloved! stammers the old woman, and kisses his hands. You are more handsome than any man on earth; your voice still makes my heart burn even today, and I love you unto death.

XIII

Johannes meets Camilla in the street; she is with her mother, her father, and young Richmond; they stop their carriage and speak kindly with him.

Camilla takes hold of his arm and says:

You did not come to see us. We had a grand celebration, you may be sure; we waited for you until the very end, but you did not come.

I was prevented, he answered.

Forgive me for not having come up to see you since then, she continued. I shall come one of these days, quite certainly, when Richmond has left. Oh, what a celebration we had! Victoria became ill; she was driven home—have you heard? I shall soon go up to see her. She is surely much better, perhaps entirely well again. I have given Richmond a medallion almost like yours. Listen, Johannes, you must promise me to tend your stove; when you write, you forget everything, and it becomes ice-cold at your place. Then you must ring for the maid.

Yes, I shall ring for the maid, he answered.

Mrs. Seier also spoke to him, asking about his work, about the piece on The Family; how was it going? She was waiting eagerly for the next thing from him.

Johannes gave the necessary answers, bowed very deeply, and watched the carriage drive away. How little the whole thing concerned him—this carriage, these people, this talk! An empty, cold mood entered him and accompanied him all the way home. By his gate, a man was loitering back and forth in the street, an old acquaintance, the former private tutor at the Castle.

Johannes greeted him.

He was dressed in a long, warm coat that had been carefully brushed, and he wore a bold and resolute expression.

You see before You Your friend and colleague, he said. Give me Your hand, young man. God has guided my paths wondrously since last we met; I am married, I have a home, a little garden, a wife. Miracles still happen in life. Have You any comment to make on my last utterance?

ohannes looks at him in astonishment.

Then it is settled. You see, I tutored her son. She has a son; the brat is from her first marriage. Naturally, she had been married before; she was a widow. Thus I married a widow. She already had the brat. I go about there, you see, looking at the garden and the widow, and for some time I entertain intense thoughts on the subject. Suddenly it comes to me, and I say to myself: very well, it was not sung over your cradle, and so forth; but I do it all the same, I take the plunge, for it is probably written in the stars. See, that is how it happened.

Congratulations! said Johannes.

Stop! Not another word! I know what You mean to say. And the first one, You mean to say—have You forgotten the eternal love of Your youth? That is precisely what You mean to say. Then may I, for my part, ask You, most honored sir, what became of my first, only, and eternal love? Did she not take an artillery captain? Moreover, I shall ask You one more little question: have You ever, ever seen a man get the woman he was meant to have? I have not. There is a legend of a man whose prayer God answered in that respect: he got his first and only love. But it brought him no particular glory. Why not? You will ask again, and see, I answer You: No, for the simple reason that she died immediately afterward—immediately afterward, do You hear, ha-ha-ha, at once afterward. That is always how it is. Naturally, a man does not get the woman he was meant to have; but if, for once, it happens by sheer damned right and reason, then she dies immediately afterward. There are always complications. Thus the man is obliged to acquire another love of the best possible kind, and he need not die from this change. I tell You, nature has arranged it so wisely that he endures it splendidly. Just look at me.

Yes, he said, I wrote that. It was so long ago; it was one night, the poplars outside my window were rustling so when I wrote it. No, are you really putting it away again? Thank you! You put it away again. Oh! he exclaimed, enraptured, and his voice was quite low, just think that you are sitting no farther away than this. I feel your arm against mine; a warmth radiates from you. Many a time, when I was alone and thought of you, I froze with emotion; but now I am warm. The last time I was home you were lovely then too; but you are lovelier now. It is the eyes and the eyebrows, your smile—no, I do not know, it is everything, everything about you.

She smiled and looked at him with half-closed eyes; beneath the long lashes there was a dark blue shadow. She had a warm glow. She seemed to be prey to the highest joy and reached toward him with her hand in an unconscious movement.

Thank you! she said.

No, Victoria, do not thank me, he answered. His whole soul streamed toward her, and he wanted to say more, say more; it became confused outbursts, he was as though intoxicated. Yes, but Victoria, if you are a little fond of me.... I do not know, but say that you are, even if it is not so. Please. Oh, I should promise you to become something, become a great deal, almost an unheard-of amount. You have no idea what I could become; I ponder it sometimes and know that I am utterly full of deeds not yet done. Many a time it pours out of me; at night I pace up and down the floor of my room because I am full of visions. There is a man in the room next door; he cannot sleep, he knocks on the wall. When morning dawns he comes in to me and is furious. It does not matter, I do not care about him; for by then I have thought of you for so long that I feel you are with me. I go to the window and sing; it is beginning to grow a little light, the poplars rustle outside. Good night! I say to the day. It is meant for you. Now she is sleeping, I think, good night, God bless her! Then I lie down. So it goes, evening after evening. But I never believed that you were as lovely as you are. Now I will remember you like this when you leave; as you are now. I will remember you so clearly....

Are you not coming home?

No. I am not finished. Yes, I am coming. I am leaving now. I am not finished, but I will do all manner of things. Do you sometimes wander in the garden at home now? Do you ever go out in the evening? I could see you, I could perhaps have the chance to greet you; it is not for anything else. But if you are a little fond of me, if you can tolerate me, endure me, then say.... Grant me that joy.... Do you know, there is a palm that blossoms only once in its life, and yet it lives to be seventy years old, the talipot palm. But it blossoms only once. I am blossoming now. Yes, I will get some money and go home. I shall sell what I have written; you see, I am writing a large book, and I shall sell it now, at once tomorrow, everything I have finished. I shall get a good deal for it. Would you then want me to come home?

a.
Thank you, thank you! Forgive me if I hope too much, believe too much; it is so lovely to believe an extraordinary amount. This is the happiest day I have lived....

He took off his hat and laid it beside him.

Victoria looked around; a lady was coming down the street, and farther up there was a woman with a basket. Victoria grew uneasy; she reached for her watch.

Must you go now? he asked. Say something before you go, let me hear your.... I love you, and I am saying it now. Whether I.... will depend on your answer. You have such absolute power over me. What is your answer?

Pause.

He lowers his head.
No, do not say it! he begged.

Not here, she answered. I shall do it down there.

They walked on.

People say that you are going to marry the little girl, the girl, the one you rescued; what is her name?

Camilla, do you mean?

Camilla Seier. People say that you are going to marry her.

Is that so. Why do you ask? She is not grown up. I have been to her home; it is so large and rich, a palace like your own; I have been there many times. No, she is not grown up.

She is fifteen years old. I have met her; we have spent time together. I became very fond of her. How lovely she is!

I am not going to marry her, he said.

Oh, you are not.

He looked at her. A twitch passed over his face.

But why are you saying this now? Do you wish to direct my attention to someone else?

She walked on with rapid steps and did not answer. They were outside the chamberlain’s house. She took his hand and pulled him through the gateway and up the stairs.

I am not going in, he said, half astonished.

She pressed the bell; she turned toward him, and her breast heaved.

I love you, she said. Do you understand that? It is you I love.

Suddenly she pulled him quickly down the stairs again, three, four steps, threw her arms around him, and kissed him. She trembled against him.

It is you I love, she said.

Johannes grabs at his papers on the table and takes a handful of large and small sheets.

Look here! he cries. I tell you, it has never gone so well for me. It was like one long flash of lightning. want this grimace to be my own.

IV

It is drawing toward morning, the day is dawning, a bluish, trembling September morning.

I am walking along the street and meet my happiness, oh, listen to me, meet my star and my happiness. Do you know, and then she kisses me. Her mouth was so red and I love her, she kisses me and intoxicates me. Have you ever trembled so violently in the mouth that you could not speak? I could not speak, my heart shook my whole body. I ran home and fell asleep; I sat here on the chair and slept. When evening came I awoke. My soul rocked up and down within me with emotion, and I began to write. What did I write? Here it is! I was possessed by a strange and glorious train of thought, the heavens opened, it was like a warm summer’s day for my soul, I received wine from an angel, I drank it; it was intoxicating wine, I drank it from a pomegranate bowl. Did I hear the clock strike? Did I see the lamp burn out? God grant that you understood it! I lived through it all anew, once again; I walked again with my beloved along the street and everyone turned to look after her. We walked in the park, we met the king, I swept my hat to the ground before him for joy, and the king turned to look after her, after my beloved, for she is so noble and lovely. We went down into the town again and all the schoolchildren turned to look after her, for she is young and wears a light-colored dress. When we came to a red stone house we went in. I followed her up the stairs and wanted to kneel before her. Then she put her arms around me and kissed me. This happened to me yesterday evening, it was no longer ago than that. If you asked me what I have written, then it is one single unceasing song to joy, to the happiness I have written. It was as though happiness lay naked before me with a long, laughing neck and desired me.

Johannes remained standing with the letter in his hand. Victoria was
dead. Again and again he spoke her name aloud, and his
voice was numb, almost hardened. He looked down at
the letter and recognized the handwriting; there were capital and lowercase letters,
the lines straight, and she who had written them was dead!

Then he makes his way in through his gate, up the stairs, finds
the right key to put into the lock, and opens the door. His room
was cold and dark. He sits down by the window and, in
the last remnant of daylight, reads Victoria’s letter.

Dear Johannes! she wrote. When you read this letter, I am
dead! Everything is so strange to me now; I am no longer ashamed
before you and am writing to you again, as though there were
nothing to prevent it. Before, while I was fully
alive, I would rather have suffered night and day than have written to
you again; but now my soul has begun to leave me, and I no longer
think that way. Strangers have seen me bleed, the doctor has
examined me and seen that I have only a remnant of one lung
left; what more have I to be ashamed of?

I have lain here on the bed and thought about the last words
I said to you. It was in the woods that evening. At the time I did
not think they would be my last words, for then I would have
said farewell to you at once and thanked you. Now I shall
never see you again, so now I regret that I did not throw
myself down before you and kiss your shoes and the ground you walked
on, and show you how inexpressibly I have loved you. I have
lain here both yesterday and today wishing that I were no sicker
than to be able to make my way home again and walk into the woods and
find the place where we sat when you held both my hands;
for then I could lie down there and see whether I could find
your traces and kiss all the heather around it. But I cannot
come home now unless perhaps I get a little better,
as Mama believes.

Dear Johannes! It is strange to think that I have
done nothing other than come into the world and
love you, and now say farewell to life. You may believe it is strange
to lie here and wait for the day and the hour. Step by step
I am moving away from life and the people in the street and the clatter
of carriages; I shall probably never see spring again either, and these
houses and the streets and the trees in the park will remain after me.
Today I was able to sit up in bed and look out of the window for a while. Down
on the corner there were two people who met; they greeted each other and clasped
each other’s hands and laughed at what they said; but then it was so strange
to me that I, who lay there watching this, was going to die. I found
myself thinking: those two down there do not know that I am lying here waiting
for my hour; but if they knew, they would probably still greet
each other and talk to each other just as they do now. Last night, when
it was dark, I thought it was going to be my final moment;
my heart began to stop, and it was as though I could already
hear eternity roaring toward me from far out. But in the next moment
I returned from far away and began to breathe again.
It was an utterly indescribable sensation. But Mama thinks that
perhaps it was only the river and the waterfall back home that I remembered.

Dear God, if only you knew how I have loved you,
Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has
stood in my way, first and foremost my own nature.
Papa too was so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter.
But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I am writing
to you once again and telling you so. I ask myself
why I am doing it, since it is nevertheless of no concern to you, especially
when I shall not even be alive anymore; but I should like
to be close to you until the end, so that at least I would not feel
more forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though
I can see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements
with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then we
are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for
you; I have no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for
you two days ago already, but I preferred to write. I also wanted most of all
for you to remember me as I once was, when I had not yet
been ill. I remember that you .... (Here some words have been omitted) .... my eyes and
eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were before. For that
reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I shall also ask
you not to see me in my coffin. I shall presumably look much as
I did when I was alive, only somewhat paler, and I shall be lying in a yellow dress; but
nevertheless you would regret it if you came and saw me.

Now I have written on this letter many times today, and
even so I have not managed to tell you a thousandth of what I
wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to;
I still hope so fervently in God that perhaps I might
get a little better, if only until spring. Then the days
are bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now, I would
certainly never be unkind to you again, Johannes.
How I have wept and thought about it! Oh, I would go out and pat
all the paving stones and stop and thank every step in the stairways
I passed and be good to everyone. It would not matter how
much pain I suffered if only I were allowed to live. I would never complain
about anything again; no, I would smile at anyone who attacked
and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were allowed to live. My
life is so unlived; I have done nothing for anyone, and this
failed life is to end now. If you knew how loath I am to die,
then perhaps you would do something, do everything in your power.
You presumably cannot do anything; but I thought that if you and
the whole world prayed for me and would not let me go, then God
would grant me life. Oh, how grateful I would be then, and
never do wrong to anyone again, but smile at everything that was
ordained for me, if only I were allowed to live.

Mama is sitting here and weeping. She also sat here all night and
wept for me. This does me a little good; it softens the bitterness of my
farewell. Today I also thought: I wonder what you would think
if one day I came right up to you in the street, when I was nicely
dressed, and said nothing hurtful anymore, but gave you a rose
that I could have bought beforehand. Then immediately afterward I thought
that I can never again do what I want; for surely I can never
recover before I die. I weep so often; I lie quietly and
weep incessantly and inconsolably; it does not hurt in my chest when
I do not sob. Johannes, dear, dear friend, my only beloved
on earth, come to me now and stay here for a while when it begins
to grow dark. I shall not weep then, but smile as well as I
can, merely from joy that you came.

Oh, good God, if only you knew how I have loved you,
Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has stood
in my way, first and foremost my own nature.
Papa was likewise so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter.
But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I am
writing to you once more and telling you. I ask myself why I do
it, since after all it is a matter of indifference to you, especially
when I shall no longer even be alive; but I would like to be near
you until the end, so that at least I would not feel more
forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though
I see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements
with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then
we are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for you; I have
no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for you two days ago,
but I preferred to write. I would also prefer you to remember me
as I once was, when I had not yet been ill. I remember
that you .... (Some words have been omitted here) .... my eyes and
eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were. For that
reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I will also ask
you not to look at me in my coffin. I shall no doubt look much as
I did when I was alive, only somewhat paler, and I shall be lying
in a yellow dress; but even so, you would regret it if you came
and saw me.

Now I have returned to writing this letter many times today, and
yet I have not managed to tell you one thousandth of what I
wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to;
I still hope so fervently in God that I might perhaps
get a little better, even if only until spring. Then the days are
bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now,
I would certainly never be cruel to you again, Johannes.
How I have wept and thought of it! Oh, I would go out and pat
all the paving stones and stop and thank every step of every
staircase I passed, and be good to everyone. It would not matter
how badly I suffered, if only I were allowed to live. I would
never complain about anything again; no, I would smile at anyone
who attacked and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were
allowed to live. My life is so unlived; I have done nothing for
anyone, and this failed life is to end now. If you knew how
reluctant I am to die, then perhaps you would do something, do
everything in your power. You probably cannot do anything; but
I thought that if you and the whole world prayed for me and
would not let me go, then God would grant me life. Oh, how
grateful I would be then, and never do wrong to anyone again,
but smile at everything that befell me, if only I were allowed
to live.

Mama is sitting here weeping. She sat here all last night as well
and wept for me. This does me a little good; it softens the
bitterness of my farewell. Today I also thought: how would you
like it if I came straight up to you in the street one day, when I
was nicely dressed, and no longer said anything hurtful, but gave
you a rose that I could have bought beforehand? Then I thought
immediately afterward that I can never again do what I want;
for I can surely never recover again before I die. I weep so
often; I lie quietly and weep ceaselessly and inconsolably; my
chest does not hurt when I do not sob. Johannes, dear, dear
friend, my only beloved on earth, come to me now and stay here
for a little while when it begins to grow dark. I shall not weep
then, but smile as well as I am able, simply for joy that you came.

No, what has become of my pride and my courage! I am not my
father’s daughter now; but that is because my strength has left
me. I have

11 — Hamsun: III

suffered for a long time, Johannes, long before these last days.
When you were abroad, I suffered, and since I came here to town
this spring, I have done nothing but suffer every day. Never
before have I known how infinitely long the night could be. I
have seen you twice in the street during this time; on one of
those occasions you were humming as you walked past me, but
you did not see me. I had hoped to see you at the Seiers’; but
you did not come. I would not have spoken to you or walked
straight in front of you, but would have been grateful merely to
see you from far away. But you did not come. I thought then that
perhaps it was because of me that you did not come. At eleven
o’clock I began to dance because I could not bear to wait any
longer. Yes, Johannes, I have loved you, loved only you throughout
my entire life. It is Victoria who is writing this, and God is
reading it over my shoulder.
And now I must bid you farewell; it has now grown almost dark,
and I can no longer see. Farewell, Johannes; thank you for every
day. When I fly away from the earth, I shall continue to thank
you until the very end and repeat your name to myself all the
way. May you fare well, then, all your life, and forgive me for
what I have done against you, and because I could not throw
myself down before you and ask your forgiveness for it. I am
doing so now in my heart. May you fare well, Johannes, and
farewell forever. And thank you once again for every single day
and hour. I can do no more.
Yours,
VICTORIA.

Now I have had the lamp lit, and it is much brighter for me.
I have lain in a stupor and once again been far away from the
earth. Thank God, it was not as frightening for me as before; I
even heard a little music, and above all, it was not dark. I am so
grateful. But now I have no strength left to write.
Farewell, my beloved ....

NORA. Only to sew on my costume. Good heavens, how unreasonable you are. (sits down on the sofa.) Now be nice, Doctor Rank; tomorrow you shall see how beautifully I shall dance; and then you must imagine that I am doing it only for your sake—yes, and then, of course, for Torvald’s; that goes without saying. (takes various things out of the box.) Doctor Rank, sit here, and I shall show you something.

RANK (sits down). What is it?

NORA. Look here. Look!

RANK. Silk stockings.

NORA. Flesh-colored. Aren’t they lovely? Yes, it is so dark in here now; but tomorrow—. No, no, no; you may only see the foot. Oh yes, you may indeed see the upper part too, if you like.

RANK. Hm—

NORA. Why do you look so critical? Perhaps you don’t think they will fit?

RANK. I cannot possibly have any well-founded opinion about that.

NORA (looks at him for a moment). Shame on you. (strikes him lightly on the ear with the stockings.) There, you deserve that. (packs them up again.)

RANK. And what other delights am I to be allowed to see?

NORA. You shall not see another scrap, because you are naughty.

(she hums a little and searches among the things.)

RANK (after a short silence). When I sit here like this, quite intimately together with you, I cannot comprehend—no, I cannot grasp—what would have become of me if I had never come into this house.

NORA (smiles). Oh, I think that, deep down, you enjoy yourself quite well with us.

RANK (more softly, staring ahead). And then to have to leave it all—

NORA. Nonsense; you are not leaving it.

RANK (as before). —and not even be able to leave behind one poor token of gratitude; scarcely even a fleeting sense of loss—nothing but an empty place that can be filled by the first person who comes along.

NORA. And if I were now to ask you to—? No—

RANK. To what?

NORA. To give me a great proof of your friendship—

RANK. Yes, yes?

NORA. No, I mean—to do me an immensely great service—

RANK. Would you really, for once, make me so happy?

NORA. Oh, you do not even know what it is.

RANK. Very well, then; say it.

NORA. No, but I cannot, Doctor Rank; it is something so unreasonably great—advice and help and a service as well—

RANK. So much the better. I cannot imagine what you can mean. But do speak. Do I not have your confidence?

NORA. Yes, you do, as no one else does. You are my most faithful and best friend; you know that. That is why I shall tell you. Very well, then, Doctor Rank; there is something you must help me prevent. You know how deeply, how indescribably dearly Torvald loves me; he would never hesitate for a moment to give his life for my sake.

RANK (leaning toward her). Nora—do you think that he is the only one—?

NORA (with a slight start). Who—?

RANK. Who would gladly give his life for your sake.

NORA (heavily). I see.

RANK. I have sworn to myself that you should know it before I went away. I would never find a better opportunity.—Yes, Nora, now you know it. And now you also know that you can confide in me as in no one else.

NORA (rises; evenly and calmly). Let me pass.

RANK (makes way for her, but remains seated). Nora—

NORA (in the doorway to the hall). Helene, bring in the lamp.—(goes over toward the stove.) Oh, dear Doctor Rank, that was really horrid of you.

RANK (rises). That I have loved you just as deeply as anyone else has? Was that horrid?

NORA. No, but that you should go and tell me so. There was no need at all—

RANK. What do you mean? Did you know—?

(The maid enters with the lamp, puts it on the table, and goes out again.)

RANK. Nora—Mrs. Helmer—I ask you, did you know anything?

NORA. Oh, how do I know what I knew or did not know? I truly cannot tell you—. How could you be so clumsy, Doctor Rank! Everything was so good as it was.

RANK. Well, at any rate, you now know for certain that I am at your disposal, body and soul. And will you now speak openly?

NORA (looks at him). After this?

RANK. I beg you, let me know what it is.

NORA. You cannot know anything now.

RANK. Yes, yes. You must not punish me like this. Allow me to do for you whatever lies within human power.

NORA. Now you can do nothing for me.—Besides, I am sure I do not need any help. You will see that it is all merely imagination. Yes, certainly it is. Of course! (sits down in the rocking chair, looks at him, smiles.) You really are a fine gentleman, Doctor Rank. Don’t you think you ought to be ashamed of yourself now that the lamp has been brought in?

RANK. No; not really. But perhaps I should go—for good?

NORA. No, you certainly must not do that. Of course you must come here as before. You know very well that Torvald cannot do without you.

RANK. Yes, but you?

NORA. Oh, I always think it becomes tremendously enjoyable here when you come.

RANK. That is precisely what led me astray. You are a riddle to me. Many times it has seemed to me that you would almost as gladly be with me as with Helmer.

NORA. Yes, you see, there are some people whom one loves most, and other people whom one would almost rather be with.

RANK. Oh yes, there is something in that.

NORA. When I was at home, naturally I loved Papa most. But I always thought it was so immensely amusing when I could steal downstairs to the maids’ room; for they did not guide me in the least, and they always talked about so many amusing things among themselves.

RANK. Aha; so it is they whom I have replaced.

NORA (springs up and goes over to him). Oh, dear, kind Doctor Rank, I did not mean that at all. But surely you can understand that with Torvald it is just as it was with Papa—

(The maid comes in from the hall.)

MAID. Madam! (whispers and hands her a card.)

NORA (glances at the card). Ah! (puts it in her pocket.)

RANK. Is something wrong?

NORA. No, no, not at all; it is only something—it is my new costume—

RANK. What? Your costume is lying right there.

NORA. Oh yes, that one; but this is another; I have ordered it—Torvald must not know—

RANK. Aha, so there we have the great secret.

NORA. Yes, indeed; just go in to him; he is sitting in the inner room; keep him occupied for a while—

RANK. Do not worry; he shall not get away from me. (he goes into Helmer’s room.)

NORA (to the maid). And he is standing waiting in the kitchen?

MAID. Yes, he came up the back stairs—

NORA. But didn’t you tell him that someone was here?

MAID. Yes, but it did no good.

NORA. He will not go away again?

MAID. No, he will not go until he has spoken with Madam.

NORA. Tomorrow I am going home—I mean, to my old hometown. It will be easiest for me there to find something or other to do.

HELMER. Oh, you blind, inexperienced creature.

NORA. I must try to gain experience, Torvald.

HELMER. Leave your home, your husband, and your children! And you do not think about what people will say.

NORA. I cannot take that into consideration. I know only that it will be necessary for me.

HELMER. Oh, it is outrageous. That you can betray your most sacred duties in this way.

NORA. What, then, do you consider my most sacred duties?

HELMER. And should I need to tell you that! Are they not your duties toward your husband and your children?

NORA. I have other duties just as sacred.

HELMER. You do not. What duties could those be?

NORA. My duties toward myself.

HELMER. First and foremost, you are a wife and mother.

NORA. I no longer believe that. I believe that first and foremost I am a human being, I, just as much as you are—or at any rate that I must try to become one. I know very well that most people agree with you, Torvald, and that something of the sort is written in the books. But I can no longer be satisfied with what most people say and what is written in the books. I must think these things over for myself and try to understand them.

HELMER. Should you not understand your position in your own home? Do you not have an infallible guide in such matters? Do you not have religion?

NORA. Oh, Torvald, I really do not properly know what religion is at all.

HELMER. What are you saying!

NORA. I know nothing beyond what Pastor Hansen said when I went to confirmation classes. He explained that religion was this and that. When I get away from all this here and am alone, I shall examine that matter too. I shall see whether what Pastor Hansen said was right, or at any rate whether it is right for me.

HELMER. Oh, such a thing is unheard of from so young a woman! But if religion cannot guide you, then at least let me awaken your conscience. Surely you have some moral sense? Or answer me—perhaps you have none?

NORA. Yes, Torvald, that is not easy to answer. I really do not know at all. I am completely at a loss about such things. I know only that I have a very different opinion of such matters from yours. I now hear, too, that the laws are different from what I thought; but that those laws should be right is something I cannot possibly get into my head. So a woman is not to have the right to spare her old, dying father, or to save her husband’s life! I do not believe in such things.

HELMER. You speak like a child. You do not understand the society in which you live.

NORA. No, I do not. But now I intend to learn about it. I must try to find out who is right, society or I.

HELMER. You are ill, Nora; you have a fever; I almost believe you are out of your mind.

NORA. I have never felt so clear and certain as I do tonight.

HELMER. And clear and certain, you are leaving your husband and your children?

NORA. Yes; I am.

HELMER. Then only one explanation is possible.

NORA. Which one?

HELMER. You no longer love me.

NORA. No, that is precisely it.

HELMER. Nora!—And you say that!

NORA. Oh, it hurts me so much, Torvald; for you have always been so kind to me. But I cannot help it. I no longer love you.

HELMER (with forced composure). Is this also a clear and certain conviction?

NORA. Yes, perfectly clear and certain. That is why I do not wish to remain here any longer.

HELMER. And will you also be able to explain to me how I have forfeited your love?

NORA. Yes, I can readily do that. It was this evening, when the wonderful thing did not happen; for then I saw that you were not the man I had imagined you to be.

HELMER. Explain yourself more fully; I do not understand you.

NORA. I have waited so patiently for eight years now; for, dear God, I understood well enough that the wonderful thing does not happen every day. Then this crushing blow came upon me; and then I was infallibly certain: now the wonderful thing will happen. When Krogstad’s letter lay out there, it never once entered my mind that you might be willing to submit to that man’s terms. I was infallibly certain that you would say to him: make the matter known to the whole world. And when that had happened—

HELMER. Yes, and then what? When I had exposed my own wife to shame and disgrace—!

NORA. When that had happened, I thought with infallible certainty that you would step forward and take everything upon yourself and say: I am the guilty one.

HELMER. Nora—!

NORA. You think I would never have accepted such a sacrifice from you? No, of course not. But what would my assurances have counted for against yours?—That was the wonderful thing for which I went on hoping in terror. And it was to prevent it that I wanted to end my life.

HELMER. I would gladly work nights and days for you, Nora—bear sorrow and privation for your sake. But no one sacrifices his honor for the person he loves.

NORA. A hundred thousand women have done so.

HELMER. Oh, you both think and speak like a foolish child.

NORA. Let that be so. But you neither think nor speak like the man to whom I could bind myself. When your fright was over—not at what threatened me, but at what you yourself were exposed to—and when all the danger was past, then for you it was as though nothing at all had happened. I was exactly as before, your little songbird, your doll, whom from then on you would carry in your hands with twice the care, since it was so fragile and frail. (rises.) Torvald—in that moment it dawned on me that for eight years I had lived here with a strange man, and that I had had three children—. Oh, I cannot bear to think of it! I could tear myself to pieces.

HELMER (heavily). I see it; I see it. An abyss has indeed opened between us.—Oh, but Nora, could it not be filled in?

NORA. As I am now, I am no wife for you.

HELMER. I have the strength to become another man.

NORA. Perhaps—if your doll is taken away from you.

HELMER. Oh, to part—to part from you! No, no, Nora, I cannot grasp that thought.

NORA (goes into the room on the right). Then it is all the more certain that it must happen. (she returns with her outer clothing and a small traveling bag, which she sets on the chair by the table.)

HELMER. Nora, Nora, not now! Wait until tomorrow.

NORA (puts on her coat). I cannot spend the night in a strange man’s rooms.

HELMER. But could we not live here as brother and sister—?

HELMER (with the letters in his hand). Look here. See how they have piled up. (leafing through them.) What is this?

NORA (at the window). The letter! Oh no, no, Torvald!

HELMER. Two calling cards—from Rank.

NORA. From Doctor Rank?

HELMER (looking at them). Doctor of Medicine Rank. They were on top; he must have slipped them in when he left.

NORA. Is there anything written on them?

HELMER. There is a black cross above the name. Look here. It is a rather uncanny idea. It is exactly as though he were announcing his own death.

NORA. That is what he is doing.

HELMER. What? Do you know something? Has he told you anything?

NORA. Yes. When those cards arrive, he has taken leave of us. He intends to shut himself in and die.

HELMER. My poor friend. I knew, of course, that I would not be allowed to keep him for long. But so soon—. And then he hides himself away like a wounded animal.

NORA. When it has to happen, it is best that it happen without words. Is that not so, Torvald?

HELMER (paces up and down). He was so closely bound up with us. I do not think I can imagine him gone. He, with his sufferings and his loneliness, gave, as it were, a clouded background to our sunlit happiness.—Well, perhaps it is best this way. For him, at any rate. (stops.) And perhaps for us too, Nora. Now the two of us are left entirely to each other alone. (puts his arms around her.) Oh, my beloved wife; I do not think I can hold you tightly enough. Do you know, Nora—many a time I wish that some imminent danger might threaten you, so that I could risk life and blood and everything for your sake.

NORA (tears herself free and says loudly and resolutely). Now you shall read your letters, Torvald.

HELMER. No, no, not tonight. I want to be with you, my beloved wife.

NORA. With the thought of your friend’s death—?

HELMER. You are right. This has shaken us both; something ugly has come between us; thoughts of death and dissolution. We must seek release from this. Until then—. We will each go our own way.

NORA (with her arms around his neck). Torvald—good night! Good night!

HELMER (kisses her on the forehead). Good night, my little songbird. Sleep well, Nora. Now I shall read through the letters. (he takes the bundle into his room and closes the door behind him.)

NORA (with wild eyes, gropes about, seizes Helmer’s domino, wraps it around herself, and whispers rapidly, hoarsely, and brokenly:) Never see him again. Never. Never. (throws her shawl over her head.) Never see the children again either. Not them either. Never; never.—Oh, the ice-cold black water. Oh, the bottomless—; this—. Oh, if only it were over.—Now he has it; now he is reading it. Oh no, no; not yet. Torvald, farewell, you and the children—

(She is about to rush out through the hall; at that same moment Helmer tears open his door and stands there with an opened letter in his hand.)

HELMER. Nora!

NORA (screams loudly). Ah—!

HELMER. What is this? Do you know what is written in this letter?

NORA. Yes, I know. Let me go! Let me get out!

HELMER (holds her back). Where are you going?

NORA (tries to tear herself free). You must not save me, Torvald!

HELMER (reels backward). True! Is what he writes true? Terrible! No, no; it is impossible that this can be true.

NORA. It is true. I have loved you above everything in the whole world.

HELMER. Oh, do not come to me with foolish evasions.

NORA (takes a step toward him). Torvald—!

HELMER. You wretched woman—what have you done!

NORA. Let me go away. You must not bear it for my sake. You must not take it upon yourself.

HELMER. No playacting. (locks the hall door.) You will remain here and answer to me. Do you understand what you have done? Answer me! Do you understand it?

NORA (looks steadily at him and says with an expression that is growing rigid:) Yes, now I am beginning to understand it to the very bottom.

HELMER (paces about the floor). Oh, what a terrible awakening this is. During all these eight years—she who was my joy and pride—a hypocrite, a liar—worse, worse—a criminal!—Oh, the bottomless ugliness that lies in all this! Shame, shame!

NORA (remains silent and continues to look steadily at him).

HELMER (stops in front of her). I should have suspected that something like this would happen. I should have foreseen it. All your father’s frivolous principles.—Be silent! You have inherited all your father’s frivolous principles. No religion, no morality, no sense of duty—. Oh, how I have been punished for turning a blind eye to him. I did it for your sake; and this is how you repay me.

NORA. Yes, this is how.

HELMER. Now you have destroyed all my happiness. You have ruined my entire future for me. Oh, it is terrible to think of. I am in the power of an unscrupulous man; he can do with me whatever he pleases, demand anything at all of me, order and command me as he sees fit—and I dare not make a sound. And I must sink so miserably and be ruined because of a frivolous woman!

NORA. When I am no longer in this world, then you will be free.

HELMER. Oh, no theatrics. Your father always had such phrases ready to hand too. What good would it do me if you were no longer in this world, as you say? It would not do me the slightest good. He could still make the matter public; and if he does, I may perhaps be suspected of having known about your criminal act. People may perhaps think that I was behind it—that it was I who urged you on! And I have you to thank for all this—you, whom I have borne upon my hands throughout our entire marriage. Do you understand now what you have done to me?

NORA (with cold calm). Yes.

HELMER. This is so incredible that I cannot grasp it. But we must try to settle matters. Take off the shawl. Take it off, I tell you! I must try to satisfy him in one way or another. The matter must be hushed up at any cost.—And as for you and me, it must appear as though everything between us were just as before. But naturally only in the eyes of the world. You will therefore continue to remain here in the house; that goes without saying. But you will not be allowed to bring up the children; I dare not entrust them to you—. Oh, to have to say this to her whom I have loved so deeply, and whom I still—! Well, it must be over. From this day forward, it is no longer a question of happiness; it is only a question of saving the remains, the fragments, the appearance. (the entrance bell rings.)

HELMER (starts). What is that? So late. Could the most terrible thing—! Could he—! Hide yourself, Nora! Say you are ill.

“I have loved you too much to let you believe that the change you perceive in me is an effect of my fickleness; I want you to know that your unfaithfulness is the cause of it. You are greatly surprised that I speak to you of your unfaithfulness; you had concealed it from me with such skill, and I took such care to conceal from you that I knew of it, that you have reason to be astonished that it is known to me. I am surprised myself that I was able to keep you from seeing any sign of it. Never has any sorrow equaled mine. I believed that you had a violent passion for me; I no longer concealed from you the passion I had for you, and at the very time when I was letting you see it in its entirety, I learned that you were deceiving me, that you loved another woman, and that, to all appearances, you were sacrificing me to this new mistress. I learned it on the day of the running at the ring; that is why I did not go. I pretended to be ill in order to conceal the disorder of my mind; but I truly became ill, and my body could not withstand so violent an agitation. When I began to recover, I still pretended to be very ill, so that I might have a pretext for neither seeing you nor writing to you. I wanted time to decide how I ought to behave toward you; twenty times I adopted and abandoned the same resolutions; but at last I found you unworthy of seeing my sorrow, and I resolved not to let it show. I wanted to wound your pride by making you see that my passion was weakening of its own accord. I believed that I would thereby diminish the value of the sacrifice you were making of it; I did not want you to have the pleasure of showing how much I loved you in order to appear more lovable on that account. I resolved to write you cold and languid letters, so as to put into the mind of the woman to whom you gave them the thought that you were ceasing to be loved. I did not want her to have the pleasure of learning that I knew she was triumphing over me, nor to increase her triumph by my despair and my reproaches. I thought that I would not punish you enough by breaking with you, and that I would cause you only slight pain if I ceased to love you when you no longer loved me. I concluded that you had to love me in order to feel the pain of not being loved, which I was experiencing so cruelly. I believed that if anything could rekindle the feelings you had once had for me, it was to make you see that mine had changed; but to make you see it while pretending to conceal it from you, and as though I had not had the strength to confess it to you. I settled upon this resolution; but how difficult it was for me to make, and, when I saw you again, how impossible it seemed to carry out! A hundred times I was on the verge of bursting forth in reproaches and tears; the state to which my health had still reduced me helped me disguise my distress and affliction from you. I was then sustained by the pleasure of dissembling with you, as you dissembled with me; nevertheless, I did myself such great violence in order to tell you and write to you that I loved you that you saw sooner than I had intended to let you see that my feelings had changed. You were hurt by it; you complained of it. I tried to reassure you; but it was in so forced a manner that you were still more thoroughly convinced that I no longer loved you. At last, I did everything I had intended to do. The capriciousness of your heart made you return to me as you saw me withdrawing from you. I have enjoyed all the pleasure that vengeance can give; it has seemed to me that you loved me more than you had ever done, and I have made you see that I no longer loved you. I have had reason to believe that you had entirely abandoned the woman for whom you had left me. I have also had reasons to be convinced that you had never spoken to her about me; but your return and your discretion have not been able to make amends for your fickleness. Your heart has been divided between me and another woman; you have deceived me. That is enough to deprive me of the pleasure of being loved by you as I believed I deserved to be, and to leave me in the resolution I have made never to see you again, at which you are so surprised.

Madame de Clèves read this letter and reread it several times, without, however, knowing what she had read. She saw only that Monsieur de Nemours did not love her as she had thought, and that he loved other women whom he deceived as he deceived her. What a sight and what knowledge for a person of her disposition, who had a violent passion, who had just given signs of it to a man she judged unworthy of it, and to another man whom she treated badly for his sake! Never had affliction been so piercing and so acute: it seemed to her that what made this affliction so bitter was what had happened that day, and that, if Monsieur de Nemours had had no reason to believe that she loved him, she would not have cared that he had loved another woman. But she was deceiving herself; and the pain she found so unbearable was jealousy, with all the horrors that may accompany it. She saw from this letter that Monsieur de Nemours had long been engaged in a love affair. She found that the woman who had written the letter had intelligence and merit; she seemed to her worthy of being loved; she found in her more courage than she found in herself, and she envied the strength she had shown in concealing her feelings from Monsieur de Nemours. She saw from the end of the letter that this person believed herself loved; she thought that the discretion this prince had shown her, and by which she had been so deeply moved, was perhaps only the effect of the passion he had for that other person, whom he feared to displease. In short, she thought of everything that could increase her affliction and her despair. How she turned her thoughts back upon herself! What reflections she made upon the advice her mother had given her! How she repented of not having persisted in withdrawing from society, despite Monsieur de Clèves, or of not having followed the thought she had had of confessing to him the inclination she had for Monsieur de Nemours! She found that she would have done better to reveal it to a husband whose goodness she knew, and who would have had an interest in concealing it, than to let it be seen by a man who was unworthy of it, who deceived her, who perhaps sacrificed her, and who desired to be loved by her only out of pride and vanity. In short, she found that all the misfortunes that could befall her, and all the extremes to which she might be driven, were less dreadful than having let Monsieur de Nemours see that she loved him and knowing that he loved another woman. All that consoled her was the thought that, after acquiring this knowledge, she at least had nothing more to fear from herself, and that she would be entirely cured of the inclination she had for this prince.”

“I have loved you too much to let you believe that the change you perceive in me is an effect of my fickleness; I wish to let you know that your unfaithfulness is the cause of it.
