Kevenhüller was no ordinary watchmaker; he wanted to become a great inventor and improver of the world.

After he had thus wandered through many lands, he also made his way to Värmland to study mill wheels and mining machinery. One beautiful summer morning, it happened that he was walking across the marketplace in Karlstad. But at that same beautiful hour of morning, the Lady of the Forest had seen fit to extend her walk all the way into the town. The tall lady was also crossing the marketplace, but from the opposite direction, and thus she met Kevenhüller.

When the major’s wife has come this far, she always looks up, gazes about her, sees the closed door, and knows where she is.

Then she wonders whether she is going mad, and sits down to think and rest. But after a while she is at it again, adding ells and fathoms into half-miles and miles, taking short rests in the Finnish huts, and sleeping neither night nor day until she has once more covered the twenty miles.

During all the time she has been held prisoner, she has hardly ever slept.

And the two women who have come to look after her watch her with anguish.

The young countess would always remember her afterward as she walked there then. She often sees her afterward in her dreams, and then awakens from the vision with her eyes wet with tears and a lament on her lips.

The old woman has deteriorated distressingly; her hair looks thin, and loose tangles protrude from the narrow braid. Her face is slack and sunken, her clothes disordered and torn. But despite all this she retains so much of the exalted ruler who commanded everyone that she inspires not only pity but also reverence.

But what the countess clearly remembered was the eyes, sunken, turned inward, not yet deprived of all the light of reason, but almost ready to go out, with a spark of wildness lurking in their depths, so that one could not help dreading and fearing that in the next moment the old woman would be upon one, her teeth ready to bite, her fingers to claw.

They have now stood there for quite some time when the major’s wife suddenly stops before the young woman and looks at her sternly. The countess takes a step backward and grasps Mrs. Scharling’s arm.

The features of the major’s wife suddenly take on life and expression; her eyes look out upon the world with full understanding.

“Oh no, oh no,” she says with a little smile, “it is not quite so bad as that, my dear young lady.”

She now invites them to sit down and also seats herself. She assumes an air of old-fashioned stateliness, familiar from the great feasts at Ekeby and the royal balls at the governor’s residence in Karlstad. They forget the rags and the prison and see only the proudest and richest lady in Värmland.

“My dear countess!” she says. “What could induce you to leave the dance to seek out a lonely old woman like me? You must be very kind.”

Countess Elisabet cannot answer. Her voice is choked with emotion. Mrs. Scharling answers in her stead that she has been unable to dance because she has been thinking of the major’s wife.

“Dear Mrs. Scharling,” the major’s wife replies, “have things now come to such a pass with me that I disturb the young in their joy? You must not weep over me, my dear young countess,” she continued. “I am a wicked old woman who deserves my fate. You do not consider it right to strike one’s mother, do you?”

“No, but—”

The major’s wife interrupts her and brushes the curly, fair hair back from her forehead.

“Child, child,” she says, “how could you go and marry that foolish Henrik Dohna?”

“But I love him.”

“I see how it is, I see how it is,” says the major’s wife. “A good child and nothing more, weeping with the sorrowful and laughing with the merry. And compelled to say ‘yes’ to the first man who says, ‘I love you.’ Yes, certainly, yes. Go in and dance now, my dear young countess! Dance and be glad! There is nothing evil in you.”

“But I wanted to do something for the major’s wife.”

“Child,” says the major’s wife solemnly, “there once lived an old woman at Ekeby who held the winds of heaven captive. Now she is imprisoned, and the winds are free. Is it strange that a storm is sweeping through the land?

I, who am old, have seen it before, countess. I know it. I know that the thundering storm of God is coming upon us. Now it rushes over the great realms, now over the small, forgotten communities. God’s storm forgets no one. It comes upon great and small alike. It is glorious to see God’s storm coming.

Storm of God, you blessed tempest of the Lord, blow over the earth! Voices in the air, voices in the waters, resound and strike terror! Make God’s storm thunder! Make God’s storm terrifying! May the gusts sweep out across the land, hurl themselves against tottering walls, break the locks that have rusted and the houses that lean toward their fall!

Anguish shall spread across the land. The little birds’ nests shall fall from their hold upon the branch. The hawk’s nest at the top of the pine shall be shaken to the ground with a great crash, and even into the owl’s nest in the mountain cleft the wind shall hiss with its dragon tongue.

We thought that all was well here among us, but it was not so. God’s storm is surely needed. I understand that, and I do not complain. I only wish that I might go to my mother.”

She suddenly collapses.

“Go now, young woman!” she says. “I have no more time. I must go. Go now, and beware of those who ride upon the storm clouds!”

With that she resumes her pacing. Her features go slack, her gaze turns inward. The countess and Mrs. Scharling must leave her.

As soon as they are back among the dancers, the young countess goes straight up to Gösta Berling.

“I am to give Mr. Berling the major’s wife’s greetings,” she says. “She expects Mr. Berling to get her out of prison.”

“Then she will have to wait, countess.”

“Oh, help her, Mr. Berling!”

Gösta stares darkly before him. “No,” he says, “why should I help her? What gratitude do I owe her? Everything she has done for me has been to my ruin.”

“But, Mr. Berling—”

“If she had not existed,” he says vehemently, “I would now be sleeping up there beneath the eternal forests. Am I obliged to risk my life for her because she made me a cavalier at Ekeby? Does the countess think that much renown comes with that office?”

The young countess turns away from him without answering. She is angry.

She goes to her place, thinking bitter thoughts about the cavaliers. They have come here with French horns and fiddles and intend to let the bows scrape across the strings until the horsehair has worn away, without thinking that the merry notes carry into the prisoner’s wretched room. They come here to dance until the soles of their shoes turn to dust, and do not think that their old benefactress may see their shadows swing past inside the misted panes. Ah, how gray and ugly the world had become! Ah, what a shadow distress and hardness cast over the young countess’s soul!

I am standing on the platform of the railway carriage. I have stood there all night,
wrapped in my cloak. I have watched the evening shadows creep up from the valleys
along the mountains, until everything was shrouded in darkness. Now day is drawing
near, a pale glow brightens on the horizon; with ever quicker piston strokes, in
time with my heart, the train rushes onward toward the foreign city.

What strange unrest has kept me awake the whole night? What anxious questions are
these for which my heart seeks answers, while I stare broodingly out into the
darkness?

I cannot, after all, doubt Maria’s love; I no longer doubt my own.

Yet I journey trembling to our meeting. For my anxious question is this: Might we
not feel like strangers to one another?

The Maria whom I am travelling out to find is not the Maria of before. She is
not the recklessly enamoured child who in the old days laid herself in my arms,
not the cheerful and ever-ready mistress, my conquest and my prize—she is surely
both the one and the other, but at the same time something greater and higher,
that which perhaps was always the background of her nature, that which I thought
I sensed the last times we were together, that which, in the final reckoning,
became the Madonna image of my solitary worship.

And she—will she recognise me? I scarcely do so myself. I won her in play; I took
her sword in hand. Every day the dance we danced was so easy. And now I come to
her with unarmed earnestness. Before, it was a matter of a dance; now, it is a
matter of life. Before, in rich high spirits, I contented myself with little; now,
in poor humility, I ask for Everything.

... We speed onward toward the dawning morning. Suddenly it is black night once
more: amid thundering noise the train hurtles through a tunnel. The darkness
presses against my chest, there is a rushing in my ears, and, dizzy, I grasp the
platform railing. It seems to me that this tunnel will never end; I grope my way
forward to reach the lighted carriage—when ... what a revelation! At the purple
rim of the sky the disc of the sun rises, spreading its golden halo far and wide,
pouring trembling, warm light over moistly gleaming grassy valleys and slopes of
grain.

Beautiful, fair Day, with joyful gratitude I kneel before You, You who delivered
me from my agonising Night and led me, with faith reborn, to Maria.




LXI.


The golden sun of reunion over mountains, the glittering tears of reunion in
silent valleys.

In wondering rapture we stand facing one another, unable to find words, unable
to ask, unable to answer, able only to sink into one another’s arms and, rejoicing,
weeping, in shared bliss praise the rising Day.

Was it truly no dream? Was it truly You and me? We look at one another; we shake
our heads in disbelief. And yet only now, it seems to us, do we truly know one
another. For this is the sublime miracle of our reunion: we meet as so often
before we met in the happy dream of our scarcely confessed longing. Now the dream
is living and breathing.

And You, lovely, living, breathing girl, with the quiet happiness of transfiguration
in your roguish eyes, with a woman’s mature thoughtfulness upon your child’s
brow, You put your arms around my neck and You say: “So at last it has happened,
at the eleventh hour, but not too late—that for which I never ceased to hope. For
it is true, is it not? Not something You will regret tomorrow, not something You
are imagining now because You have longed a little for your mistress?”

I answer: “As surely as I have always preferred to tell You too little rather than
too much, so surely do I love You. I love You in joy and in distress, on weekdays
and feast days. You are the one with whom I wish to die, but first I wish to live
with You for a very, very long time. Indeed, I have longed for my lovely mistress’s
caresses. But most of all I have longed for all the rest that is also You: your
faithful heart, your pure thought, your gentle speech, your bright smile, which
is my sun in doubt, your good handclasp, which is my strength upon the road.”

But when I tell Maria this, she weeps because she understands that I am speaking
the truth, and because she is happy.




LXII.


Someone tugs me from behind by the sleeve. I am sitting with Maria on my lap and
say angrily: “Who dares disturb us?”

But a voice whispers: “I come as a deputation from the readers. Your book, which
was dreadful at the beginning, has gradually taken a better course. There are
even some among us who have had tears in their eyes. But now we are so afraid that
in the end it will nevertheless go astray. For God’s sake: surely you intend to
marry Maria? Remember, you have taken her from her suitor, who had the most
respectable intentions?”

My stern lady censor, do not be afraid. Maria, tell the kind lady that she may
leave us alone without any scruples.




LXIII.


The Bishop stands before the altar in his golden vestment, shining in rivalry
with the candelabra. The venerable marble statues in the niches have been washed,
and at the organ sits the venerable old Master, with a silk skullcap on his head
and the Grand Cross upon his breast.

The pews are filled with the country’s most enamoured young women and men. They
have flowers in their hands; they sit in pairs, the young women with white roses,
the young men with red. They all stare down toward the entrance door, where twelve
kindly old priests in black velvet robes stand arrayed, six on either side.

Then the Master begins to play. The tones of the organ surge beneath the lofty
vaults. The young women and men rise.

The heavy oak door is flung open; a dazzling light fills the opening: there stands
Maria in her white bridal gown, surrounded by the billowing folds of the long
veil. A blushing maiden with downcast eyes. Heavenly majesty, blessed happiness
radiate from her.

A murmur of admiration passes through the church; the Bishop at the altar turns,
puts on his spectacles, and when he sees how lovely Maria is, he hastens to meet
her, bows to her, and leads her by the hand to the altar.

The young women and men scatter their roses, the red and the white, over her as
she passes; some of the roses remain caught in the veil, and Maria smiles when
she sees the flower-strewn gown.

But the old Master has stopped playing; he leans out over the balustrade of the
organ loft to see Maria, and curious angels’ faces peer through the apertures in
the vaults.

... Then, with the words of the Old and New Testaments, Maria is given into my
hand; I lead her out, followed by the Bishop and the twelve priests, as well as
all the enamoured young couples, while the old Master plays with one hand and
waves to us with the other.

Outside, the carriage with the white horses is waiting, and we climb in to drive
home to me, home to us. And then the bells begin to peal.

CYRANO:
  Why!
  I had taken it upon myself: I was interpreting thy passion!
  Sometimes I wrote without telling thee: I am writing!

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah?

CYRANO:
  It is quite simple!

CHRISTIAN:
  But how didst thou manage,
  Since we have been blockaded, to?...

CYRANO:
  Oh!...before dawn
  I could cross over...

CHRISTIAN (folding his arms):
  Ah! it is quite simple again?
  And how many times a week did I write?...Twice?—Three times?—
  Four?—

CYRANO:
  More.

CHRISTIAN:
  Every day?

CYRANO:
  Yes, every day.—Twice.

CHRISTIAN (violently):
  And that intoxicated thee, and the intoxication was such
  That thou didst brave death...

CYRANO (seeing Roxane returning):
  Be silent! Not before her!
  (He quickly goes back into his tent.)



Scene 4.VIII.

Roxane, Christian; in the background, cadets coming and going. Carbon and De
Guiche give orders.


ROXANE (running to Christian):
  And now, Christian!...

CHRISTIAN (taking her hands):
  And now, tell me
  Why, by these dreadful roads, why
  Through all these ranks of soldiers and troopers,
  Thou hast joined me here?

ROXANE:
  It is because of the letters!

CHRISTIAN:
  What dost thou say?

ROXANE:
  So much the worse for you if I run these dangers!
  It is your letters that have intoxicated me! Ah! consider
  How many you have written me for the past month,
  And always more beautiful!

CHRISTIAN:
  What! For a few little
  Love letters...

ROXANE:
  Be silent! Thou canst not know!
  My God, I adored thee, it is true, from the night when,
  In a voice I had not known was thine, beneath my window,
  Thy soul began to make itself known...
  Well! Thy letters, thou seest, for the past month,
  Are as though all the while I heard it, thy voice
  From that night, so tender, and which enfolds you!
  So much the worse for thee, I hasten here. The wise Penelope
  Would not have remained beneath her roof embroidering,
  Had Lord Ulysses written as thou dost,
  But, to join him, as mad as Helen,
  She too would have sent her balls of wool packing!...

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

ROXANE:
  I read, I read again, I swooned,
  I was thine. Each of those little sheets
  Was like a petal blown from thy soul.
  In every word of those letters of flame one feels
  Love, powerful, sincere...

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah! Sincere and powerful?
  It can be felt, Roxane?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! How it can be felt!

CHRISTIAN:
  And you come?...

ROXANE:
  I come (O my Christian, my master!
  You would raise me if I wished to kneel
  At your feet, so it is my soul I lay there,
  And you will never be able to raise it again!)
  I come to ask thy forgiveness (and it is indeed the hour
  To ask forgiveness, since we may die!)
  For having at first, in my frivolity,
  Insulted thee by loving thee for thy beauty alone!

CHRISTIAN (in terror):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  And later, my friend, less frivolous,
  —A bird that hops before it fully takes flight,—
  Thy beauty holding me, thy soul drawing me onward,
  I loved thee for the two together!...

CHRISTIAN:
  And now?

ROXANE:
  Well! At last thy true self triumphs over thyself,
  And it is now for thy soul alone that I love thee!

CHRISTIAN (drawing back):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  Then be happy. For to be loved
  Only for that in which one is costumed for a moment
  Must torture an eager and noble heart;
  But thy dear mind effaces thy face,
  And the beauty by which at first thou didst please me,
  Now I see more clearly...and I no longer see it!

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh!...

ROXANE:
  Dost thou still doubt such a victory?...

CHRISTIAN (painfully):
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  I understand, thou canst not believe
  In this love?...

CHRISTIAN:
  I do not want this love!
  I want to be loved more simply for...

ROXANE:
  For
  What women have loved in you until this hour?
  Then let yourself be loved in a better way!

CHRISTIAN:
  No! It was better before!

ROXANE:
  Ah! Thou understandest nothing about it!
  It is now that I love more, that I love rightly!
  It is that which makes thee thyself, dost thou hear, that I adore!
  And less handsome...

CHRISTIAN:
  Be silent!

ROXANE:
  I would love thee still!
  If all thy beauty suddenly flew away...

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh! Do not say that!

ROXANE:
  Yes, I say it!

CHRISTIAN:
  What? Ugly?

ROXANE:
  Ugly! I swear it!

CHRISTIAN:
  God!

ROXANE:
  And is thy joy profound?

CHRISTIAN (in a stifled voice):
  Yes...

ROXANE:
  What is the matter with thee?

CHRISTIAN (gently pushing her away):
  Nothing. Two words to say: one second...

ROXANE:
  But?...

CHRISTIAN (showing her a group of cadets in the background):
  My love took thee away from those poor fellows:
  Go and smile upon them a little, since they are going to die...go!

ROXANE (moved):
  Dear Christian!...
  (She goes upstage toward the Gascons, who respectfully crowd around
  her.)



Scene 4.IX.

Christian, Cyrano; in the background, Roxane talking with Carbon and a few cadets.


CHRISTIAN (calling toward Cyrano's tent):
  Cyrano?

CYRANO (reappearing, armed for battle):
  What is it? Thou art pale!

CHRISTIAN:
  She no longer loves me!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is thee she loves!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  She loves nothing but my soul now!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes!
  So it is indeed thee she loves—and thou lovest her too!

CYRANO:
  I?

CHRISTIAN:
  I know it.

CYRANO:
  It is true.

CHRISTIAN:
  Like a madman.

CYRANO:
  More.

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Look at my face!

CHRISTIAN:
  She would love me ugly!

CYRANO:
  She told thee so!

CHRISTIAN:
  There!

CYRANO:
  Ah! I am very glad she told thee that!
  But come, come, do not believe such a mad thing!
  —My God, I am glad she thought
  To say it—but come, do not take her at her word;
  Come, do not become ugly: she would resent me too much for it!

CHRISTIAN:
  That is what I want to see!

CYRANO:
  No, no!

CHRISTIAN:
  Let her choose!
  Thou art going to tell her everything!

CHRISTIAN:
  But how did you manage it,
  Since we have been blockaded, to—?...

CYRANO:
  Oh!... before dawn

CHRISTIAN (folding his arms):

CYRANO:
  More.

CHRISTIAN:
  Every day?

CYRANO:
  Yes, every day.—Twice.

CYRANO (seeing Roxane returning):

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

ROXANE:
  I read, I reread, I swooned,
  I was yours. Each of those little sheets
  Was like a petal flown from your soul.
  In every word of those letters of flame one feels
  Love, powerful, sincere...

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah! Sincere and powerful?
  One can feel that, Roxane?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! How clearly one can feel it!

CHRISTIAN:
  And you have come?...

ROXANE:
  I have come (O my Christian, my master!
  You would raise me up if I wished to kneel
  At your feet, and so it is my soul I lay there,
  And you will never be able to raise it again!)
  I have come to ask your forgiveness (and it is indeed the hour
  To ask forgiveness, since we may die!)
  For having at first, in my frivolity,
  Insulted you by loving you for your beauty alone!

CHRISTIAN (in horror):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  And later, my friend, less frivolous,
  —A bird that hops before it fully takes flight,—
  Your beauty holding me back, your soul drawing me onward,
  I loved you for the two together!...

CHRISTIAN:
  And now?

ROXANE:
  Well! You yourself at last triumph over yourself,
  And it is now for your soul alone that I love you!

CHRISTIAN (stepping back):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  Then be happy. For to be loved
  Only for what one is costumed in for a moment
  Must torture an eager and noble heart;
  But your dear mind effaces your face,
  And the beauty by which you first pleased me,
  Now I see more clearly... and I no longer see it!

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh!...

ROXANE:
  Do you still doubt such a victory?...

CHRISTIAN (painfully):
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  I understand, you cannot believe
  In this love?...

CHRISTIAN:
  I do not want this love!
  I want to be loved more simply for...

ROXANE:
  For
  What women have loved in you until now?
  Then let yourself be loved in a better way!

CHRISTIAN:
  No! It was better before!

ROXANE:
  Ah! You understand nothing about it!
  It is now that I love better, that I love well!
  It is what makes you you, do you hear, that I adore!
  And less dazzling...

CHRISTIAN:
  Be quiet!

ROXANE:
  I would still love you!
  If all your beauty suddenly flew away...

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh! Do not say that!

ROXANE:
  Yes, I say it!

CHRISTIAN:
  What? Ugly?

ROXANE:
  Ugly! I swear it!

CHRISTIAN:
  God!

ROXANE:
  And is your joy profound?

CHRISTIAN (in a stifled voice):
  Yes...

ROXANE:
  What is the matter?

CHRISTIAN (gently pushing her away):
  Nothing. Two words to say: one second...

ROXANE:
  But?...

CHRISTIAN (pointing out a group of cadets to her in the background):
  My love took you away from those poor fellows:
  Go and smile at them a little, since they are going to die... go!

ROXANE (moved):
  Dear Christian!...
  (She goes upstage toward the Gascons, who respectfully crowd around
  her.)



Scene 4.IX.

Christian, Cyrano; in the background, Roxane conversing with Carbon and several cadets.


CHRISTIAN (calling toward Cyrano's tent):
  Cyrano?

CYRANO (reappearing, armed for battle):
  What is it? You are pale!

CHRISTIAN:
  She no longer loves me!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is you she loves!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  She now loves only my soul!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes!
  So it is indeed you she loves—and you love her too!

CYRANO:
  I?

CHRISTIAN:
  I know it.

CYRANO:
  It is true.

CHRISTIAN:
  Like a madman.

CYRANO:
  More than that.

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Look at my face!

CHRISTIAN:
  She would love me ugly!

CYRANO:
  She told you that!

CHRISTIAN:
  There!

CYRANO:
  Ah! I am very glad she told you that!
  But come, come, do not believe such a mad thing!
  —My God, I am glad the thought occurred to her
  To say it—but come, do not take her at her word,
  Come, do not become ugly: she would hold it too much against me!

CHRISTIAN:
  That is what I want to see!

CYRANO:
  No, no!

CHRISTIAN:
  Let her choose!
  You are going to tell her everything!

CYRANO:
  No, no! Not that torment.

CHRISTIAN:
  Would I destroy your happiness because I am handsome?
  It is too unjust!

CYRANO:
  And would I send yours to the grave
  Because, thanks to the chance that governs birth,
  I have the gift of expressing... what you perhaps feel?

CYRANO:
  It is my wound
  From Arras...which...sometimes...you know...

ROXANE:
  Poor friend!

CYRANO:
  But it is nothing. It will soon be over.
  (He smiles with effort):
  It is over.

ROXANE (standing near him):
  Each of us has a wound: I have mine.
  Still raw, it is there, that old wound,
  (She puts her hand on her breast):
  It is there, beneath the letter with its yellowing paper
  Where tears and blood can still be seen!
  (Twilight begins to fall.)

CYRANO:
  His letter!...Had you not said that one day, perhaps,
  You would let me read it?

ROXANE:
  Ah! you wish to?...His letter?

CYRANO:
  Yes...I wish to...Today...

ROXANE (giving him the pouch hanging from her neck):
  Here!

CYRANO (taking it):
  May I open it?

ROXANE:
  Open it...read!...
  (She returns to her embroidery frame, folds it up, puts away her wool.)

CYRANO (reading):
  Roxane, farewell, I am going to die!...

ROXANE (stopping, surprised):
  Aloud?

CYRANO (reading):
  It will be this evening, I think, my beloved!
  My soul is still heavy with unexpressed love,
  And I am dying! Never again, never will my intoxicated eyes,
  My gaze, for which they were...

ROXANE:
  How you read it,
  His letter!

CYRANO (continuing):
  ...for which they were trembling festivities,
  Kiss in their flight the gestures that you make;
  I see again one little gesture familiar to you,
  With which you touch your brow, and I would like to cry out...

ROXANE (troubled):
  How you read it—this letter!
  (Night falls imperceptibly.)

CYRANO:
  And I cry:
  Farewell!...

ROXANE:
  You read it...

CYRANO:
  My dear one, my darling,
  My treasure...

ROXANE (dreamily):
  In a voice...

CYRANO:
  My love!...

ROXANE:
  In a voice...
  (She starts):
  But...one that I am not hearing for the first time!
  (She approaches very softly, without his noticing, passes behind the armchair, leans over noiselessly, and looks at the letter.—The darkness deepens.)

CYRANO:
  My heart never left you for a single second,
  And I am and shall be, even in the other world,
  The one who loved you beyond measure, the one...

ROXANE (placing her hand on his shoulder):
  How can you read now? It is dark.
  (He starts, turns around, sees her there very close to him, makes a gesture of fright, and lowers his head. A long silence. Then, in the now complete darkness, she says slowly, clasping her hands):
  And for fourteen years, he played this role
  Of being the old friend who comes to be amusing!

CYRANO:
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  It was you!

CYRANO:
  No, no, Roxane, no!

ROXANE:
  I should have guessed when he said my name!

CYRANO:
  No, it was not I!

ROXANE:
  It was you!

CYRANO:
  I swear to you...

ROXANE:
  I see the whole generous deception:
  The letters—it was you...

CYRANO:
  No!

ROXANE:
  The tender, mad words,
  It was you...

CYRANO:
  No!

ROXANE:
  The voice in the night—it was you!

CYRANO:
  I swear to you it was not!

ROXANE:
  The soul—it was yours!

CYRANO:
  I did not love you.

ROXANE:
  You loved me!

CYRANO (struggling):
  It was the other one!

ROXANE:
  You loved me!

CYRANO (in a weakening voice):
  No!

ROXANE:
  Already you say it more softly!

CYRANO:
  No, no, my dear love, I did not love you!

ROXANE:
  Ah! how many things have died...how many have been born!
  —Why did you remain silent for fourteen years,
  Since on this letter, in which he had no part,
  These tears were yours?

CYRANO (holding out the letter to her):
  That blood was his.

ROXANE:
  Then why let this sublime silence
  Be broken today?

CYRANO:
  Why?...
  (Le Bret and Ragueneau run in.)



Scene 5.VI.

The same, Le Bret and Ragueneau.


LE BRET:
  What recklessness!
  Ah! I was quite sure of it! He is here!

CYRANO (smiling and straightening up):
  Well, by heaven!

LE BRET:
  He has killed himself, Madame, by getting up!

ROXANE:
  Great God!
  But just now, then...that weakness?...that?...

CYRANO:
  It is true! I had not finished my gazette:
  ...And on Saturday the twenty-sixth, one hour before dinner,
  Monsieur de Bergerac died, assassinated.
  (He bares his head; it can be seen that his head is wrapped in bandages.)

ROXANE:
  What is he saying?—Cyrano!—His head bandaged!...
  Ah, what have they done to you? Why?

CYRANO:
  “Struck by a hero
  With a sword thrust, to fall with its point in my heart!”...
  —Yes, that is what I used to say!...Fate is a mocker!...
  And now I am killed in an ambush,
  From behind, by a lackey, with a blow from a log!
  It is very fitting. I shall have failed in everything, even my death.

RAGUENEAU:
  Ah, Monsieur!...

CYRANO:
  Ragueneau, do not weep so loudly!...
  (He holds out his hand to him):
  What has become of you now, my fellow artist?

RAGUENEAU (through his tears):
  I am a snuffer of...of...candles, in Molière’s company.

CYRANO:
  Molière!

RAGUENEAU:
  But I mean to leave him tomorrow:
  Yes, I am outraged!...Yesterday they were performing Scapin,
  And I saw that he had taken a scene from you!

LE BRET:
  An entire scene!

RAGUENEAU:
  Yes, Monsieur, the famous: “What the devil was he doing there?...”

LE BRET (furiously):
  Molière took it from you!

CYRANO:
  Hush! hush! He did well!...
  (To Ragueneau):
  The scene does make a great impression, does it not?

RAGUENEAU (sobbing):
  Ah! Monsieur, they laughed! they laughed!

CYRANO:
  Yes, my life
  Was to be the one who prompts—and whom they forget!
  (To Roxane):
  Do you remember the evening when Christian spoke to you
  Beneath the balcony? Well! my whole life is there:
  While I remained below, in the black shadow,
  Others climbed up to gather the kiss of glory!
  It is just, and I approve upon the threshold of my grave:
  Molière has genius, and Christian was handsome!
  (At that moment, the chapel bell having rung, the nuns can be seen passing at the rear, along the path, on their way to the service):
  Let them go and pray, since their bell is ringing!

ROXANE (rising to call out):
  Sister! Sister!

CYRANO (holding her back):
  No! no! do not go to fetch anyone:
  By the time you returned, I would no longer be here.
  (The nuns have entered the chapel; the organ can be heard):
  I was lacking a little harmony...there it is.

CYRANO (growing more and more overcome with emotion):
  Let us savor for a while...
  This opportunity that offers itself...to be able
  To speak softly to each other, without seeing each other.

ROXANE:
  Without seeing each other?

CYRANO:
  Why yes, it is delightful. We can barely make each other out.
  You see the blackness of a long trailing cloak,
  I glimpse the whiteness of a summer dress:
  I am nothing but a shadow, and you nothing but light!
  You cannot know what these moments are to me!
  If ever I was eloquent...

ROXANE:
  You were!

CYRANO:
  Until now, my speech has never come
  From my true heart...

ROXANE:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Because...until now
  I spoke through...

ROXANE:
  What?

CYRANO:
  ...the dizziness in which anyone beneath your gaze
  Trembles!...But tonight, it seems to me...
  That I am going to speak to you for the first time!

ROXANE:
  It is true that you have a wholly different voice.

CYRANO (drawing nearer feverishly):
  Yes, wholly different, for in the night that shields me
  I dare at last to be myself, and I dare...
  (He stops and, distracted):
  Where was I?
  I do not know...all this—forgive my agitation—
  Is so delightful...it is so new to me!

ROXANE:
  So new?

CYRANO (overwhelmed, still trying to recover his words):
  So new...why yes...to be sincere:
  The fear of being mocked always grips my heart...

ROXANE:
  Mocked for what?

CYRANO:
  Why, for...for a surge of feeling!...Yes, my heart
  Always clothes itself in my wit, out of modesty:
  I set out to pluck down the star, and I stop,
  For fear of ridicule, to pick a little flower!

ROXANE:
  The little flower has its merits.

CYRANO:
  Tonight, let us disdain it!

ROXANE:
  You had never spoken to me like this!

CYRANO:
  Ah! What if, far from quivers, torches, and arrows,
  We escaped for a while toward things...more fresh!
  Instead of drinking, drop by drop, from a dainty
  Thimble of fine gold, the insipid water of the Lignon,
  What if we tried to see how the soul slakes its thirst
  By drinking deeply straight from the great river!

ROXANE:
  But wit?...

CYRANO:
  I used it at first to make you stay,
  But now it would be an insult
  To this night, these fragrances, this hour, to Nature,
  To speak like a love letter by Voiture!
  Let the sky, with a single glance from its stars,
  Disarm us of all that is artificial in us:
  I fear so much that amid our exquisite alchemy
  The truth of feeling may evaporate,
  That the soul may be emptied by these vain pastimes,
  And that the finest of the fine may be the final end!

ROXANE:
  But wit?...

CYRANO:
  I hate it in love! It is a crime,
  When one loves, to prolong this fencing match too much!
  Besides, the moment inevitably comes
  —And I pity those for whom that moment never comes!—
  When we feel that within us a noble love exists
  Which every pretty word we utter makes sorrowful!

ROXANE:
  Well then! If that moment has come for us both,
  What words will you say to me?

CYRANO:
  All those, all those, all those
  That come to me; I shall throw them to you in a mass,
  Without arranging them in a bouquet: I love you, I am suffocating,
  I love thee, I am mad, I can bear no more, it is too much;
  Thy name is in my heart as in a little bell,
  And since all the time, Roxane, I shiver,
  All the time the bell trembles, and the name rings out!
  I remember everything about thee; I have loved it all:
  I know that last year, one day, on the twelfth of May,
  To go out in the morning thou changed thy hairstyle!
  I have so taken thy hair for brightness
  That, as when one has stared too long at the sun
  And afterward sees a crimson circle over everything,
  Upon everything, when I have left the fires with which thou floodest me,
  My dazzled gaze lays golden patches!

ROXANE (in a troubled voice):
  Yes, that is indeed love...

CYRANO:
  Certainly, this feeling
  That overwhelms me, terrible and jealous, truly is
  Love; it has all love’s sorrowful fury!
  Love—and yet it is not selfish!
  Ah! For thy happiness I would give my own,
  Even if thou wert never to know anything of it,
  If only, sometimes, from afar, I might hear
  The happiness born of my sacrifice laugh a little!
  Every glance of thine awakens a new virtue,
  A new courage in me! Dost thou begin
  To understand now? Come, dost thou realize?
  Dost thou feel my soul, a little, rising through this darkness?...
  Oh! But truly, tonight, it is too beautiful, it is too sweet!
  I tell you all this; you listen to me—to me, you!
  It is too much! Even in my least modest hope,
  I never hoped for so much! Nothing remains for me
  But to die now! It is because of the words
  I speak that she trembles among the blue branches!
  For you tremble like a leaf among the leaves!
  For thou tremblest! For I have felt, whether thou willest it
  Or not, the adored trembling of thy hand
  Descend all along the jasmine branches!
  (He wildly kisses the end of a hanging branch.)

ROXANE:
  Yes, I tremble, and I weep, and I love thee, and am thine!
  And thou hast intoxicated me!

CYRANO:
  Then let death come!
  This intoxication—it is I, I, who knew how to cause it!
  I ask for only one thing more...

CHRISTIAN (beneath the balcony):
  A kiss!

ROXANE (drawing back):
  What?

CYRANO:
  Oh!

ROXANE:
  You ask for?...

CYRANO:
  Yes...I...
  (Softly to Christian):
  Thou art going too fast.

CHRISTIAN:
  Since she is so overcome, I must take advantage of it!

CYRANO (to Roxane):
  Yes, I...I did ask, it is true...but good heavens!
  I understand that I was far too bold.

ROXANE (a little disappointed):
  You do not insist any more than that?

CYRANO:
  Yes! I insist...
  Without insisting!...Yes, yes! Your modesty is distressed!
  Well then! But this kiss...do not grant it to me!

CHRISTIAN (to Cyrano, tugging at his cloak):
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Be quiet, Christian!

ROXANE (leaning out):
  What are you saying so softly?

CYRANO:
  Why, I am scolding myself for having gone too far;
  I was saying to myself: be quiet, Christian!...
  (The theorbos begin to play):
  One moment...
  Someone is coming!
  (Roxane closes the window. Cyrano listens to the theorbos, one of which is playing a frolicsome tune and the other a mournful tune):
  Sad tune? Merry tune?...What, then, is their purpose?
  Is it a man? A woman?—Ah! It is a Capuchin!
  (A Capuchin enters, going from house to house with a lantern in his hand, looking at the doors.)

THE DUENNA (rapturously):
  Oh, look! The knocker is wrapped in cloths! . . .
  (To the knocker):
  They have gagged you so that your metal
  Would not disturb the fine speeches—you little brute!
  (She lifts it with infinite care and knocks softly.)

ROXANE (seeing that the door is being opened):
  Let us go in! . . .
  (From the threshold, to Cyrano):
  If Christian comes, as I presume he will,
  Have him wait for me!

CYRANO (quickly, as she is about to disappear):
  Ah! . . .
  (She turns around):
  On what, according to your custom,
  Do you intend to question him today?

ROXANE:
  On . . .

CYRANO (quickly):
  On?

ROXANE:
  But you will keep silent about it!

CYRANO:
  Like a wall.

ROXANE:
  On nothing! . . . I shall say to him: Go on! Give yourself free rein!
  Improvise. Speak of love. Be splendid!

CYRANO (smiling):
  Good.

ROXANE:
  Hush! . . .

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .

ROXANE:
  Not a word! . . .
  (She goes inside and closes the door again.)

CYRANO (bowing to her once the door is closed):
  With thanks to you.
  (The door opens again and Roxane puts her head out.)

ROXANE:
  He might prepare himself! . . .

CYRANO:
  Devil, no! . . .

BOTH TOGETHER:
  Hush! . . .
  (The door closes.)

CYRANO (calling):
  Christian!



Scene 3.IV.

Cyrano, Christian.


CYRANO:
  I know everything that is needed. Ready thy memory.
  Here is the opportunity to cover oneself with glory.
  Let us lose no time. Do not look so sullen.
  Quickly, let us go back to thy house; I am going to teach thee . . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No!

CYRANO:
  Eh?

CHRISTIAN:
  No! I am waiting for Roxane here.

CYRANO:
  What madness
  Has seized thee? Come quickly and learn . . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No, I tell thee!
  I am weary of borrowing my letters, my speeches,
  And of playing this part, and of always trembling! . . .
  It was fine at first! But I feel that she loves me!
  Thank thee. I am no longer afraid. I shall speak for myself.

CYRANO:
  Indeed!

CHRISTIAN:
  And who tells thee that I would not know how? . . .
  I am not so stupid, after all! Thou shalt see!
  But, my dear fellow, thy lessons have been profitable to me.
  I shall know how to speak alone! And, by all the devils,
  I shall always know how to take her in my arms! . . .
  (Catching sight of Roxane, who is coming back out of Clomire’s house):
  —It is she! Cyrano, no, do not leave me!

CYRANO (bowing to him):
  Speak on your own, sir.
  (He disappears behind the garden wall.)



Scene 3.V.

Christian, Roxane, some précieux and précieuses, and the duenna,
for a moment.


ROXANE (coming out of Clomire’s house with a company from whom she
  takes her leave, with curtsies and bows):
  Barthénoïde!—Alcandre!—Grémione! . . .

THE DUENNA (despairingly):
  We missed the discourse on Tenderness!
  (She goes into Roxane’s house.)

ROXANE (still bidding farewell):
  Urimédonte! . . . Farewell! . . .
  (They all bow to Roxane, bow again to one another, part, and
  move away along different streets. Roxane sees Christian):
  It is you! . . .
  (She goes to him):
  Evening is falling.
  Wait. They are far away. The air is mild. Not a passerby.
  Let us sit down. Speak. I am listening.

CHRISTIAN (sits near her on the bench. A silence):
  I love you.

ROXANE (closing her eyes):
  Yes, speak to me of love.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee.

ROXANE:
  That is the theme.
  Embroider, embroider.

CHRISTIAN:
  I . . . you . . .

ROXANE:
  Embroider!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee so much.

ROXANE:
  Of course! And then?

CHRISTIAN:
  And then . . . I would be so happy
  If you loved me!—Tell me, Roxane, that thou lovest me!

ROXANE (pouting):
  You offer me gruel when I was hoping for creams!
  Tell me a little how you love me? . . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Why . . . greatly.

ROXANE:
  Oh! . . . Unlabyrinth your feelings!

CHRISTIAN (having drawn closer and devouring the fair nape of her neck with his eyes):
  Thy neck!
  I would like to kiss it! . . .

ROXANE:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee!

ROXANE (trying to rise):
  Again!

CHRISTIAN (quickly, holding her back):
  No! I do not love thee!

ROXANE (sitting down again):
  That is fortunate!

CHRISTIAN:
  I adore thee!

ROXANE (rising and moving away):
  Oh!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes . . . I am becoming stupid!

ROXANE (dryly):
  And that displeases me!
  As it would displease me if you became ugly.

CHRISTIAN:
  But . . .

ROXANE:
  Go and gather up your fleeing eloquence!

CHRISTIAN:
  I . . .

ROXANE:
  You love me, I know. Farewell.
  (She goes toward the house.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Not yet!
  I shall tell you . . .

ROXANE (pushing open the door to go inside):
  That you adore me . . . yes, I know.
  No! No! Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  But I . . .
  (She shuts the door in his face.)

CYRANO (who returned a moment ago without being seen):
  It is a success.



Scene 3.VI.

Christian, Cyrano, the pages, for a moment.


CHRISTIAN:
  Help!

CYRANO:
  No, sir.

CHRISTIAN:
  I shall die if I do not regain
  Her favor this very instant . . .

CYRANO:
  And how the devil can I
  Teach you this very instant? . . .

CHRISTIAN (seizing his arm):
  Oh! There, look, see!
  (The balcony window has lit up.)

CYRANO (moved):
  Her window!

CHRISTIAN (shouting):
  I am going to die!

CYRANO:
  Lower your voice!

CHRISTIAN (very softly):
  Die! . . .

CYRANO:
  The night is dark . . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Well?

CYRANO:
  It can be repaired.
  You do not deserve it . . . Stand there, wretch!
  There, in front of the balcony! I shall place myself beneath it . . .
  And I shall prompt thee with thy words.

CHRISTIAN:
  But . . .

CYRANO:
  Be quiet!

THE PAGES (reappearing at the back, to Cyrano):
  Hey!

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .
  (He signals to them to speak softly.)

FIRST PAGE (in a low voice):
  We have just serenaded
  Montfleury! . . .

CYRANO (softly, quickly):
  Go and lie in ambush,
  One at that street corner, and the other at this one;
  And if some troublesome passerby comes this way,
  Play a tune!

SECOND PAGE:
  What tune, Monsieur Gassendist?

CYRANO:
  A merry one for a woman, and for a man, a sad one!
  (The pages disappear, one at each street corner.—To Christian):
  Call her!

CHRISTIAN:
  Roxane!

CYRANO (picking up pebbles, which he throws at the windowpanes):
  Wait! A few pebbles.



Scene VII.

Roxane, Christian, Cyrano, at first hidden beneath the balcony.


ROXANE (partly opening her window):
  Who is calling me?

CYRANO:
  No, no, my dear love, I did not love you!

ROXANE:
  Ah! How many things have died... how many have been born!
  —Why did you remain silent for fourteen years,
  Since, upon this letter in which he had no part,
  Those tears were yours?

CYRANO (holding out the letter to her):
  That blood was his.

ROXANE:
  Then why let that sublime silence
  Be broken today?

CYRANO:
  Why?...
  (Le Bret and Ragueneau run in.)



Scene 5.VI.

The same, Le Bret and Ragueneau.


LE BRET:
  What recklessness!
  Ah! I was certain of it! He is here!

CYRANO (smiling and straightening up):
  Well, by God!

LE BRET:
  He has killed himself, Madame, by getting up!

ROXANE:
  Great God!
  But just now, then... that weakness?... that?...

CYRANO:
  That is true! I had not finished my gazette:
  ...And on Saturday the twenty-sixth, one hour before dinner,
  Monsieur de Bergerac died by assassination.
  (He removes his hat; his head is seen wrapped in bandages.)

ROXANE:
  What is he saying?—Cyrano!—His head bandaged!...
  Ah, what have they done to you? Why?

CYRANO:
  “Struck by a hero with a sword,
  To fall with its point in my heart!”...
  —Yes, that is what I used to say!... Fate is mocking!...
  And now I am killed in an ambush,
  From behind, by a lackey, with a blow from a log!
  That is just fine. I shall have failed in everything, even my death.

RAGUENEAU:
  Ah, Monsieur!...

CYRANO:
  Ragueneau, do not cry so hard!...
  (He holds out his hand to him.)
  What has become of thee now, my fellow craftsman?

RAGUENEAU (through his tears):
  I am a snuffer of... of... candles, in Molière’s company.

CYRANO:
  Molière!

RAGUENEAU:
  But I mean to leave him tomorrow:
  Yes, I am indignant!... Yesterday they were performing Scapin,
  And I saw that he had taken a scene from you!

LE BRET:
  A whole one!

RAGUENEAU:
  Yes, Monsieur, the famous: “What the devil was he doing?...”

LE BRET (furiously):
  Molière took it from thee!

CYRANO:
  Hush! Hush! He did well!...
  (To Ragueneau.)
  The scene has a great effect, does it not?

RAGUENEAU (sobbing):
  Ah! Monsieur, they laughed! They laughed!

CYRANO:
  Yes, my life
  Has been to be the one who prompts—and whom they forget!
  (To Roxane.)
  Do you remember the evening when Christian spoke to you
  Beneath the balcony? Well! My entire life is there:
  While I remained below, in the black shadow,
  Others climbed up to gather glory’s kiss!
  It is just, and I approve upon the threshold of my tomb:
  Molière has genius, and Christian was handsome!
  (At that moment, the chapel bell having rung, the nuns can be seen
  passing in the background, along the path, on their way to the service.)
  Let them go and pray, since their bell is ringing!

ROXANE (rising to call out):
  Sister! Sister!

CYRANO (restraining her):
  No! No! Do not go and fetch anyone:
  Even if you came back, I would no longer be here.
  (The nuns have entered the chapel; the organ is heard.)
  I was lacking a little harmony... there it is.

ROXANE:
  I love you; live!

CYRANO:
  No! For it is in the fairy tale
  That when one says, “I love thee!” to the shame-filled prince,
  He feels his ugliness melt at those sunlit words...
  But thou wouldst notice that I remain the same.

ROXANE:
  I have caused your unhappiness! I! I!

CYRANO:
  You?... On the contrary!
  I did not know feminine tenderness. My mother
  Did not find me handsome. I had no sister.
  Later, I feared the mistress with the mocking eye.
  I owe it to you that I had, at least, a woman friend.
  Thanks to you, a gown passed through my life.

LE BRET (showing him the moonlight descending through the branches):
  Thy other friend is there, coming to see thee!

CYRANO (smiling at the moon):
  I see.

ROXANE:
  I loved only one being, and I lose him twice!

CYRANO:
  Le Bret, I am going to ascend into the opaline moon,
  With no need today to invent a machine...

LE BRET:
  What are you saying?

CYRANO:
  Why, yes, it is there, I tell you,
  That they are going to send me to make my paradise.
  More than one soul I love must be exiled there,
  And I shall find Socrates and Galileo again!

LE BRET (protesting):
  No, no! It is too stupid, after all, and too
  Unjust! Such a poet! A heart so great, so noble!
  To die like this!... To die!...

CYRANO:
  There is Le Bret growling!

LE BRET (bursting into tears):
  My dear friend...

CYRANO (raising himself, his eyes wandering):
  They are the Cadets of Gascony...
  —Elementary mass... Why, yes!... there is the rub...

LE BRET:
  His science... in his delirium!

CYRANO:
  Copernicus
  Said...

ROXANE:
  Oh!

CYRANO:
  But also, what the devil was he doing,
  What the devil was he doing in that galley?...
  Philosopher, physicist,
  Rhymer, swordsman, musician,
  And traveler through the air,
  Great master of the swift retort,
  Lover too—not for his own good!—
  Here lies Hercule-Savinien
  De Cyrano de Bergerac,
  Who was everything, and who was nothing,
  ...But I am leaving; forgive me, I cannot keep them waiting:
  You see, the moonbeam is coming to take me!
  (He falls back into a sitting position; Roxane’s tears recall him to reality.
  He looks at her and caresses her veils.)
  I do not want you to mourn any less for that charming,
  That good, that handsome Christian; but I want only
  That when the great cold has seized my vertebrae,
  You give a double meaning to those mourning veils,
  And that your mourning for him become, a little, mourning for me.

ROXANE:
  I swear it to you!...

CYRANO (shaken by a great shudder and rising abruptly):
  Not there! No! Not in that armchair!
  (They try to rush toward him.)
  —Do not support me!—No one!
  (He goes and braces himself against the tree.)
  Nothing but the tree!
  (Silence.)
  She is coming. I already feel myself booted in marble,
  —Gloved in lead!
  (He stiffens.)
  Oh! But... since she is on her way,
  I shall await her standing,
  (He draws his sword.)
  And with sword in hand!

LE BRET:
  Cyrano!

ROXANE (fainting):
  Cyrano!
  (All recoil in terror.)

CYRANO:
  I believe she is looking...
  That she dares to look at my nose, that Snub-Nosed One!
  (He raises his sword.)
  What do you say?... It is useless?... I know!
  But one does not fight in the hope of success!
  No! No! It is far finer when it is useless!
  —Who are all those?—Are there a thousand of you?
  Ah! I recognize you, all my old enemies!
  Falsehood?
  (He strikes the empty air with his sword.)
  Take that, take that!—Ha! Ha! Compromises!
  Prejudices, Cowardices!...
  (He strikes.)
  That I should make terms?
  Never, never!—Ah! There thou art, Folly!
  —I know full well that in the end you will strike me down;
  No matter: I fight! I fight! I fight!
  (He makes immense sweeping strokes and stops, gasping.)
  Yes, you tear everything from me, the laurel and the rose!
  Tear them away! In spite of you, there is something
  That I carry with me, and tonight, when I enter God’s house,
  My salute will sweep broadly across the blue threshold,
  Something that, without a crease, without a stain,
  I carry with me in spite of you,
  (He springs forward, sword held high.)
  And it is...
  (The sword slips from his hands; he staggers and falls into the arms of
  Le Bret and Ragueneau.)

ROXANE (seeing that the door is being opened):
  Let us go in! . . .
  (From the threshold, to Cyrano):
  If Christian comes, as I presume he will,
  Tell him to wait for me!

CYRANO (quickly, as she is about to disappear):
  Ah! . . .
  (She turns around):
  On what, as is your custom,
  Do you intend to question him today?

ROXANE:
  On. . .

CYRANO (quickly):
  On?

ROXANE:
  But you will keep silent about it!

CYRANO:
  Like a wall.

ROXANE:
  On nothing! . . .I shall tell him: Go on! Give yourself free rein!
  Improvise. Speak of love. Be splendid!

CYRANO (smiling):
  Good.

ROXANE:
  Hush! . . .

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .

ROXANE:
  Not a word! . . .
  (She goes inside and closes the door again.)

CYRANO (bowing to her once the door is closed):
  With my thanks.
  (The door opens again and Roxane puts her head out.)

ROXANE:
  He might prepare himself! . . .

CYRANO:
  Good heavens, no! . . .

BOTH (together):
  Hush! . . .
  (The door closes.)

CYRANO (calling):
  Christian!



Scene 3.IV.

Cyrano, Christian.


CYRANO:
  I know everything that is needed. Prepare thy memory.
  Here is the opportunity to cover ourselves with glory.
  Let us waste no time. Do not look so sullen.
  Quickly, let us go back to thy place; I am going to teach thee. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  No! I am waiting for Roxane here.

CYRANO:
  What madness
  Has seized thee? Come quickly and learn. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No, I tell thee!
  I am weary of borrowing my letters and my speeches,
  And of playing this part, and of always trembling! . . .
  It was fine at first! But I feel that she loves me!
  Thank thee. I am no longer afraid. I shall speak for myself.

CYRANO:
  Indeed!

CHRISTIAN:
  And who tells thee that I would not know how? . . .
  I am not so stupid, after all! Thou shalt see!
  But, my dear fellow, thy lessons have been useful to me.
  I shall know how to speak alone! And, by all the devils,
  I shall certainly always know how to take her in my arms! . . .
  (Catching sight of Roxane, who is coming out of Clomire's house):
  —There she is! Cyrano, no, do not leave me!

CYRANO (bowing to him):
  Speak by yourself, sir.
  (He disappears behind the garden wall.)



Scene 3.V.

Christian, Roxane, several male and female précieuses, and the duenna,
for a moment.


ROXANE (leaving Clomire's house with a company from whom she is taking
  her leave: curtsies and bows):
  Barthenoïde!—Alcandre!—Grémione! . . .

THE DUENNA (in despair):
  We missed the discourse on Tenderness!
  (She goes into Roxane's house.)

ROXANE (still taking leave):
  Urimédonte! . . .Farewell! . . .
  (They all bow to Roxane, bow again to one another, part, and
  go off along different streets. Roxane sees Christian):
  It is you! . . .
  (She goes to him):
  Evening is falling.
  Wait. They are far away. The air is mild. No passersby.
  Let us sit down. Speak. I am listening.

CHRISTIAN (sits down near her on the bench. A silence):
  I love you.

ROXANE (closing her eyes):
  Yes, speak to me of love.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee.

ROXANE:
  That is the theme.
  Embroider, embroider.

CHRISTIAN:
  I. . .you. . .

ROXANE:
  Embroider!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee so much.

ROXANE:
  No doubt! And then?

CHRISTIAN:
  And then. . .I would be so happy
  If you loved me!—Tell me, Roxane, that thou lovest me!

ROXANE (pouting):
  You offer me gruel when I had hoped for creams!
  Tell me how you love me. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Why. . .very much.

ROXANE:
  Oh! . . .Unlabyrinth your feelings!

CHRISTIAN (having moved closer and devouring the fair nape of her neck with his eyes):
  Thy neck!
  I would like to kiss it! . . .

ROXANE:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee!

ROXANE (trying to rise):
  Again!

CHRISTIAN (quickly, holding her back):
  No! I do not love thee!

ROXANE (sitting down again):
  That is fortunate!

CHRISTIAN:
  I adore thee!

ROXANE (rising and moving away):
  Oh!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes. . .I am becoming a fool!

ROXANE (dryly):
  And that displeases me!
  As it would displease me if you were to become ugly.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

ROXANE:
  Go and gather up your fleeing eloquence!

CHRISTIAN:
  I. . .

ROXANE:
  You love me, I know. Farewell.
  (She goes toward the house.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Not yet!
  I shall tell you. . .

ROXANE (pushing the door open to go inside):
  That you adore me. . .yes, I know.
  No! No! Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  But I. . .
  (She shuts the door in his face.)

CYRANO (who came back in some time ago without being seen):
  It is a success.



Scene 3.VI.

Christian, Cyrano, the pages, for a moment.


CHRISTIAN:
  Help!

CYRANO:
  No, sir.

CHRISTIAN:
  I shall die if I do not regain
  Her favor this very instant. . .

CYRANO:
  And how the devil can I
  Make you learn this very instant? . . .

CHRISTIAN (seizing his arm):
  Oh! There, look, see!
  (The balcony window has lit up.)

CYRANO (moved):
  Her window!

CHRISTIAN (shouting):
  I am going to die!

CYRANO:
  Lower your voice!

CHRISTIAN (very softly):
  Die! . . .

CYRANO:
  The night is dark. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Well?

CYRANO:
  It can be repaired.
  You do not deserve it. . .Stand there, wretch!
  There, in front of the balcony! I shall stand underneath. . .
  And prompt thee with thy words.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

CYRANO:
  Be silent!

THE PAGES (reappearing at the back, to Cyrano):
  Hey!

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .
  (He motions to them to speak quietly.)

FIRST PAGE (in a low voice):
  We have just serenaded
  Montfleury! . . .

CYRANO (quietly, quickly):
  Go and lie in ambush,
  One at that street corner and the other at this one;
  And if some troublesome passerby comes this way,
  Play a tune!

SECOND PAGE:
  What tune, Mr. Gassendist?

CYRANO:
  A merry one for a woman, and for a man, a sad one!
  (The pages disappear, one at each street corner.—To Christian):
  Call her!

CHRISTIAN:
  Roxane!

CYRANO (picking up pebbles, which he throws at the windowpanes):
  Wait! A few pebbles.



Scene VII.

Roxane, Christian, Cyrano, at first hidden beneath the balcony.


ROXANE (partly opening her window):
  Who is calling me?

CHRISTIAN:
  I am.

ROXANE:
  Who is “I”?

CHRISTIAN:
  Christian.

ROXANE (with disdain):
  It is you?

ROXANE:
  Ah! How many things that were dead . . . have been born!
  —Why did you remain silent for fourteen years,
  Since, on this letter in which he had no part,
  Those tears were yours?

CYRANO (holding out the letter to her):
  That blood was his.

ROXANE:
  Then why let this sublime silence
  Be broken today?

CYRANO:
  Why? . . .
  (Le Bret and Ragueneau run in.)



Scene 5.VI.

The same, Le Bret and Ragueneau.


LE BRET:
  What recklessness!
  Ah! I was sure of it! He is here!

CYRANO (smiling and straightening up):
  Well, by God!

LE BRET:
  He has killed himself, Madame, by getting up!

ROXANE:
  Great God!
  But just now, then . . . that weakness? . . . that? . . .

CYRANO:
  It is true! I had not finished my gazette:
  . . . And on Saturday the twenty-sixth, one hour before dinner,
  Monsieur de Bergerac was murdered.
  (He bares his head; it is seen to be wrapped in bandages.)

ROXANE:
  What is he saying?—Cyrano!—His head all wrapped up! . . .
  Ah, what have they done to you? Why?

CYRANO:
  “Struck by a hero with a sword-thrust,
  To fall with its point in my heart!” . . .
  —Yes, that is what I used to say! . . . Fate is a mocker! . . .
  And now I am killed in an ambush,
  From behind, by a lackey, with a blow from a log!
  Very well. I shall have failed at everything, even my death.

RAGUENEAU:
  Ah, Monsieur! . . .

CYRANO:
  Ragueneau, do not weep so loudly! . . .
  (He holds out his hand to him):
  What has become of you now, my fellow craftsman?

RAGUENEAU (through his tears):
  I am a snuffer of . . . of . . . candles, in Molière’s company.

CYRANO:
  Molière!

RAGUENEAU:
  But I mean to leave him tomorrow:
  Yes, I am indignant! . . . Yesterday they were performing Scapin,
  And I saw that he had taken a scene from you!

LE BRET:
  An entire scene!

RAGUENEAU:
  Yes, Monsieur, the famous: “What the devil was he doing? . . .”

LE BRET (furiously):
  Molière took it from you!

CYRANO:
  Hush! Hush! He did well! . . .
  (To Ragueneau):
  The scene has quite an effect, does it not?

RAGUENEAU (sobbing):
  Ah! Monsieur, they laughed! They laughed!

CYRANO:
  Yes, my life
  Was to be the one who prompts—and is forgotten!
  (To Roxane):
  Do you remember the evening when Christian spoke to you
  Beneath the balcony? Well! My whole life is there:
  While I remained below, in the black shadow,
  Others climbed up to pluck the kiss of glory!
  It is just, and I approve upon the threshold of my grave:
  Molière has genius, and Christian was handsome!
  (At that moment, the chapel bell having chimed, the nuns can be seen
  passing at the back, along the path, on their way to the service):
  Let them go and pray, since their bell is ringing!

ROXANE (rising to call out):
  Sister! Sister!

CYRANO (restraining her):
  No! No! Do not go and fetch anyone:
  By the time you returned, I would no longer be here.
  (The nuns have entered the chapel; the organ is heard):
  I was lacking a little harmony . . . there it is.

ROXANE:
  I love you; live!

CYRANO:
  No! For it is in the fairy tale
  That when one says, “I love thee!” to the shame-filled prince,
  He feels his ugliness melt at those words of sunlight . . .
  But you would realize that I remain the same.

ROXANE:
  I have caused your unhappiness! I! I!

CYRANO:
  You? . . . On the contrary!
  I knew nothing of feminine tenderness. My mother
  Did not find me handsome. I had no sister.
  Later, I dreaded the sweetheart with the mocking eye.
  To you I owe having had, at least, a woman friend.
  Thanks to you, a dress has passed through my life.

LE BRET (showing him the moonlight descending through the branches):
  Your other friend is there, coming to see you!

CYRANO (smiling at the moon):
  I see.

ROXANE:
  I loved only one being, and I lose him twice!

CYRANO:
  Le Bret, I am going to ascend into the opaline moon,
  Without any need to invent a machine today . . .

LE BRET:
  What are you saying?

CYRANO:
  Why yes, it is there, I tell you,
  That they are going to send me to make my paradise.
  More than one soul I love must be exiled there,
  And I shall find Socrates and Galileo again!

LE BRET (rebelling):
  No, no! It is too stupid in the end, and it is too
  Unjust! Such a poet! So great, so lofty a heart!
  To die like this! . . . To die! . . .

CYRANO:
  There is Le Bret growling!

LE BRET (bursting into tears):
  My dear friend . . .

CYRANO (raising himself, his eyes wandering):
  They are the Gascon Cadets . . .
  —The elementary mass . . . Why yes! . . . there is the rub . . .

LE BRET:
  His science . . . in his delirium!

CYRANO:
  Copernicus
  Said . . .

ROXANE:
  Oh!

CYRANO:
  But then, what the devil was he doing,
  What the devil was he doing in that galley? . . .
  Philosopher, physicist,
  Rhymer, swordsman, musician,
  And aerial voyager,
  Great master of the swift retort,
  A lover too—not for his own good!—
  Here lies Hercule-Savinien
  De Cyrano de Bergerac,
  Who was everything, and who was nothing,
  . . . But I must go; forgive me, I cannot keep them waiting:
  You see, the moonbeam is coming to take me!
  (He falls back into a sitting position; Roxane’s tears recall him to reality;
  he looks at her and caresses her veils):
  I do not want you to mourn any less for that charming,
  That good, that handsome Christian; but I want only
  That when the great cold has seized my vertebrae,
  You should give a double meaning to those funeral veils,
  And that your mourning for him should become a little mourning for me.

ROXANE:
  I swear it to you! . . .

CYRANO (is shaken by a great shudder and rises abruptly):
  Not there! No! Not in that armchair!
  (They try to rush toward him):
  —Do not support me!—No one!
  (He goes and braces himself against the tree):
  Nothing but the tree!
  (Silence):
  She is coming. I already feel myself shod in marble,
  —Gloved in lead!
  (He stiffens):
  Oh! But . . . since she is on her way,
  I shall await her standing,
  (He draws his sword):
  And sword in hand!

LE BRET:
  Cyrano!

ROXANE (fainting):
  Cyrano!
  (They all recoil in terror.)

CYRANO:
  I think she is looking . . .
  That she dares to look at my nose, that noseless crone!
  (He raises his sword):
  What do you say? . . . It is useless? . . . I know!
  But one does not fight in the hope of success!
  No! No! It is far finer when it is useless!
  —Who are all those?—Are there a thousand of you?
  Ah! I recognize you, all my old enemies!
  Falsehood?
  (He strikes the empty air with his sword):
  Take that, take that!—Ha! Ha! Compromises!
  Prejudices, Cowardices! . . .
  (He strikes):
  You want me to come to terms?
  Never, never!—Ah! There you are, Folly!
  —I know very well that in the end you will bring me down;
  No matter: I fight! I fight! I fight!
  (He makes immense sweeping passes and stops, panting):
  Yes, you tear everything from me, the laurel and the rose!
  Tear them away! Despite you, there is something
  That I carry with me, and tonight, when I enter God’s house,
  My salute will sweep broadly across the blue threshold,
  Something that, without a crease, without a stain,
  I carry away despite you,
  (He springs forward, sword raised):
  And that is . . .
  (The sword slips from his hands; he staggers and falls into the arms of
  Le Bret and Ragueneau.)

CYRANO:
  A kiss! The word is sweet.
  I do not see why your lip does not dare it;
  If it already burns her, what will the thing itself be?
  Do not make it into something terrifying:
  Did you not, just now, almost imperceptibly,
  Leave banter behind and glide without alarm
  From smile to sigh, and from sigh to tears!
  Glide a little farther, imperceptibly:
  From tears to a kiss there is but a shiver!

ROXANE:
  Be quiet!

CYRANO:
  A kiss—when all is said and done, what is it?
  An oath made at somewhat closer quarters, a promise
  More precise, a confession that seeks confirmation,
  A rosy dot placed over the i in the verb to love;
  It is a secret that takes the mouth for an ear,
  An instant of infinity that makes the sound of a bee,
  A communion with the taste of a flower,
  A way of breathing in a little of each other's heart,
  And of tasting a little of each other's soul upon the lips!

ROXANE:
  Be quiet!

CYRANO:
  A kiss is so noble, Madame,
  That the queen of France allowed the happiest of lords
  To take one from her—the queen herself!

ROXANE:
  Well then!

CYRANO (growing impassioned):
  Like Buckingham, I suffered in silence;
  Like him, I adore the queen that you are;
  Like him, I am sorrowful and faithful...

ROXANE:
  And you are
  Handsome like him!

CYRANO (aside, brought back to earth):
  That is true, I am handsome—I had forgotten!

ROXANE:
  Well, then! Climb up and pluck this peerless flower...

CYRANO (pushing Christian toward the balcony):
  Climb!

ROXANE:
  This taste of the heart...

CYRANO:
  Climb!

ROXANE:
  This sound of a bee...

CYRANO:
  Climb!

CHRISTIAN (hesitating):
  But now it seems to me that this is wrong!

ROXANE:
  This instant of infinity!...

CYRANO (pushing him):
  Climb, then, you animal!
  (Christian springs forward and, by way of the bench, the foliage, and the pillars,
  reaches the balusters and climbs over them.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah, Roxane!
  (He embraces her and bends over her lips.)

CYRANO:
  Ow! What a strange pang in my heart!
  —Kiss, feast of love at which I am Lazarus!
  Here in the darkness, a crumb of you comes to me—
  Yes, I feel my heart receiving you a little,
  Since upon that lip where Roxane is deceived,
  She kisses the words I spoke just now!
  (The theorbos are heard):
  A sad tune, a merry tune: the Capuchin!
  (He pretends to run as though arriving from far away, and calls in a clear voice):
  Ho there!

ROXANE:
  What is it?

CYRANO:
  Me. I was passing by... Is Christian still here?

CHRISTIAN (greatly surprised):
  Why, Cyrano!

ROXANE:
  Good day, cousin!

CYRANO:
  Good day, cousin!

ROXANE:
  I am coming down!
  (She disappears into the house. At the back, the Capuchin reenters.)

CHRISTIAN (catching sight of him):
  Oh! Again!
  (He follows Roxane.)



Scene 3.XI.

Cyrano, Christian, Roxane, the Capuchin, Ragueneau.


THE CAPUCHIN:
  It is here—I insist—
  Magdeleine Robin!

CYRANO:
  You said: Ro-lin.

THE CAPUCHIN:
  No: Bin. B, i, n, bin!

ROXANE (appearing on the threshold of the house, followed by Ragueneau,
  who is carrying a lantern, and by Christian):
  What is it?

THE CAPUCHIN:
  A letter.

CHRISTIAN:
  What?

THE CAPUCHIN (to Roxane):
  Oh! It can only concern something holy!
  It is a worthy lord who...

ROXANE (to Christian):
  It is De Guiche!

CHRISTIAN:
  He dares?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! But he is not going to pester me forever!
  (Breaking the seal on the letter):
  I love you, and if...
  (By the light of Ragueneau's lantern, she reads in a low voice, apart):
  Mademoiselle,
  The drums
  Are beating; my regiment is fastening its surcoats;
  It is leaving; as for me, they think I have already left: I am staying.
  I disobey you. I am in this convent.
  I am about to come, and I inform you beforehand
  Through a friar as simple as a goat,
  Who can understand nothing of this. Your lip
  Smiled too much at me earlier: I wished to see it again.
  Send everyone away, and deign to receive
  The audacious man who is already forgiven, I hope,
  And who signs himself your most... et cetera...
  (To the Capuchin):
  Father,
  Here is what this letter tells me. Listen:
  (They all draw nearer; she reads aloud):
  Mademoiselle,
  You must submit to the wishes
  Of the Cardinal, however hard that may be for you.
  That is why, to place
  These lines in your charming hands, I have chosen a most holy,
  Most intelligent and discreet Capuchin;
  We desire him to give you, in your own home,
  The nuptial
  (She turns the page):
  blessing at once.
  Christian must secretly become your husband;
  I am sending him to you. He displeases you. Resign yourself.
  Remember that Heaven will bless your zeal,
  And be entirely assured, Mademoiselle,
  Of the respect of him who was and who shall be
  Always your most humble and most... et cetera.

THE CAPUCHIN (beaming):
  Worthy lord!... I said so. I had no fears!
  It could only concern something holy!

ROXANE (softly to Christian):
  Do I not read letters very well?

CHRISTIAN:
  Hm!

ROXANE (aloud, despairingly):
  Ah!... It is dreadful!

THE CAPUCHIN (who has directed the light of his lantern onto Cyrano):
  Is it you?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is I!

THE CAPUCHIN (turning the light toward him and, as though a doubt
  occurred to him on seeing his beauty):
  But...

ROXANE (quickly):
  Postscript:
  Give the convent one hundred and twenty pistoles.

THE CAPUCHIN:
  Worthy,
  Worthy lord!
  (To Roxane):
  Do you resign yourself?

ROXANE (like a martyr):
  I resign myself!
  (While Ragueneau opens the door for the Capuchin, whom Christian invites
  to enter, she says softly to Cyrano):
  You—keep De Guiche here! He is going to come!
  Do not let him enter until...

CYRANO:
  Understood!
  (To the Capuchin):
  To bless them,
  you need?...

THE CAPUCHIN:
  A quarter of an hour.

CYRANO (pushing them all toward the house):
  Go! I shall remain!

ROXANE (to Christian):
  Come!...
  (They enter.)



Scene XII.

Cyrano, alone.


CYRANO:
  How can I make De Guiche lose a quarter of an hour?
  (He rushes to the bench and climbs the wall toward the balcony):
  There!... Let us climb!... I have my plan!...
  (The theorbos begin playing a mournful phrase):
  Oh! It is a man!
  (The tremolo becomes sinister):
  Oh! Oh!
  This time it is one!...
  (He is on the balcony; he pulls his felt hat down over his eyes, removes his
  sword, wraps himself in his cloak, then leans over and looks outside):
  No, it is not too high!...
  (He climbs over the balusters and, pulling toward himself the long branch of one of
  the trees that extend over the garden wall, grips it with both hands,
  ready to let himself drop):
  I am going to disturb this atmosphere slightly!...

CYRANO:
  That is possible.
  But one does not abdicate the honor of being a target.
  (Cards, dice, smoke subside, fall, fly away with increasing
  satisfaction):
  Had I been present when the sash slipped off
  —Our courage, sir, differs in this respect—
  I would have picked it up and put it on.

DE GUICHE:
  Yes, more Gascon boasting!

CYRANO:
  Boasting?...
  Lend it to me. I offer to go up, this very evening,
  First into the assault, with it across my chest.

DE GUICHE:
  Another Gascon offer! You know that the sash
  Remained with the enemy, on the banks of the Scarpe,
  In a place that grapeshot has since riddled—
  Where no one can go to retrieve it!

CYRANO (drawing the white sash from his pocket and holding it out to him):
  Here it is.
  (Silence. The cadets stifle their laughter in their cards and in their
  dice cups. De Guiche turns around and looks at them: they immediately
  resume their gravity, their games; one of them whistles with
  indifference the mountain tune played by the fife.)

DE GUICHE (taking the sash):
  Thank you. With this scrap of light-colored cloth, I shall
  Be able to give a signal—which I was hesitating to give.
  (He goes to the embankment, climbs it, and waves the sash several times in the air.)

ALL:
  Eh!

THE SENTRY (at the top of the embankment):
  That man down there, running away!...

DE GUICHE (coming back down):
  He is a sham Spanish spy. He renders us
  Great services. The information he carries
  To the enemy is what I give him, so
  That their decisions can be influenced.

CYRANO:
  He is a scoundrel!

DE GUICHE (nonchalantly tying on his sash):
  It is very convenient. What were we saying?...
  —Ah! I was about to tell you something. This very night,
  Attempting one supreme stroke to resupply us,
  The marshal went off toward Dourlens, without drums;
  The King's sutlers are there; across the plowed fields
  He will join them; but in order to return without mishap,
  He took so many troops with him
  That anyone attacking us would certainly have an easy time of it:
  Half the army is absent from the camp!

CARBON:
  Yes, if the Spaniards knew, it would be serious.
  But they do not know of this departure?

DE GUICHE:
  They know.
  They are going to attack us.

CARBON:
  Ah!

DE GUICHE:
  My sham spy
  Came to warn me of their assault.
  He added: “I can determine its location;
  At what point do you want the attack to take place?
  I shall say that it is the least defended of all,
  And the force of the attack will fall upon it.”—I answered:
  “Very well. Leave the camp. Keep your eyes on the line:
  It will be at the point from which I signal to you.”

CARBON (to the cadets):
  Gentlemen, prepare yourselves!
  (They all rise. Sound of swords and sword belts being buckled.)

DE GUICHE:
  It will be in an hour.

FIRST CADET:
  Ah!... very well!...
  (They all sit down again. The interrupted game resumes.)

DE GUICHE (to Carbon):
  We must gain time. The marshal is returning.

CARBON:
  And to gain time?

DE GUICHE:
  You will be so kind
  As to have yourselves killed.

CYRANO:
  Ah! So that is the revenge?

DE GUICHE:
  I shall not claim that, if I loved you,
  I would have chosen you and your men; but,
  Since no courage compares with yours,
  It is my King I serve by serving my rancor.

CYRANO (saluting):
  Allow me to be grateful to you, sir.

DE GUICHE (saluting):
  I know that you like to fight one against a hundred.
  You will not complain of lacking work.
  (He climbs back up, with Carbon.)

CYRANO (to the cadets):
  Well then! To Gascony's coat of arms,
  Which bears six chevrons, gentlemen, azure and gold,
  We are going to add a chevron of blood that it still lacked!
  (De Guiche speaks in a low voice with Carbon de Castel-Jaloux, at the rear. Orders
  are given. The defense is prepared. Cyrano goes toward Christian, who has
  remained motionless, his arms folded.)

CYRANO (putting his hand on Christian's shoulder):
  Christian?

CHRISTIAN (shaking his head):
  Roxane!

CYRANO:
  Alas!

CHRISTIAN:
  At least, I would like to put
  All my heart's farewell into a beautiful letter!...

CYRANO:
  I suspected that it would be today.
  (He draws a note from his doublet):
  And I have written your farewells.

CHRISTIAN:
  Show me!...

CYRANO:
  You want to?...

CHRISTIAN (taking the letter from him):
  Why, yes!
  (He opens it, reads, and stops):
  Look!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  This little circle?...

CYRANO (quickly taking back the letter and looking at it with an innocent air):
  A circle?...

CHRISTIAN:
  It is a tear!

CYRANO:
  Yes... A poet gets caught up in his own game—that is the charm!...
  You understand... this note—it was very moving:
  I made myself weep while writing it.

CHRISTIAN:
  Weep?...

CYRANO:
  Yes... because... dying is not terrible.
  But... never seeing her again... that is what is horrible!
  For after all I do not...
  (Christian looks at him):
  we do not...
  (Quickly):
  you do not...

CHRISTIAN (snatching the letter from him):
  Give me that note!
  (A commotion is heard in the distance, in the camp.)

A SENTRY'S VOICE:
  By God's belly, who goes there?
  (Gunshots. Sounds of voices. Jingle bells.)

CARBON:
  What is it?...

THE SENTRY (who is on the embankment):
  A carriage!
  (They rush to look.)

SHOUTS:
  What! In the camp?—It is coming in!
  —It looks as though it comes from the enemy!—The devil!
  Fire!—No! The coachman shouted!—Shouted what?—
  He shouted: On the King's service!
  (Everyone is on the embankment, looking outside. The jingle bells draw
  nearer.)

DE GUICHE:
  Eh? The King!...
  (They come back down and form ranks.)

CARBON:
  Hats off, everyone!

DE GUICHE (offstage):
  The King!—Stand aside, vile rabble,
  So that it may describe its curve with pomp!
  (The carriage enters at a fast trot. It is covered with mud and
  dust. The curtains are drawn. Two lackeys stand behind. It stops dead.)

CARBON (shouting):
  Beat the salute!
  (Roll of drums. All the cadets uncover their heads.)

DE GUICHE:
  Lower the step!
  (Two men rush forward. The carriage door opens.)

ROXANE (jumping from the carriage):
  Good day!
  (The sound of a woman's voice makes all these deeply bowed men
  straighten up at once.—Astonishment.)

ROXANE:
  Let me have your hand—come now, it has a fever.—
  But I saw the confession trembling on his lips.

CYRANO:
  Ah!...

ROXANE (finishing a little bandage for him with her handkerchief):
  And just imagine—why, as it happens,
  Yes, cousin, he serves in your regiment!

CYRANO:
  Ah!...

ROXANE (laughing):
  For he is a cadet in your company!

CYRANO:
  Ah!...

ROXANE:
  His brow bespeaks wit and genius;
  He is proud, noble, young, intrepid, handsome...

CYRANO (rising, deathly pale):
  Handsome!

ROXANE:
  What? What is the matter with you?

CYRANO:
  Nothing... It is... it is...
  (He points to his hand, with a smile):
  It is this little hurt.

ROXANE:
  In short, I love him. Besides, I must tell you
  That I have never seen him except at the theater...

CYRANO:
  So you have not spoken to each other?

ROXANE:
  Only our eyes have.

CYRANO:
  But then how do you know?

ROXANE:
  Beneath the lindens
  Of the Place Royale, people talk... Some gossips
  Informed me...

CYRANO:
  He is a cadet?

ROXANE:
  A cadet in the Guards.

CYRANO:
  His name?

ROXANE:
  Baron Christian de Neuvillette.

CYRANO:
  What?...
  He is not in the Cadets.

ROXANE:
  Yes, since this morning:
  Captain Carbon de Castel-Jaloux.

CYRANO:
  How swiftly,
  How swiftly one gives away one’s heart!... But, my poor little one...

THE DUENNA (opening the door at the back):
  I have finished the cakes, Monsieur de Bergerac!

CYRANO:
  Well, then! Read the verses printed on the bag!
  (The duenna disappears):
  ...My poor child, you who love only fine language
  And brilliant wit—what if he were a philistine, a savage?

ROXANE:
  No, he has the hair of one of d’Urfé’s heroes!

CYRANO:
  What if his speech were as foul as his hair is fine!

ROXANE:
  No, every word he says is refined—I can tell!

CYRANO:
  Yes, every word is refined when the mustache is fine.
  —But what if he were a fool!...

ROXANE (stamping her foot):
  Well then, I would die of it, there and then!

CYRANO (after a pause):
  You asked me to come so that you could tell me this?
  I do not quite see the point of it, madame.

ROXANE:
  Ah, it is because yesterday someone filled my soul with mortal dread
  By telling me that all of you, all of you are Gascons
  In your company...

CYRANO:
  And that we challenge
  Every beardless boy who, through favor, gains admittance
  Among the pure Gascons we are, without being one himself?
  Is that what you were told?

ROXANE:
  And you can imagine how I
  Trembled for him!

CYRANO (between his teeth):
  Not without reason!

ROXANE:
  But I thought,
  When yesterday you appeared before us, invincible and great,
  Punishing that scoundrel, standing up to those brutes—
  I thought: if he were willing, he whom they will all fear...

CYRANO:
  Very well, I shall protect your little baron.

ROXANE:
  Oh! You will protect him for me, will you not?
  I have always felt such tender friendship for you.

CYRANO:
  Yes, yes.

ROXANE:
  You will be his friend?

CYRANO:
  I shall.

ROXANE:
