  And he will never have to fight a duel?

CYRANO:
  I swear it.

ROXANE:
  Oh! I am very fond of you. I must be going.
  (She quickly puts her mask back on, arranges a lace veil over her brow, and,
  distractedly):
  But you have not told me about the battle
  Last night. Truly, it must have been extraordinary!...
  —Tell him to write to me.
  (She blows him a little kiss from her hand):
  Oh! I love you!

CYRANO:
  Yes, yes.

ROXANE:
  A hundred men against you? Come, farewell.—We are
  Great friends!

CYRANO:
  Yes, yes.

ROXANE:
  Have him write to me!—A hundred men!—
  You will tell me later. I cannot now.
  A hundred men! What courage!

CYRANO (bowing to her):
  Oh! I have done better since then.
  (She exits. Cyrano remains motionless, his eyes on the ground. A silence. The
  door on the right opens. Ragueneau puts his head through.)



Scene 2.VII.

Cyrano, Ragueneau, the poets, Carbon de Castel-Jaloux, the cadets, the
crowd, etc., then De Guiche.


RAGUENEAU:
  May we come back in?

CYRANO (without moving):
  Yes...
  (Ragueneau signals, and his friends come back in. At the same time, Carbon
  de Castel-Jaloux appears at the door at the back, dressed as a captain in
  the Guards, making broad gestures when he catches sight of Cyrano.)

CARBON DE CASTEL-JALOUX:
  There he is!

CYRANO (raising his head):
  My captain!...

CARBON (exultantly):
  Our hero! We know everything! Some thirty
  Of my cadets are here!...

CYRANO (drawing back):
  But...

CARBON (trying to pull him along):
  Come! They want to see you!

CYRANO:
  No!

CARBON:
  They are drinking across the way, at the Croix du Trahoir.

CYRANO:
  I...

CARBON (going up to the door and shouting into the wings in a voice of
  thunder):
  The hero refuses. He is in a surly mood!

A VOICE (outside):
  God’s blood!
  (Commotion outside, the sound of swords and boots drawing nearer.)

CARBON (rubbing his hands):
  Here they come, crossing the street!

THE CADETS (entering the pastry shop):
  A thousand gods!—God’s head!—God’s death!—By God’s little head!

RAGUENEAU (drawing back in terror):
  Gentlemen, are you all from Gascony, then?

THE CADETS:
  All of us!

A CADET (to Cyrano):
  Bravo!

CYRANO:
  Baron!

ANOTHER (shaking his hands):
  Long live Cyrano!

CYRANO:
  Baron!

THIRD CADET:
  Let me embrace you!

CYRANO:
  Baron!...

SEVERAL GASCONS:
  Let us embrace him!

CYRANO (not knowing which one to answer):
  Baron!... Baron!... Please...

RAGUENEAU:
  Are you all barons, gentlemen?

THE CADETS:
  All?

RAGUENEAU:
  Are they?...

FIRST CADET:
  One could build a tower from our coronets alone!

LE BRET (entering and running to Cyrano):
  They are looking for you! A delirious crowd, led
  By those who followed behind you last night...

CYRANO (horrified):
  You did not tell them where I am?...

LE BRET (rubbing his hands):
  I did!

A BURGHER (entering, followed by a group):
  Monsieur, the whole Marais is having itself carried here!
  (Outside, the street has filled with people. Sedan chairs and carriages
  draw to a halt.)

LE BRET (softly, smiling, to Cyrano):
  And Roxane?

CYRANO (sharply):
  Be quiet!

THE CROWD (shouting outside):
  Cyrano!...
  (A mob rushes into the pastry shop. Jostling. Cheers.)

CYRANO (growing more and more overcome with emotion):
  Allow us awhile to take advantage...
  Of this opportunity that offers itself...to be able
  To speak softly to each other, without seeing each other.

ROXANE:
  Without seeing each other?

CYRANO:
  Why yes, it is delightful. We can scarcely make each other out.
  You see the blackness of a long trailing cloak,
  I glimpse the whiteness of a summer dress:
  I am but a shadow, and you but a radiance!
  You have no idea what these moments are to me!
  If sometimes I was eloquent...

ROXANE:
  You were!

CYRANO:
  Until now, my speech has never issued
  From my true heart...

ROXANE:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Because...until now
  I spoke through...

ROXANE:
  What?

CYRANO:
  ...the dizziness in which anyone beneath your gaze
  Trembles!...But tonight, it seems to me...
  That I am going to speak to you for the first time!

ROXANE:
  It is true that you have an altogether different voice.

CYRANO (drawing nearer feverishly):
  Yes, altogether different, for in the night that protects me
  I dare at last to be myself, and I dare...
  (He stops and, distractedly):
  Where was I?
  I do not know...all this—forgive my agitation—
  Is so delightful...it is so new to me!

ROXANE:
  So new?

CYRANO (deeply shaken, still trying to recover his words):
  So new...why yes...to be sincere:
  The fear of being mocked always constricts my heart...

ROXANE:
  Mocked for what?

CYRANO:
  Why, for...for an outburst!...Yes, my heart
  Always clothes itself in my wit, out of modesty:
  I set out to pluck down the star, and I stop,
  For fear of ridicule, to gather the little flower!

ROXANE:
  The little flower has its merits.

CYRANO:
  Tonight, let us disdain it!

ROXANE:
  You had never spoken to me like that!

CYRANO:
  Ah! if, far from quivers, torches, and arrows,
  We could escape awhile toward things...more refreshing!
  Instead of drinking drop by drop, from a dainty
  Thimble of fine gold, the insipid water of the Lignon,
  What if we tried to see how the soul quenches its thirst
  By drinking deeply straight from the great river!

ROXANE:
  But wit?...

CYRANO:
  I used it at first to make you stay,
  But now it would be an insult
  To this night, these perfumes, this hour, Nature,
  To speak like a love letter by Voiture!
  Let us allow the sky, with a single glance from its stars,
  To disarm us of all our artifice:
  I fear so greatly that amid our exquisite alchemy
  The truth of feeling may evaporate,
  That the soul may empty itself in these vain pastimes,
  And that the height of refinement may be the end of all ends!

ROXANE:
  But wit?...

CYRANO:
  I hate it in love! It is a crime,
  When one loves, to prolong this fencing match too far!
  Besides, the moment inevitably comes
  —And I pity those for whom that moment never comes!—
  When we feel that within us there exists a noble love
  That every pretty word we utter makes sorrowful!

ROXANE:
  Well then! If that moment has come for us both,
  What words will you say to me?

CYRANO:
  All those, all those, all those
  That come to me, I shall fling them to you in a mass,
  Without arranging them in a bouquet: I love you, I am suffocating,
  I love thee, I am mad, I can bear no more, it is too much;
  Thy name is in my heart as in a little bell,
  And since all the time, Roxane, I shudder,
  All the time the bell stirs, and the name rings out!
  Of thee, I remember everything, I have loved everything:
  I know that last year, one day, on the twelfth of May,
  To go out in the morning thou changed thy hairstyle!
  I have so utterly taken thy hair for radiance
  That, as when one has stared too long at the sun,
  One afterward sees a crimson circle upon everything,
  Upon everything, once I have left the fires with which thou floodest me,
  My dazzled gaze casts golden patches!

ROXANE (in a troubled voice):
  Yes, that truly is love...

CYRANO:
  Indeed, this feeling
  That invades me, terrible and jealous, truly is
  Love; it has all love’s sorrowful fury!
  Love—and yet it is not selfish!
  Ah! How gladly I would give my happiness for thine,
  Even if thou shouldst never know anything of it,
  If only, sometimes, from afar, I might hear
  The happiness born of my sacrifice laugh a little!
  Every glance from thee awakens a new virtue,
  A new courage in me! Dost thou begin
  To understand now? Come, dost thou realize?
  Dost thou feel my soul, a little, rising through this darkness?...
  Oh! But truly, tonight, it is too beautiful, it is too sweet!
  I say all this to you, and you listen to me—you, to me!
  It is too much! Even in my least modest hopes,
  I never hoped for so much! Nothing remains for me
  But to die now! It is because of the words
  I speak that she trembles there among the dark-blue branches!
  For you tremble, like a leaf among the leaves!
  For thou tremblest! For I have felt, whether thou wouldst
  Or not, the adored trembling of thy hand
  Descend all along the jasmine branches!
  (He kisses the tip of a hanging branch wildly.)

ROXANE:
  Yes, I tremble, and I weep, and I love thee, and am thine!
  And thou hast intoxicated me!

CYRANO:
  Then let death come!
  This intoxication—it was I, I, who knew how to cause it!
  I ask for only one thing more...

CHRISTIAN (beneath the balcony):
  A kiss!

ROXANE (drawing back):
  What?

CYRANO:
  Oh!

ROXANE:
  You are asking for?...

CYRANO:
  Yes...I...
  (Softly to Christian):
  Thou art going too fast.

CHRISTIAN:
  Since she is so deeply moved, I must take advantage of it!

CYRANO (to Roxane):
  Yes, I...I did ask, it is true...but good heavens!
  I understand that I was far too bold.

ROXANE (a little disappointed):
  You do not press your request any further than that?

CYRANO:
  Yes! I insist...
  Without insisting!...Yes, yes! Your modesty is distressed!
  Well then! But that kiss...do not grant it to me!

CHRISTIAN (to Cyrano, tugging at his cloak):
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Be quiet, Christian!

ROXANE (leaning out):
  What are you saying so softly?

CYRANO:
  Why, I am scolding myself for having gone too far;
  I was saying to myself: be quiet, Christian!...
  (The theorbos begin to play):
  One moment...
  Someone is coming!
  (Roxane closes the window again. Cyrano listens to the theorbos, one of which plays a frolicsome tune and the other a mournful one):
  A sad tune? A merry tune?...What then is their purpose?
  Is it a man? A woman?—Ah! It is a Capuchin!
  (A Capuchin enters, going from house to house, a lantern in his hand, looking at the doors.)

ROXANE:
  Not a word! . . .
  (She goes back inside and closes the door again.)

CYRANO (bowing to her, once the door is closed):
  Thank you.
  (The door opens again and Roxane puts her head out.)

ROXANE:
  He might be preparing himself! . . .

CYRANO:
  Good heavens, no! . . .

BOTH (together):
  Hush! . . .
  (The door closes.)

CYRANO (calling):
  Christian!



Scene 3.IV.

Cyrano, Christian.


CYRANO:
  I know everything that is needed. Prepare your memory.
  Here is the opportunity to cover oneself with glory.
  Let us waste no time. Do not look so sullen.
  Quickly, let us go back to your place; I am going to teach you. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  No! I am waiting for Roxane here.

CYRANO:
  What madness
  Has seized you? Come quickly and learn. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No, I tell you!
  I am tired of borrowing my letters, my speeches,
  And of playing this role, and of always trembling! . . .
  It was fine at first! But I feel that she loves me!
  Thank you. I am no longer afraid. I am going to speak for myself.

CYRANO:
  Oh, really!

CHRISTIAN:
  And who tells you that I would not know how? . . .
  I am not so stupid, after all! You will see!
  But, my dear fellow, your lessons have been useful to me.
  I shall know how to speak on my own! And, by all the devils,
  I shall always know well enough how to take her in my arms! . . .
  (Catching sight of Roxane, who is coming out of Clomire's house):
  —There she is! Cyrano, no, do not leave me!

CYRANO (bowing to him):
  Speak on your own, Monsieur.
  (He disappears behind the garden wall.)



Scene 3.V.

Christian, Roxane, several male and female précieuses, and the duenna,
for a moment.


ROXANE (leaving Clomire's house with a company from whom she takes
  her leave, with curtsies and bows):
  Barthénoïde!—Alcandre!—Grémione! . . .

THE DUENNA (in despair):
  We missed the discourse on Tenderness!
  (She goes into Roxane's house.)

ROXANE (still bidding farewell):
  Urimédonte! . . .Farewell! . . .
  (They all bow to Roxane, bow again to one another, part, and
  go off down different streets. Roxane sees Christian):
  It is you! . . .
  (She goes to him):
  Evening is falling.
  Wait. They are far away. The air is mild. Not a passerby.
  Let us sit down. Speak. I am listening.

CHRISTIAN (sits beside her on the bench. A silence):
  I love you.

ROXANE (closing her eyes):
  Yes, speak to me of love.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love you.

ROXANE:
  That is the theme.
  Embroider, embroider.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love. . .

ROXANE:
  Embroider!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love you so much.

ROXANE:
  No doubt! And then?

CHRISTIAN:
  And then. . .I would be so happy
  If you loved me!—Tell me, Roxane, that you love me!

ROXANE (pouting):
  You offer me gruel when I was hoping for creams!
  Tell me a little how you love me? . . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Why. . .very much.

ROXANE:
  Oh! . . .Unlabyrinth your feelings!

CHRISTIAN (who has moved closer and is devouring the fair nape of her neck with his eyes):
  Your neck!
  I would like to kiss it! . . .

ROXANE:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love you!

ROXANE (trying to rise):
  Again!

CHRISTIAN (quickly, holding her back):
  No! I do not love you!

ROXANE (sitting down again):
  That is fortunate!

CHRISTIAN:
  I adore you!

ROXANE (rising and moving away):
  Oh!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes. . .I am becoming a fool!

ROXANE (dryly):
  And that displeases me!
  As it would displease me if you were to become ugly.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

ROXANE:
  Go and gather up your fugitive eloquence!

CHRISTIAN:
  I. . .

ROXANE:
  You love me, I know. Farewell.
  (She goes toward the house.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Not yet!
  I will tell you. . .

ROXANE (pushing the door open to go inside):
  That you adore me. . .yes, I know.
  No! No! Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  But I. . .
  (She shuts the door in his face.)

CYRANO (who came back in some time ago without being seen):
  It is a success.



Scene 3.VI.

Christian, Cyrano, the pages, for a moment.


CHRISTIAN:
  Help!

CYRANO:
  No, Monsieur.

CHRISTIAN:
  I shall die if I do not regain
  Her favor this very instant. . .

CYRANO:
  And how the devil can I
  Teach you this very instant? . . .

CHRISTIAN (seizing his arm):
  Oh! There, look, see!
  (The balcony window has lit up.)

CYRANO (moved):
  Her window!

CHRISTIAN (shouting):
  I am going to die!

CYRANO:
  Lower your voice!

CHRISTIAN (very softly):
  Die! . . .

CYRANO:
  The night is dark. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Well?

CYRANO:
  It can be repaired.
  You do not deserve it. . .Stand there, wretch!
  There, in front of the balcony! I shall stand beneath it. . .
  And prompt you with your words.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

CYRANO:
  Be quiet!

THE PAGES (reappearing at the back, to Cyrano):
  Hey!

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .
  (He motions to them to speak softly.)

FIRST PAGE (in a low voice):
  We have just serenaded
  Montfleury! . . .

CYRANO (softly, quickly):
  Go and lie in ambush,
  One at that street corner, and the other at this one;
  And if some troublesome passerby comes this way,
  Play a tune!

SECOND PAGE:
  What kind of tune, Monsieur Gassendist?

CYRANO:
  A merry one for a woman, and for a man, a sad one!
  (The pages disappear, one at each street corner.—To Christian):
  Call her!

CHRISTIAN:
  Roxane!

CYRANO (picking up pebbles and throwing them at the windowpanes):
  Wait! A few pebbles.



Scene VII.

Roxane, Christian, Cyrano, at first hidden beneath the balcony.


ROXANE (partly opening her window):
  Who is calling me, then?

CHRISTIAN:
  Me.

ROXANE:
  Who is “me”?

CHRISTIAN:
  Christian.

ROXANE (disdainfully):
  It is you?

CHRISTIAN:
  I would like to speak to you.

CYRANO (beneath the balcony, to Christian):
  Good. Good. Almost in a whisper.

ROXANE:
  No! You speak too poorly. Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  Please! . . .

ROXANE:
  No! You no longer love me!

CHRISTIAN (as Cyrano prompts him with the words):
  To accuse me—just gods!—
  Of loving no more. . .when. . .I love more!

ROXANE (who was about to close her window again, stopping):
  Well! That is better!

CHRISTIAN (the same business):
  Love grows, rocked within my anxious soul. . .
  Which that. . .cruel brat took for. . .a cradle!

ROXANE (coming forward onto the balcony):
  That is better!—But since it is cruel, you were foolish
  Not to smother that love in its cradle!

ROXANE (standing near him):
  Each of us has a wound: I have mine.
  Still raw, it is there, that old wound,
  (She places her hand on her breast):
  It is there, beneath the letter with its yellowing paper,
  Where tears and blood can still be seen!
  (Twilight begins to fall.)

CYRANO:
  His letter! . . . Had you not said that one day, perhaps,
  You would let me read it?

ROXANE:
  Ah! you wish to? . . . His letter?

CYRANO:
  Yes. . . I wish to. . . Today. . .

ROXANE (giving him the pouch hanging from her neck):
  Here!

CYRANO (taking it):
  May I open it?

ROXANE:
  Open it. . . read! . . .
  (She returns to her embroidery frame, folds it up, and puts away her wool.)

CYRANO (reading):
  Roxane, farewell, I am going to die! . . .

ROXANE (stopping, astonished):
  Aloud?

CYRANO (reading):
  It is to be this evening, I think, my beloved!
  My soul is still heavy with unexpressed love,
  And I am dying! Never again, never will my intoxicated eyes,
  My gaze, whose. . .

ROXANE:
  How you read it,
  His letter!

CYRANO (continuing):
  . . .whose thrilling delight it was,
  Kiss in passing the gestures that you make;
  I see again a little one familiar to you,
  With which you touch your brow, and I should like to cry out. . .

ROXANE (disturbed):
  How you read it—this letter!
  (Night falls imperceptibly.)

CYRANO:
  And I cry:
  Farewell! . . .

ROXANE:
  You read it. . .

CYRANO:
  My dear one, my darling,
  My treasure. . .

ROXANE (dreamily):
  In a voice. . .

CYRANO:
  My love! . . .

ROXANE:
  In a voice. . .
  (She starts):
  But. . . which I am not hearing for the first time!
  (She approaches very softly, without his noticing, passes behind the armchair, bends over noiselessly, and looks at the letter.—The shadows deepen.)

CYRANO:
  My heart never left you for a single second,
  And I am and shall be, even in the other world,
  He who loved you beyond measure, he who. . .

ROXANE (placing her hand on his shoulder):
  How can you read now? It is dark.
  (He starts, turns, sees her there very close to him, makes a frightened gesture, and bows his head. A long silence. Then, in the now complete darkness, she speaks slowly, clasping her hands):
  And for fourteen years, he played this part:
  Being the old friend who comes to be amusing!

CYRANO:
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  It was you!

CYRANO:
  No, no, Roxane, no!

ROXANE:
  I should have guessed when he spoke my name!

CYRANO:
  No, it was not I!

ROXANE:
  It was you!

CYRANO:
  I swear to you. . .

ROXANE:
  I see the whole generous imposture:
  The letters—it was you. . .

CYRANO:
  No!

ROXANE:
  The tender, wild words,
  It was you. . .

CYRANO:
  No!

ROXANE:
  The voice in the night—it was you!

CYRANO:
  I swear to you it was not!

ROXANE:
  The soul—it was yours!

CYRANO:
  I did not love you.

ROXANE:
  You loved me!

CYRANO (struggling):
  It was the other man!

ROXANE:
  You loved me!

CYRANO (in a weakening voice):
  No!

ROXANE:
  Already you say it more softly!

CYRANO:
  No, no, my dear love, I did not love you!

ROXANE:
  Ah! how many things have died. . . how many have been born!
  —Why did you remain silent for fourteen years,
  Since upon this letter, in which he had no part,
  Those tears were yours?

CYRANO (holding out the letter to her):
  That blood was his.

ROXANE:
  Then why let this sublime silence
  Be broken today?

CYRANO:
  Why? . . .
  (Le Bret and Ragueneau enter at a run.)



Scene 5.VI.

The same, Le Bret and Ragueneau.


LE BRET:
  What recklessness!
  Ah! I was sure of it! He is here!

CYRANO (smiling and straightening up):
  Well, by thunder!

LE BRET:
  He has killed himself, Madame, by getting up!

ROXANE:
  Great God!
  But just now, then. . . that weakness? . . . that? . . .

CYRANO:
  That is true! I had not finished my gazette:
  . . . And on Saturday the twenty-sixth, one hour before dinner,
  Monsieur de Bergerac died by assassination.
  (He uncovers his head; it is seen to be wrapped in bandages.)

ROXANE:
  What is he saying?—Cyrano!—His head bandaged! . . .
  Ah, what have they done to you? Why?

CYRANO:
  “Struck by a hero with a sword thrust,
  To fall with its point in my heart!” . . .
  —Yes, that is what I used to say! . . . Fate is a mocker! . . .
  And here I am, killed in an ambush,
  From behind, by a lackey, with a blow from a log!
  That is very good. I shall have failed at everything, even my death.

RAGUENEAU:
  Ah, Monsieur! . . .

CYRANO:
  Ragueneau, do not weep so loudly! . . .
  (He holds out his hand to him):
  What has become of you now, my fellow craftsman?

RAGUENEAU (through his tears):
  I am a snuffer of. . . of. . . candles, at Molière’s theater.

CYRANO:
  Molière!

RAGUENEAU:
  But I mean to leave him tomorrow:
  Yes, I am outraged! . . . Yesterday they were performing Scapin,
  And I saw that he had taken a scene from you!

LE BRET:
  A whole one!

RAGUENEAU:
  Yes, Monsieur, the famous: “What the devil was he doing? . . .”

LE BRET (furiously):
  Molière took it from you!

CYRANO:
  Hush! hush! He did well! . . .
  (To Ragueneau):
  The scene has a great effect, does it not?

RAGUENEAU (sobbing):
  Ah! Monsieur, they laughed! They laughed!

CYRANO:
  Yes, my life
  Was to be the one who prompts—and is forgotten!
  (To Roxane):
  Do you remember the evening when Christian spoke to you
  Beneath the balcony? Well! My whole life is there:
  While I remained below, in the black shadows,
  Others climbed up to gather glory’s kiss!
  It is just, and I approve upon the threshold of my grave:
  Molière has genius and Christian was handsome!
  (At that moment, the chapel bell having rung, the nuns are seen passing at the back, along the path, on their way to the service):
  Let them go and pray, since their bell is ringing!

ROXANE (rising to call out):
  Sister! Sister!

CYRANO (restraining her):
  No! no! do not go and fetch anyone:
  By the time you returned, I should no longer be here.
  (The nuns have entered the chapel; the organ is heard):
  I was lacking a little harmony. . . there it is.

ROXANE:
  I love you—live!

ROXANE:
  On nothing! . . . I shall tell him: Go! Set forth with the reins loose!
  Improvise. Speak of love. Be splendid!

CYRANO (smiling):
  Good.

ROXANE:
  Hush! . . .

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .

ROXANE:
  Not a word! . . .
  (She goes inside and closes the door again.)

CYRANO (saluting her once the door is closed):
  With thanks to you.
  (The door opens again and Roxane puts her head out.)

ROXANE:
  He might prepare himself! . . .

CYRANO:
  Good Lord, no! . . .

BOTH TOGETHER:
  Hush! . . .
  (The door closes.)

CYRANO (calling):
  Christian!



Scene 3.IV.

Cyrano, Christian.


CYRANO:
  I know everything that is needed. Ready thy memory.
  Here is the chance to cover oneself with glory.
  Let us waste no time. Do not look so sullen.
  Quickly, let us go to thy home; I shall teach thee. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  No! I am waiting for Roxane here.

CYRANO:
  What fit of madness
  Has seized thee? Come quickly and learn. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No, I tell thee!
  I am weary of borrowing my letters, my speeches,
  And of playing this role, and of always trembling! . . .
  It was all very well at first! But I feel that she loves me!
  Thank thee. I am no longer afraid. I shall speak for myself.

CYRANO:
  Indeed!

CHRISTIAN:
  And who tells thee that I would not know how? . . .
  I am not so stupid, after all! Thou shalt see!
  But, my dear fellow, thy lessons have been of use to me.
  I shall know how to speak on my own! And, by all the devils,
  I shall always know how to take her in my arms! . . .
  (Noticing Roxane, who is coming out of Clomire’s house again):
  —There she is! Cyrano, no, do not leave me!

CYRANO (saluting him):
  Speak by yourself, sir.
  (He disappears behind the garden wall.)



Scene 3.V.

Christian, Roxane, several male and female précieuses, and the duenna,
for a moment.


ROXANE (emerging from Clomire’s house with a company from whom she
  is taking leave; curtsies and bows):
  Barthénoïde!—Alcandre!—Grémione! . . .

THE DUENNA (despairingly):
  We missed the discourse on Tenderness!
  (She goes into Roxane’s house.)

ROXANE (still taking her leave):
  Urimédonte! . . . Farewell! . . .
  (They all bow to Roxane, bow again to one another, part, and
  move away along different streets. Roxane sees Christian):
  It is you! . . .
  (She goes to him):
  Evening is falling.
  Wait. They are far away. The air is mild. Not a passerby.
  Let us sit down. Speak. I am listening.

CHRISTIAN (sits beside her on the bench. A silence):
  I love you.

ROXANE (closing her eyes):
  Yes, speak to me of love.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee.

ROXANE:
  That is the theme.
  Embroider upon it, embroider.

CHRISTIAN:
  I. . . you. . .

ROXANE:
  Embroider!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee so much.

ROXANE:
  No doubt! And then?

CHRISTIAN:
  And then. . . I should be so happy
  If you loved me!—Tell me, Roxane, that thou lovest me!

ROXANE (pouting):
  You offer me gruel when I was hoping for cream!
  Tell me a little how you love me? . . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Why. . . greatly.

ROXANE:
  Oh! . . . Lead your feelings out of their labyrinth!

CHRISTIAN (having moved closer and devouring the fair nape of her neck with his eyes):
  Thy neck!
  I should like to kiss it! . . .

ROXANE:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee!

ROXANE (about to rise):
  Again!

CHRISTIAN (quickly, restraining her):
  No! I do not love thee!

ROXANE (sitting down again):
  That is fortunate!

CHRISTIAN:
  I adore thee!

ROXANE (rising and moving away):
  Oh!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes. . . I am becoming a fool!

ROXANE (dryly):
  And that displeases me!
  As it would displease me if you became ugly.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

ROXANE:
  Go and gather up your fleeing eloquence!

CHRISTIAN:
  I. . .

ROXANE:
  You love me, I know. Farewell.
  (She goes toward the house.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Not yet!
  I shall tell you. . .

ROXANE (pushing open the door to go inside):
  That you adore me. . . yes, I know.
  No! No! Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  But I. . .
  (She shuts the door in his face.)

CYRANO (who came back in a moment ago without being seen):
  It is a success.



Scene 3.VI.

Christian, Cyrano, the pages, for a moment.


CHRISTIAN:
  Help!

CYRANO:
  No, sir.

CHRISTIAN:
  I shall die if I do not regain
  Her favor this very instant. . .

CYRANO:
  And how the devil can I
  Make you learn this very instant? . . .

CHRISTIAN (seizing his arm):
  Oh! There, look, see!
  (The balcony window has lit up.)

CYRANO (moved):
  Her window!

CHRISTIAN (shouting):
  I am going to die!

CYRANO:
  Lower your voice!

CHRISTIAN (very softly):
  Die! . . .

CYRANO:
  The night is dark. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Well?

CYRANO:
  It can be repaired.
  You do not deserve it. . . Stand there, wretch!
  There, in front of the balcony! I shall stand beneath it. . .
  And prompt thee with thy words.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

CYRANO:
  Be quiet!

THE PAGES (reappearing at the back, to Cyrano):
  Hey!

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .
  (He motions to them to speak softly.)

FIRST PAGE (in a half-voice):
  We have just serenaded
  Montfleury! . . .

CYRANO (softly, quickly):
  Go and lie in ambush,
  One at that street corner and the other at this one;
  And if some troublesome passerby comes this way,
  Play a tune!

SECOND PAGE:
  What sort of tune, Monsieur Gassendist?

CYRANO:
  A merry one for a woman, and for a man, a sad one!
  (The pages disappear, one at each street corner.—To Christian):
  Call her!

CHRISTIAN:
  Roxane!

CYRANO (picking up pebbles and throwing them at the windowpanes):
  Wait! A few pebbles.



Scene VII.

Roxane, Christian, Cyrano, at first hidden beneath the balcony.


ROXANE (partly opening her window):
  Who is calling me?

CHRISTIAN:
  I.

ROXANE:
  Who is “I”?

CHRISTIAN:
  Christian.

ROXANE (disdainfully):
  It is you?

CHRISTIAN:
  I should like to speak to you.

CYRANO (beneath the balcony, to Christian):
  Good. Good. Almost in a whisper.

ROXANE:
  No! You speak too poorly. Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  Please! . . .

ROXANE:
  No! You no longer love me!

CHRISTIAN (as Cyrano prompts him with his words):
  To accuse me—righteous gods!—
  Of loving no longer. . . when. . . I love more!

ROXANE (who was about to close her window, stopping):
  Why, that is better!

CHRISTIAN (the same business):
  Love grows, cradled within my troubled soul. . .
  Which that cruel brat took for. . . a cradle!

CYRANO:
  Ah! If, far from quivers, torches, and arrows,
  We fled awhile toward things... fresher!
  Instead of drinking drop by drop, from a dainty
  Thimble of fine gold, the insipid water of the Lignon,
  What if we tried to see how the soul slakes its thirst
  By drinking deeply straight from the great river!

ROXANE:
  But wit?...

CYRANO:
  I used it at first to make you stay,
  But now it would be an insult
  To this night, these perfumes, this hour, Nature,
  To speak like a love letter by Voiture!
  —Let heaven, with a single glance from its stars,
  Disarm us of all our artifice:
  I fear so greatly that amid our exquisite alchemy
  The truth of feeling may evaporate,
  That the soul may empty itself in these vain pastimes,
  And that the height of refinement may be the end of everything!

ROXANE:
  But wit?...

CYRANO:
  I hate it in love! It is a crime,
  When one loves, to prolong this fencing match too much!
  Besides, the moment inevitably comes
  —And I pity those for whom that moment never comes!—
  When we feel that a noble love exists within us,
  Which every pretty word we utter makes sad!

ROXANE:
  Well then! If that moment has come for us both,
  What words will you say to me?

CYRANO:
  All those, all those, all those
  That come to me—I shall fling them to you in a bunch,
  Without arranging them into a bouquet: I love you, I am suffocating,
  I love you, I am mad, I can bear no more, it is too much;
  Your name is in my heart as in a little bell,
  And since I am trembling all the time, Roxane,
  All the time the bell is shaken, and the name rings out!
  I remember everything about you; I have loved everything:
  I know that last year, one day, on the twelfth of May,
  You changed your hairstyle to go out in the morning!
  I have so taken your hair for light
  That, as when one has stared too long at the sun
  And afterward sees a crimson circle upon everything,
  Upon everything, when I have left the blaze with which you flood me,
  My dazzled gaze casts golden patches!

ROXANE (in a troubled voice):
  Yes, that truly is love...

CYRANO:
  Indeed, this feeling
  That overwhelms me, terrible and jealous, truly is
  Love; it has all love's sorrowful fury!
  Love—and yet it is not selfish!
  Ah! How gladly I would give my happiness for yours,
  Even if you were never to know of it,
  If only, now and then, from afar, I might hear
  The happiness born of my sacrifice laugh a little!
  —Every glance of yours brings forth a new virtue,
  A new courage in me! Are you beginning
  To understand now? Come, do you realize?
  Do you feel my soul, a little, rising through this darkness?...
  Oh! But truly, tonight, it is too beautiful, it is too sweet!
  I am telling you all this, and you are listening to me—to me, you!
  It is too much! Even in my least modest hope,
  I never hoped for so much! Nothing remains for me
  But to die now! It is because of the words
  I speak that she trembles among the blue branches!
  For you are trembling like a leaf among the leaves!
  For you are trembling! For I have felt, whether you wished it
  Or not, the adored trembling of your hand
  Descend all along the jasmine branches!
  (He frantically kisses the tip of a hanging branch.)

ROXANE:
  Yes, I am trembling, and I am weeping, and I love you, and I am yours!
  And you have intoxicated me!

CYRANO:
  Then let death come!
  This intoxication—it is I, I, who knew how to cause it!
  I ask for only one thing more...

CHRISTIAN (beneath the balcony):
  A kiss!

ROXANE (drawing back):
  What?

CYRANO:
  Oh!

ROXANE:
  You are asking for?...

CYRANO:
  Yes... I...
  (Softly to Christian):
  You are going too fast.

CHRISTIAN:
  Since she is so deeply moved, I must take advantage of it!

CYRANO (to Roxane):
  Yes, I... I did ask, it is true... but good heavens!
  I understand that I was far too bold.

ROXANE (a little disappointed):
  You do not insist any more than that?

CYRANO:
  Yes! I insist...
  Without insisting!... Yes, yes! Your modesty is distressed!
  Well then! But that kiss... do not grant it to me!

CHRISTIAN (to Cyrano, pulling him by his cloak):
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Be quiet, Christian!

ROXANE (leaning forward):
  What are you saying under your breath?

CYRANO:
  Why, I am scolding myself for having gone too far;
  I was saying to myself: be quiet, Christian!...
  (The theorbos begin to play):
  One moment!...
  Someone is coming!
  (Roxane closes the window again. Cyrano listens to the theorbos, one of which is playing a frolicsome tune and the other a mournful one):
  A sad tune? A merry tune?... What can their purpose be?
  Is it a man? A woman?—Ah! It is a Capuchin!
  (A Capuchin enters, going from house to house, a lantern in his hand, looking at the doors.)



Scene 3.VIII.

Cyrano, Christian, a Capuchin.


CYRANO (to the Capuchin):
  What is this game of Diogenes begun anew?

THE CAPUCHIN:
  I am looking for the house of Madame...

CHRISTIAN:
  He is in our way!

THE CAPUCHIN:
  Magdeleine Robin...

CHRISTIAN:
  What does he want?...

CYRANO (showing him an uphill street):
  This way!
  Straight ahead—always straight ahead...

THE CAPUCHIN:
  For your sake, I shall—thank you—
  Say my rosary as far as the great bead.
  (He exits.)

CYRANO:
  Good luck! My good wishes follow your cowl!
  (He goes back down toward Christian.)



Scene 3.IX.

Cyrano, Christian.


CHRISTIAN:
  Obtain that kiss for me!...

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Sooner or later!...

CYRANO:
  That is true!
  It will come, that moment of intoxicated rapture
  When your mouths will move toward one another, because
  Of your blond mustache and her rosy lip!
  (To himself):
  I would rather it were because of...
  (The sound of the shutters reopening; Christian hides beneath the balcony.)



Scene 3.X.

Cyrano, Christian, Roxane.


ROXANE (coming forward onto the balcony):
  Is that you?
  We were speaking of... of... a...

CYRANO:
  Kiss! The word is sweet.
  I do not see why your lip dares not speak it;
  If the word already burns it, what will the deed be like?
  Do not make it into something terrifying:
  Did you not just now, almost imperceptibly,
  Leave jesting behind and glide without alarm
  From smiles to sighs, and from sighs to tears!
  Glide a little farther in the same imperceptible way:
  From tears to a kiss there is only a shiver!

ROXANE:
  Be silent!

CYRANO:
  A kiss—when all is said and done, what is it?
  An oath made from a little nearer, a promise
  More precise, a confession seeking confirmation,
  A rosy dot placed upon the i of the verb to love;
  It is a secret that takes the mouth for an ear,
  An instant of infinity that makes the sound of a bee,
  A communion with the taste of a flower,
  A way of breathing in each other's hearts a little,
  And of tasting each other's souls a little at the edge of the lips!

THE DUENNA (in rapture):
  Oh, look! The knocker is wrapped in cloths!...
  (To the knocker):
  They have gagged you so that your metal
  Will not disturb the lovely speeches—little brute!
  (She lifts it with infinite care and knocks softly.)

ROXANE (seeing that the door is being opened):
  Let us go in!...
  (From the threshold, to Cyrano):
  If Christian comes, as I presume he will,
  Let him wait for me!

CYRANO (quickly, as she is about to disappear):
  Ah!...
  (She turns around):
  On what, as is your custom,
  Do you intend to question him today?

ROXANE:
  On...

CYRANO (quickly):
  On?

ROXANE:
  But you will keep silent about it!

CYRANO:
  Like a wall.

ROXANE:
  On nothing!... I shall tell him: Go on! Set forth with no rein!
  Improvise. Speak of love. Be splendid!

CYRANO (smiling):
  Good.

ROXANE:
  Hush!...

CYRANO:
  Hush!...

ROXANE:
  Not a word!...
  (She goes inside and closes the door again.)

CYRANO (bowing to her once the door is closed):
  With thanks to you.
  (The door opens again and Roxane puts her head out.)

ROXANE:
  He might prepare himself!...

CYRANO:
  Good heavens, no!...

BOTH TOGETHER:
  Hush!...
  (The door closes.)

CYRANO (calling):
  Christian!



Scene 3.IV.

Cyrano, Christian.


CYRANO:
  I know everything we need. Ready thy memory.
  Here is the chance to cover oneself with glory.
  Let us waste no time. Do not look so sullen.
  Quickly, let us go back to thy lodgings; I am going to teach thee...

CHRISTIAN:
  No!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  No! I am waiting for Roxane here.

CYRANO:
  What fit of madness
  Has seized thee? Come quickly and learn...

CHRISTIAN:
  No, I tell thee!
  I am weary of borrowing my letters, my speeches,
  And of playing this part, and of always trembling!...
  It was all very well at first! But I feel that she loves me!
  Thank you. I am no longer afraid. I shall speak for myself.

CYRANO:
  Indeed!

CHRISTIAN:
  And who tells thee that I would not know how?...
  I am not so stupid, after all! Thou shalt see!
  But, my dear fellow, thy lessons have been useful to me.
  I shall know how to speak alone! And, by all the devils,
  I shall certainly always know how to take her in my arms!...
  (Catching sight of Roxane, who is coming out of Clomire’s house again):
  —It is she! Cyrano, no, do not leave me!

CYRANO (bowing to him):
  Speak by yourself, sir.
  (He disappears behind the garden wall.)



Scene 3.V.

Christian, Roxane, several précieuses and their admirers, and the duenna,
for a moment.


ROXANE (leaving Clomire’s house with a company from which she now
  parts, amid curtsies and bows):
  Barthénoïde!—Alcandre!—Grémione!...

THE DUENNA (in despair):
  We missed the discourse on the Tender!
  (She goes into Roxane’s house.)

ROXANE (still taking her leave):
  Urimédonte!... Farewell!...
  (They all bow to Roxane, bow to one another again, part, and
  go off down different streets. Roxane sees Christian):
  It is you!...
  (She goes to him):
  Evening is falling.
  Wait. They are far away. The air is mild. Not a passerby.
  Let us sit down. Speak. I am listening.

CHRISTIAN (sitting beside her on the bench. A silence):
  I love you.

ROXANE (closing her eyes):
  Yes, speak to me of love.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee.

ROXANE:
  That is the theme.
  Embroider, embroider.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love you...

ROXANE:
  Embroider!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee so much.

ROXANE:
  No doubt! And then?

CHRISTIAN:
  And then... I should be so happy
  If you loved me!—Tell me, Roxane, that thou lovest me!

ROXANE (pouting):
  You offer me gruel when I had hoped for creams!
  Tell me somewhat how you love me?...

CHRISTIAN:
  Why... very much.

ROXANE:
  Oh!... Unlabyrinth your feelings!

CHRISTIAN (having drawn closer and devouring the fair nape of her neck with his eyes):
  Thy neck!
  I should like to kiss it!...

ROXANE:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love thee!

ROXANE (about to rise):
  Again!

CHRISTIAN (quickly, holding her back):
  No! I do not love thee!

ROXANE (sitting down again):
  That is fortunate!

CHRISTIAN:
  I adore thee!

ROXANE (rising and moving away):
  Oh!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes... I am becoming foolish!

ROXANE (dryly):
  And that displeases me!
  As it would displease me if you became ugly.

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

ROXANE:
  Go and gather up your fugitive eloquence!

CHRISTIAN:
  I...

ROXANE:
  You love me, I know. Farewell.
  (She goes toward the house.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Not yet!
  I shall tell you...

ROXANE (pushing the door open to go inside):
  That you adore me... yes, I know.
  No! No! Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  But I...
  (She shuts the door in his face.)

CYRANO (who returned a moment ago without being seen):
  It is a success.



Scene 3.VI.

Christian, Cyrano, the pages, for a moment.


CHRISTIAN:
  Help!

CYRANO:
  No, sir.

CHRISTIAN:
  I shall die if I do not regain
  Her favor this very instant...

CYRANO:
  And how the devil can I
  Teach you this very instant?...

CHRISTIAN (seizing his arm):
  Oh! There, look, see!
  (The balcony window has lit up.)

CYRANO (moved):
  Her window!

CHRISTIAN (shouting):
  I am going to die!

CYRANO:
  Lower your voice!

CHRISTIAN (very softly):
  Die!...

CYRANO:
  The night is dark...

CHRISTIAN:
  Well?

CYRANO:
  It can be repaired.
  You do not deserve it... Get over there, wretch!
  There, in front of the balcony! I shall stand underneath...
  And prompt thee with thy words.

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

CYRANO:
  Be quiet!

THE PAGES (reappearing at the back, to Cyrano):
  Hey!

CYRANO:
  Hush!...
  (He signals to them to speak softly.)

FIRST PAGE (in a half whisper):
  We have just serenaded
  Montfleury!...

CYRANO (softly, quickly):
  Go and lie in ambush,
  One at that street corner and the other at this one;
  And if some troublesome passerby comes this way,
  Play a tune!

SECOND PAGE:
  What sort of tune, Mr. Gassendist?

CYRANO:
  A merry one for a woman, and a sad one for a man!
  (The pages disappear, one at each street corner.—To Christian):
  Call her!

CHRISTIAN:
  Roxane!

CYRANO (picking up pebbles and throwing them at the windowpanes):
  Wait! A few pebbles.



Scene VII.

LISE (to Cyrano, who, passing in front of her counter, has absentmindedly squeezed her hand):
  What is the matter with your hand?

CYRANO:
  Nothing. A sword cut.

RAGUENEAU:
  Did you run into some danger?

CYRANO:
  No danger at all.

LISE (threatening him with her finger):
  I believe you are lying!

CYRANO:
  Would my nose be twitching?
  It would have to be for an enormous lie!
  (Changing his tone):
  I am expecting someone here. Unless it is under the elm,
  You will leave us alone.

RAGUENEAU:
  But I cannot;
  My versifiers will be coming...

LISE (ironically):
  For their first meal.

CYRANO:
  Thou wilt send them away when I give thee the sign...
  The time?

RAGUENEAU:
  Ten past six.

CYRANO (sitting down nervously at Ragueneau’s table and taking some paper):
  A pen?...

RAGUENEAU (offering him the one he has behind his ear):
  A swan’s quill.

A MUSKETEER (magnificently mustachioed, enters and speaks in a stentorian voice):
  Greetings!
  (Lise quickly goes upstage toward him.)

CYRANO (turning around):
  What is that?

RAGUENEAU:
  A friend of my wife’s. A fearsome
  Warrior—so he says!...

CYRANO (taking up the pen again and motioning Ragueneau away):
  Hush!...
  Write—fold it—
  (To himself):
  Give it to her—flee...
  (Throwing down the pen):
  Coward!... But may I die
  If I dare speak to her, say a single word to her...
  (To Ragueneau):
  The time?

RAGUENEAU:
  A quarter past six!...

CYRANO (striking his chest):
  —a single word of all those I have in here!
  Whereas, by writing...
  (He takes up the pen again):
  Very well! Let us write it,
  That love letter I have composed within myself
  And composed again a hundred times, so that it is ready,
  And, placing my soul beside the paper,
  All I have to do is simply copy it out.
  (He writes.—Behind the glass panes of the door, thin, hesitant silhouettes can be seen moving about.)



Scene 2.IV.

Ragueneau, Lise, the musketeer, Cyrano, writing at the small table,
the poets, dressed in black, their stockings sagging, covered in mud.


LISE (entering, to Ragueneau):
  Here are your mud-spattered lot!

FIRST POET (entering, to Ragueneau):
  Fellow craftsman!...

SECOND POET (likewise, shaking his hands):
  Dear fellow craftsman!

THIRD POET:
  Eagle of pastry cooks!
  (He sniffs):
  It smells good in your eyrie,

FOURTH POET:
  O Phoebus of the Roasting Spit!

FIFTH POET:
  Apollo, master cook!...

RAGUENEAU (surrounded, embraced, shaken):
  How quickly one feels at ease with them!...

FIRST POET:
  We were delayed by the crowd gathered
  At the Porte de Nesle!...

SECOND POET:
  Slashed open by sword blows,
  Eight bloodied villains adorned the cobblestones!

CYRANO (raising his head for a moment):
  Eight?... Well, I thought there were seven.
  (He resumes his letter.)

RAGUENEAU (to Cyrano):
  Do you know
  The hero of the fight?

CYRANO (casually):
  I?... No!

LISE (to the musketeer):
  And you?

THE MUSKETEER (twirling his mustache):
  Perhaps!

CYRANO (writing, aside—he can be heard murmuring from time to time):
  I love you...

FIRST POET:
  One man alone, they said, managed to put
  A whole band to flight!...

SECOND POET:
  Oh! It was a curious sight!
  Pikes and clubs littered the ground!...

CYRANO (writing):
  ...your eyes...

THIRD POET:
  Hats were found as far away as the Quai des Orfèvres!

FIRST POET:
  Good heavens! He must have been a savage brute...

CYRANO (doing the same):
  ...your lips...

FIRST POET:
  A fearsome giant, the author of these exploits!

CYRANO (doing the same):
  ...And I faint with fear when I see you.

SECOND POET (snatching a cake):
  What new thing hast thou put into verse, Ragueneau?

CYRANO (doing the same):
  ...he who loves you...
  (He stops just as he is about to sign, and rises, putting his letter into his doublet):
  No need to sign it. I shall give it to her myself.

RAGUENEAU (to the second poet):
  I have put a recipe into verse.

THIRD POET (settling himself beside a tray of cream puffs):
  Let us hear these verses!

FOURTH POET (looking at a brioche he has taken):
  This brioche has put its cap on crooked.
  (He knocks its cap off with one bite.)

FIRST POET:
  This gingerbread follows the famished rhymester
  With its almond-shaped eyes and angelica eyebrows!
  (He snatches the piece of gingerbread.)

SECOND POET:
  We are listening.

THIRD POET (lightly squeezing a cream puff between his fingers):
  This puff is drooling cream. It is laughing.

SECOND POET (biting directly into the large pastry lyre):
  For the first time, the Lyre is feeding me!

RAGUENEAU (who has prepared himself to recite, cleared his throat, adjusted his cap, and struck a pose):
  A recipe in verse...

SECOND POET (to the first, nudging him with his elbow):
  Art thou breakfasting?

FIRST POET (to the second):
  Thou art dining!

RAGUENEAU:
  How to make almond tartlets.
  Beat, until they are frothy,
  Several eggs;
  Into their froth incorporate
  The juice of a choice citron;
  Pour into it
  Good sweet almond milk;
  Put custard pastry
  Along the sides
  Of tartlet molds;
  With a nimble finger, glaze
  The edges with apricot;
  Drop by tiny drop
  Your froth into these wells; then
  Let these wells
  Go into the oven, and, golden,
  Emerging in merry little troops,
  These are the
  Almond tartlets!

THE POETS (their mouths full):
  Exquisite! Delicious!

A POET (choking):
  Homph!
  (They move upstage, eating.)

CYRANO (who has been watching, comes toward Ragueneau):
  Lulled by thy voice,
  Dost thou not see how they are stuffing themselves?

RAGUENEAU (more quietly, with a smile):
  I see it...
  Without looking, for fear it might disturb them;
  And reciting my verses like this gives me double pleasure,
  Since I satisfy a sweet weakness of mine
  While letting those who have not eaten eat!

CYRANO (slapping him on the shoulder):
  Thou—I like thee!...
  (Ragueneau goes to rejoin his friends. Cyrano watches him go, then, somewhat abruptly):
  Ho there, Lise?
  (Lise, in tender conversation with the musketeer, starts and comes downstage toward Cyrano):
  This captain...
  Is he laying siege to you?

CHRISTIAN:
  What did you say?

ROXANE:
  So much the worse for you if I run these risks!
  It is your letters that have intoxicated me! Ah! just think
  How many you have written me over the past month,
  And always more beautiful!

CHRISTIAN:
  What! For a few little
  Love letters...

ROXANE:
  Be quiet! You cannot know!
  My God, I adored you, it is true, ever since one evening,
  In a voice I had not known you possessed, beneath my window,
  Your soul began to make itself known...
  Well! Your letters, you see, for the past month,
  Have been as though all the while I were hearing it, your voice
  From that evening, so tender, and which enfolds you!
  So much the worse for you, I hasten here. The wise Penelope
  Would not have remained beneath her roof embroidering,
  Had Lord Ulysses written like you;
  But to join him, as mad as Helen,
  She too would have sent her balls of wool packing!...

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

ROXANE:
  I read, I reread, I swooned,
  I was yours. Each of those little sheets
  Was like a petal blown from your soul.
  In every word of those letters of flame one feels
  Powerful, sincere love...

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah! Sincere and powerful?
  One can feel that, Roxane?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! One certainly can!

CHRISTIAN:
  And you have come?...

ROXANE:
  I have come (oh, my Christian, my master!
  You would raise me up if I wished to kneel
  At your feet, so it is my soul that I lay there,
  And you will never be able to raise it again!)
  I have come to ask your forgiveness (and it is indeed the hour
  To ask forgiveness, since we may die!)
  For having at first, in my frivolity,
  Insulted you by loving you for your beauty alone!

CHRISTIAN (in terror):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  And later, my friend, less frivolous,
  —A bird that hops before it fully takes flight—
  Your beauty holding me back, your soul drawing me onward,
  I loved you for both together!...

CHRISTIAN:
  And now?

ROXANE:
  Well! At last, you yourself have triumphed over yourself,
  And now it is only for your soul that I love you!

CHRISTIAN (recoiling):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  Then be happy. For to be loved
  Only for that in which one is costumed for a moment
  Must torture an eager and noble heart;
  But your dear mind effaces your face,
  And the beauty through which you pleased me at first,
  Now I see more clearly... and I no longer see it!

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh!...

ROXANE:
  Do you still doubt such a victory?...

CHRISTIAN (painfully):
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  I understand, you cannot believe
  In this love?...

CHRISTIAN:
  I do not want this love!
  I want to be loved more simply for...

ROXANE:
  For
  What women have loved in you until now?
  Then let yourself be loved in a better way!

CHRISTIAN:
  No! It was better before!

ROXANE:
  Ah! You understand nothing about it!
  It is now that I love better, that I love truly!
  It is what makes you yourself, do you hear me, that I adore!
  And less brilliant...

CHRISTIAN:
  Be quiet!

ROXANE:
  I would love you still!
  If all your beauty suddenly flew away...

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh! Do not say that!

ROXANE:
  Yes, I do say it!

CHRISTIAN:
  What? Ugly?

ROXANE:
  Ugly! I swear it!

CHRISTIAN:
  God!

ROXANE:
  And is your joy profound?

CHRISTIAN (in a stifled voice):
  Yes...

ROXANE:
  What is the matter with you?

CHRISTIAN (gently pushing her away):
  Nothing. Two words to say: one second...

ROXANE:
  But?...

CHRISTIAN (showing her a group of cadets at the back):
  My love took you away from those poor fellows:
  Go and smile upon them a little, since they are going to die... go!

ROXANE (moved):
  Dear Christian!...
  (She goes upstage toward the Gascons, who respectfully crowd around
  her.)



Scene 4.IX.

Christian, Cyrano; at the back, Roxane conversing with Carbon and several cadets.


CHRISTIAN (calling toward Cyrano's tent):
  Cyrano?

CYRANO (reappearing, armed for battle):
  What is it? You are deathly pale!

CHRISTIAN:
  She no longer loves me!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is you she loves!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  She loves only my soul now!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes!
  So it is indeed you she loves—and you love her too!

CYRANO:
  I?

CHRISTIAN:
  I know it.

CYRANO:
  It is true.

CHRISTIAN:
  Like a madman.

CYRANO:
  More than that.

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Look at my face!

CHRISTIAN:
  She would love me ugly!

CYRANO:
  She told you that!

CHRISTIAN:
  Just now!

CYRANO:
  Ah! I am very glad she told you that!
  But come, come, do not believe such a mad thing!
  —My God, I am glad she thought
  To say it—but come, do not take her at her word;
  Come, do not become ugly: she would hold it against me too much!

CHRISTIAN:
  That is what I want to see!

CYRANO:
  No, no!

CHRISTIAN:
  Let her choose!
  You are going to tell her everything!

CYRANO:
  No, no! Not that torture.

CHRISTIAN:
  Should I destroy your happiness because I am handsome?
  It is too unjust!

CYRANO:
  And should I send yours to the grave
  Because, thanks to the accident of birth,
  I have the gift of expressing... what you perhaps feel?

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her everything!

CYRANO:
  He persists in tempting me; it is wrong!

CHRISTIAN:
  I am weary of carrying a rival within myself!

CYRANO:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  Our union—without witnesses—clandestine,
  —Can be broken—if we survive!

CYRANO:
  He persists!...

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes, I want to be loved for myself, or not at all!
  —I am going to see what they are doing, there! I will go to the far end
  Of the outpost; I will return: speak, and let her prefer
  One of the two of us!

CYRANO:
  It will be you!

CHRISTIAN:
  But... I hope so!
  (He calls):
  Roxane!

“Germain,” little Marie replied, “is it settled, then, that you love me?”

“It angers thee, I know, but it is not my fault. If thou couldst change thy mind, I should be only too happy, and no doubt I do not deserve that it should be so. Come, look at me, Marie; am I really so frightful?”

“No, Germain,” she replied with a smile, “you are handsomer than I am.”

“Do not mock me; look at me indulgently. I have not yet lost either a hair or a tooth. My eyes tell thee that I love thee. Look into my eyes, then; it is written there, and every girl knows how to read that kind of writing.”

Marie looked into Germain’s eyes with her playful assurance; then, all at once, she turned her head away and began to tremble.

“Ah, my God! I frighten thee,” said Germain. “Thou lookest at me as though I were the farmer of Les Ormeaux. Do not fear me, I beg thee; it hurts me too much. I shall not say wicked things to thee, not I; I shall not kiss thee against thy will, and when thou wantest me to go away, thou needst only show me the door. Come, must I go out so that thou wilt stop trembling?”

Marie held out her hand to the plowman, but without turning her head away from where it was bowed toward the hearth, and without saying a word.

“I understand,” said Germain. “Thou pitiest me, for thou art good; thou art sorry to make me unhappy. But still, thou canst not love me?”

“Why do you say such things to me, Germain?” little Marie replied at last. “Do you mean to make me cry?”

“Poor little girl, thou hast a good heart, I know; but thou dost not love me, and thou hidest thy face from me because thou art afraid to let me see thy displeasure and thy repugnance. And I do not even dare to clasp thy hand! In the woods, when my son was asleep and thou wert asleep too, I nearly kissed thee very softly. But I would have died of shame rather than ask it of thee, and I suffered as much that night as a man who was being burned over a slow fire. Since then, I have dreamed of thee every night. Ah, how I kissed thee, Marie! But thou, all that time, wert sleeping without dreaming. And now, dost thou know what I think? It is that if thou wert to turn around and look at me with eyes like those I have for thee, and if thou wert to bring thy face close to mine, I believe I should fall down dead with joy. And thou, thou thinkest that if such a thing happened to thee, thou wouldst die of anger and shame!”

Germain spoke as though in a dream, without hearing what he was saying. Little Marie was still trembling; but as he was trembling even more, he no longer noticed it. All at once she turned around; she was in tears and looked at him reproachfully. The poor plowman thought this was the final blow, and, without waiting for her judgment, he rose to leave; but the young girl stopped him by putting both arms around him and, hiding her head against his breast, said to him between sobs:

“Ah, Germain, have you really not guessed that I love you?”

Germain would have gone mad if his son, who was looking for him and who came galloping into the cottage astride a stick, with his little sister riding behind him and whipping this imaginary steed with a willow switch, had not brought him back to himself. I


THE COUNTRY WEDDING


Here ends the story of Germain’s marriage, just as he told it to me himself—the fine plowman that he is! I beg thy pardon, friendly reader, for not having known how to translate it better for thee; for the ancient and artless speech of the peasants of the region that I _sing_ (as they used to say in former times) truly requires translation. Those people speak too much French for us, and since Rabelais and Montaigne, the progress of the language has caused us to lose many old riches. So it is with all progress; one must resign oneself to it. Yet it is still a pleasure to hear these picturesque idioms prevailing upon the old soil of central France, all the more because they are the true expression of the mockingly placid and pleasantly fluent character of those who use them. Touraine has preserved a certain precious number of patriarchal turns of phrase. But Touraine became greatly civilized during and after the Renaissance. It became covered with châteaux, roads, foreigners, and activity. Berry has remained stationary, and I believe that, after Brittany and a few provinces in the extreme south of France, it is the most _preserved_ region to be found at the present time. Certain customs are so strange, so curious, that I hope to amuse thee for another moment, dear reader, if thou wilt allow me to recount in detail a country wedding—for example, Germain’s, which I had the pleasure of attending some years ago.

For alas! everything is passing away. Merely in the time that I have been alive, more change has taken place in the ideas and customs of my village than had been seen during the centuries before the Revolution. Already half of the Celtic, pagan, or medieval ceremonies that I still saw in full vigor in my childhood have vanished. Another year or two, perhaps, and the railways will carry their level across our deep valleys, bearing away, with the speed of lightning, our ancient traditions and our marvelous legends.

It was winter, around carnival time, the season of the year when it is fitting and proper among us to hold weddings. UNDER THE STARS


“This time I give up!” said Germain, stamping his foot. “Someone has cast a spell on us, that is certain, and we shall not get out of here until broad daylight. This place must be bedeviled.”

“It is done; here is the bed, and a few pricks are not saber cuts,” replied the brave little girl.

She once again set about putting little Pierre to bed. This time he was so sound asleep that he noticed nothing at all of this new journey. Germain put so much wood on the fire that the whole forest glowed with it all around; but little Marie could go no farther, and although she complained of nothing, her legs could no longer support her. She was pale, and her teeth were chattering with cold and weakness. Germain took her in his arms to warm her; and anxiety, compassion, and impulses of irresistible tenderness, taking possession of his heart, silenced his senses. His tongue was loosened as though by a miracle, and, all shame gone, he said:

“Marie, I like you, and I am very unhappy that you do not like me. If you were willing to accept me as your husband, neither father-in-law, nor parents, nor neighbors, nor advice could prevent me from giving myself to you. I know that you would make my children happy, that you would teach them to respect their mother’s memory, and, with my conscience at peace, I could satisfy my heart. I have always felt affection for you, and now I feel so much in love that, if you asked me to spend my whole life doing your every wish, I would swear to do so this very moment. See, I beg you, how I love you, and try to forget my age. Consider that it is a false notion people have when they think that a man of thirty is old. Besides, I am only twenty-eight! A young girl is afraid of being criticized if she takes a man ten or twelve years older than she is, because that is not the custom of the region; but I have heard it said that in other regions people pay no attention to that; that, on the contrary, they prefer to give a young woman, as her support, a sensible man whose mettle has been well tested rather than a young fellow who may go astray and, though believed to be a good sort, turn into a good-for-nothing. Besides, years do not always determine age. It depends on the strength and health one has. When a man is worn out by too much work and hardship, or by bad conduct, he is old before he is twenty-five. “Yes, I am, Germain; I hear you perfectly well,” little Marie replied, “but I am thinking about what my mother has always told me: that a woman of sixty is much to be pitied when her husband is seventy or seventy-five and can no longer work to support her. “Parents are right to say that, I agree, Marie,” Germain resumed; “but then they would sacrifice all the years of youth, which are the best, to worrying about what one will become at an age when one is no longer good for anything and it makes no difference whether one ends in one way or another. Besides, I shall love you so much, you see, that it will keep me from growing old. They say that when a man is happy, he keeps well, and I know that I am younger than Bastien when it comes to loving you; for he does not love you—he is too stupid, too childish to understand how pretty and good you are, and how worthy you are of being sought after. Come, Marie, do not hate me; I am not a bad man. I made my Catherine happy; before God, on her deathbed, she said that she had never had anything from me but happiness, and she urged me to marry again. Germain yielded, and the handsome trio dashed through the ranks at the triumphant gallop of the _Gray Mare_.

And indeed, although the people of Saint-Chartier were great mockers and somewhat given to teasing the neighboring parishes that had gathered in theirs, it did not occur to them to laugh when they saw so handsome a bridegroom, so pretty a bride, and a child who would have been the envy of a king’s wife. Little Pierre had a complete suit of cornflower-blue cloth, and a red waistcoat so smart and so short that it scarcely reached below his chin. The village tailor had made the armholes so tight that he could not bring his two little arms together. And how proud he was! He had a round hat with a black-and-gold band, and a peacock feather jutting boldly from a tuft of guinea-fowl feathers. A bouquet of flowers larger than his head covered his shoulder, and its ribbons floated down to his feet. The hemp-dresser, who was also the local barber and wigmaker, had cut his hair in a circle by covering his head with a bowl and trimming off everything that protruded, an infallible method for ensuring an even cut. Dressed up in this fashion, the poor child was assuredly less poetic than with his long hair blowing in the wind and his sheepskin in the manner of Saint John the Baptist; but he did not think so, and everyone admired him, saying that he looked like a little man. His beauty triumphed over everything; and over what, indeed, would the incomparable beauty of childhood not triumph?

His little sister Solange wore, for the first time in her life, a bonnet instead of the printed-cotton cap worn by little girls until the age of two or three. And what a bonnet! Taller and broader than the poor little thing’s whole body. And how beautiful she thought herself! She did not dare turn her head and held herself perfectly stiff, thinking that people would take her for the bride.

As for little Sylvain, he was still in a gown, and, asleep on his grandmother’s lap, he had scarcely any notion of what a wedding was.

Germain looked lovingly at his children, and upon arriving at the town hall, he said to his betrothed:

“Look, Marie, I arrive here a little happier than on the day when I brought you home from the woods of Chanteloube, believing that you would never love me; I took you in my arms to set you on the ground, just as I do now; but I thought that we would never again find ourselves together on the poor good Gray Mare with this child on our knees. Look, I love you so much, I love these poor little ones so much, I am so happy that you love me, and that you love them, and that my parents love you, and I love your mother and my friends and everyone so much today that I wish I had three or four hearts to hold it all. Truly, one is too little to house so much affection and so much happiness! It almost gives me a pain in my stomach.”

There was a crowd at the doors of the town hall and the church to look at the pretty bride. Why should we not describe her attire? It suited her so well! Her bonnet of sheer muslin, embroidered all over, had lappets trimmed with _rientelle_ lace. In those days peasant women did not permit themselves to show a single hair; and although beneath their bonnets they conceal magnificent heads of hair wound in white cotton ribbons to support the headdress, even today it would be considered indecent and shameful to appear before men bareheaded. Nevertheless, they now permit themselves to leave a narrow band of hair visible across the forehead, which greatly enhances their beauty. But I regret the classical headdress of my day: that white lace lying directly against the skin possessed a quality of ancient chastity that seemed to me more solemn, and when a face was beautiful framed in that way, its beauty had a charm and artless majesty that nothing can express.

Little Marie still wore that headdress, and her forehead was so white and pure that it defied the whiteness of the linen to make it look dark. Although she had not closed her eyes all night, the morning air, and above all the inward joy of a soul as limpid as the sky, together with a little secret ardor, restrained by adolescent modesty, brought to her cheeks a radiance as sweet as peach blossom in the first rays of April.

Her white kerchief, chastely crossed over her breast, revealed only the delicate contours of a neck rounded like a turtledove’s; her jacket of fine myrtle-green cloth outlined her small waist, which seemed perfect but was yet to grow and develop, for she was not seventeen. She wore a pansy-purple silk apron with a bib, which our village women were wrong to do away with and which lent so much elegance and modesty to the bosom. Today they display their kerchiefs with greater pride, but their attire no longer possesses that delicate bloom of ancient chasteness that made them resemble Holbein virgins. They are more coquettish, more graceful. In former times, good style consisted of a kind of severe stiffness that made their rare smiles deeper and more ideal.

At the offertory, Germain placed in his betrothed’s hand, according to custom, the _treizain_, that is, thirteen silver coins. He slipped onto her finger a silver ring, of a form unchanged for centuries, but which has now been replaced by the _gold wedding band_. On leaving the church, Marie said softly to him:

“Is it really the ring I wished for? The one I asked you for, Germain?”

“Yes,” he replied, “the one my Catherine wore on her finger when she died. It is the same ring for both my marriages.”

She once again set about putting little Pierre to bed; this time he was so sound asleep that he noticed nothing at all of this new journey. Germain put so much wood on the fire that the whole forest shone with it all around; but little Marie could bear no more, and although she complained of nothing, she could no longer stand on her legs. She was pale, and her teeth were chattering from cold and weakness. Germain took her in his arms to warm her; and anxiety, compassion, and impulses of irresistible tenderness, taking possession of his heart, silenced his senses. His tongue was loosened as if by a miracle, and all shame fell away:

“Marie,” he said to her, “thou pleasest me, and I am very unhappy not to please thee. If thou wouldst accept me as thy husband, there would be neither father-in-law, nor parents, nor neighbors, nor advice that could prevent me from giving myself to thee. I know that thou wouldst make my children happy, that thou wouldst teach them to respect their mother’s memory, and, with my conscience at rest, I could satisfy my heart. I have always felt affection for thee, and now I feel so much in love that if thou askedst me to do thy every bidding all my life, I would swear it to thee this very hour. See, I beg thee, how I love thee, and try to forget my age. Think that it is a false notion people have when they believe that a man of thirty is old. Besides, I am only twenty-eight! A young girl fears being criticized if she takes a man ten or twelve years older than herself, because that is not the custom of the region; but I have heard it said that in other regions they pay no attention to that; that, on the contrary, they prefer to give a young woman, as her support, a sensible man of well-proven courage rather than a young fellow who may go astray and, though thought a good sort, turn into a worthless rascal. Besides, years do not always make age. It depends on the strength and health one has. When a man is worn out by too much work and hardship, or by bad conduct, he is old before twenty-five. Whereas I... But thou art not listening to me, Marie.”

“Indeed I am, Germain; I hear you clearly,” little Marie replied, “but I am thinking of what my mother has always told me: that a woman of sixty is much to be pitied when her husband is seventy or seventy-five and can no longer work to feed her. He becomes infirm, and she must care for him at the age when she herself would begin to have great need of care and rest. That is how one ends up dying on straw.”

“Parents are right to say that, I admit it, Marie,” Germain resumed; “but then they would sacrifice all of youth, which is the best time, to foreseeing what one will become at an age when one is no longer good for anything and when it makes no difference whether one ends one way or another. But I am in no danger of starving in my old age. I am in a position to save something, since, living with my wife’s parents, I work a great deal and spend nothing. Besides, I shall love thee so much, dost thou see, that it will keep me from growing old. They say that when a man is happy, he keeps well, and I feel sure that I am younger than Bastien when it comes to loving thee; for he does not love thee: he is too stupid, too much of a child to understand how pretty and good thou art, and how deserving of being sought after. Come, Marie, do not detest me; I am not a wicked man. I made my Catherine happy; before God, on her deathbed, she said that she had never received anything from me but happiness, and she urged me to marry again. It seems that her spirit spoke this evening to her child, just as he was falling asleep. Didst thou not hear what he was saying? And how his little mouth trembled while his eyes gazed upward at something we could not see! He saw his mother, be sure of it, and it was she who made him say that he wanted thee to take her place.”

“Germain,” Marie replied, utterly astonished and thoughtful, “you speak honorably, and everything you say is true. I am sure I would do well to love you, if that did not displease your parents too much; but what would you have me do about it? My heart is not inclined toward you. I am very fond of you, but although your age does not make you unattractive, it frightens me. It seems to me that you are something to me like an uncle or a godfather; that I owe you respect, and that there would be times when you would treat me like a little girl rather than like your wife and your equal. In short, my companions might make fun of me, and although it is foolish to pay attention to that, I think I would feel ashamed and a little sad on my wedding day.”

“Those are a child’s reasons; thou speakest exactly like a child, Marie!”

“Well, yes, I am a child,” she said, “and that is why I fear a man who is too sensible. You can plainly see that I am too young for you, since already you reproach me for speaking without reason! I cannot have more reason than my age allows.”

“Alas, my God, how greatly I am to be pitied for being so clumsy and expressing what I think so badly!” Germain exclaimed. “Marie, you do not love me; that is the fact of it. You find me too simple and too dull. If you loved me a little, you would not see my faults so clearly. But you do not love me, that is all!”

“Well, it is not my fault,” she replied, a little hurt that he was no longer addressing her as ‘thou’; “I am doing my best as I listen to you, but the more I try, the less I can get it into my head that we ought to be husband and wife.”

Germain did not reply. He put his head in both his hands, and it was impossible for little Marie to know whether he was weeping, sulking, or asleep. She was a little worried to see him so gloomy and not to be able to guess what was passing through his mind; but she did not dare speak to him any further, and as she was too astonished by what had just happened to feel like going back to sleep, she waited impatiently for daylight, still tending the fire and watching over the child, whom Germain appeared no longer to remember. Germain, however, was not asleep; he was not reflecting on his fate, and was making neither courageous resolutions nor plans of seduction. He was suffering; he had a mountain of sorrow upon his heart. He wished he were dead. Everything seemed bound to turn out badly for him, and if he had been able to weep, he would not have done so by halves. But there was a little anger against himself mingled with his grief, and he was choking, unable and unwilling to complain.

The irresolution of Oswald's character, increased by his misfortunes, inclined him to fear every irrevocable course. In his uncertainty, he had not even dared to ask Corinne the secret of her name and her fate, and yet his love for her was gaining new strength every day; he never looked at her without emotion; in company, he could scarcely move away, even for an instant, from the place where she was sitting; she did not utter a word that he did not feel; she did not have an instant of sadness or gaiety whose reflection was not depicted on his own countenance. But, even as he admired, even as he loved Corinne, he remembered how ill such a woman accorded with the English way of life, how much she differed from his father's conception of the woman it would be fitting for him to marry; and what he said to Corinne bore the marks of the agitation and constraint that these reflections aroused in him.

Corinne was only too well aware of it; but it would have cost her so much to break with Lord Nelvil that she herself acquiesced in there being no decisive explanation between them; and as there was a certain lack of foresight in her character, she was happy with the present as it was, although it was impossible for her to know what would come of it.

She had withdrawn entirely from society to devote herself to her feelings for Oswald. But at last, wounded by his silence about their future, she resolved to accept an invitation to a ball where her presence was eagerly desired. Nothing is regarded with more indifference in Rome than withdrawing from society and reappearing in it by turns, as it suits one: it is the country where people concern themselves least with what elsewhere is called gossip; everyone does as he pleases without anyone inquiring into it, unless in others one encounters an obstacle to one's love or ambition. The Romans are no more concerned about the conduct of their compatriots than about that of the foreigners who come and go through their city, the meeting place of Europeans. When Lord Nelvil learned that Corinne was going to the ball, he felt vexed. For some time he had thought he saw in her a melancholy disposition that sympathized with his own; all at once she appeared to him keenly preoccupied with dancing, with that talent in which she excelled, and her imagination seemed animated by the prospect of a celebration. Corinne was not a frivolous person, but every day she felt herself more subjugated by her love for Oswald, and she wanted to try to weaken its force. She knew from experience that reflection and sacrifices have less power over passionate natures than distraction does, and she thought that reason consists not in triumphing over oneself according to the rules, but as best one can.

“I must,” she said to Lord Nelvil, who was reproaching her for this intention, “I must nevertheless find out whether there is no one but you left in the world who can fill my life, whether what pleased me formerly can no longer amuse me, and whether the feeling you inspire in me must absorb every other interest and every other thought.”—“So you wish to cease loving me?” Oswald replied.—“No,” Corinne answered; “but only in domestic life can it be sweet to feel oneself thus ruled by a single affection. For me, who need my talents, my wit, my imagination, to sustain the brilliance of the life I have adopted, it hurts me, and hurts me greatly, to love as I love you.”—“So you would not sacrifice to me,” Oswald said to her, “that homage, that glory?”—“What does it matter to you,” Corinne said, “to know whether I would sacrifice them to you! Since we are not destined for one another, you must not forever blight for me the kind of happiness with which I must content myself.” Lord Nelvil did not reply, because, in expressing his feeling, he would also have had to say what design that feeling inspired in him; and his heart did not yet know. He therefore remained silent, sighing, and followed Corinne to the ball, although it cost him a great deal to go there.

It was the first time since his misfortune that he had again seen a large gathering; and the tumult of a celebration produced in him such an impression of sadness that he remained for a long time in a room adjoining the ballroom, his head resting on his hand, without even seeking to watch Corinne dance. He listened to that dance music which, like all music, makes one dream, although it seems intended only for joy. The Count d’Erfeuil arrived, utterly delighted by a ball, a gathering, in short, by a numerous company that reminded him a little of France. “I have done all I could,” he said to Lord Nelvil, “to find some interest in those ruins about which there is so much talk in Rome; I see nothing beautiful in them: admiration for those fragments covered with brambles is a prejudice. I shall give my opinion of them when I return to Paris, for it is time that this enchantment with Italy should end. There is not a monument in Europe still standing whole today that is not worth more than those broken columns, those bas-reliefs blackened by time, which can be admired only by dint of erudition. A pleasure that must be purchased with so much study does not seem to me very keen in itself; for no one needs to grow pale over books in order to be enraptured by the spectacles of Paris.” Lord Nelvil made no reply. The Count d’Erfeuil questioned him again about the impression Rome had made on him. “In the midst of a ball,” Oswald said, “this is hardly the time to speak of it seriously, and you know that I do not know how to speak otherwise.”—“Very well,” the Count d’Erfeuil replied; “I am gayer than you, I admit it; but who knows whether I am not wiser?
