Alas, dear friend, we are going to be separated for a fortnight, perhaps a month! Come, I do thee justice, thou wilt suffer as much as I. But after all, this is the only way to counteract the effect of that anonymous letter; it is not the first my husband has received, and about me, too. Alas! how I used to laugh at them!

The entire purpose of my conduct is to make my husband think that the letter comes from Monsieur Valenod; I do not doubt that he is its author. If thou leavest the house, do not fail to settle in Verrières. I shall arrange matters so that my husband conceives the idea of spending a fortnight there, to prove to the fools that there is no coolness between him and me. Once in Verrières, make friends with everyone, even with the liberals. I know that all those ladies will seek thy company.

Do not go and quarrel with Monsieur Valenod, nor cut off his ears, as thou saidst one day; on the contrary, show him all thy charm. The essential thing is that people in Verrières should believe that thou art going to enter the Valenod household, or some other, to educate the children.

That is something my husband will never tolerate. Even if he should resign himself to it, well! at least thou wilt live in Verrières, and I shall see thee sometimes. My children, who love thee so much, will go to see thee. Great God! I feel that I love my children more because they love thee. What remorse! How will all this end?… I am wandering… At any rate, thou understandest how thou must conduct thyself; be gentle, polite, not disdainful with those coarse people, I beg it of thee on my knees: they are going to be the arbiters of our fate. Do not doubt for an instant that my husband will act toward thee as public opinion dictates to him.

Julien was already cold and haughty. He gave thanks, but in very vague terms that committed him to nothing. Could it really be possible, he said to himself, that I am the natural son of some great lord exiled to our mountains by the terrible Napoleon? At every moment, this idea seemed less improbable to him... My hatred for my father would be proof of it... I would no longer be a monster!

A few days after this monologue, the Fifteenth Hussar Regiment, one of the most brilliant in the army, was drawn up in battle formation on the parade ground at Strasbourg. Monsieur the Chevalier de La Vernaye rode the finest horse in Alsace, which had cost him six thousand francs. He had been commissioned as a lieutenant without ever having been a second lieutenant except on the rolls of a regiment of which he had never heard.

His impassive manner, his stern and almost malicious eyes, his pallor, and his unalterable composure began to establish his reputation from the very first day. Soon afterward, his perfect and measured courtesy, and his skill with pistols and weapons, which he made known without too much affectation, discouraged any thought of joking aloud at his expense. After five or six days of hesitation, the prevailing opinion in the regiment declared itself in his favor. There is everything in this young man, the old, mocking officers said, except youth.

From Strasbourg, Julien wrote to M. Chélan, the former curé of Verrières, who was now approaching the utmost limits of extreme old age.

“You will have learned, with a joy of which I have no doubt, of the events that have led my family to enrich me. Here are five hundred francs, which I beg you to distribute quietly, without any mention of my name, to the unfortunate, poor now as I once was, whom you no doubt assist as you once assisted me.”

       *       *       *       *       *

Julien was intoxicated with ambition and not with vanity; nevertheless, he devoted a great deal of his attention to outward appearance. His horses, his uniforms, and his servants’ liveries were maintained with a correctness that would have done honor to the punctuality of a great English lord. Having been a lieutenant, by favor, for barely two days, he was already calculating that, in order to be commander in chief by the age of thirty at the latest, like all the great generals, he had to be more than a lieutenant at twenty-three. He thought only of glory and of his son.

It was in the midst of the transports of the most unbridled ambition that he was surprised by a young footman from the Hôtel de La Mole, who arrived as a courier.

“Everything is lost,” Mathilde wrote to him, “come as quickly as possible, sacrifice everything, desert if necessary. As soon as you arrive, wait for me in a hired carriage near the small garden gate, at No. ... in the Rue ... I shall come and speak to you; perhaps I shall be able to get you into the garden. Everything is lost, and I fear beyond remedy; rely on me, you will find me devoted and steadfast in adversity. I love you.”

Within a few minutes, Julien obtained leave from the colonel and set out from Strasbourg at full gallop; but the dreadful anxiety consuming him did not allow him to continue traveling in this fashion beyond Metz. He threw himself into a post-chaise; and it was with almost incredible speed that he arrived at the appointed place, near the small garden gate of the Hôtel de La Mole. The gate opened, and at once Mathilde, forgetting all regard for propriety, flung herself into his arms. Fortunately, it was only five in the morning, and the street was still deserted.

“He is said to be the son of a carpenter from our mountains, but I would sooner believe him the natural son of some rich man. I saw him receive an anonymous or pseudonymous letter with a bill of exchange for five hundred francs.”

“Ah! That is Julien Sorel,” said the marquis.

“How do you know his name?” said the astonished abbé; and when he blushed at his own question:

“That is something I shall not tell you,” replied the marquis.

“Well then,” the abbé resumed, “you might try making him your secretary; he has energy and judgment; in short, it is an experiment worth trying.”

“Why not?” said the marquis. “But would he be the sort of man to let the prefect of police or anyone else grease his palm to act as a spy in my house? That is my only objection.”

After Abbé Pirard’s favorable assurances, the marquis took out a thousand-franc note:

“Send this traveling money to Julien Sorel; have him come to me.”

“The habit of living in Paris must indeed, Monsieur le Marquis, produce this illusion in your mind; because you occupy a high social position, you do not know the tyranny that weighs upon us poor provincials, and particularly upon priests who are not friends of the Jesuits. They will not be willing to let Julien Sorel leave; they will know how to cloak themselves in the cleverest pretexts. I shall be told that he is ill, the post will have lost the letters, and so on and so forth.”

“One of these days I shall obtain a letter from the minister to the bishop,” said the marquis.

“I was forgetting a precaution,” said the abbé. “Although this young man was born very low, he has a proud spirit; he will be of no use whatsoever in your affairs if his pride is alarmed; you would make him stupid.”

“I like that,” said the marquis. “I shall make him my son’s companion; will that suffice?”

Some time later, Julien received a letter in an unfamiliar hand and bearing the Châlon postmark. In it he found a payment order upon a merchant in Besançon and instructions to go to Paris without delay. The letter was signed with an assumed name, but upon opening it Julien had started: a large blot of ink had fallen in the middle of the thirteenth word. It was the signal he had agreed upon with Abbé Pirard.

“Do speak more quietly,” she said to him with a frightened look. Julien was trying to recall the phrases from an odd volume of the _New Heloise_ that he had found at Vergy. His memory served him well; for ten minutes he had been reciting the _New Heloise_ to a delighted Mademoiselle Amanda, and he was happy in his boldness, when suddenly the beautiful woman from Franche-Comté assumed an icy air. One of her lovers had appeared at the door of the café.

He approached the counter, whistling and swaggering his shoulders; he looked at Julien. At once, Julien’s imagination, always running to extremes, was filled with nothing but thoughts of a duel. He turned very pale, pushed his cup away, put on a confident expression, and looked at his rival very attentively. As this rival lowered his head while familiarly pouring himself a glass of brandy at the counter, Amanda ordered Julien with a glance to lower his eyes. He obeyed and, for two minutes, remained motionless in his place, pale, resolute, and thinking only of what was about to happen; he was truly admirable at that moment. The rival had been surprised by Julien’s eyes; having swallowed his glass of brandy in one gulp, he said a word to Amanda, put both hands into the side pockets of his heavy overcoat, and approached a billiard table, puffing and looking at Julien. Julien rose, carried away by anger; but he did not know how to go about being insolent. He put down his little bundle and, with the most swaggering air he could manage, walked toward the billiard table.

In vain prudence told him: But with a duel as soon as you arrive in Besançon, your ecclesiastical career is ruined.

What does it matter? It shall not be said that I let an insolent fellow escape me.

Amanda saw his courage; it formed a pretty contrast with the ingenuousness of his manners; in an instant, she preferred him to the tall young man in the overcoat. She rose and, while pretending to be following someone passing in the street with her eyes, quickly came and placed herself between him and the billiard table:

“Take care not to look askance at that gentleman; he is my brother-in-law.”

“What do I care? He looked at me.”

“Do you want to make me unhappy? Of course he looked at you; perhaps he is even going to come and speak to you. I told him that you are a relative of my mother’s and that you have just arrived from Genlis. He is from Franche-Comté and has never gone beyond Dole on the road to Burgundy; so say whatever you like, and do not be afraid.”

Julien was still hesitating; she added very quickly, her imagination as a woman behind a counter supplying her with lies in abundance:

“Of course he looked at you, but that was when he was asking me who you were; he is a man who is boorish with everyone; he did not mean to insult you.”

Julien’s eye followed the supposed brother-in-law; he saw him buy a number in the pool being played at the farther of the two billiard tables. Julien heard his loud voice cry in a threatening tone, “I’ll take the play.” He passed quickly behind Mademoiselle Amanda and took a step toward the billiard table. Amanda seized him by the arm:

“Come and pay me first,” she said to him.

That is fair, thought Julien; she is afraid I shall leave without paying.

Amanda was as agitated as he was and very red; she gave him his change as slowly as she could, all the while repeating to him in a low voice:

“Leave the café this instant, or I shall no longer love you; and yet I love you dearly.”

Julien did leave, but slowly. Is it not my duty, he kept asking himself, to go and stare at that coarse fellow in my turn, puffing as I do so? This uncertainty kept him for an hour on the boulevard in front of the café; he watched to see whether his man would come out. He did not appear, and Julien went away.

He had been in Besançon for only a few hours, and already he had acquired a remorse. The old surgeon-major had once given him, despite his gout, a few fencing lessons; that was all the skill Julien could find to put at the service of his anger. But this difficulty would have been nothing if he had known how to become angry otherwise than by administering a slap in the face; and if it came to fisticuffs, his rival, an enormous man, would have beaten him and then left him there.

For a poor devil like me, Julien said to himself, without protectors and without money, there will not be much difference between a seminary and a prison; I must leave my civilian clothes at some inn, where I shall put my black coat back on. If I ever manage to get out of the seminary for a few hours, I can quite easily put on my civilian clothes and see Mademoiselle Amanda again. This reasoning was excellent; but as Julien passed all the inns, he did not dare enter any of them.

At last, as he passed the Hôtel des Ambassadeurs again, his anxious eyes met those of a stout woman, still fairly young, ruddy, with a happy and cheerful air. He approached her and told her his story.

“Certainly, my pretty little abbé,” the landlady of the Ambassadeurs said to him, “I shall keep your civilian clothes for you and even have them dusted often. At this time of year, it is not wise to leave a woolen coat untouched.” She took a key and herself led him to a room, recommending that he write down a list of what he was leaving.

“Good Lord! How handsome you look like that, Monsieur l’Abbé Sorel,” the stout woman said to him when he came down to the kitchen. “I am going to have a good dinner served to you, and,” she added in a low voice, “it will cost you only twenty sous instead of the fifty everyone else pays; for you must take care of your little nest egg.”

“I have ten louis,” Julien replied with a certain pride.

“Oh, good Lord!” the kind landlady answered in alarm. “Do not speak so loudly; there are many bad characters in Besançon. They will steal that from you in no time. Above all, never go into the cafés; they are full of bad characters.”

“Really!” said Julien, to whom this remark gave food for thought.

“Never go anywhere but here; I shall have coffee made for you. Remember that you will always find a friend here and a good dinner for twenty sous; that is plain speaking, I hope. Go and sit down at the table; I shall serve you myself.”

“I could not eat,” Julien told her. “I am too agitated; I am going to enter the seminary when I leave here.”

The good woman did not let him leave until she had filled his pockets with provisions. At last Julien set out for the terrible place; from her doorway, the landlady pointed out the way to him.

She goes to the washbasin and washes her face and hands.

There! Give me a towel!—oh—the sun is rising!

JEAN

And then the troll bursts!

MISS

Yes, it is the trolls who have been abroad tonight!—But Jean, listen! Come with me, for now I have the means!

JEAN

hesitating.

Enough?

MISS

Enough to begin with! Come with me, for I cannot travel alone today. Just think, Midsummer Day, on a stifling train, packed in among crowds of people who will gape at one; standing still at the stations when one wanted to fly—no, I cannot, I cannot! And then the memories come; childhood memories of Midsummer Days, with the church decked in greenery—the birch leaves and lilacs; dinner with the table laid, the relatives, the friends; the afternoon in the park, dancing, music, flowers, and games! Oh, one flees, flees, but the memories follow in the baggage van, and remorse and pangs of conscience!

JEAN

I shall go with you! But now, at once, before it is too late! This very moment!

MISS

There! Get dressed, then!

Takes the birdcage.

JEAN

But no luggage! Then we shall be discovered!

MISS

No, nothing! Only what one can take in the compartment!

JEAN

has taken his hat.

What sort of thing have you there? What is it?

MISS

It is only my greenfinch! I do not want to leave it!

JEAN

Well, there we are! Are we to bring a birdcage now too! You are out of your mind! Put down the cage!

MISS

The only thing I am taking with me from home; the only living creature that is fond of me, since Diana was unfaithful to me! Do not be cruel! Let me take it with me!

JEAN

Put down the cage, I say—and do not speak so loudly—Kristin will hear us!

MISS

No, I will not leave it in strangers’ hands! Kill it instead, then!

JEAN

Bring the wretched creature here, then, and I shall wring its neck!

MISS

Yes, but do not hurt it! Do not—no, I cannot!

JEAN

Bring it here; I can!

MISS

takes the bird out of the cage and kisses it.

Oh, my little Serine, are you to die and leave your mistress now?

JEAN

Please do not make a scene; it is your life, your welfare, that is at stake! Come, quickly!

Snatches the bird from her; carries it to the chopping block and takes the kitchen axe.

Miss turns away.

JEAN

You should have learned to slaughter chickens instead of shooting a revolver—

strikes

Then you would not have fainted at a drop of blood!

MISS

screams.

Kill me too! Kill me! You who can slaughter an innocent animal without your hand trembling. Oh, I hate and loathe you; there is blood between us! I curse the hour when I saw you, I curse the hour when I was born in my mother’s womb!

JEAN

Yes, what good does it do for you to curse! Go!

MISS

approaches the chopping block as though drawn there against her will.

No, I do not want to go yet; I cannot—I must see—quiet! There is a carriage driving outside—

Listens toward the outside, all the while keeping her eyes fixed on the block and the axe.

Do you think I cannot look at blood! Do you think I am so weak—oh—I should like to see your blood, your brain on a wooden block—I should like to see your whole sex swimming in a lake like that—I think I could drink from your skull, I should like to bathe my feet in your chest and I could eat your heart roasted whole!—You think I am weak; you think I love you because the fruit of my womb desired your seed; you think I want to carry your offspring beneath my heart and nourish it with my blood—bear your child and take your name—do you hear, what is your name?—I have never heard your surname—you probably have none, I suppose. I should become Mrs. “Gatehouse”—or Madam Dunghill—you dog who wears my collar, you farmhand who wears my owner’s mark on your buttons—I, share with my cook, rival my maid—oh! oh! oh!—You think I am cowardly and want to flee! No, now I shall stay—and let the thunder roll! My father comes home—finds his escritoire broken open—his money gone—then he rings—that bell—twice for the valet—and then he sends for the sheriff—and then I tell everything! Everything! Oh, it will be good to have an end—if only it would end—and then he has a stroke and dies!—then we shall all be finished—and then there will be calm—peace—eternal rest—and then the coat of arms is shattered against the coffin—the count’s line is extinguished and the valet’s line continues in a foundling home—wins its laurels in a gutter and ends in a prison!

JEAN

Now it is the royal blood speaking! Good, Miss Julie! Just put the miller in the sack too!

Kristin enters, dressed for church, with a hymnbook in her hand.

MISS

Hurries toward her and falls into her arms as though seeking protection.

Help me, Kristin! Help me against this man!

KRISTIN

motionless and cold.

What sort of spectacle is this on a holy-day morning!

Looks at the chopping block.

And how you have fouled things up here!—What is the meaning of this? And all this screaming and noise!

MISS

Kristin! You are a woman and you are my friend! Beware of this scoundrel!

JEAN

abashed.

While the ladies discuss matters, I shall go in and shave!

Slips out to the right.

MISS

You must understand me; and you must listen to me!

KRISTIN

No, I really do not understand this sort of sluttishness! Where is Miss going, dressed for travel like this—and he is standing there with his hat on—eh?—eh?—

MISS

Hear me, Kristin; listen to me, and I shall tell you everything—

KRISTIN

I do not want to know anything—

MISS

You must hear me—

KRISTIN

What is it about? Is it about the foolishness with Jean! Well, you see, I do not care about that at all! For I do not meddle in it. But if Miss means to trick him into running away, we shall put a stop to that!

MISS

extremely nervous.

Try now to remain calm, Kristin, and listen to me! I cannot stay here and Jean cannot stay here—we must therefore leave...

KRISTIN

Hm, hm!

MISS

brightening.

But you see, I have just had an idea—what if all three of us were to go—abroad—to Switzerland and set up a hotel together—I have money, you see—and Jean and I would run the whole thing—and you, I had thought, would take care of the kitchen—would that not be good!—Say yes now! And come with us, and then everything is arranged!—Say yes! Do!

Embraces Kristin and pats her.

KRISTIN

cold and thoughtful.

Hm, hm!

MISS

presto tempo.

You have never been away traveling, Kristin—you must go out and see the world—you cannot imagine how amusing it is to travel by train—new people incessantly—new countries—and then we shall come to Hamburg and see the Zoological Garden in passing—you will like that—and then we shall go to the theater and listen to opera.—And when we come to Munich, we have the museums—you—and there are Rubens and Raphael, those great painters, as you know—you have heard of Munich, where King Ludwig lived—the king, I mean—who went mad—and then we shall see his castles—he still has castles that are furnished exactly as in fairy tales—and from there it is not far to Switzerland—with the Alps, you know—just think, the Alps with snow on them in the middle of summer—and there oranges and laurels grow and remain green all year round—

Flee? But where? We cannot get out! And we cannot go to Kristin!

JEAN

Well then! Into my room? Necessity knows no law; and you can trust me,
for I am your true, sincere, and respectful friend!

MISS JULIE

But think!—suppose they look for you there?

JEAN

I shall bolt the door, and if anyone tries to break in, I shall shoot!—Come!

On his knees.

Come!

MISS JULIE

meaningfully.

Do you promise me—

JEAN

I swear!

Miss Julie exits hastily to the right. Jean rushes after her.

BALLET

The country folk enter in festive dress, with flowers in their hats; a
fiddler at their head; a keg of small beer and a small cask of brandy,
decorated with greenery, are set on the table; glasses are brought out.
Then they drink. Afterward they form a ring and sing and dance the singing
game: “There Came Two Ladies from the Woods.”

When this is over, they leave, still singing.

Miss Julie enters alone; sees the devastation in the kitchen; clasps her
hands; then picks up a powder puff and powders her face.

JEAN

enters; exalted.

There, you see! And you have heard! Do you consider it possible to remain
here?

MISS JULIE

No! I do not! But what, then, are we to do?

JEAN

Flee, travel, far away from here!

MISS JULIE

Travel? Yes, but where?

JEAN

To Switzerland, to the Italian lakes;—you have never been there?

MISS JULIE

No! Is it beautiful there?

JEAN

Oh, an eternal summer, orange trees, laurels, oh!

MISS JULIE

But what shall we do there afterward?

JEAN

There I shall establish a hotel with first-class goods and first-class
customers.

MISS JULIE

A hotel?

JEAN

That is a life, believe me; constantly new faces, new languages; not a
minute’s leisure for brooding or nerves; no searching for something to do,
for the work presents itself; night and day, the bell ringing, the train
whistling, the omnibus coming and going; while the gold pieces roll onto
the bureau. That is a life!

MISS JULIE

Yes, that is living! And I?

JEAN

Mistress of the house; the ornament of the firm. With your looks and your
manner—oh—it is a certain success! Colossal! You sit like a queen in the
office and set the slaves in motion by pressing an electric button; the
guests file past your throne and timidly lay their tribute on your table—you
would never believe how people tremble when they are handed a bill—I shall
salt the accounts, and you shall sugar them with your loveliest smile—ah!
let us travel away from here—

Takes a timetable from his pocket.

at once, on the next train!—we shall be in Malmö at six thirty; Hamburg at
eight forty early tomorrow morning; Frankfurt—Basel in one day, and in Como
by the Gotthard Railway in, let me see, three days! Three days!

MISS JULIE

All that is well and good! But Jean—you must give me courage—say that you
love me! Come and embrace me!

JEAN

hesitating.

I want to—but I dare not! Not here in this house anymore! I love you—without
a doubt—can you doubt it?

MISS JULIE

shyly, truly womanly.

Not “you”!—Say “thou”! There are no barriers between us anymore!—Say “thou”!

JEAN

in anguish.

I cannot!—There are still barriers between us, as long as we remain in this
house—there is the past, there is the Count—and I have never met anyone for
whom I have such respect—I need only see his gloves lying on a chair, and I
feel small—I need only hear the bell upstairs, and I start like a skittish
horse—and when I now see his boots standing there so straight and
self-assured, I feel my back bending!

Kicks the boots.

Superstition, prejudices that we have been taught since childhood—but that
one can forget just as easily. Just come to another country where there is
a republic, and people fall flat on their faces before my doorman’s livery—on
their faces they shall fall, you see; but I shall not! I was not born to
fall on my face, for there is substance in me, there is character, and once
I get hold of the first branch, you shall see me climb!

I am a servant today, but next year I shall be a proprietor, in ten years I
shall be a man of independent means, and then I shall travel to Romania,
have myself decorated, and may—mark well, I say may—end as a count!

MISS JULIE

Beautiful, beautiful!

JEAN

Ah, in Romania one buys oneself the title of count, and then you will be a
countess after all! My countess!

MISS JULIE

What do I care about all that, which I am now casting behind me!—Say that
you love me, otherwise—yes, what am I otherwise?

JEAN

I shall say it a thousand times—afterward—only not here! And above all, no
feelings, unless everything is to be lost! We must approach the matter
coldly! Like sensible people!

Takes out a cigar, clips and lights it.

Now sit down there! Then I shall sit here, and we shall talk as though
nothing had happened!

MISS JULIE

despairingly.

Oh my God! Have you no feelings, then?

JEAN

I! There is no one as full of feeling as I am; but I can restrain myself.

MISS JULIE

Just now you could kiss my shoe—and now!

JEAN

harshly.

Yes, that was then! Now we have other things to think about!

MISS JULIE

Do not speak harshly to me!

JEAN

No, but sensibly! One folly has been committed; do not commit more! The
Count may be here at any moment, and before then our fates must be decided.
What do you think of my plans for the future? Do you approve of them?

MISS JULIE

They seem quite acceptable to me, but just one question: so large an
enterprise requires considerable capital; do you have it?

JEAN

chews the cigar.

I! Certainly! I have my professional knowledge, my vast experience, my
knowledge of languages! That is capital of real worth, I should think!

MISS JULIE

But with that you cannot even buy a railway ticket.

JEAN

That is certainly true; but that is why I am looking for a backer who can
advance the funds!

MISS JULIE

Where will you find one in such haste?

JEAN

You shall find one, if you are willing to become my partner!

MISS JULIE

I cannot, and I own nothing myself.

Pause.

JEAN

Then the whole matter falls through—

MISS JULIE

And—

JEAN

Things will remain as they are!

MISS JULIE

Do you think I shall remain under this roof as your mistress? Do you think
I am willing to let the people point their fingers at me; do you imagine I

THE FRUIT OF SIN

Oh no, she had not had an easy time of it during these months she had been at Husaby. She had talked a little with Erlend in the evening, on the day they had been to Medalby. Then she understood that he had thought she was angry with him because he had brought this upon her.

“I remember well enough,” he said very softly. “That day in the spring when we walked in the woods north of the church. I remember well enough that you begged me to leave you be—”

Kristin had been glad because he said this. At other times she often wondered how many things Erlend seemed to have forgotten. But then he said:

“And yet I would not have believed this of you, Kristin—that you could go on like this, nursing a secret grudge against me, while behaving just as sweetly and happily as ever. For you must have known for a long time what was happening to you. I had believed you were as open and honest as the shining sun—”

“Ah, Erlend,” she said sorrowfully. “You of all people in the world know best that I have gone by secret ways and been false to those who trusted me most.” But she wanted so much for him to understand. “And now I do not know whether you remember, my friend, that before this you acted toward me in a way that some would not call honorable. And God and the Virgin Mary know that I bore no grudge, and I loved you no less—”

Erlend’s face softened.

“That was how I thought of it,” he said quietly. “But you know this too—I strove through all these years to make right what I had broken. I comforted myself with the thought that in the end it would come to pass that I could reward you for being so faithful and patient.”

Then she had asked him:

“You have surely heard of my grandfather’s brother and Lady Bengta, who fled from Sweden against the will of her kinsmen. God chastised them by giving them no child together. Have you never feared during all these years that He might punish us in the same way—”

Trembling and softly, she had said to him:

“You can surely understand, my Erlend, that I was not very happy here this summer when this was the first thing that happened to me. And yet I thought— I thought that if you were to die and leave me before we were married, I would rather be left with your child than be alone. I thought that if I were to die bearing it, that would still be better than for you not to have a lawful son who could take your place in the high seat when you must depart from this world—”

Erlend answered vehemently:

“Then I would think my son had been bought far too dearly if he were to cost your life. Do not speak so, Kristin— I do not hold Husaby so dear,” he said a little later. “Especially since I came to understand that Orm can never inherit the ancestral estate after me—”

“Do you care more for her son than for mine?” Kristin asked then.

“Your son—” Erlend laughed a little. “Of him I know no more at present than that he will come here half a year or so earlier than is good. Orm I have loved for twelve years—”

After a while Kristin asked:

“Do you ever long for those children of yours?”

“Yes,” the man answered. “In former times I often went inland to see them in Østerdalen, where they are.”

“You could travel there now during Advent,” Kristin said softly.

“Would you not resent it, then?” Erlend asked happily.

Kristin had answered that she would find it reasonable. Then he had asked whether she would object if he brought the children home with him for Christmas. “At some time you must see them.” And again she had answered that this too seemed reasonable to her.

“I remember,” he began, “a day in the month of March, when you came to see me at my house for the first time. I was asleep. You were almost a child then, or seemed to be, and you showed me a gold bracelet. Yes!… and now I no longer have that house, or at least I must leave it, because there has been a scandal and people avoid greeting me… Do you know? It means that you will have a house, and one more beautiful and richer than mine, since Rafa spends willingly. Provided, however, that you do not grow too fat… Rafa, I warn you, abhors women who are too fat. Then I also remember an excursion we took together, on the shores of a certain lake… But it was for one night only; perhaps you have lost all memory of it amid so many things.”

He looked at her, questioned her, intimidated her with his sinister eyes.

“Tell me a little about your life, then!… Have you no voice left?”

His sister asked in a firm, simple tone:

“Why have you come?”

He stared at her for a moment, his eyes gleaming brightly:

“I was passing by,” he answered; “the wall is not high; I felt like paying you a visit.”

“Why have you come?” she repeated again, in a deeper voice.

“Ah!… Perhaps you thought you would never see me again? Had you already put your heart at rest?”

A wicked, gloomy anger showed fleetingly in her, as it did in her brother’s face.

“I have done you no harm,” she said sharply, with complete certainty.

“You?”

“No harm,” she insisted, even more sharply.

He sprang to his feet, livid, as though to seize her.

“No, do not touch me!” she commanded, shielding herself with both arms. “If you wanted me, I was yours; you could freely have done with me whatever you pleased… Do not forget that!”

“What are you saying?” he murmured, surprised by these words, struck full on by this truth.

“When I was, as you said, a child, when I came to your house for the first time, and afterward, and always, until the day you fled, you could have done with me whatever you pleased. I would never have taken revenge or complained.”

She too paused, since he was silent, struck with astonishment.

“But what are you asking of me now?” Loretta added.

“What am I asking you?… A little clarification, a trifling thing: for what reason did you become Rafa’s mistress?”

She turned her eyes irresolutely elsewhere, toward the motionless trees, toward the trembling stars, toward the luminous shadow of the cerulean night.

“Answer!”

“I do not know.”

“For love?”

“No.”

“For money?”

“Not that either.”

“Did he perhaps take you by force?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“I do not know, I do not know!…” she said nervously. “Why do you want to torment me?”

“Answer: did you love him? Do you love him?”

“No. I said no.”

She sensed that she was saving herself with these words, and repeated once more:

“Neither before nor now; I do not love him.”

And moreover, it was indeed true.

A kind of vertigo passed through the eyes of the man staring at her; a sign, almost already a smile, almost a kiss, creased his bitter mouth.

“Then why did you do this?”

“I myself could not tell you,” his sister confessed. “It was madness, a moment of thoughtlessness, something unforeseen and easy, without seriousness yet almost necessary… One day I did this, and I cannot even tell you the reason. Perhaps because you had tormented me so much, perhaps because I made the mistake of climbing a staircase… I do not know, I do not know!”

And now she was no longer afraid of him; she spoke to him almost gently, her lovely color returning to her blooming cheeks, passing a ringed hand over her white temple and smoothing her hair with one of her habitual gestures.

“And I?” her brother murmured after being silent.

“You?”

“Yes, Lora, I, who loved you with such anguish, I, who fled desperately so as not to hurt you?…”

She hesitated a little, then said:

“You did not want me… you did not want me even when I wept over it, therefore…”

In the terrible simplicity of these words she gathered all the logic of her little woman’s heart, solved her little feminine enigma, in which the maddest love had ultimately been nothing but a murky curiosity. She could go no further; the whole story of her great sin ended in this little reflection: “You did not want me, therefore…”

And he lowered his face, then began rapping his knuckles on the little wicker table, which rocked.

“Therefore,” he said, with bitterness and mockery, “you simply needed someone to lay you down hard, with your shoulders upon a pillow, someone to make you finally utter that little cry… Who that person was mattered little. I had tormented you greatly… did you say tormented?… Very well, so be it! But in any case you chose yourself a rich man, to sweeten the pains of martyrdom; in exchange you wanted a few dresses, a few jewels, a house that will end by becoming yours… there, and you have all this!”

“I wanted,” she explained, “to choose for myself a life different from the one I was leading: nothing else. Perhaps I was also mistaken.”

He stared at her again with a doubtful look, then changed his mind:

“Why are you alone this evening?”

“I am alone many times,” she answered.

They fell silent; a long silence held sway over their uneasiness. He waited for her to speak; she was waiting for his words. And they scrutinized one another attentively; each sought to read the other’s heart.

“Then,” he resumed after that pause, “then you have nothing to tell me?”

“Yes, many things… but I am afraid of you.”

“And you are right,” her brother said. “I have reached that hour when nothing and no one is respected any longer, when an entire history goes to meet its final peril. Yet I am listening, if you have something to tell me, and I am still listening kindly, Lora, because I am still the same… I repeat: still the same.”

And in these last words he put into his voice an accent as gentle as a caress.

“Sit down,” he added; “come closer to me.”

“No!” she said twice, “no.”

“Are you afraid?”

She did not answer; but it seemed that an anguish, a pity, a compassion almost bordering on revulsion, was choking her soul in that refusal.

On the threshold of the half-dark room, Lazzara’s figure appeared, full of hesitation, yet with the air of being there to bring her help.

The man turned toward her with a sudden movement:

“What do you want?” he assailed her.

The girl did not answer; her frightened eyes moved from one to the other, as though trying to guess.

But Loretta said to her:

“Do not be afraid, Lazzara. Go up to your room and sleep. My brother will leave shortly.”

“Your brother, madam?…” the girl uttered, unable to believe herself for amazement.

“Go up and sleep, Lazzara,” Lora commanded briefly.

She withdrew in small steps, saying nothing, and disappeared into the darkness. Shortly afterward, from within the thickness of the ancient wall there burst forth the sound of running water, which in the resonance of the night filled the deep house with sound. Then it ceased: the lofty rooms fell asleep.

“Well?” she asked when they had returned to the drawing room and were seated facing one another, perplexed.

Outside, summer blazed with its rivers of light, its pyres of splendor; there in the deep drawing room, behind the closed shutters, behind the lowered blinds, a restful coolness breathed.

Then he took one of her hands and slowly, with a kind of stealth, caressed it.

“It is strange,” he said, “but you intimidate me. I have always been rather afraid of you. So often I see a kind of mockery on your lips...”

“Really? How odd!”

“Besides, you are right: you must find me almost grotesque. Men in love are very often ridiculous.”

“And women?” she said.

“Women, I believe, almost never are.”

“What? Grotesque?”

“No, in love.”

“Ah, I could not say... But they certainly confess it more rarely.”

“Tell me,” he resumed warmly, “tell me that you will come often, that you will come every day... I want to see you every day! We are so perfectly safe here...”

“I am thirsty,” she replied.

Rafa brought her an orangeade so cold that it misted the crystal of the carafe; then he drank in turn, from the same glass.

“In other years, by this time, I am already in the country,” Rafa said. “The heat is bad for me. This year, however, it is impossible for me to leave; the thought of no longer seeing you is unbearable to me. But what do you intend to do during the summer?”

“I do not know yet; it does not depend on me.”

“And on whom does it depend?”

“Perhaps on my parents, perhaps...” she added hesitantly, “on my brother.”

“And not on me, in any event?”

“On you? How on you?”

“You once told me, while speaking of other things: ‘My family bores me; perhaps a day will come when I shall be free, entirely free, because I want to sing.’ Do you remember telling me that?”

“Yes, I remember, and I repeat: A day will come, perhaps soon, when I shall be free.”

“There, and thinking of that day, I too have had a dream... but one so beautiful that I do not dare tell you.”

“Dreams...” she joked, “dreams have this virtue: they serve to tell things that are too difficult to say.”

“You are right, Loretta,” he admitted. “Then, a dream. That I should get you a small villa, not too far from Villa Giuliani, a little one, for you alone. A hidden villa, with a beautiful garden, an orchard, a stable. You would be free; no one would know who you were. Sometimes, so as not to remain alone, you would open the gate to me.”

“Ah... and that is the dream?”

“Yes, that is it.”

She reflected for a moment, then said:

“Go on.”

“What do you mean?”

“After the summer...”

“Well, after the summer you may choose whatever you like. In autumn, for example, a lovely journey, a little escape by motorcar, if you wish, even abroad, if you wish... And in winter, your house in the city, a lady companion to preserve appearances, a teacher to teach you singing.”

“And in spring,” she exclaimed, tempted nonetheless, “since the year blossoms again, another is put in Lora’s place, and everything begins again: the same villa, the journey, the house in the city... No, thank you!”

“Another? What are you saying? Have you still not understood that I love you, that I have loved you for long months, more strongly every day? That you can make me obey like a child, and that you alone, you alone, must give me back the peace I no longer have?... Another? That word has no meaning! But think for a moment. Do you believe I do not know what risks I run in making you this proposal? Well, what do I care? I do not want to, I can no longer reflect! No danger frightens me. Only say yes! Ask me for whatever you want, but say yes!”

“I am asking for nothing,” she said, regretting having allowed herself to seem so calculating.

“Then listen, hear me...” And he knelt before her armchair and encircled her with his arms.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?”

“Nothing; I am begging you on my knees. Love me a little; be kind to me for once!”

Thus on his knees, leaning toward her in the ardor of his desire, with passionate eyes and a pleading voice, Rafa was almost handsome, and she looked at him.

“Come, leave me alone...” she said, with a certain annoyance.

He held her tightly around the waist and, bearing down on her a little, covered her dress and her wrists with tiny kisses.

“How many mistresses have you had sit in this armchair?” she asked suddenly.

“How many? None.”

“Oh, come now! I am asking out of curiosity.”

“Perhaps,” he said, “some woman has come here, but I do not remember. They were not mistresses, they were not you. If you do not like it, we shall change houses. I had no love before knowing you. Now you seem the first to me. I love you, I love you in every way; you haunt me and you please me. You are beautiful. You have such an indefinable grace that I suffer when I am near you. Be kind to me, do not laugh!...”

She was indeed laughing, but with a somewhat nervous laugh, and her mouth, her eyes, her hands were no longer so calm.

“No, leave me alone...” she pleaded. “Let me go, please... you are hurting me terribly...”

In the half-light he saw her turn pale; he hid his face in her lap, and with his arms he clasped her knees.

She tried to lift his burning forehead, tried to push away that troublesome mouth, but unable to overcome his strength, in sudden anger she thrust her convulsed fingers into his hair.

Then the struggle was brief: desperately, the girl closed her eyes and let herself be carried away...

But she saw another room, at night, with its windows open over a lake white with moonlight, and the stars close and infinite; another man bent over her, covering her with caresses and kisses. And she saw herself again in that bed, and relived the agony of that vanished hour, and it seemed to her, for an instant, that he had returned, that he was there, on his knees, and was kissing her terribly as he had then, and that his hands were running feverishly, ardently, all over her inflamed body, and a mouth was rising, rising to her lips, full of anguish, fever, voluptuousness, and terror...

A little later, the adjoining room was dark, and from room to room, throughout the silent house, the cry of her lost virginity was suddenly heard.




II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and, having ordered an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several others were playing poker.

Arrigo was watching her: she had set her feet on the same footrest against which he himself pressed as he arched back to row; her short skirt had slipped up a little, and he could see her slender ankles emerging from her low-cut shoes, then rising with equal symmetry, like perfect spindles, and disappearing among the lace of her little skirt into the beginnings of darkness. She wore ash-colored silk stockings, openworked and gleaming. With the tips of her restless little feet, every now and then in play, she touched his. And they laughed, they both laughed, without speaking to each other.

In that peace, in the slowness of the rowing, in the rocking of the moving boat, they understood that the sweetest thing was to look at each other and be silent.

He observed her. In the sun, in the great blaze, her flesh took on a golden transparency, like the calyxes of tea roses; the down on her skin glistened minutely, and its shadows seemed darker. He examined her, and realized, perhaps for the first time, that she did not have a pure mouth, not the mouth of her twenty years, limpid and almost light like herself, but a sensual mouth, warm, too red, too alive, the mouth of a woman already much kissed, already versed in all the lusts that love teaches. And slackening in his stroke, his body leaning backward and his eyes half closed, he stretched beneath the kiss of that impure mouth with a long sensual shudder.

In the heat of the day, amid the glare of the dazzling sun, she too let her eyelids fall halfway over eyes somewhat intoxicated by the light; a sense of blissful weariness spread across her face, through her whole body, flooding her with repose as after exertion. And in her he no longer saw the girl who had skipped among the flowers in the garden, throwing pebbles into the fountains, but another, who bore on her lips the smile of the fallen woman, and seemed almost to be falling asleep after suffering a violent pleasure; another, whom he pictured lying in a bed of love, naked, her languid arms along her sides, abandoned in the sweet repose of the pleasure endured, naked and weary in a bed of love, her head turned to one side amid her half-loosened hair, her mouth moist, her eyes faded, dark as violets...

He rowed slowly, slowly, in the infinite light. One bank receded, the other was still far away; everything seemed to be yielding to sleep, to feel itself oppressed by the splendor, in that sunny afternoon. They passed near a fisherman, whose boat lay still and whose line was in the water. Slowly, without making a sound, they glided on.

He observed her: she held the two tiller cords, one in each hand; but both hands rested in her lap, half open, almost asleep, so that at the slightest tug of the rudder they might perhaps have let the two ropes slip away. The sun gilded those hands; they looked somewhat dark against the whiteness of her skirt. They too, like her mouth, revealed no purity. They were made for every sin, they were destined to inflict tormenting caresses, and in their innocent shape they bore some sign that betrayed their aptitude for vice. And across his hot face, across his somewhat parched mouth, over his whole body wearied by long desire, he felt the caress of those lascivious hands pass, a caress that enervated and twisted him, lavishing upon him a voluptuousness full of death, from the roots of his hair to his last veins. Then he let go of the oars, bent forward, and kissed her.

“What are you doing?...” she said as though awakening, astonished.

“I love you,” he replied, encircling her with his arms and looking into her sun-filled eyes, his whole body reaching and bending over her, his mouth immersed in her living breath. To shake herself free of that torpor, she stretched languidly beneath him as he weighed a little upon her, and, raising her arms, with a movement full of love she clasped them around his neck, throwing her head backward, closing her eyes, blissful.

Over the water, over all the water, the beating of their enamored souls seemed to race in a tremor of light.

“Kiss me...” she uttered, as though she wished to translate into words for him that fullness of joy which intoxicated her senses. “Kiss me once more, as you did before... like this... like this...”

He kissed her again upon her moist mouth, greedily, as one sucks a honeycomb. And she ran her fingers through his hair, uncovering his temples and forehead, slowly combing his hair with a lingering caress.

“I feel happy...” she repeated, her young throat swelling with her breath. “I should like to say so many inexpressible things... I should almost like to sing, yes, to sing for joy!...”

And she turned her eyes all around, over that infinite blaze, and it seemed to her that she embraced within herself all the splendor she saw.

He stared deeply at her, with a steadfast power in his eyes:

“You are mine, or what do you think?” he asked breathlessly, almost angrily. And he clasped her so tightly in his rough arms that she seemed to feel pain from it.

“Why do you ask me that? Why are you acting like this?...” she said, with a shadow of fear.

“Nothing, it is nothing... pay no attention to what I say. Laugh, Loretta, laugh again!”

And he rose and began rowing once more. Over his face had again descended that expression of violence and torment which often distorted it; his extraordinarily agile body bent and straightened, impetuous in the effort of pulling hard at the oars; the slender little boat sped along; the lashed water leapt in swift rainbows.

“What is the matter with you? Why are you tiring yourself like this?”

He did not answer; indeed, he rowed harder.

“Let me try,” she said. “I want to row too.”

And she made as if to rise.

“Do not move, do not move, or you will fall.”

“I want to row too; let me try.”

“Yes, wait.” And, panting, he abandoned the oars.

“How strong you are! We were going so fast just now!”

He smiled at her as he wiped away the sweat that ran down his forehead.

“So you want to row?”

“Yes.”

“Very well, let us try: I shall sit on the other bench and you will come here.”

He changed places, put another pair of oars into the water, and held out a hand to support her as she crossed over. When she was seated, he kissed her again on the nape and the temple, encircled her, and held her captive. Laughing, she pressed her cheek against his bare neck; then she said:

“Why did you ask me that question, Rigo?”

“I wanted to know whether you love me, whether you truly love me...” he replied with a lover’s timidity.

“Do you not know it, then?”

He did not answer; he taught her how to hold the oars and guided her arm through the stroke.

“It is easy!” the girl replied. “You see that I know how to row too?”

Whenever they were alone, whenever it was a little dark, whenever they touched,
the inner phantom took possession of their agitation. It was an affliction
that began with the desire for a kiss and passed from one to the other,
like a chain tightening around their sibling flesh; then it twisted,
coiling into the tightest of knots, until it bent them both beneath
the oppression of its weight. She felt the need to abandon herself
in his arms; he felt, with anger, the temptation to seize her and
squeeze her until it hurt; but in both of them, even in her
who offered herself, there was an invincible fear. An icy fear, rooted
in their very being, a fear that drew them together in different ways and in different ways
kept them apart. They were like two people dying of thirst, bound beside the same fountain,
so that they could stretch their lips to within an inch of the water, close enough
to feel its clear freshness and breathe its moisture, yet without ever
managing to dip their lips into it. Between their thirst and the fountain there was that
inch of space that did not let them drink.

“I wish a man could tell me why on earth I had to love you!”
Arrigo exclaimed. “I wish a man who knows all
souls and all sins would tell me, a priest, for example. But I do not dare
confess this sin. And besides, what use would it be? They too know
nothing; no one knows anything about all this.”

This religious allusion to confession frightened the girl,
as if, all at once, the priest’s black habit, the shadow
between the columns, the mystical clouds of incense, the warm breath
passing through the grille with the whisper of guilty words, and
the rebuke, and the condemnation, and the threat of perpetual penances,
were forming in her terrified heart the image of her mortal sin.

“Why do you say such dark things?” she asked. And she pressed herself against him,
closer, as though to find refuge in him. The singers’ boat
was receding into the moonlit evening, and faintly, from time to time, the merry
refrain could be heard:

      “Very fine linen cloth
    that is put on every morning...”

“Have you thought,” he resumed, “have you thought about what would happen
if I were, for once, to have the courage, the terrible courage I have lacked
until now?”

“I have thought two things: either that you do not truly love me, or that your
mind is sick. If our happiness lies within us, why must we
frighten it away with so much reflection? Little by little you are passing your
illness on to me. When this immense desire first stirred me,
I would have wanted to be yours at once. Looking any further seemed useless
to me; it still seems useless.”

“But tell me,” he said, “you who speak so lightly, do you then know
the value of the offering you are making me? Do you understand what
this phrase you repeat without dismay means: ‘To be yours’? Do you understand that it
means giving away, sacrificing your whole life to me?”

She seemed astonished by these words; nevertheless, she answered with her lips alone,
without conviction:

“Yes, of course, I understand.”

“No, Lora,” he corrected her indulgently, “you do not understand.
A day would inevitably come, and perhaps not a very distant one, when
you would say to your brother: ‘Give me back my life now, because it is
mine, and I want to live it.’ But do you think that then I could yield you to
another man? Do you think that, after a crime like this, one can calmly
start again along the road one was following before? You perhaps could,
because you are twenty and have a carefree heart. But I? Tell me, what
would I do then? Do you know jealousy? Do you know that other, greater
torment called remorse? You see: there is a fundamental difference
between us: you love me because you can forget, because you do not know, and
hardly even realize that I am your brother... whereas I love you precisely,
and more desperately, because I know, because I know with profound fear,
that you are my sister...”

With her head bowed, looking at the treacherous water, which glittered like a
dark fabric woven with silver threads and made a scarcely perceptible
sound as it struck the wall of the dock, she seemed to be pondering
deeply the meaning of those words.

“No, Rigo!” she suddenly exclaimed, clutching his arm with
convulsive force, “no! You are not my brother. I have never thought
for a moment that you were my brother. I like you, and when I am with you
I feel that you desire me like a true lover. Take me!... do with me what
you wish, for an hour or forever, as long as I am beautiful and your love
finds me beautiful... Can’t you smell it? I am fragrant all over like a sheaf
of roses... Take me!... hold me tightly in your arms, as if I were a
great sheaf of roses... But laugh! Laugh!... because I can no longer bear to see you
so gloomy... Laugh once more... laugh!”

The boat was passing again in the distance, and the singing could be heard:

      “Everything I would give her
    to do as you do with her...”




XIV


“Go up and undress, Lora,” he had said to her at the foot of the lift,
perhaps because he was afraid of hastening that imminent nocturnal hour.
“Go to bed early and rest well.”

“But aren’t you coming up?” she asked, lingering.

“Yes, in a little while. I’m not sleepy yet; I’ll stay and smoke another
cigarette.”

“I’m not sleepy either...” she said.

But he gently persuaded her:

“Tomorrow we will go on an outing; we shall have to get up early. Go and sleep.”

He remained walking in the entrance hall for a long time, then went down again into the
garden and returned toward the lake. He saw the illuminated room on the terrace
of the first floor; that intense light fascinated him, drawing him away from
every other thought.

“Lora is undressing,” he thought. And he saw the clothes she was taking off and smelled
their scent.

Her arms tormented him; the breast emerging from her batiste chemise
blossomed in his thoughts like a bouquet of fresh roses; he saw her little feet,
still shod, moving here and there about the room with that restlessness,
now languid, now hurried, of a woman undressing. “And now Lora is combing
her hair,” he thought. And he heard the crackling of the tortoiseshell comb
in her loosened braid. The scent of that hair filled the air wherever he passed.

He saw her bending over the washbasin to refresh her face; he imagined that,
out of feminine coquetry, she powdered herself all over before going to bed.
The soft scent of the powder mingled with that of her perfumed skin
breathed beneath his nostrils like a living thing. And he saw her
sit down beside the bed, stretch a little in the languor and delight
of the approaching rest, cross one leg over the other to remove
her little shoe, let it fall onto the bedside rug, then slowly roll
the exquisitely fine black stocking down her calf, and the little
foot emerge from it, polished like an ivory jewel, restless in its slender
shape, nervous as a hand. He saw her linger a little as she likewise removed
the other little shoe, the other stocking, look around with the listless
gaze of a woman who would rather not sleep alone, then rise,
take from the coverlet a beautiful nightgown all lace and ribbons,
arrange it with a few caressing movements, unfasten the one
she was wearing and let it slip down like a sheath, with a slow smile...”

And he thought of putting out the light in the room so as to have more courage,
but he wanted a glimmer to filter in, a half-light gradually becoming more
discernible, perhaps from the streetlamps on the road, perhaps from a shaded lamp
in the adjoining room. And he smelled the diffused scent of her body,
that same scent, but sweeter, which she had on her mouth when kissing him; an
intense and manifold scent that blossomed from her skin, as though roses were
hidden in the folds of her body. He savored the freshness
of that springtime flesh, imagined caressing her round
bare shoulder, slipped his groping hand into the velvety warmth of her
armpits, gathered her torso, supple as a young shoot, into his clasping arms,
felt against himself the unrestrainable throbbing of
her womb, the entwining her body would make against his
body, in order to offer herself and defend herself, conceived the savage joy of
being able to stun her, heard in her throat the death rattle of her fleeing virginity,
heard her weep in ecstasy, laugh in pain... then he
saw her as she was, slender, arched, strong in her slightness, turning pale for a
moment with that pallor which is close to death, and flashing forth in all her beauty
with love in that exultant hatred with which the virgin gives herself...

But suddenly she had felt ill. Truly, as in his
vision, he had seen her blanch with that same pallor, had felt
her convulsive hands seize his arms, then, seeing her
stagger, had supported her against himself.

“What is wrong, Lora?”

She did not answer; her teeth were chattering; she was trembling.

“Lora! Lora! What is wrong?”

“Nothing...” she stammered, “it will pass...”

It was only dizziness, and her mouth soon smiled at him again. They retraced
their way; he supported her as far as the carriage.

The coachman chattered; the little horse began trotting again toward the city
of its martyrdom, where there were rough stone, slippery rails,
the stand, and the stable. On either side of the two hedges, fragrant in the
white night, the tilled earth was growing grain and fruit for the
voracious city; some cricket enamored of the moon raised its shrill song,
infinitely greater than itself.

Now her head hurt; around her temples she had an iron band that
hammered. To soothe that pain she took one of her brother’s hands and
bound her forehead with it.

“Are you suffering?”

“Yes, a little.”

He encircled her forehead, from one temple to the other, with so many little
kisses.

“Hold me close, very close... and I shall recover.”

In a garden they passed, the roses of May were opening their
calyxes swollen with spring.

“Do you still feel ill?”

“Yes, a sweet pain...”

Beyond a row of poplars there reappeared, like a vast cloud suspended
in the firmament, the red blaze of the city. They came upon the first
houses, with walls white in the moonlight. Now the crickets were a hundred, were
a thousand, lost in the May hay, and one, more wrathful than all the rest,
seemed to pursue them close at hand along the hawthorn hedge.

All at once she let her head fall back against his shoulder, as though the onset
of a faint were overpowering her.

“Rigo, I feel ill...” she stammered, pressing her breast.

“But what is wrong?” he said, bewildered. “Why are you suffering so?”

She closed her eyes and still tried to smile at him from her wholly white face.

“I feel dizzy... I do not know...”

“Do you want to stop? What do you want to do?”

“Nothing; it will pass now... it will pass... I love you...”

When they reached the last farmhouse, the cricket’s wandering song
faded far away, infinitely far away, and died. But ahead there appeared
the monumental customs gate, majestic as a triumphal arch beneath the starry sky.
The customs guards, seated beside the booth, laughed and smoked, chatting
with women of ill repute. Amid throngs of children, some vagrants
were playing in a street vendor’s raffle; a swallower of burning tow gaped
his enormous soot-blackened mouth before the astonished spectators.

“I love you...” she said again, in a breath, to her pale lover.

And the hair shirt of the inexpiable sin clothed their desperate flesh like a
mantle of thorns.




VIII


He arrived unexpectedly at Clara Michelis’s house around lunchtime.
For several days she had not seen him; she had written to him
several times without receiving an answer, had repeatedly gone to his house, but
without ever finding him. She could not regard it as unusual that
Arrigo should neglect her; yet he had never shown himself indifferent to such a degree.

Mother and daughter were sitting at the table when he arrived. It was the
servant who first asked him whether he had already had lunch.

After he answered no, his usual place was laid for him, and there he
sat down with the air of a broken man.

“I have had a great deal to do these past few days,” he said by way of apology. “Forgive me for not coming.”

Neither the daughter nor the servants were any longer surprised at his presence
in that house; he had become somewhat its master, everyone knew in what capacity,
and by now no one paid any attention to it. That day his
face was pale and agitated, his eyes full of fever, his hands somewhat restless.

“I have been extremely busy,” he repeated, as though he did not know what else
to say.

Out of regard for her daughter, Clara did not answer a word, but remained
watching him, staring at him, with her gentle eyes full of tenderness and
resignation. She was greatly afraid of him when she saw him arrive in
that state. She too looked worn, and since she had expected to be alone,
she had come to lunch in a dressing gown without having finished doing herself up.
The face powder left a visible trace on her somewhat worn skin;
her neck, which emerged slenderly from the lace of her neckline,
had the appearance of something sickly; as she ate, a few very faint
wrinkles formed at the corners of her mouth and near the arches of her
eyebrows. Perhaps she had wept during the sleepless night; her eyes
seemed to have grown dim, and they turned toward her lover a gaze full
of anguished sweetness.

Adelina, on the other hand, appeared entirely fresh in her blooming seventeen years;
but that Signor Arrigo made her somewhat uncomfortable when, instead of joking
with her as usual, he came with that mastiff-like face of his
and from time to time looked at her with his violent eyes, like those of a
nocturnal bird of prey.

“What could you possibly have had to do all these days?” Clara finally
asked, trying to give her words a playful tone.

“And not from me, in any case?”

“From you? What do you mean, from you?”

“You once told me, while speaking to me of other things: ‘My family bores me; perhaps a day will come when I shall be free, entirely free, because I want to sing.’ Do you remember telling me that?”

“Yes, I remember, and I repeat: A day will come, perhaps soon, when I shall be free.”

“There, and thinking of that day, I too have had a dream... but one so beautiful that I do not dare tell you.”

“Dreams...” she said teasingly, “dreams have this good quality: they serve to tell things that are too difficult to say.”

“You are right, Loretta,” he admitted. “So, a dream. That I should get you a little villa, not too far from Villa Giuliani, small, for you alone. A secluded little villa, with a beautiful garden, an orchard, a stable. You would be free; no one would know who you are. Sometimes, so as not to remain alone, you would open the gate to me.”

“Ah... and that is the dream?”

“Yes, that is it.”

She reflected for a moment, then said:

“Go on.”

“What do you mean?”

“After the summer...”

“Well, after the summer you may choose whatever you please. In the autumn, for example, a lovely journey, a little escape by motorcar, if you like, even abroad, if you like... And in winter, your house in the city, a lady companion to preserve appearances, a teacher to teach you singing.”

“And in the spring,” she exclaimed, still tempted, “since the year blossoms anew, someone else is put in Lora’s place, and everything begins again: the same villa, the journey, the city house... No, thank you!”

“Someone else? What are you saying? Have you still not understood that I love you, that I have loved you for many months, more strongly every day? That you can make me obey like a child, and you alone, you alone, must give me back the peace I no longer have?... Someone else? That word makes no sense! But think for a moment. Do you believe I do not know what risks I am running by making you this proposal? Well, what do I care? I do not want to, I can no longer think! No danger frightens me. Only say yes! Ask me for whatever you want, but say yes!”

“I ask for nothing,” she said, regretting having let herself appear so calculating.

“Then listen, hear me...” And he knelt before her armchair and encircled her with his arms.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?”

“Nothing; I am begging you on my knees. Love me a little; be kind to me for once!”

Thus on his knees, leaning toward her in the ardor of his desire, with passionate eyes and a pleading voice, Rafa was almost handsome, and she looked at him.

“Come, leave me alone...” she said, with a certain annoyance.

He held her tightly around the waist and, leaning a little against her, covered her dress and her wrists with tiny kisses.

“How many mistresses have you had sit in this armchair?” she suddenly asked.

“How many? None.”

“Oh, come now! I am asking out of curiosity.”

“Perhaps,” he said, “some woman has come here, but I do not remember. They were not mistresses; they were not you. If you do not like it, we shall change houses. I had no love before meeting you. Now you seem the first to me. I love you, I love you in every way; you haunt me and you delight me. You are beautiful. You have such an indefinable grace that I suffer when I am near you. Be kind to me; do not laugh!...”

She was indeed laughing, but with a somewhat nervous laugh, and her mouth, her eyes, her hands were no longer so calm.

“No, leave me alone...” she pleaded. “Let me go, please... you are hurting me terribly...”

In the half-light he saw her turn pale; he hid his face in her lap and clasped her knees with his arms.

She tried to lift his burning forehead, tried to push away that importunate mouth, but, unable to overcome his strength, in sudden anger she thrust her convulsed fingers into his hair.

Then the struggle was brief: desperately, the girl closed her eyes and let herself be carried away...

But she saw another room, at night, with its windows open over a lake white with moonlight and the stars near, infinite; another man bent over her, covering her with caresses and kisses. And she saw herself again in that bed, and relived the agony of that vanished hour, and for an instant it seemed to her that he had returned, that he was there, on his knees, and was kissing her as terribly as he had then, and that his hands were running, feverish, burning, all over her inflamed body, and that a mouth was rising, rising to her lips, full of anguish, fever, voluptuousness, and terror...

A little later, it was dark in the adjoining room, and from room to room, throughout the silent house, the cry of her lost virginity was suddenly heard.




II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and, after ordering an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several others were playing poker.

Beppe Cianella was hot and wiped his sweaty brow with a brightly colored silk handkerchief. He unbuttoned his waistcoat, lit a cigar, and blissfully closed his eyes as though about to doze off. But it was too hot to sleep. In a still-drowsy voice, Beppe Cianella called the servant and asked him to turn the fan toward him.

When the cool air struck him, he stretched out more comfortably on the sofa and, with a feeling of true bliss, tried to close his mischievous eyes.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair,” he said with a slight yawn.

“So much the better for him!” replied one of the players.

Sacco Berni had attempted a daring “bluff,” but Gigi Saponetta, an extremely skillful player, had forced him to declare his hand, and the others, laughing wildly over it, mocked the trickster who had been tricked.

Count Berrini passed by at the back, in his shirtsleeves, shouting at the servants because he could not find a newspaper; Lello Fornara, the languishing one, was writing his daily love letter in a corner; through the open door leading into the billiard room, the balls could be heard striking one another amid the noisy quarrels of old Baron Gioacchini and his young pupil Leonardo Sergi.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair!” Beppe Cianella, who could not fall asleep, repeated between one yawn and the next.

Outside, summer blazed with its torrents of light, with its pyres of
splendor; there in the deep room, behind the closed shutters, behind the
lowered mats, a restful coolness breathed.

Then he took one of her hands and slowly, with a kind of stealth, caressed
it.

“It is strange,” he said, “but you intimidate me. I have always been
somewhat afraid of you. So often I see a kind of mockery on your lips...”

“Really? How odd!”

“Besides, you are right: you must find me almost grotesque. Men in love
are very often ridiculous.”

“And women?” she said.

“Women, I believe, almost never are.”

“What? Grotesque?”

“No, in love.”

“Ah, I could not say... But they certainly confess it less often.”

“Tell me,” he resumed warmly, “tell me that you will come often, that you

Rafa brought her an orangeade so cold that it misted the crystal of the

“I do not know yet; it does not depend on me.”

“And on whom does it depend?”
