II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and,
having ordered an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near
the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several
others were playing poker.

The young man turned down an avenue that grew thick among the trees;
she made a long circuit there. She walked slowly, thoughtful, nervous;
with her parasol she bothered the grass at the edges of the meadows. She
was in an extremely perplexed state of mind. Despite her long
reflections, she no longer understood herself or her brother now, and
she no longer knew what to do with this Rafa, so devoted and so rich. In
the depths of her heart she also felt sad; love was consuming her,
melancholy rose from the depths of her being, causing her a kind
of slow suffocation. The day before she had been at Arrigo’s house,
because she could no longer bear to remain without seeing him; she had
found him absorbed and almost hostile. He had not kissed her, had not
allowed himself to be kissed; he had sought a thousand pretexts to send
her away, and, when near her, he seemed to be on tenterhooks. He had not
even wanted to hear Rafa spoken of; he had said to her roughly:

— Do whatever you like with him! I no longer care about anything.

And she had grown meek, had tried to caress him, had said to him:

— I shall have to see him tomorrow: give me some good advice.

Then he had begun to laugh, with a bitter, malicious laugh whose
meaning she could not understand; then he had begun to pace about the
room, agitated, scowling.

— You will see him tomorrow?

— Yes.

— Then tell him he is an imbecile! In his place I would already have
taken you.

— Why do you speak like that, Rigo? — she had asked him with tears
in her eyes. And he had shrugged his shoulders without answering. Then
he had begged her to leave, because his head hurt and he wanted to be
alone. But at the door he had taken her in his arms, had clasped her in
his arms passionately, and had pushed her out.

Later, toward evening, on the pretext of asking her father for some
information, he had come to their house, perhaps to see her for a
moment, to smile at her for an instant, after having been so rough.

And they had kissed again, in secret, with greater anxiety, in her
father’s house.

She could not understand him properly. Perhaps he was being consumed
by a foolish jealousy of this man whom, deep down, she mocked and about
whom she was making a calculation so different, so remote from love.
But she would have renounced Rafa a thousand times over if he had said
just one word to her! And why did he not want her? Why did he, with such
obstinacy, make both of them endure such wearing suffering?

Behind the gate she saw the automobile standing there; she ran quickly
to it and got in. The chauffeur had already been given his orders: they
set off in haste.

In the hot afternoon the countryside glittered like gold: a motionless
cloud of dust hung over the road; enormous carts, loaded with furniture
or merchandise, drawn by many horses in single file, obstructed its
middle and moved slowly aside, with a great creaking, at the signals of
the horn. When another automobile sped past, with shrieks of its siren,
everything, for a long stretch, grew clouded in a thick haze of dust,
everything: even the sun.

Rafa put an arm around her waist; she tried to push him away, but
weakly; she was no longer talkative or merry.

— You see, — she said, — I cannot trust you...

He obeyed and began again.

— Are we going far?

— Not very.

— Well, what have you to tell me?

— Not now; we shall talk afterward.

— Ah, afterward...

— Are you sad today?

— Yes, a little.

— Why?

— Because of so many things... so many things...

— Tell me about them, Loretta.

— No, what good would it do? In any case, you consider me a very
frivolous girl... I am here with you... you even have the right to think
so!

She was now mingling cunning with sincerity in a singular way, without
realizing it. The young man bent over her, almost to the point of
kissing her.

— Do not say that, Loretta; you know very well it is not true. I also
feel a profound respect for you: otherwise I would not love you.

— No, you desire me; that is the right word. But as for loving me,
that is quite another matter; you would not have me come here.

— Use the familiar form with me again, Loretta, as you did the other
times.

— Not today, not today!

— Then you do not believe that I care for you?

She shook her head, incredulous, smiling.

— Are you certain of it?

— Absolutely certain.

In a little over half an hour they reached a small village that spread
its white houses across the great plain, encircled by an almost dry
little ditch, with both its banks covered in yellow flowers among the
dusty grasses.

The automobile stopped in the square, and a swarm of barefoot,
shirtless urchins came running up, hopping over the cobblestones. There
was a small garden full of coolness and peace beside the little church;
a gilded sunburst blazed, struck full by the sun, on the church façade,
and it shone so brightly that it seemed to be turning; the parish
house, behind the greenery, had the shutters of its two windows partly
closed; from one hung a sheet, from the other a white-and-blue-striped
percale shirt. A large tawny dog scrabbled along the wall.

— Come, — said Rafa; — there is a little inn at the end of the village:
we shall drink white wine there.

— No; I want to go into the church, — Loretta replied.

— Into the church?

— Yes.

— Very well, let us go, if you wish.

The chauffeur went to the inn to wait for them; they crossed the
square, the little garden full of shade, and climbed the four steps to
the churchyard. Many urchins ran after the noisy automobile.

It was not late; all the sounds of the village could still be heard:
the blacksmiths hammering, the carpenters planing, the weavers working
their looms. A chubby little boy dressed as a cleric was reading a book
while seated in the shade in the garden. He looked at them and did not
move. Beneath the luminous arch of the main doorway, swarms could be
seen buzzing. They entered. The church was poor, but devout and bright
like the soul of a sower; through the tall windows the sunlight poured,
broken into golden dust. Only an old woman, indistinct in the shadow of
the colonnades, was praying with her face in her hands; but she was so
still, so firmly kneeling, that she seemed one of the church’s
furnishings.

The girl dipped her hand into the holy-water font and crossed herself,
bending her knee slightly. A drop remained on her forehead, clear as a
pearl. Then they walked all around the apse, looking at the paintings of
the Passion of Christ.

The cool air smelled of faded incense.

— Why did you want to enter this church?

— A whim.

She walked ahead with a springy step, almost so as not to make any
noise; her shadow stretched obliquely across the polished floor. She
bent her knee again as she passed before the altar, then sat down on a
pew in the shadow of the colonnade and rested her forehead in her hand.

The crucified Christ glittered anew beneath his silver crown.

— And what are you doing now? — Rafa asked.

— Nothing. I like it.

He leaned against the column beside her, slightly stooped.

— I love churches, — said Loretta, — and the singing and the organs in
churches.

Rafa looked at her for a long time, then said:

— I am not making a scene; I am only telling you that I cannot go on without seeing you, without speaking to you now and then. In short, listen, Loretta: I have fallen in love with you, foolishly in love, because all this serves only to make you laugh... Yet you will understand that one does not give up in a single day the thing dearest to one.

— I have never laughed at you, Rafa, — she said gently.

— Yes, laughed, laughed, and you want to do nothing but laugh!... But it does not matter. I am only telling you this, Loretta: do not think of taking away from me that very little which you have granted me until now, because in that case I do not know what might happen.

That timid man had found a tone so full of energy that Loretta was astonished by it.

— Come now, Rafa, calm yourself, — she said. — Do not take things this way, and do not look at me like that, because you almost frighten me. I should like you to reason instead, to think of one thing, of one thing only: What if my brother were to find out?...

— He will not find out.

— Oh, that is easily said! You do not know him; he is capable of... I know what he is capable of! In short, I should be a ruined girl, and let that suffice for you.

Rafa calmed down a little in the face of such arguments.

— Very well, we shall increase our precautions; I shall do whatever you wish.

— In this world, my dear, everything comes to be known, and when we suppose ourselves well hidden, a thousand eyes are watching us.

— But in short, this danger existed before as well, and yet...

— Precisely, precisely; it is something that cannot go on any longer. I have been imprudent, very imprudent with you, but I cannot go any further.

— Loretta, — he said softly, in a persuasive voice, — think that I love thee, think that thou art in my thoughts all day long, that thou art so deeply in my soul that I cannot give thee up... Do not be so cruel, I beg thee!

He took hold of her arm, and she did not try to draw it away.

— Be quiet, Rafa... — she murmured, — be quiet!

But he went on:

— I have left everything behind, solely to enjoy these few moments thou givest me. Thou seest, I am not demanding, I shall insist no more; for now I am content to see thee, to speak to thee now and then... If one day thou wert to break off so abruptly the sweetness of the love I bear thee, it would have been better never to allow me to draw near thee. Now it is too late.

— But no, Rafa, thou... you do not understand!

— I understand perfectly; I am a matter of indifference to thee, I amused thee for a little while, and now thou hast had enough; thou art afraid, and darest risk nothing for me.

— You do not understand, I tell you. If I had no family, if I did not have so many appearances to preserve, if, in short, I were free, alone... then, perhaps... But as things are, I repeat, woe, woe if my brother were to have the slightest suspicion of this!

— We shall make sure he knows nothing.

— No, Rafa. And then there is another danger...

— What danger?

— Oh God! There is another danger, I tell you; do not insist.

— Come, out with it, tell me! Be honest for once!

They were walking; she stopped and assumed a mischievous air:

— Why dost thou address me as “thou,” for example? Thou knowest very well that I do not want thee to.

— That does not matter; go on: what is the danger?...

— In short, you say that I laugh, that I laugh... It is easy to say! Yet it might be that, when all is said and done, I too was afraid that I might cease to laugh...

— How I love thee, Loretta! — he exclaimed ingenuously, encircling her waist with one arm.

— Keep still... keep still, come now! — And she continued: — Naturally, I too am made neither of wax nor of tow... One day or another, what do I know? finding ourselves alone, for example, with the things you are always saying to me... or by chance, or by mistake, or for any other reason at all, I might perhaps lose... In short, it takes no time at all to commit a foolish act!

She twirled her parasol again, thrust it deep into a hedge, and added:

— And then?...

Rafa tried to answer, but she gave him no time:

— Of course, you men are quick about it: good day, good evening, and that is the last one sees of you! We girls pay for both. The thoughtlessness, the intoxication of a moment, may cost us who knows what price, and you say that one laughs? Naturally one laughs, one laughs... as long as one can...

— But I am an honorable man, Loretta! — he proclaimed resoundingly.

— Very well. And because you are an honorable man, I ought to give myself to you? That is not a good reason, do you think? But I, dearest Rafa, have my whole life to live, and there are, I repeat, certain reasons of my own which forbid me the luxury of doing what perhaps I too would enjoy. I am certainly not a street girl, nor do I have, like some other woman, a coat of arms and several millions to assure me of impunity. If I found myself in either of those two situations, well then, yes, I might perhaps be the sort to say to a man—to you, for example: “My dear Rafa, I like thee; do with me what thou wilt.” But in my case this would mean offering you my entire life, gambling my whole future, material and moral, on the recklessness of a moment... And that is a little too much, do you not think?

Having delivered this fine speech to him, she involuntarily thought of Arrigo, regretting that he could not hear her. She felt like saying these two words to herself; indeed, she said them inwardly: “How clever you are!”

Rafa took some time to extricate himself from his difficulty; during that interval they both passed once more in front of the old man who was reading the newspaper one syllable at a time, and through the greenery, along another path, they saw the infantry soldier returning with his ruddy maidservant.

— Loretta, — he said at the end of that silence, — I have already spoken to thee once with great clarity; but thou wilt not even hear certain things discussed.

— I know very well what you are alluding to!... — she said sarcastically. — Since we have spoken of it once, we may speak of it again. And I prefer clear situations and plain words. You offered me money... a great deal of money!...

— Not like that, Loretta... — he exclaimed, blushing.

— Just like that, just like that! What is the use of circumlocutions? That is the naked truth.

She paused, and he did not dare interrupt her.

— Now listen, Rafa. I do not know what opinion you have of me; indeed, I do not care. Everything may lead you to believe that I am capable even of selling myself... and that does not offend me, because once again I admit that the fault was mine. You see that I am speaking openly, as I have not done before. Nevertheless, if you believe that, you are mistaken. I need nothing: from my family I receive everything I require, and I could receive much more if I were willing to submit to certain family disciplines that are contrary to my character. We are not extremely rich, yet you can see that my brother, for example, leads an enviable life. If I wished to marry tomorrow, I could choose, and choose well, as my sister did, for I have a sister too. But none of this pleases me. I have already told you that I am a girl unlike the others. Precisely because of my singular ideas, I have already come into conflict with my family; I have laid claim to a kind of independence, and I would have done even more if I were not afraid of my brother in particular.

He saw her bent over the washbasin, cooling her face; he imagined that, out of some feminine coquetry, she powdered herself all over before going to bed. That soft scent of the powder and of her perfumed skin, mingled together, breathed beneath his nostrils like a living thing. And he saw her sit down beside the bed, stretch a little in her languor, in the delight of imminent rest, cross one leg over the other to take off her little shoe, let it fall upon the bedside rug, then slowly roll the very fine black stocking down her calf, and the small foot emerge from it, polished like an ivory jewel, restless in its slender shape, nervous as a hand. Linger a little as she likewise took off the other little shoe, the other stocking, look around with that listless gaze of a woman who would not wish to sleep alone, then rise, take from atop the coverlet a beautiful nightgown all lace and ribbons, lay it out with a few caressing movements, unfasten the one she wore and let it slip down like a sheath, with a slow smile....

She would go to look in the mirror one last time, then go to bed.

He pictured these things minutely, agonizingly, like someone drinking an exquisite poison in little sips. The tepid night swathed him in scents too strong; an indefinable silence full of agitation hung between heaven and earth; the hidden nocturnal life multiplied around him in the drunken garden.

Through the foliage of the trees he gazed with a kind of stupefaction at that lighted window on the first-floor terrace.

Suddenly, he could no longer withstand those visions; he crossed the garden in haste and went upstairs.

She had gone out onto the deserted terrace, had stretched out languidly in the reclining chair, and was now waiting for him, gazing into the miracle of the night, where the magnificence of the stars trembled with a kind of furious intensity.

“What are you doing out there? Haven’t you gone to bed, then?”

A little intoxicated by the stars, by the silence, and by love, she held out both arms to him without answering.

“Why don’t you undress?” he asked again.

“I was waiting for you,” she replied in a slow, slightly veiled voice.

The light breath of night had passed through her hair; the whiteness of the moonbeam shone upon her face. “It is damp in the evening,” he observed; “do not stay outside too long.”

Then, turning quickly, he said to her, “It is late now; sleep well. Farewell.”

“Rigo...” she uttered softly, as though she were still lost in the dream. And there was a little intoxication in her feminine languor, in her ambiguous manner, in the voice with which she called him. “Rigo, come here: sit down.”

She made a little room for him beside her. He obeyed silently. The warmth of that sweet body spread through his veins like a poisoned, exceedingly slow pleasure. He was bent over her face; the girl’s hands caressed his hair, his forehead.

Then she began to speak to him softly, with long pauses, trembling.

“You must not leave me alone.... Tonight more than ever I feel the need to be close to you, very close, because it would be truly melancholy to put a wall, to close a door, between you and me.... Do you not see what a magnificent night it is? There is a scent of jasmine drifting through the air like an intoxicating powder. And then I feel so full of torpor tonight.... Kiss me!... My hands are hot, feel.... They hurt.... They burn. I want to stay here all night, talking to you, caressing you, rather than remain alone.”

She thrust her fingers into his thick hair, as one sometimes does into warm furs in winter. And she continued:

“Down there, in the garden, you said such grave things to me that I am troubled by them; I should like to weep, but in the depths of my heart there is a joy that laughs, a kind of inexpressible hope.... Do not leave me alone. Or I should even like to do something I have never done: come into your bed, fall asleep beside you.... Kiss me! And then tell me something truly dangerous.... Even an innocent word, if you do not wish to tell me anything else.... I love you, and alone I shall not be able to sleep... because I want you to kiss me. Feel how much in love my mouth is.... Kiss me! I am yours... yours... take me! I desire nothing but to suffer from you... for you.... Hurt me a little... give me a kiss, only one, without end... bend down....”

These words, spoken close to his mouth, lulled him like the music of a sweet enchantment, swathed his aching senses in ineffable relief, and, closing his eyes, he stiffened in order to listen to her. A great shudder of pleasure passed over his cold flesh; an imperceptible wasting, an endless yearning spread through him beneath the caress of that voice.

She spoke again, enervated, exhausted:

“Look: I am closing my eyes... I am asleep. Bend down a little, kiss me!... I am so sleepy... I love you. Be gentle with me.... Listen: there is no sound, no one is watching us... kiss me!”

Like a madman he kissed her mouth, her forehead, her temples, her neck, her wrists, her hands, with a hoarse pant in his constricted throat, and he kissed her all over her perfumed flesh until his breath failed him. Then he rose, his hair disheveled, tore himself free from her as she held him, thrust her violently back upon the cushions, ran into his own room, and locked himself in.

She gave a little cry and, still quivering beneath the scourge of those kisses, burst into a convulsion of tears, then for a few moments remained almost lifeless.

The half-moon was rising above the mountains, high, clear, far from the stars.

He flung himself onto the bed, biting the pillows, clutching at the covers, to master the tumult that was rending him within, and not to hear that hushed voice pleading with him from behind the door, and not to look any further into the terrible possibility of that hour.

The night advanced, clear, almost trembling, toward the heights of its glorious radiance, strewing across the vault of infinity a still greater magnificence of stars. The lake and the shores, inhabited by the shadows of night, pervaded by the ambiguity of silence, clothed themselves in white splendors beneath the enchantment of the night.

A span of time passed that seemed infinite to him; then he thought he understood that she had begun to undress. He no longer heard upon the floor the sound of her slender heels, but the soft tread of two slippers moving hurriedly; then he was tempted to go to the inner door that separated them and listen. But instead the door to the corridor suddenly opened, and she entered.

She was in a dressing gown, frightened, pale, and stopped on the threshold. He sprang down from the bed and stood staring at her in astonishment.

“What do you want?...” he stammered in a choked voice.

“Nothing,” she replied. She looked at him. There was an unfamiliar light in her altered eyes; the expression of that face was singularly changed. There was something harsh and wild in her too, in her mouth, usually so smiling.

“Will you not sleep tonight?”

“No.”

Then her brother began to pace gloomily about the room, without going near her, as though he were contemplating some horrible act against her.

But abruptly he opened the window and went out onto the terrace.

“You are so beautiful!” he said again; “so beautiful that you hurt me...”

She felt no shame; she raised her face, and her mouth laughed, vivid, crimson, full of guilt. Her eyes shone: she felt no shame.

“And then why?...” she asked hesitantly.

“What are you saying?”

“...why don’t you want me?”

The question was so grave that she herself hid again. The other made no reply; he lit a cigarette, as though he wished to intoxicate himself with smoke.

Then, when she no longer expected any answer:

“Because you are my sister,” he said.

She shrugged her shoulders and reflected.

“Does that name seem so terrible to you?”

“You are a child,” he observed gravely.

“A child?...” And she smiled, shaking her head. “No, rather, it is something else, something very simple: I suffer, and I no longer want to suffer. I love you, you alone, and whoever you may be, I love you! After all, what do you reproach me for? For feeling this love? But it is not my fault. Perhaps for speaking of it? But what good would silence do, if you, though you too are silent, do nothing but think continually of the same thing?”

And her little hands clasped his tightly, while he did not know how to answer and no longer dared look at her. Then she became gentle, persuasive, insistent:

“Listen to me, Rigo, listen to me! I was the first to have the courage that you ought to have. Now do not condemn me: help me! There is a certain fear in all this, it is true, but we shall have to overcome it...”

He looked at her in astonishment.

“We must not overcome it,” he said darkly. “On the contrary, we must be cured of it.”

“Is it, then, so great an evil?”

“Yes, a horrible evil. Even speaking of it, even thinking about it, is wrong.”

“No,” she said firmly. “No!”

“You see, if you could have some name other than sister... Do you not hear how wrong it sounds on my lips?”

“A name!... what is a name?” she said.

“But it is everything, since it means something, since it contains the greatest sin there is in love.”

She made a vague gesture and smiled.

“It does not matter,” she replied. “I do not regard you as such; I do not feel at all that you are my brother. Paolo is my brother; you are not. It is something entirely different. I no longer even remember what you were like when you were my brother, that is, when we were children. Now you are someone else.”

She paused, then began again:

“Besides, it is natural that there should be a difference between us. You have had so many other lovers; you have been caressed, kissed, adored by so many... What you may feel for me resembles, at most, the desire you might feel for another woman. Whereas I...”

“No, Lora, do not say that! Do not say it! It is absurd! Can you not see, then, that I am making a terrible effort against myself to save you?”

“To save me? To save me, you say? But I do not want to be saved! To what end? So that perhaps one day Rafa, or someone else like Rafa, may take me? I am free, do you understand? Free to do with myself what I please. And it is I who seek you, not you who seek me. If you are afraid of remorse, I want to take it all upon myself. Look: I am reasoning calmly; I know what I am saying. I love you; I want to be yours; that alone pleases me. I want to caress you, to have you caress me, to live close to you, to be in love with you, jealous over you... And it is I who want it, not you; I alone... is that enough for you?”

He looked at that twenty-year-old girl, that simple flower whose calyx was so deep and mature, so fragrant and perverse. A kind of silent admiration arose within him, as though he were afraid of it.

“Loretta,” he said, “at your age one cannot yet know what is good and what is evil, or at least which evil is too great.”

“The too-great evil is not having the courage to be happy,” she said, perhaps unaware of her own words.

Two young dandies came in, merry and boisterous, out carousing that evening in the company of two little courtesans, so red with rouge and so eccentrically dressed that many among those sated bourgeois appeared scandalized by them. The two talkative girls, holding the arms of their escorts, walked on high heels with a loose-jointed gait and an indecent swaying of their hips, every so often bursting into shrill laughter that struck other people’s eardrums like a false note from an out-of-tune guitar. They were low-class pleasure-seekers or night revelers and women of low gallantry; as they passed, they glanced at Arrigo’s table, and one of the men greeted him. Old acquaintances, perhaps from the days when he used to frequent taverns with a band of dubious idlers in disreputable drinking shops. The newcomers sat down at a nearby table and plainly began talking about him. Arrigo, guessing the tenor of their conversation, regretted for the first time that they had caught him in that country tavern, a place almost clandestine for a young gentleman, and had caught the two of them alone, looking like lovers, bound to look like lovers to everyone, perhaps bearing on their faces the indelible shadow of their sin.

Loretta understood that something was troubling him and asked:

“Who is that fellow who greeted you?”

“A little lawyer with no clients,” Arrigo replied; “an unsavory character.”

“And those two girls?”

“Oh, I wouldn’t know!”

“They are talking about us.”

“I noticed.”

“What can they be saying?”

“Nothing good, certainly. I am very sorry they have seen us together, because the world guesses certain things, God knows how.”

“Do you think so?”

“Perhaps not these people; but once we have been seen together too many times, someone else—who knows...”

“Very well, we shall think about it later.”

They both fell silent. Laughter rang through the garden; those who had eaten too much allowed their stomachs to perform the labor of digestion in peace; meanwhile, warmed by wine, they exchanged cheerful remarks. The children had been given free rein and went racing beneath the arbors with loud cries; men and women, their faces flushed with that heat which comes from excessive food and generous wine, poured over the still-cluttered tables the salt of anecdotes and the pepper of bawdy jokes. Husbands, lovers, and sweethearts thought of the approaching night.

Upstairs they were dancing. That surge of somewhat tempestuous music spilled onto the terrace through the open windows; from time to time a girl appeared there, all overheated, her hair disheveled, with a honey-tongued admirer hovering around her. They drew a breath of air, then off they went again, tightly, fiercely, into the commotion of the dance.

And he thought of putting out the light in the room so as to have more courage,
but he wished for a glimmer to filter in, a half-light growing gradually more
discernible, perhaps from the streetlamps in the road, perhaps from a shaded
lamp in the adjoining room. And he smelled the fragrance of her body diffused
about him, that same fragrance, but sweeter, which he had had upon his mouth
when kissing her; an intense and manifold fragrance that blossomed from her
skin, as though roses were hidden in the folds of her body. He savored the
freshness of that springtime flesh, imagined caressing her round bare shoulder,
slipped his groping hand into the velvety warmth of her armpits, gathered her
torso, pliant as a young shoot, into his tight embrace, felt against himself the
unrestrainable throbbing of her womb, the way her body would entwine itself with
his body, to offer itself and to defend itself, conceived the savage joy of
being able to stun her, heard in her throat the death rattle of fleeing
virginity, heard her weep in rapture, laugh in pain... then he saw her as she
was, slender, arched, strong in her slightness, grow pale for a moment with that
pallor which is near to death, and flash forth in all her beauty with love amid
that exultant hatred with which the virgin gives herself...

But suddenly she had felt ill. Truly, just as in his vision, he had seen her
turn white with that same pallor, had felt his arms seized by her convulsed
hands, then, seeing her stagger, had supported her against himself.

“What is it, Lora?”

She did not answer; her teeth were chattering; she was trembling.

“Lora! Lora! What is it?”

“Nothing...” she stammered, “it will pass...”

It was only a dizzy spell, and soon her mouth smiled at him again. They resumed
their journey; he supported her as far as the carriage.

The coachman prattled; the little horse began trotting again toward the city of
its martyrdom, where there were the rough paving stone, the slippery rail, the
posting station, and the stable. On either side of the two hedges, fragrant in
the white night, the tilled earth was growing grains and fruits for the
voracious city; some cricket in love with the moon raised its shrill song,
infinitely greater than itself.

Now her head hurt; around her temples she had an iron band that hammered. To
soothe that pain she took one of her brother’s hands and wrapped it around her
forehead.

“Are you suffering?”

“Yes, a little.”

He encircled her forehead, from one temple to the other, with countless little
kisses.

“Keep me close, very close... and I shall recover.”

In a garden they passed, the May roses were opening their calyxes swollen with
spring.

“Do you still feel ill?”

“Yes, a sweet pain...”

Beyond a row of poplars, the city’s red blaze reappeared like a vast cloud
suspended in the firmament. They reached the first houses, with walls white in
the moonlight. Now the crickets were a hundred, were a thousand, lost in the
May hay, and one, more wrathful than all the others, seemed to pursue them close
behind along the hawthorn hedge.

Suddenly she let her head fall back against his shoulder, as though the onset
of a faint were overcoming her.

“Rigo, I feel ill...” she stammered, pressing her breast.

“But what is it?” he said, distraught. “Why are you suffering so?”

She closed her eyes and tried once more to smile at him from her wholly white
face.

“I feel dizzy... I don’t know...”

“Do you want to stop? What do you want to do?”

“Nothing; it will pass now... it will pass... I love you...”

When they reached the last farmhouse, the cricket’s wandering song faded far
away, infinitely far away, and died. But before them appeared the monumental
tollhouse, majestic as a triumphal arch beneath the starry sky. The customs
guards, seated near the booth, laughed and smoked, chatting with women of ill
repute. Amid throngs of children, several vagrants were playing a peddler’s
raffle game; an eater of flaming tow gaped his enormous soot-blackened mouth
before the astonished spectators.

“I love you...” she said again, in a breath, to her pale lover.

And the hair shirt of unconsumable guilt clothed their desperate flesh like a
mantle of thorns.




VIII


He arrived unexpectedly at Clara Michelis’s house around lunchtime. She had
not seen him for several days; she had written to him several times without
receiving an answer, and had repeatedly gone to his house, but had never found
him there. She could not regard Arrigo’s neglecting her as unusual; yet he had
never shown himself indifferent to such a degree.

Mother and daughter were sitting at the table when he arrived. The servant was
the first to ask him whether he had already eaten lunch.

After he answered no, his customary place was laid for him, and he sat down
there with the air of a broken man.

“I have had a great deal to do these past few days,” he said by way of apology.
“Forgive me for not coming.”

Neither the daughter nor the servants were any longer surprised by his presence
in that house; he had become something of its master, everyone knew in what
capacity, and by now no one paid any further attention to it. That day his face
was pale and agitated, his eyes full of fever, his hands somewhat restless.

“I have been extremely busy,” he repeated, as though he did not know what else
to say.

Out of regard for her daughter, Clara did not say a word, but remained looking
at him, staring at him, with her gentle eyes full of tenderness and
resignation. She was greatly afraid of him when she saw him arrive in that
state. She too looked worn, and because she had expected to be alone, she had
come to lunch in a dressing gown without having finished making herself
presentable. Face powder left a visible trace upon her somewhat worn skin; her
neck, emerging slenderly from the lace around the low neckline, had the
appearance of something diseased; as she ate, a few very slight wrinkles formed
at the corners of her mouth and near the arches of her eyebrows. Perhaps she
had wept during the sleepless night; her eyes seemed to have grown dim, and
they turned toward her lover a gaze full of anguished tenderness.

Adelina, by contrast, appeared wholly fresh in her blooming seventeen years;
but that Signor Arrigo made her a little uncomfortable when, instead of joking
with her as usual, he came with that mastiff’s face of his and from time to time
looked at her with eyes as fierce as those of some great nocturnal bird.

“What ever have you had to do all these days?” Clara finally asked, trying to
give her words a playful tone.

“Many things,” he said. “I shall tell you.”

And at once, to change the subject, he turned to the young lady:

“And you, Lela, how are you?” He tried to smile, but his face was tense.

“Lela is very well,” the girl replied merrily. “It seems to me, though, that
you are not very well.”

“Why?”

“Why, did you not look at yourself in the mirror this morning?”

“Ah... I had no time to shave: that is the reason. And then my head hurts a
little.”

“And you are not eating?”

“Yes, I am eating; but I have little appetite.”

“Perhaps you would like to take something for your headache?” Clara
interrupted, looking at him with eyes already full of forgiveness.

And the little horse trotted on; the little horse, insensible to the warmth of spring, equally weary and resigned in the storms of winter and in the dog days of summer, limped over the hostile stones, slowly, slowly, with that immovable philosophy which comes after despair; a poor old machine made of bones and aches, indifferent to the tugs, the lashes, the impatience of the customers, as though by now it knew that its entire destiny was to keep going, by dint of stumbling and wheezing, slowly, but to keep going.

The nearby countryside sent a few rural scents among the last houses, and already appeared entirely open, almost wrapped in a violet air, along the side roads that were no longer paved. The driver turned into one of them.

“I have never come this far,” Loretta said. “It feels as though we are in the country; smell how lovely it is!”

Some meadow nearby had been mown; the haymaking stacks gave off vegetal fragrances in the spring evening. Even the nag, at that scent of savory May hay, seemed to feel its greedy soul swell within its lean flanks, and pulled harder. The driver stuck a cigar stub between his teeth and began to hum; with cracks of his whip he accompanied his monotonous singsong. This made Loretta laugh.

“How funny he is!” she said softly to her brother. And she drew close to him with a little laugh that breathed her fresh breath into his face.

He did not speak; a sort of torpor, a sensation he had never known, gently enveloped his spirit, imparting to him a physical weariness, a kind of sensual languor. For one brief hour he liked to forget that his little companion, she whose arm it was sweet to feel beneath his arm and whose breath upon his face, was his very own sister, come from the same womb that had given him life, nourished with the same milk, rocked in the same cradle: the daughter of his father and his mother, his full sister.

At the same time he felt an immense horror, an unconscious horror, of himself, and yet in this he found his greatest voluptuous pleasure. He liked to hear her speak; that voice, which he felt he had never known before, entered the innermost depths of his heart, lavishing upon him something like a slow and exhausting caress. That she said she loved him, that she dared tell him that she loved him, that her desire was so manifest to him, so ready to let itself be seized, that she had an almost morbid need to wrap herself around his person and make him feel the trembling of her soft, still untouched limbs, that she spoke to him as to her first sweetheart... all this dazed him, tempted him, intoxicated him, set a vehement pulse beating in his strong heart, a shiver almost of terror in his excited veins, a kind of torment in his rough nerves, whose every perversity he savored slowly.

In her truly lay forbidden possession, the joy that was not to be known, the crime and the supreme voluptuous pleasure.

When she spoke to him of love, he would have liked, in turn, to answer her: “Yes, I love you! You are the first I love, the only one I shall ever be able to love... You stir a great tempest within me that intoxicates me...” But he was ashamed of this, and the words that resounded within him seemed impossible to utter. So he remained silent, leaving it to her to speak—to her, since she was almost a child, a little child, and could say anything.

But merely in calling to her, in speaking to her, in uttering her name, he put an infinite love. It was no longer merely his desire for her, that vehement desire which had assailed him, enslaving him and twisting him to the point of pain; now it was something more, a kind of sadness, a pent-up and murky frenzy that possessed him to his innermost depths and wounded him like a thorn driven into his heart.

He, who had never faced his own conscience, was now afraid of himself. He feared something obscure; between him and her there was an indefinable, unknown force that terrified him; over his guilty love there hung something like a more-than-human threat. He wanted to be harsh, and could only manage to be gentle; he wanted not to look at her, and his eyes, despite himself, went to meet hers. Even when he was far away and distracted, her image remained fixed in his mind without respite. He wanted to think of other women, other loves, and she furtively nestled in his arms with a stronger promise; he wanted to thrust her away from him, as though to purify himself of this guilt, and the guilt came back to him, flowed into his heart through every vein, like a wave of voluptuous pleasure.

The little horse trotted on; the uniform countryside rested from the day’s labor, broken by farmhouses, crossed by roads, marked by hedges. A row of poplars here and there, across the vaporous plain, receded out of sight into the white night. Behind them the city loomed, overhung by a reddish glow which, in the still air, was the reflection of its many lights.

Beyond a hedge they saw a flock of sheep spending the night; it had spread across the little meadow in small groups, and slept there, gleaming white. The dog rushed to the verge, its fur all bristling, and barked.

“Look,” Loretta said with childlike wonder, “look how white they are and how close together they sleep.”

Those sleeping little sheep inspired a singular tenderness in her child’s heart. She added:

“Life in the country must be better than in the cities. Why don’t you take me away, Rigo?”

“Take you away? But where?”

“It doesn’t matter where. Just for one week. I should like to take a little journey with you, to stay close to you always, day and night, never to leave you, day and night... What happiness—just think!”

Her brother shook his head and, without speaking, caressed the backs of her hands, then her knees.

“Take me away...” she said again, pleadingly.

“It cannot be done.”

At that moment they passed a merry party returning to the city singing. A village appeared in the distance, and, before the village, behind a house, a cluster of thick trees where many lights shone.

“You see: that is where we are dining,” Arrigo said, pointing to the glow. “Many people come in summer because the food is good there.”

He said that he had thought about himself and about her—about her above all—and had understood that they were both preparing, with their own hands, an irreparable ruin. That she was young and had to live, while he would never have consented to share her with anyone. And she must let no illusion blind her. Today, perhaps, her greatest joy lay in sacrificing herself, but inevitably a day would come, and perhaps not a distant one, when she would repent of it too late. Indeed, how many aspirations, how many impatient longings were already tormenting her ardent youth! For she was a child of twenty, and at twenty love, even so troubled a love, can be nothing but a gust of sentiment, a breath of perverse ardor, which fades and passes and leaves no memory of itself... Then, in the long run, nothing can be hidden. People, sooner or later, would notice. And then?... Did she feel she had the courage to endure such shame openly? Everyone would execrate them, shun them like two leprous dogs, like two creatures possessed, and for them there would remain neither family, nor friends, nor future, nor peace, nor any of those human comforts that are, after all, necessary to every creature. Moreover, they were not rich, and it was therefore necessary that each, along a separate path, provide for the future, since both had chosen a road different from the one marked out in their destiny. If they had been rich, perhaps, very rich, they could have fled to a country where no one knew them or could ever come to know them, and there forget that they had been born of the same mother, the same father, remembering only that they loved one another.

But even if that were so, would they ever have found peace in their own consciences? “Remember!—he said to her—everything can be silenced except the inexorable voice that rises from the depths of our heart. And remorse, you see, is the most terrible enemy of all those life holds in store for us.”

And not only that: but what if a child were born of their sin? What if they should ever give the world a creature so accursed from its very origin? What if from the two of them, brother and sister, there should be born an infamous creature, excluded from all human laws, who would make them tremble whenever its childish mouth uttered those first words that are babbled: “mamma, papa...”

Had she ever thought of all this? Certainly not; because she was still young, inexperienced in every danger, and let herself be seized unthinkingly by the madness of her love, which was only “her first love...”

For him too it was the first, the only, truly the one and only. And she would certainly recover from it; he would not. He would do everything possible to forget, but all this would serve only to mingle his poisonous malady more deeply into his veins. For her, without a doubt, it was nothing but a slight caprice, a gust of wind, an impetuous wave of heat in the freshness of her twenty years... Oh, she must not say no! He knew it well, and this was perhaps his greatest torment. But he, on the other hand, was already a mature man and, indeed, a man who until then had remained insensible to every passion; and so a dark storm had been unleashed in his soul, one of those storms that overwhelm and destroy an entire life. However much he struggled with all his strength, there was now no escape; another man had suddenly entered into him, utterly different from the man he had been until then; his mind, his heart, his senses—everything had changed. His free youth had been chained on the day he had begun to love her, and now he lived as though under the magic of a spell; he no longer knew how to master himself; he was beside himself.

He had to arm himself with all his strength so as not to drag her too into his own ruin; he had to love her with an infinite love, more than love, with a boundless adoration, in order to come and tell her what he was telling her:

—“I am leaving, I am fleeing; you will never see me again. I must stay far from you even if it kills me; I must renounce you so that you may be happy later. I must find within my human strength the pitiless strength not to take you, and to go away, alone, to seek refuge who knows where—I who love you, I who do not live a single moment without thinking of you, I who, wherever I go, shall carry in my senses and in my soul the memory of you, more vivid and more terrible than you yourself... And that is not all. You are defended, watched over; there is your father, our father, who defends you. Every time my lips wished to kiss you, I would see him now. Last night, when we were together, when you were almost mine, all at once he came; I saw him. He was there, between you and me, looking at me with his unwavering eyes. His face merged with your face. I heard our father cursing us. And now his specter no longer leaves me. Do you understand, Loretta, do you understand that it would drive me mad?...

“I ask only one thing of you: have pity on me. Do nothing to keep me here; do not weep; do not repeat that you would have wished to be mine. Instead you must hate me, because this love I have for you—remember!—is a horrible thing. Do as you wish: go back home, or stay, or go wherever you will be happy. But do not forget that a man is fleeing, casting his dead heart out of life, to save you, solely to save from ruin the sister whom he loved...

“Later, when you are a woman, remember that if my guilt was great, I also struggled as much as a man can struggle to rebel against this guilt. And do not say anything to me, Lora... never seek me again. I am leaving at once, this morning, in an hour...”


And he left.

I


She remained in that hotel for two days, lost, inert, astonished, bewildered. What was happening was new, unexpected, to her. The revelation of this desperate love, the tragic aspect of this passion, at first gave her a sense of painful wonder.

She did not understand love in this way; for her, love could be nothing but a romantic tangle of sad and joyful sensations, of words that come to the lips to be transformed into a kiss, of unsatisfied curiosities, of vehement aspirations toward a physical contentment unknown to her. For her, then, love was meant to be a joyous thing.

She was nothing but a little wasp, light, fickle, stinging: she felt a sense of unease before this love so tragic. She had become enamored of her brother, but without finding in it the slightest savor of incest; indeed, she had loved him by instinct, without thinking of his name, without even realizing that she was violating a sacred prohibition. She had met him when, in her voluptuous lover’s womb, still sealed, she felt an invincible need for self-surrender, wrapped in the obscure lusts that torment the fire of virginity. From him she had undergone her first temptation; for him she had felt the first dark unrest of love arise in her blood; her virgin womb, thus and in no other way, loved him.

She was at once so simple and so perverse that she could feel an incestuous love purely; the evil lay so well hidden within her that she did not know she was contaminated by it.

Man, who in his actions is often impulsive, nevertheless loves to question himself, to debate his own passions; woman, who by nature instead has a reflective spirit, when a strong passion binds her, debates no longer and allows her desire to surrender itself to it without a shadow of fear. Nothing is so pleasing to her as escaping the dominion of her own will, whereas it is always with great regret that we relinquish power over ourselves.

“Perhaps from my parents, perhaps...” she added hesitantly, “from my brother.”

“And not from me, in any case?”

“From you? How from you?”

“You once told me, while speaking to me of other things: ‘My family bores me; perhaps a day will come when I shall be free, entirely free, because I want to sing.’ Do you remember telling me that?”

“Yes, I remember, and I repeat: A day will come, perhaps soon, when I shall be free.”

“There, and thinking of that day, I too had a dream... but one so beautiful that I dare not tell it to you.”

“Dreams...” she joked, “dreams have this good thing about them: they serve to tell things that are too difficult to say.”

“You are right, Loretta,” he admitted. “Then, a dream. That I should get you a little villa, not too far from Villa Giuliani, small, for you alone. A hidden little villa, with a beautiful garden, an orchard, a stable. You would be free; no one would know who you are. Sometimes, so as not to remain alone, you would open the gate for me.”

“Ah... and that is the dream?”

“Yes, that is it.”

She reflected for a moment, then said:

“Go on.”

“What do you mean?”

“After the summer...”

“Well, after the summer you will be able to choose whatever you like. In autumn, for example, a beautiful journey, a little getaway, by motorcar, if you wish, even abroad, if you wish... And in winter, your house in the city, a lady companion to preserve appearances, a teacher to teach you singing.”

“And in spring,” she exclaimed, still tempted, “since the year blooms again, another is put in Lora’s place, and everything begins again: the same villa, the journey, the house in the city... No, thank you!”

“Another? But what are you saying? Have you still not understood that I love you, that I have loved you for many months, more strongly every day? That you can make me obey like a child, and that you alone, you alone, must give me back the peace I no longer have?... Another? That word has no meaning! But think for a moment. Do you believe I do not know what risks I am running by making you this proposal? Well, what do I care? I do not want to, I can no longer think! No danger frightens me. Only say yes to me! Ask me for whatever you want, but say yes to me!”

“I am not asking for anything,” she said, regretting that she had allowed herself to appear so calculating.

“Then listen, listen to me...” And he knelt before her armchair and encircled her with his arms.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?”

“Nothing; I am begging you on my knees. Care for me a little; be good to me for once!”

Thus on his knees, leaning toward her in the ardor of his desire, with passionate eyes and a pleading voice, Rafa was almost handsome, and she looked at him.

“Come, leave me alone...” she said, with a certain annoyance.

He held her tightly around the waist and, leaning on her a little, covered her dress and her wrists with tiny kisses.

“How many mistresses have you had sit in this armchair?” she asked suddenly.

“How many? None.”

“Oh, come now! I am asking out of curiosity.”

“Perhaps,” he said, “some woman has come here, but I do not remember. They were not mistresses; they were not you. If you do not like it, we shall change houses. I had no love before I met you. Now you seem the first to me. I love you, I love you in every way; you persecute me and you please me. You are beautiful. You have such an indefinable grace that I suffer when I am near you. Be good to me; do not laugh!...”

She was indeed laughing, but with a somewhat nervous laugh, and her mouth, her eyes, her hands were no longer so calm.

“No, leave me alone...” she pleaded. “Let me go, please... you are hurting me terribly...”

In the half-light he saw her turn pale; he hid his face in her lap, and with his arms he clasped her knees.

She tried to lift his burning forehead, tried to push away that troublesome mouth, but, unable to overcome his strength, with sudden anger she thrust her convulsed fingers into his hair.

Then the struggle was brief: desperately, the girl closed her eyes and let herself be carried away...

But she saw another room, at night, with its windows open above a lake white with moonlight, and the stars close and infinite; another man bent over her, covering her with caresses and kisses. And she saw herself again in that bed, and relived the agony of that vanished hour, and for an instant it seemed to her that he had returned, that he was there, on his knees, and was kissing her terribly as he had then, and that his hands were running feverishly, ardently, over all her tormented body, and that a mouth was rising, rising to her lips, full of anguish, fever, voluptuousness, and terror...

A little later, the adjoining room was dark, and from room to room, through the silent house, there was suddenly heard the cry of her lost virginity.




II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and, after ordering an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several others were playing poker.

Beppe Cianella was hot and wiped his sweating forehead with a brightly colored silk handkerchief. He unbuttoned his waistcoat, lit a cigar, and blissfully closed his eyes as if to doze off. But it was too hot to sleep. In a still drowsy voice, Beppe Cianella called the servant and asked him to turn the fan toward him.

When the cool air struck him, he stretched out more comfortably on the sofa and, with a feeling of true bliss, tried to close his mischievous eyes.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair,” he said with a slight yawn.

“So much the better for him!” replied one of the players.

Sacco Berni had attempted a daring “bluff,” but Gigi Saponetta, a highly skilled player, had forced him to show his hand, and the others, laughing wildly over it, mocked the trickster who had been tricked.

Count Berrini passed by at the back, in his shirtsleeves, bellowing at the servants because he could not find a newspaper; Lello Fornara, the languishing one, was writing his daily love letter in a corner; through the open doorway leading into the billiard room, the balls could be heard striking one another amid the noisy quarrels of old Baron Gioacchini and his young pupil Leonardo Sergi.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair!” Beppe Cianella, who could not fall asleep, repeated between one yawn and the next.

She had gone out onto the deserted terrace, had stretched herself lazily in the reclining chair, and now she was waiting for him, gazing into the miracle of the night, where the magnificence of the stars trembled with a kind of furious intensity.

“What are you doing out there? Have you not gone to bed, then?”

A little intoxicated by the stars, by the silence, and by love, she held out both arms to him without answering.

“Why do you not undress?” he asked again.

“I was waiting for you,” she replied in a slow, slightly veiled voice.

The light breath of night had passed through her hair; the whiteness of the moonbeam shone upon her face. “It is damp in the evening,” he observed; “do not stay outside too long.”

Then, turning quickly, he said to her, “It is late now; sleep well. Goodbye.”

“Rigo...” she uttered softly, as though she were still lost in the dream. And there was a little intoxication in her feminine languor, in her ambiguous manner, in the voice with which she called him. “Rigo, come here: sit down.”

She made a little room for him beside her. He obeyed in silence. The warmth of that sweet body spread through his veins like a poisoned, very slow pleasure. He was bent over her face; the girl’s hands caressed his hair, his forehead.

Then she began speaking softly to him, with long pauses, in trepidation.

“You must not leave me alone... Tonight more than ever I feel the need to be close to you, very close, because it would be truly melancholy to put a wall, to close a door, between you and me... Do you not see what a magnificent night it is? There is a scent of jasmine flying through the air like intoxicating dust. And then I feel full of torpor tonight... Kiss me!... My hands are hot, feel... They hurt... They are burning. I want to stay here all night, talking to you, caressing you, rather than remain alone.

She plunged her fingers into his thick hair, as one sometimes does in warm furs in winter. And she continued:

“There, in the garden, you told me things so grave that I am troubled by them; I should like to weep, but in the depths of my heart there is a joy that laughs, a kind of inexpressible hope... Do not leave me alone. Or I should also like to do something I have never done: come into your bed, fall asleep beside you... Kiss me! And then tell me something truly dangerous... Even an innocent word, if you do not wish to tell me anything else... I love you, and I shall not be able to sleep alone... because I want you to kiss me. Feel how much in love my mouth is... Kiss me! I am yours... yours... take me! I desire nothing but to suffer from you... for you... Hurt me a little... give me a kiss, just one, without end... bend down...”

These words, spoken close to his mouth, lulled him like the music of a gentle spell, swathed his aching senses in an ineffable relief, and, closing his eyes, he stiffened in order to listen to her. A great shiver of pleasure passed over his cold flesh; an imperceptible wasting away, an endless languishing spread through him beneath the caress of that voice.

She spoke again, enervated, exhausted:

“Look: I am closing my eyes... I am asleep. Bend down a little, kiss me!... I am so sleepy... I love you. Be gentle with me... Listen: there is no sound, no one is watching us... kiss me!”

Like a madman he kissed her mouth, her forehead, her temples, her neck, her wrists, her hands, with a hoarse panting in his constricted throat, and he kissed her all over her fragrant flesh until his breath failed him. Then he rose, disheveled, tore himself away from her as she held him, thrust her violently back onto the cushions, ran into his own room, and locked himself in.

She gave a little cry and, trembling as she was beneath the lash of those kisses, broke into a convulsion of tears, then remained for a few moments almost lifeless.

The half-moon was rising above the mountains, high, clear, far from the stars.

He threw himself onto the bed, biting the pillows, clutching at the covers, to master the tumult that was rending him within, and not to hear that subdued voice pleading with him behind the door, and not to look any further into the terrible possibility of that hour.

The night advanced, clear, almost trembling, toward the heights of its glorious radiance, scattering a still greater magnificence of stars across the curve of infinity. The lake and the shores, inhabited by nocturnal shadows, pervaded by the ambiguity of silence, clothed themselves in white splendors beneath the enchantment of the night.

A length of time passed that seemed infinite to him; then he thought he understood that she had begun to undress. He no longer heard the sound of her slender heels on the floor, but the soft tread of two slippers moving hurriedly; then he was tempted to approach the inner door that divided them and begin listening. But instead the door to the corridor suddenly opened, and she entered.

She was in a dressing gown, frightened and pale, and stopped on the threshold. He sprang down from the bed and stood gazing at her in astonishment.

“What do you want?...” he stammered in a stifled voice.

“Nothing,” she replied. She looked at him. There was an unusual light in her altered eyes; the expression of that face was singularly changed. There was also something harsh and wild in her, in her mouth that was usually so smiling.

“Will you not sleep tonight?”

“No.”

Then her brother began pacing gloomily about the room, without going near her, as though he were plotting some horrible thing against her.

But he quickly opened the window and went out onto the terrace.

All the stars wheeled through the trembling immensity like a whirlwind of golden confetti.

Stealthily, she glided after him, so lightly that he did not hear her, and hung upon his neck. She no longer wore a corset; she wore nothing but an almost diaphanous dressing gown, which scarcely concealed her swelling chemise and short petticoat; her body wrapped itself around him as a soft silk scarf wraps itself, in the wind, around the neck of the person wearing it. Her hair, which was held by a single comb, also came loose and, without falling completely, thick and soft, crowded about the nape of her neck.

Painfully, bitterly, their mouths joined. She felt the agony of surrender so near that she twined herself around him like ivy, wound herself around him like a knot.

Berto saw her turn frightfully pale at once; drawing an armchair near for her, he made her sit down, knelt before her, and Loredana remained like that for a moment, her face white, her eyes closed, while Berto kept kissing her gloved hands. Then she became aware that gently, gently, with consummate skill, he was removing her hat and veil, and, kneeling again, was pressing his lips to her hands.

She reopened her eyes, and, looking at him at her feet, noticed the shiny, burning scar that crossed his face like a formidable lash of a riding crop.

“I have come to you,” she said. “I have fled. I have left Filippo. I still love him, I love him always, I love no one but him; but his mother is dying, and I must flee from him.... I have come to take refuge with you.... How hot it is in this room; I feel as though I am suffocating!”

Without rising to his feet, he unfastened her fur coat and let it fall around her, so that her slender torso seemed to emerge from that white, soft nest mottled with black. Looking around, she saw herself in a mirror; she no longer had her hat, no longer her fur coat; she was undressed, as though she had returned to her own home; and that man was at her feet, mute, humble, and already her master....

The sight revealed her to herself. She sprang upright, exclaiming:

“No; what am I doing? I am mad....”

Berto too had risen, and, placing himself before her, said quickly:

“Do not flee: you are in the home of a gentleman. Calm yourself. I need to know and to speak to you. If you wish to leave here, I shall not detain you.... Grant me the bitter satisfaction of asking your forgiveness. I have paid for my error. I was truly guilty, but I appeared guiltier in your eyes because you believed it a whim, whereas I loved you and love you with profound feeling.... Do not flee, I implore you....”

Loredana sat down again, gathering the white fur coat around herself.

As soon as Berto saw her thus, calm and astonished, he left the drawing room and returned precipitately, holding a bottle in one hand and a glass in the other. Neither he nor the young woman noticed the ridiculousness of that dash; Berto pushed toward Loredana a small table supported by four slender griffins and, pouring, set the glass beside his guest.

“Drink,” he said, “I beg you: it will give you strength.”

Loredana had seen that the bubbling liquid was champagne; she made a gesture of refusal and replied:

“No, it is not possible; it would make me ill.”

Candriani was not listening to her; drunk with joy, able to gaze at her with the intensity of a desire no longer restrained, he looked over all of her avidly, from her head to her small feet, the tips of which emerged from the very edge of her skirt.

“I shall make you forget Filippo,” he said suddenly. “You will no longer love him; I am free and alone, I can devote my entire life to you.... Love him still today, it does not matter; it is right that you should love him; it will be for me to erase his image from your heart.”

And suddenly he burst out:

“I am happy; I am happy to see you beside me; you remembered that I offered you my friendship in a desperate situation, and that consoles me for many sorrows.... Ah, I assure you, Loredana, that I am no longer the thoughtless man you once knew! I love you tenderly, and I hope I can reassure you....”

She cut off his words with a gesture.

“No,” she replied. “I shall never love you.”

She looked around and, seeing the glass, raised it to her lips, which felt parched by an inner fever.

“Listen to me,” she continued imperiously. “I am here not because I love you, not because I believe in your friendship, but because I wish and must ruin myself.”

“Loredana, Loredana, for pity’s sake!” Berto interrupted.

“I must ruin myself. He is about to commit a crime. His sick mother asked him to leave me, and he refused.... No, I cannot accept this sacrifice; it is a horrible thing; I must leave him, and in such a way that he will no longer seek me, no longer desire me.... I do not wish to harm his mother, who has already suffered so much because of me.... If she were to die, ah, if she were to die, what remorse, what shame!... And one day he would awaken from this madness; and between him and me, always, always, I would see his mother’s corpse.... I must prevent him from dishonoring himself!”

Berto, standing upright, listened with a sense of wonder to the young woman, who spoke rapidly, agitated by violent excitement; her first pallor had given way to a feverish flush that crimsoned her cheeks, made her eyes shine intensely, and reddened her lips, giving them the color of living blood.

She pleased him so much, stretched out in the armchair and sunk into the snowy fur, that Berto bent down once more to kiss her hands. Loredana pushed him away.

“I wanted to kill myself,” she continued, “but it would have been a new scandal; they might have accused Filippo of my death.... Ah, how malicious they all are!... I was told to my face that I am your mistress, that my honor is worth nothing because no one believes me, that a man is a thief when everyone calls him a thief.... How many frightful things I have learned! And then I thought they were right. The only one who did not doubt me was Filippo; he believes in my love and in my honor, which everyone laughs at; and so he too must cease to believe, so that he may save himself.... I thought that, since they call me your mistress, every effort is useless, and I shall never again be able to free myself from this accusation....”

“Do not speak like that,” Berto interrupted. “It hurts you too much....”

She stared at him with wide eyes; that informal “you” seemed to her more brutal than a kiss that had suddenly closed her mouth; but Berto noticed and added:

“I beg your pardon; I did not mean to offend you. I love you, and I did not know how to control myself.”

“No,” said Loredana, rising, “let me go!”

Berto dared to lay a hand on her.

“I beg you,” he murmured, “stay a little longer.....”

Loredana shuddered; gathering up the fur coat, she looked for her hat. But just as she was about to take it, she stopped as though struck by a thought.

Where was she going? To her own home? Filippo would take her back. To Filippo’s home? His mother would die of it.
