The girl did not have the courage to extricate herself from that tormenting situation: the entire Gianella family—Adolfo’s mother, father, uncles, and cousins—surrounded her, extolling the young man’s virtues, making plans for the future, showing themselves so certain, so delighted by that singularly happy marriage, that Loredana suffocated and remained silent. But it would have been impossible to find a man more incapable of understanding her than Adolfo, so much so that she, who was kind to everyone, was always irritated, nervous, and sorrowful with him.

Lately he had even wanted to read the letters she received from her friends, whom he did not trust at all; one morning, while he had gone to bid his fiancée good morning, the letter carrier arrived, and Adolfo seized the mail, opened a letter from a girl who was writing to Loredana from a town in the province, asked about the people mentioned in it, and ended by putting the letter in his pocket.

When Filippo arrived toward evening, the girl was still quivering all over with indignation and anger; she told her friend everything, even what she had kept silent until that day: Adolfo’s harassment, stinginess, insulting distrust, unreasonable jealousy, and presumption.

“I do not want him, I do not want him, I do not want him!” she exclaimed, her eyes flashing with rage. “Anything rather than this marriage! Never, never, never!”

Filippo had listened in silence, looking at the floor of red and white tiles and marking the rhythm of a march with his foot.

Suddenly he raised his head, grasped his friend’s hands, and asked:

“Would you come with me?”

The girl did not understand at once.

“Where?” she asked.

“Away, far away, out of Venice, forever!” Filippo pressed her.

“Run away? Run away with you?” she said in a low voice, already trembling without knowing why.

“Listen to me,” Filippo murmured.

He went as far as the threshold of the little sitting room, saw that Mama was intently reading a poorly bound book, and continued as he returned to Loredana:

“What we call friendship is nothing but love. Have you realized it?”

She remained rigid and motionless, her eyes wide open, and did not answer.

“I have realized it,” Filippo went on. “I know that I love you, I feel that I love you, I feel that we can be happy. I cannot marry you; understand me clearly, I cannot marry you because my whole family would cause us so many, so very many sorrows that, by comparison, what you have suffered until now would seem a joy to you. They are ignorant, stubborn, and ferocious.... But I offer you my love and my life all the same.... I too am tired; I too can no longer drag out this tormenting and useless existence. Tell me that you accept, and we shall be happy.... We shall leave at once....”

Loredana withdrew her hands from Filippo’s and rose to her feet: she took a few steps as though to leave the room, but stopped and leaned back against the wall; she was weeping in silence, and the tears ran down her cheeks.

Filippo approached her again. He was pale, and his voice trembled. He said:

“Are you offended?”

She shook her head.

“Then you are not in love with me, as I am with you?”

No answer came. Loredana looked at her friend through the veil of her tears. He took a step as though to move away, but the girl quickly, instinctively, stopped him with a gesture.

“Yes, I love you too,” she murmured in a low voice.

Filippo seized her around the waist and kissed her on the mouth.

“Think about it,” he said. “Think how very happy we shall be.... Mama will forgive you. She loves you too dearly to condemn you. She will understand that you had the right to live, to escape a dreadful future. You will know how to make her forgive you, will you not? For you know the way to reach Mama’s heart! Tell me that you accept, and we shall leave at once....”

She, still leaning against the wall, still motionless, her eyes full of tears, did not answer. But a peal of the doorbell made both her and Filippo start.

The girl hastily dried her eyes and ran into the little sitting room.

“It must be Adolfo,” she said to Mama. “I have a migraine, I do not want to see him, I am going to shut myself in my room!”

Mama sighed and raised her eyes to the ceiling. Loredana returned to Filippo and clasped his hands while he kissed her once more on the mouth.

“Think about it!” Filippo repeated.

She made a vague gesture and disappeared, to shut herself in her little room.

Adolfo Gianella was coming up the stairs, and Filippo, hearing his footsteps, was saying to Signora De Carolis:

“I am very sorry that the young lady is indisposed; I hope it is nothing....”

“Is she ill?” Adolfo asked as he arrived, greeting Filippo with a cold salutation and a sidelong glance. “Where was she last evening? She must have caught cold, or eaten something indigestible....”

Filippo left at once, and despite himself he said inwardly, laughing:

“You will soon have to eat something indigestible yourself!...”

That night he thought again about the idea of running away, which had flashed upon him so suddenly; and the more he thought about it, the better it seemed to him. Signora De Carolis would not have dared do anything against her adored daughter; Adolfo would have found consolation in the thought that a girl capable of running away with Count Vagli was unworthy of him.... In the end, the affair would have become known only to a few, and imperfectly, and it would have been diminished, pulverized, so to speak, in the classic gossip of Venice. Filippo found the honesty in his dishonesty; he loved Loredana; he felt that he would be faithful to her, that he would make her happy, that she would not suffer, and since it was absurd to speak of marriage because of the formidable opposition he would encounter in his family, running away—a prudent flight, without too much scandal, without commotion—would put an end to a situation that was unbearable for him and for his little friend.

The thought of Fausta also came to him; but in that period the unfortunate woman had fallen utterly in his eyes because of her strange humble behavior, which he could not understand at all. He thought regretfully of his mistress’s devotion: Fausta was not made to obey, to remain silent, to suffer; every woman has her own charm and her own destiny. Subservience had dimmed the beautiful flame of those sky-blue eyes and robbed her face of the complexion of fresh youth.

Every day they went back to the beginning; Adolfo's passionate nature flared up and grew more venomous; the young man would have liked Mrs. De Carolis to intervene on his behalf, but the mother judged with her daughter's mind, and did not even remember ever having scolded her once in eighteen years. Indeed, seeing that her daughter was sad, Mrs. De Carolis too began to think, without having the courage to say so, that Adolfo was brutal; and she regretted having welcomed and encouraged the proposal of the Gianella family, who wished to unite the two young people. It could not be denied: the peace of the little white house had been disturbed by Adolfo Gianella; Loredana, always cheerful, had changed in character because of him; jealous, restless, full of suspicion, he scowled at everyone, did not want them to go to the theater, grew irritated at Loredana's lightheartedness, offended her with incessant remarks, demanded that she already be as serious and prudent as a mother of a family, and finally, even in his better moments, he was querulous and tiresome, pedantic and petty.

Because of that incessant conflict, the girl was dejected; and more than once Filippo found her with red, swollen eyes.

“You must not marry him, you know,” he would say firmly. “It is an impossible marriage. What will that young man do when he is your husband and has the most stupid and disagreeable rights? Would you like me to speak to your mother?”

The girl did not have the courage to extricate herself from that tormenting situation: the entire Gianella family—Adolfo's mother, father, uncles, aunts, and cousins—surrounded her, extolling the young man's virtues, making plans for the future, showing themselves so certain, so delighted by that singularly happy marriage, that Loredana felt stifled and remained silent. But it would have been impossible to find a man more incapable than Adolfo of understanding her, so much so that she, kind to everyone, was always irritated, nervous, and sorrowful with him.

At last he even wanted to read the letters she received from her female friends, whom he did not trust in the least; one morning, while he had gone to bid his fiancée good morning, the postman arrived, and Adolfo seized the mail, opened a letter from a girl who was writing to Loredana from a town in the province, asked for news of the people mentioned in it, and ended by putting the letter into his pocket.

When Filippo arrived toward evening, the girl was still trembling all over with indignation and anger; she told her friend everything, even what she had kept silent about until that day: Adolfo's acts of oppression, his stinginess, his insulting distrust, his unreasonable jealousy, his conceit.

“I do not want him, I do not want him, I do not want him!” she exclaimed, her eyes flashing with rage. “Anything rather than this marriage! Never, never, never!”

Filippo had listened in silence, looking at the floor of red and white tiles and beating out the rhythm of a march with his foot.

Suddenly he raised his head, seized his friend's hands, and asked:

“Will you come with me?”

The girl did not understand at once.

“Where?” she asked.

“Away, far away, out of Venice, forever!” Filippo pressed her.

“Run away? Run away with you?” she said in a low voice, already trembling without knowing why.

“Listen to me,” Filippo murmured.

He went as far as the threshold of the little sitting room, saw that her mother was intently reading a poorly bound book, and continued, returning to Loredana:

“What we call friendship is nothing but love. Have you noticed?”

She remained motionless and rigid, her eyes wide open, and did not answer.

“I have noticed,” Filippo continued. “I know that I love you, I feel that I love you, I feel that we can be happy. I cannot marry you; understand me well, I cannot marry you because my whole family would cause us so many and such great sorrows that, by comparison, what you have suffered until now would seem a joy to you. They are ignorant, obstinate, and ferocious.... But I offer you my love and my life all the same.... I too am weary; I too can no longer drag out this tormenting and useless existence. Tell me that you accept, and we shall be happy.... We shall leave at once....”

Loredana withdrew her hands from Filippo's and rose to her feet: she took a few steps as if to leave the room, but stopped and leaned back against the wall; she was weeping silently, and the tears ran down her cheeks.

Filippo approached her again. He was pale and his voice trembled. He said:

“Are you offended?”

She shook her head.

“Then you do not love me with love, as I love you?”

No answer came. Loredana looked at her friend through the veil of her tears. He took a step as if to move away, but the girl quickly, instinctively, stopped him with a gesture.

“Yes, I love you too,” she murmured in a low voice.

Filippo seized her around the waist and kissed her on the mouth.

“Think about it,” he said. “Think how happy we shall be.... Your mother will forgive you. She loves you too much to condemn you. She will understand that you had the right to live, to escape a dreadful future. You will know how to make her forgive you, will you not? For you know the way to reach your mother's heart! Tell me that you accept, and we shall leave at once....”

She, still leaning against the wall, still motionless, her eyes full of tears, did not answer. But the ringing of the doorbell made both her and Filippo start.

The girl quickly dried her eyes and ran into the little sitting room.

“It must be Adolfo,” she said to her mother. “I have a migraine, I do not want to see him, I am going to shut myself in my room!”

Her mother sighed and raised her eyes to the ceiling. Loredana returned to Filippo and clasped his hands while he kissed her once more on the mouth.

“Think about it!” Filippo repeated.

She made a vague gesture and disappeared, to shut herself in her little room.

Adolfo Gianella was coming up the stairs, and Filippo, hearing his footsteps, was saying to Mrs. De Carolis:

“I am very sorry that the young lady is unwell; I hope it is nothing....”

“Is she ill?” Adolfo asked as he arrived, greeting Filippo with a cold salutation and a sidelong glance. “Where was she last night? She must have caught cold, or eaten something indigestible....”

Filippo left at once and, despite himself, said inwardly with a laugh:

“You will soon have something indigestible to eat!...”

That night he thought again about the idea of running away, which had flashed upon him so suddenly; and the more he thought about it, the better it seemed to him. Mrs. De Carolis would not have dared do anything against her adored daughter; Adolfo would have found consolation in the thought that a girl capable of running away with Count Vagli was not worthy of him.... In the end, few people would have learned of the matter, and learned of it imperfectly, and it would have dwindled, been pulverized, so to speak, in the classic Venetian gossip. Filippo found the honesty in his dishonesty; he loved Loredana; he felt that he would be faithful to her, that he would make her happy, that she would not suffer, and since it was absurd to speak of marriage because of the formidable opposition he would have encountered in his family, running away—a prudent flight, without too much scandal, without an uproar—would put an end to a situation unbearable for him and for his little friend.

She saw again that accursed female with goat-like feet, half naked, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. She turned, and on the other side saw Berto, who did not dare move to detain her, did not dare speak for fear of frightening her, and kept watching her, to divine from her gestures the decision she would make.

She returned to her armchair, let herself fall into it, and said not a word.

Thus followed an anguished silence of several minutes, during which Loredana and Berto stared keenly at each other, motionless, as though scrutinizing one another; but Berto could endure it no longer, approached her again, and seized her hands.

“Stay!” he said, his voice veiled by passion. “Stay! I implore thee! I know thou dost not love me, and that does not frighten me....”

He was trying to remove one of her gloves; she noticed, and unbuttoned it with a swift gesture, offering him her bare hand and wrist to kiss; but when she felt those avid lips upon her flesh, she turned her head away as though in revulsion.

“No!” she said. “Wait!”

She seized the goblet and drained it avidly, then held it out to Berto again so that he might pour more, and again she drank; but, catching sight of herself in the mirror, she threw the empty goblet to the floor, where it shattered.

“What do you want to do with me?” she then said.

“Everything thou shalt command me to do,” Berto replied. “I am free; I can leave this very day, tonight, tomorrow, whenever thou askest it of me.”

“Yes,” Loredana declared. “We shall leave at once. We shall go to Rome.”

She burst into such a harsh and sardonic laugh that Berto looked at her in fright.

“To Rome,” Loredana repeated. “I was to go there with Flopi; I shall go with you. Is it not the same? Am I not your mistress? Did they not want me to be your mistress? One man or another, it matters little.... Why do we not go to Sirmione as well?... I want to trample upon all my past, I want to destroy every memory, I want nothing to remain, nothing at all of what was so dear to me and would make me blush!... Ah, you do not know the horror I feel for life!... You think only of taking possession of me; I see it in your eyes, and you do not understand that I am no longer alive, you do not understand that I hate you, and the nearer you come to me, the more I hate you!...”

Berto did not reply, but the hand that held the young woman’s hand loosened its grip; he drew back, struck by the savage vehemence of those words.

“Why do you want me?” Loredana continued, casting him a contemptuous glance. “I love Filippo, and I sacrifice myself for him. Is that not clear? Is it not clear that I want to ruin myself in order to save him? Have I not told you already! And I chose you in particular, so that he may despise me so much that he will no longer seek me!... And you lend yourself to this game?... If I consented to become your mistress, that would be the moment when I loved Filippo most, because it would be the gravest sacrifice I could make for him.... And did you not understand it? How must I tell you that I shall never love you?”

Hemmed in by the ferocious logic, which seemed dictated by that need to bite and destroy with which Loredana felt her whole being vibrate, Berto at first found no answer; then he uttered the one word that explained any madness:

“But I love thee,” he said. “I love thee, Loredana; and I know nothing else....”

The young woman looked at him, feeling that he was not lying; he seemed subdued and vanquished to her, and she pitied him.

“Come,” she murmured, rising, “let me go!”

“Where, where dost thou want to go?” Berto asked, taking a step toward her. “Where dost thou want to go, like this?”

She had made her way toward the door, without a hat, like a madwoman.

Berto looked at her, elegant and slender in her perfectly smooth amethyst-colored dress, gracefully adorned with a strip of dark fur that ran around her breast and along the very hem of her skirt like a little snake.

She was going out, leaving, fleeing; suddenly she had felt that the sacrifice was too repugnant, that it was better to die, to rest, to think of no one anymore, and she had remembered the black, deep canal that flowed before Berto’s house.

The hour was late, the light faint, the people few on that winter evening. Loredana could have thrown herself into the water and drowned there without anyone coming to her aid.

“Where dost thou want to go?” Berto repeated.

They met upon the threshold and stared at one another, he with eyes blazing with desire, she with the lost gaze of despair; but because she wished to go on, he seized her by the arms and held her back.

Loredana again broke into laughter.

In her mouth she had the taste of that mire from which human beings drink, that mire which is all of life, and an unslaked thirst burned in her veins, as though she had swallowed liquid fire....

Someone behind Berto—perhaps the half-naked female with goat-like feet—suggested a thought to him: the young woman would never bring herself either to leave or to remain, either to live or to die; she had to be forced.

He drew her abruptly to his breast, sealed her mouth with his own, giving her so long a kiss that he seemed to wish to drink from her her life, her soul, her blood; he felt Loredana gradually yielding, falling backward, and he followed the movement without taking his mouth from the longed-for mouth, and laid her down upon the broad divan.




XVII.


It was a joyous spring, that of 1894 in Venice. An immense host of foreigners descended from every part of the world, the women and men already intoxicated with delights and desire, their souls vibrating with that sensual romanticism which torpid Venice inspires.

Where was she going? Home—to her own home? Filippo would have taken her back. To Filippo’s house?

XVII.


It was a joyous spring, that of 1894 in Venice. An immense host of foreigners descended from every part of the world, women and men already drunk with delight and desire, their souls vibrating with that sensual romanticism inspired by languid Venice.

New passions and new dramas sprang up amid that throng of people, and on certain evenings Saint Mark’s Square became a wondrous drawing room through which the fashionable women of New York and Paris, London and Vienna, Berlin and Petersburg wandered, leaving in their wake a trail of exotic perfumes.

They saw Venice through the eyes of legend and history, and their souls were transformed, pouring themselves forth and becoming perverted among the treasures of art and the deathly silence of the voluptuous city. The gondola, slow and caressing, agile and silent, made them dream the erotic dreams and swift tragedies of novels; the night, whether illumined by moonlight upon the narrow waterways and canals, or dark, or veiled, seemed to them as enigmatic and extravagant as in no other city in the world.

“Ah, there we are!” said Filippo. “I went to the Grand Hôtel and came out with Uncle Roberto, who seized the opportunity to give me one of his usual sermons. We became heated; he threatened to disinherit me, and I told him I did not give a damn; apparently, Uncle’s two million have thus gone up in smoke, but I prefer my full and absolute freedom to them. That is all, Lori; you see it was not even worth mentioning.”

Loredana, having quickly freed herself from her skirt, stood dumbfounded.

“Two million!” she suddenly repeated.

“A little more, a little less,” said Filippo. “But I have never needed his money, and you know it.”

The girl tossed her clothes onto a chair and remained standing before the mirrored wardrobe....

“Because of me!” she exclaimed.

“Lori, please,” said Filippo. “It pains me when you talk like that: it is not your fault, but my relatives’. This is nothing new: do you remember that I had told you? My relatives do not understand, and arguments are of no use....”

“They want you to leave me?” Loredana pressed him.

“Of course!” Filippo replied. “Poor Uncle Roberto is merely my mother’s instrument: she makes him act and speak, and he acts and speaks, simply to have some peace.”

“They want you to leave me?” Loredana repeated. “And they want nothing else?”

“By Jove!” Filippo exclaimed, laughing. “That seems enough to me....”

“No, they might want more,” said the girl after a moment’s hesitation. “They might want you to marry.... Because, Flopi, I do not understand.... If you left me, what would you do? Would you live without mistresses and without a wife? Is that what your relatives demand?... Do they not want you to marry? Do they not have some young lady they like and are offering you?”

Filippo fell silent, astonished, and wondered how little Lori, whom he still considered scarcely more than a child, had arrived at the truth with the sole aid of logic. To conceal his embarrassment, he rose and said:

“No, no: whatever put that into your head?... Let me look at you....”

Loredana made a gesture to keep him away and insisted:

“Truly, Flopi, have they never spoken to you about marriage? Do they not want you to marry?”

“No, indeed; those are fantasies of yours!” Filippo repeated.

“Are you prepared to swear it to me?”

“I swear it to you....”

“Are you prepared to give me your word of honor?”

Filippo hesitated for a moment; but by then he could no longer turn back.

“I give you my word of honor!” he said.

The girl covered her face with her hands and burst into tears.

“What!” Filippo exclaimed in surprise. “Now you are crying? Aren’t you happy? Perhaps you do not believe me?”

She stood before him with her arms and breast bare; she wore batiste drawers that came down to her knees, gray silk stockings, and low white slippers: she looked like a dainty little Pierrot.

“So pretty,” said Filippo, “and so wicked! But aren’t you happy, I ask you again?”

Loredana managed to answer between sobs:

“Yes,” she declared, lying in her turn, “I am crying because I am happy!”

Filippo began to laugh and clasped her to his breast, lifting her off the ground.

“Come,” he said. “Come, lovely little mask, dear little viper. You are so beautiful, I love you so much....”

The young woman twined her arms around his neck, let herself be laid upon the bed, and through her tears sought the mouth of the man who lied and kissed so well....




VIII.


The winter was unusually harsh and long that year in Venice; it snowed several times, and on clear days an icy bora blew violently. Many families left the countryside ahead of time and began the season of receptions and festivities earlier than usual; by mid-November, because of the rigors of winter, fashionable life was already flourishing in all its splendor.

Filippo was gradually drawn back into it, almost without realizing it; he found his friends again and resumed the usual round of visits and habitual engagements among those familiar groups of people to which he was accustomed.

But he took the most solicitous care of Loredana. The murmuring of society and the spitefulness of his relatives had made the girl even dearer to him, and he often gave up some social entertainment to devote his time to her. He had surrounded her with luxury, procuring outfits for her in Milan, giving her jewels, covering her in silks and lace and furs, so that her beauty might have a worthy setting.

Loredana let him do as he pleased.

She had changed; a dull, profound sorrow had been gnawing at her since the day she discovered that her Flopi lied; and lied because his friendship with Giselda Fioresi must have a meaning he could not confess to her. At first, when she realized that Filippo was resuming his social habits, the young woman anxiously followed him in her thoughts; each time, she had him tell her what he had seen and what he had said; she noticed that he never uttered the name of the young Countess Fioresi, even when it could be learned from the newspapers that the young countess attended the parties and gatherings in which Filippo took part. A thousand times Loredana had been on the point of asking for explanations, and a thousand times she had restrained herself, thinking that he would lie again.

Then, little by little, she managed to master herself; she no longer wished to know, no longer asked questions. She was his mistress, who awaited him with inexpressible longing and gave herself wholly to him with infinite voluptuousness; she silenced the terrible jealousy that poisoned her heart, swallowed her tears in silence, and always appeared cheerful and smiling. It was a heroism of every day, of every hour, which Filippo did not know of and would never know of.

Even the luxury surrounding her seemed excessive to her; she put on her fur coat and slipped the precious rings onto her fingers with a certain little shiver, thinking that the name of kept woman suited her then better than ever. She did not care; the world was so unknown and so distant to her that she did not wish to concern herself with it; but her mother, the good Signora Emma, had grown worried about her.

Loredana still went to visit Mama in the little white house on the secluded small square. Every time, she was certain to encounter along the way Adolfo Gianella, her former fiancé, who lay in wait for her. He had remained strangely faithful to her through the storm of scandal and malicious gossip that had engulfed the young woman’s name. He followed her at a distance for long stretches, gazed at her with intense pleasure, and was perhaps more in love with her than in the days when she was a virgin and innocent. Adolfo had learned everything from the mouths of the curious and the idle—Loredana’s life and love—and then he had discovered the lovers’ nest and begun to loiter in that neighborhood, to gaze at those windows, to spy upon that happiness. Humble and timid, he confided his sorrows to no one and did not speak of Loredana at home, because his family hated her. He contented himself with following the girl and seeing her beautiful, flourishing, happy.

Candriani was not listening to her; drunk with joy, now able to gaze at her with all the intensity of a desire no longer restrained, he gazed avidly over her whole body, from her head to her little feet, whose tips peeped out from beneath the very hem of her skirt.

“I shall make you forget Filippo,” he said suddenly. “You will no longer love him; I am free and alone, I can devote my entire life to you.... Love him still today, it does not matter; it is right that you should love him; it will be for me to erase his image from your heart.”

And all at once he burst out:

“I am happy; I am happy to see you here beside me; you remembered that I offered you my friendship in a desperate situation, and that consoles me for many sorrows.... Ah, I assure you, Loredana, that I am no longer the thoughtless man you once knew! I love you tenderly and hope that I may reassure you....”

She cut off his words with a gesture.

“No,” she replied. “I shall never love you.”

She looked around, and, seeing the goblet, raised it to lips that she felt were parched by an inward fever.

“Listen to me,” she continued imperiously. “I am here not because I love you, not because I believe in your friendship, but because I wish and must ruin myself.”

“Loredana, Loredana, for pity’s sake!” Berto interrupted.

“I must ruin myself. He is about to commit a crime. His sick mother has asked him to leave me, and he has refused.... No, I cannot accept this sacrifice; it is a horrible thing; I must leave him, and in such a way that he will no longer seek me, no longer desire me.... I do not wish to hurt his mother, who has already suffered so much because of me.... If she were to die—ah, if she were to die—what remorse, what shame!... And one day he would awaken from this madness; and between him and me, always, always, I would see his mother’s corpse.... I must prevent him from dishonoring himself!”

Berto, standing upright, listened with a sense of wonder to the young woman, who spoke rapidly, agitated by violent excitement; her initial pallor had given way to a feverish flush that crimsoned her cheeks, made her eyes shine intensely, and reddened her lips, giving them the color of living blood.

She pleased him so much thus stretched out in the armchair and sunk into the white fur that Berto bent down once more to kiss her hands. Loredana pushed him away.

“I wanted to kill myself,” she continued, “but it would have caused a fresh scandal; they might have accused Filippo of my death.... Ah, how malicious everyone is!... I have been told to my face that I am your mistress, that my honesty is worth nothing because no one believes me, that a man is a thief when everyone calls him a thief.... How many dreadful things I have learned! And then I thought that they were right. The only person who did not doubt me was Filippo; he believes in my love and in my honesty, which everyone laughs at; and so he too must cease to believe, in order that he may be saved.... I thought that, since they call me your mistress, every effort is useless, and I shall never be able to free myself from this accusation....”

“Do not speak so,” Berto interrupted. “It does thee too much harm....”

She stared at him with wide-open eyes; that “thee” seemed to her more brutal than a kiss that had suddenly closed her mouth; but Berto noticed it and added:

“I beg your pardon; I did not mean to offend you. I love you, and I was unable to master myself.”

“No,” said Loredana, rising, “let me go!”

Berto dared to lay a hand on her.

“I beg you,” he murmured, “stay a little longer.....”

Loredana shuddered; gathering up the fur, she searched for her hat with her eyes. But just as she was about to take it up again, she stopped, as though struck by a thought.

Where was she going? To her own home? Filippo would take her back. To Filippo’s home? His mother would die of it. And by then Filippo must already have read the few lines Loredana had left him: “I shall never forget thee; I shall always love thee; the farther away I may seem to thee, the more wholly thine I shall be....” And after this, was she to return to him, with bowed head, like a repentant schoolgirl, and forever too late to be forgiven?

Once more she saw that accursed woman with goatlike feet, half-naked, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. She turned, and on the other side saw Berto, who dared not move for fear of detaining her, dared not speak for fear of frightening her, and kept watching her, seeking to divine from her gestures the decision she would make.

She returned to her armchair, let herself fall into it, and said not a word.

There followed in this manner an anguished silence of several minutes, during which Loredana and Berto stared keenly at one another, motionless, almost as though searching each other’s souls; but Berto could endure it no longer, approached her again, and seized her hands.

“Stay!” he said, his voice veiled by passion. “Stay! I implore thee! I know that thou dost not love me, and that does not frighten me....”

He was trying to remove one of her gloves; she noticed and unbuttoned it with a swift gesture, offering him her bare hand and wrist to kiss; but when she felt those avid lips upon her flesh, she turned her head away, almost in disgust.

“No!” she said. “Wait!”

She seized the goblet and drained it avidly, then held it out to Berto again so that he might pour more, and drank once more; but, catching sight of herself in the mirror, she threw the empty goblet to the floor, where it shattered.

“What do you wish to do with me?” she then said.

“Anything thou commandest me,” Berto replied. “I am free; I can leave this very day, tonight, tomorrow, whenever thou askest it of me.”

“Yes,” Loredana declared. “We shall leave at once. We shall go to Rome.”

She gave such a harsh and sardonic laugh that Berto looked at her in alarm.

“To Rome,” Loredana repeated. “I was to go there with Flopi; I shall go with you. Is it not the same? Am I not your mistress? Did they not want me to be your mistress? One man or another, it matters little.... Why do we not go to Sirmione as well?... I wish to trample upon my entire past, I wish to destroy every memory, I wish nothing to remain, nothing at all, of what was so dear to me and would make me blush!... Ah, you do not know the horror I feel for life!... You think of nothing but taking possession of me; I see it in your eyes, and you do not understand that I am no longer alive, you do not understand that I hate you, and the nearer you come to me, the more I hate you!...”

Berto did not reply, but the hand holding the young woman’s hand loosened its grip; he drew back, struck by the savage vehemence of those words.

“I am happy; I am happy to see you here with me; you remembered that I offered you my friendship in an extreme case, and this consoles me for many sorrows.... Ah, I assure you, Loredana, that I am no longer the thoughtless man you once knew! I love you tenderly, and I hope to be able to reassure you....”

She cut off his words with a gesture.

“No,” she replied. “I shall never love you.”

She looked around, and, seeing the glass, raised it to her lips, which she felt were parched by an inward fever.

“Listen to me,” she continued imperiously. “I am here not because I love you, not because I believe in your friendship, but because I wish and must ruin myself.

“Loredana, Loredana, for pity’s sake!” Berto interrupted.

“I must ruin myself. He is about to commit a crime. His ailing mother asked him to abandon me, and he refused.... No, I cannot accept this sacrifice; it is a horrible thing; I must leave him, and in such a way that he will no longer seek me, no longer desire me.... I do not wish to harm his mother, who has already suffered so much because of me.... If she were to die, ah, if she were to die, what remorse, what shame!... And one day he would awaken from this madness; and between him and me, always, always, I would see his mother’s corpse.... I must prevent him from dishonoring himself!”

Berto, standing erect, listened with a sense of wonder to the young woman, who spoke rapidly, agitated by violent excitement; her initial pallor had given way to a feverish flush that crimsoned her cheeks, made her eyes gleam intensely, and reddened her lips, giving them the color of living blood.

He liked her so much thus stretched out in the armchair and sunk into the white fur that Berto bent down once more to kiss her hands. Loredana pushed him away.

“I wanted to kill myself,” she continued, “but it would have been another scandal; perhaps they would have accused Filippo of my death.... Ah, how malicious they all are!... I was told to my face that I am your mistress, that my honor is worth nothing because no one believes me, that a man is a thief when everyone calls him a thief.... How many frightful things I have learned! And then I thought that they were right. The only one who did not doubt me was Filippo; he believes in my love and in my honor, which everyone laughs at; and so he too must cease to believe, so that he may be saved.... I thought that since they call me your mistress, every effort is useless, and I shall never be able to free myself from this accusation....”

“Do not speak like that,” Berto interrupted. “It hurts you too much....”

She stared at him with wide-open eyes; that informal ‘you’ seemed to her more brutal than a kiss that had suddenly sealed her mouth; but Berto noticed and added:

“I beg your pardon; I did not mean to offend you. I love you, and I could not control myself.”

“No,” said Loredana, rising, “let me go!”

Berto dared to lay a hand on her.

“I beg you,” he murmured, “stay a little longer.....”

Loredana shuddered; gathering up the fur, she looked about for her hat. But just as she was about to pick it up again, she stopped as though struck by a thought.

Where was she going? Home, to her own house? Filippo would take her back. To Filippo’s house? His mother would die of it. And by that time Filippo must already have read the few lines Loredana had left him: “I shall never forget you; I shall always love you; the farther away I may seem to you, the more I shall be yours....” And after that, was she to return to him, head bowed, like a repentant schoolgirl, and always too late to be forgiven?

She saw again that accursed half-naked woman with goat’s feet, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. I wish to trample upon all my past, I wish to destroy every memory, I wish nothing to remain, nothing at all of what was so dear to me, and what would make me blush!... Ah, you do not know the horror I feel for life!... You think only of taking possession of me; I see it in your eyes, and you do not understand that I am no longer alive, you do not understand that I hate you, and the closer you come to me, the more I hate you!...”

Berto did not reply, but the hand that held the young woman’s relaxed its grip; he drew back, stricken by the savage vehemence of those words.

“Why do you want me?” Loredana continued, casting him a contemptuous glance. “I love Filippo, and I am sacrificing myself for him. Is that not clear? Is it not clear that I wish to ruin myself in order to save him? Have I not already told you! And I chose you of all people so that he will despise me so much that he will no longer seek me!... And you lend yourself to this game?... If I consented to become your mistress, that would be the moment when I loved Filippo most, because that would be the gravest sacrifice I could make for him.... And you did not understand that? How must I tell you that I shall never love you?”

She saw again that accursed female with goat’s feet, half naked, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. And you lend yourself to this game?... If I consented to become your mistress, that would be the moment when I loved Filippo most, because it would be the gravest sacrifice I could make for him.... And you did not understand that? How must I tell you that I shall never love you?”

Constrained by the ferocious logic, which seemed dictated by that need to bite and destroy with which Loredana felt her whole being quivering, Berto at first found no answer; then he uttered the one phrase that explained every madness:

“But I love you,” he said. “I love you, Loredana; and I know nothing else....”

The young woman looked at him, sensing that he was not lying; he seemed subdued and defeated to her, and she pitied him.

“Come now,” she murmured, rising, “let me go!”

“Where, where do you want to go?” Berto asked, taking a step toward her. “Where do you want to go, like this?”

She had started toward the door, without a hat, like a madwoman.

Berto looked at her, elegant and slender in her smooth amethyst-colored dress, gracefully adorned with a strip of dark fur that ran around her breast and along the very edge of the skirt like a little snake.

She was going out, leaving, fleeing; suddenly she had felt that the sacrifice was too repugnant, that it was better to die, to rest, to think of no one anymore, and she had remembered the deep black canal that flowed in front of Berto’s house.

The hour was late, the light dim, and few people were abroad on that winter evening. Loredana could have thrown herself into the water and drowned there without anyone coming to her aid.

“Where do you want to go?” Berto repeated.

They met on the threshold and stared at each other, his eyes blazing with desire, hers lost in despair; but because she meant to go on, he seized her by the arms and held her back.

Loredana broke into laughter again.

In her mouth she had the taste of that mud from which human beings drink their fill, that mud which is all of life, and an unquenched burning scorched her veins, as though she had swallowed liquid fire....

Someone behind Berto—perhaps the half-naked female with goat’s feet—suggested a thought to him: the young woman would never decide either to leave or to stay, either to live or to die; she had to be forced.

He abruptly drew her to his breast, sealed her mouth with his own, giving her so long a kiss that it seemed he wished to drink her life, her soul, her blood; he felt Loredana slowly yielding, falling backward, and followed the movement without taking his mouth from the longed-for mouth, and laid her upon the broad divan.




XVII.


It was a joyous spring, that of 1894 in Venice. A boundless host of foreigners descended from every part of the world, women and men already intoxicated with delights and desire, their souls vibrating with that sensual romanticism inspired by languid Venice.

New passions and new dramas sprang up amid that throng of people, and on certain evenings Saint Mark’s Square became a prodigious drawing room through which the fashionable women of New York and Paris, London and Vienna, Berlin and St. Petersburg wandered, leaving in their wake a trail of exotic perfumes.

They saw Venice through the eyes of legend and history, and their souls were transformed, pouring themselves out and becoming perverted amid the treasures of art and the deathly silence of the voluptuous city. The gondola, slow and caressing, agile and silent, made them dream the erotic dreams and swift tragedies of novels; the night, whether illuminated by moonlight upon the streams and canals, or dark, or veiled, seemed to them as enigmatic and extravagant as in no other city in the world.

—Even if it is false, it matters little, because when everyone thinks the same way, it is as though it were true. Do you understand me? If someone is accused of being a thief, in order to go about with him and remain his friend, it is not enough to believe and even to know that he is honest; it takes a courage that I do not have, because other people believe he is a thief, and I cannot be the friend of a thief.... All appearances are against you, and all Venice speaks of you as a dangerous little hussy; and what can I do about it?... Besides, there must be something to it; it cannot all have been invented.... But even if there is nothing, absolutely nothing true in it, I have my family reproaching me for loving you and following you, I have my friends laughing, I have the director of the Bank, who does not want his employees associating with bad women; and how am I to persuade all these people that you are not a bad woman, after a scandal that has been talked about for so many days and in such detail in every corner of the city?... It may not be your fault, let us grant that, but you are dishonored, there it is; and your protests are lost in the din, and by now, whatever good and beautiful thing you may do, it will be of no use to you....

He seized the mug of beer, raised it to his lips, and did not put it back on the saucer until he had emptied it.

—But then,—said Loredana with a shiver of terror,—does being innocent mean nothing?

—It means.... it means.... How should I know what it means?—replied Adolfo, who did not perceive his own cruelty, himself astounded by the soundness of his facile arguments.—What matters in the world is to be believed, rightly or wrongly; even miracles are of no use if no one believes in them.... And no one believes in your honesty.... It would be better for you to be dishonest, truly dishonest, and for everyone to praise your virtue....

A fine ocher-colored background, boldly laid in with vigorous strokes, framed in the sketchbook the little head of the young woman with golden glints in her hair; an effect of light and shade that the artist compared with the original, moving his head to right and left and holding the drawing at a distance.

—If that idiot does not stop tormenting her,—he muttered under his breath,—I’ll make a caricature of him!

But Adolfo did not stop, exalted by the voluptuous pleasure of torturing the woman who had always been victorious over him, driven by the need to trample upon and destroy his love, darkly satisfied to see his one-time fiancée reduced to defenselessness, drunk with ferocity against her and against himself....

—And besides, why discuss your innocence? I do not believe in it, come now!... Is it possible that an entire city would turn against a woman, a girl, like this, merely on a whim?... You will tell me that those who speak ill of you gain nothing by it!... Why do they not speak ill of so many others?... You see, when people warn me that one must be wary of gossip, I laugh; gossip is spread about those who deserve it; nothing has ever been said about me, for instance?... It would be better not to speak of your innocence, which, besides, even if it existed, would not be worth a damn by now.... What have you set against the specific and precise accusations? That it is all false! But I expected that; you are hardly going to tell me about your love affairs—to me, who truly, honestly loved you.... And you were so afraid of my judgment that you stopped me in the street and asked whether I knew.... There is another proof.... And then, I must add....

Loredana rose slowly.

—Thank you,—she interrupted in an unsteady voice.—You have told me some very useful things....

She made to leave and staggered....

—Do not move,—she added, leaning against a corner of the table.—I want to go out alone....

After a few uncertain steps, while Adolfo watched her with lifeless eyes, Loredana regained her strength, walked on resolutely, and passed close to the artist, who, looking back and forth between the pastel and the young woman, felt that he loved them both.... Adolfo remained motionless, slumped on his bench; suddenly remorse invaded his soul, leaving him open-mouthed, with an expression of blank bewilderment.

Loredana felt the urge to snatch from the artist’s hands the sketchbook in which she knew she had been portrayed and strike him in the face with it. She had to close her eyes to master herself.

She went out into the fog; the fog had descended suddenly, with a faint smell of burning, broken here and there by the reddish halos of the gas flames.

And the young woman set off again toward the Zattere, toward Flopi, the one and the other seeming lost in that infinite, dense, acrid expanse.

—What am I bringing him?—Loredana asked herself.

She was bringing him her body, which the crowd said had been mauled by others, and dishonor.

Certainly he was deluding himself, Filippo; no one had hurled all the accusations in his face, and he did not know how much his mistress was despised; she was bringing ridicule into his home like a poisoned fluid. Adolfo Gianella’s words were the echo of that wisdom found on the ground, among the spittle and greasy papers, which is called public opinion. He spoke truly: what matters is not to be, but to appear; when a slander is repeated by everyone, it has the force of truth: evil is what is seen, not what is committed. Aphorisms that kill; stubborn bestiality; the majority’s tyranny, against which there is no appeal.... But life proceeds on this chariot of death, and every day someone falls beneath its wheels because of one mistaken gesture.

Loredana blushed for herself; having drunk for long hours from the stream of mud, she felt as though her mouth were full of it, her body splattered, her hands macerated. How could she allow herself to be embraced and kissed by Filippo, who would notice on her face the traces of the sufferings she had endured, a furrow on her brow, a bruise beneath her eyes? To kiss and love each other amid the audience’s jeers? To tremble beneath sardonic gazes? To live beside a man who, unless he quickly and decisively broke away from her, would become ridiculous?

The crowd had fallen upon her love and torn it to pieces.

Safe and strong protection, tender confidences and fleeting moments of joy, secret tenderness and impetuous outbursts of passion, long oblivion of every mortal thing, dreamed-of journeys, the little house on the Zattere, the beautiful sun of Sirmione—all drowned in the fog forever!

She wanted to run home and say to Filippo:

—You had me when I was still a child, and through your love you made me a woman. Take me; love me one last time; extinguish in your arms this life that is yours, and do not let others slowly kill, out of hatred, the woman who wants to die for you.

Every day they went back to the beginning; Adolfo’s passionate nature flared up and grew embittered; the young man would have liked Signora De Carolis to intervene on his behalf, but the mother judged with her daughter’s mind, and could not even remember having reprimanded her once in eighteen years. Indeed, seeing that her daughter was sad, Signora De Carolis too began to think, without having the courage to say so, that Adolfo was brutal; and she regretted having welcomed and encouraged the proposal of the Gianella family, who wanted to unite the two young people. It could not be denied: the peace of the little white house had been disturbed by Adolfo Gianella; Loredana, always cheerful, had changed in character because of him; he, jealous, uneasy, full of suspicion, glared at everyone, did not want them to go to the theater, became irritated by Loredana’s lightheartedness, offended her with incessant remarks, demanded that she already be as serious and prudent as a mother of a family, and finally, even in his good moments, was querulous and tiresome, pedantic and petty.

Because of that ceaseless conflict, the girl was dejected; and more than once Filippo found her with red, swollen eyes.

“You must not marry him, you know,” he would say firmly. “It is an impossible marriage. What will that young man do when he is your husband and has the most foolish and obnoxious rights? Would you like me to speak to your mother?”

The girl did not have the courage to extricate herself from that tormenting situation: the entire Gianella family—Adolfo’s mother, father, uncles, aunts, and cousins—crowded around her, extolling the young man’s virtues, making plans for the future, showing themselves so certain, so delighted about that exceptionally happy marriage, that Loredana stifled herself and kept silent. But no man could have been found who was more incapable than Adolfo of understanding her, so much so that she, kind to everyone, was always irritated, nervous, and distressed with him.

At last he even wanted to read the letters she received from her female friends, whom he did not trust at all; one morning, while he had gone to bid his fiancée good morning, the postman arrived, and Adolfo seized the mail, opened the letter from a girl who was writing to Loredana from a town in the province, asked for information about the people mentioned in it, and ended by putting the letter into his pocket.

When Filippo arrived toward evening, the girl was still trembling all over with indignation and anger; she told her friend everything, even what she had kept silent about until that day: Adolfo’s harassment, stinginess, insulting mistrust, unreasonable jealousy, and conceit.

“I do not want him, I do not want him, I do not want him!” she exclaimed, her eyes blazing with rage. “Anything rather than this marriage! Never, never, never!”

Filippo had listened in silence, looking at the floor of red and white tiles and marking out the rhythm of a march with his foot.

All at once he raised his head, grasped his friend’s hands, and asked:

“Will you come with me?”

The girl did not understand at once.

“Where?” she asked.

“Away, far away, out of Venice, forever!” Filippo pressed.

“Run away? Run away with you?” she said in a low voice, already trembling without knowing why.

“Listen to me,” Filippo murmured.

He went as far as the threshold of the sitting room, saw that her mother was attentively reading a poorly bound book, and continued, returning to Loredana:

“What we call friendship is nothing but love. Have you realized it?”

She, still and rigid, her eyes wide open, did not answer.

“I have realized it,” Filippo went on. “I know that I love you, I feel that I love you, I feel that we can be happy. I cannot marry you; understand me well, I cannot marry you because my whole family would cause us so much grief that, by comparison, what you have suffered until now would seem a joy to you. They are ignorant, stubborn, and ferocious.... But I offer you my love and my life all the same.... I too am weary; I too can no longer drag out this tormented and useless existence. Tell me that you accept, and we shall be happy.... We shall leave at once....”

Loredana withdrew her hands from Filippo’s and stood up: she took a few steps as though to leave the room, but stopped and leaned back against the wall; she was weeping silently, and the tears ran down her cheeks.

Filippo approached her again. He was pale, and his voice trembled. He said:

“Are you offended?”

She shook her head.

“Then you do not love me with romantic love, as I love you?”

No answer came. Loredana looked at her friend through the veil of tears. He took a step as though to move away, but the girl quickly, instinctively detained him with a gesture.

“Yes, I love you too,” she murmured in a low voice.

Filippo seized her around the waist and kissed her on the mouth.

“Think about it,” he said. “Think how happy we shall be.... Your mother will forgive you. She loves you too much to condemn you. She will understand that you had the right to live, to escape a dreadful future. You will know how to make her forgive you, will you not? For you know the road that leads to your mother’s heart! Tell me that you accept, and we shall leave at once....”

She, still leaning against the wall, still motionless, her eyes full of tears, did not answer. But the ringing of the doorbell made both her and Filippo start.

The girl quickly dried her eyes and ran into the sitting room.

“It must be Adolfo,” she said to her mother. “I have a migraine, I do not want to see him, I am going to shut myself in my room!”

Her mother sighed and raised her eyes to the ceiling. Loredana returned to Filippo and clasped his hands while he kissed her on the mouth again.

“Think about it!” Filippo repeated.

She made a vague gesture and disappeared, to shut herself in her little room.

Adolfo Gianella was coming up the stairs, and Filippo, hearing his footsteps, was saying to Signora De Carolis:

“I am very sorry that the young lady is indisposed; I hope it is nothing....”

“Is she ill?” Adolfo asked as he arrived, greeting Filippo with a cold salutation and a sidelong glance. “Where was she last night? She must have caught cold, or eaten something indigestible....”

Filippo left at once, and involuntarily said to himself, laughing inwardly:

“You will soon have to swallow something indigestible yourself!...”

That night he thought again about the idea of running away, which had flashed upon him so suddenly; and the more he thought about it, the better it seemed to him. Signora De Carolis would not have dared do anything against her adored daughter; Adolfo would have found consolation in the thought that a girl capable of running away with Count Vagli was not worthy of him.... Finally, few people would learn of the matter, and only imperfectly, and it would dwindle, be pulverized, so to speak, in the classic Venetian gossip. Filippo found the honesty within his dishonesty; he loved Loredana; he felt that he would be faithful to her, that he would make her happy, that she would not suffer, and since it was absurd to speak of marriage because of the formidable opposition he would encounter in his family, running away—a discreet flight, without too much scandal, without commotion—would put an end to a situation unbearable for him and for his little friend.
